But if in that dwelling, one blocks it off with walls and so on and fits a separate door, it becomes of different precincts. If, however, one only blocks it off and does not fit a separate door, it should be understood that “this too is of a single precinct, like an inner chamber with its door sealed with clay, etc.” Otherwise, for one who enters an inner chamber and has the chamber door sealed with clay and so on to be free from the offense of lying down together with unordained persons sleeping in the antechamber, etc., there would be no offense even for one who has it opened when dawn has arisen.

Tesaṃ payoge payoge bhikkhussa āpattīti ettha keci “anuṭṭhahanena akiriyasamuṭṭhānā āpatti vuttā tasmiṃ khaṇe sayantassa kiriyābhāvā. Idañhi sikkhāpadaṃ siyā kiriyāya samuṭṭhāti, siyā akiriyāya samuṭṭhāti. Kiriyāsamuṭṭhānatā cassa tabbahulavasena vuttāti vadati. Yathā cetaṃ, evaṃ divāsayanampi. Anuṭṭhahanena, hi dvārāsaṃvaraṇena cetaṃ akiriyasamauṭṭhānampi hotī”ti vadanti. Idañca yuttaṃ viya dissati, vīmaṃsitvā gahetabbaṃ.

Regarding the statement, “For the monk, there is an offense at each and every application,” some say: “An offense originating from non-action is stated because of not getting up, due to the absence of action on the part of the one sleeping at that moment. Indeed, this training rule sometimes arises from action, and sometimes arises from non-action. And its nature of originating from action is stated by way of its prevalence.” And they say: “Just as this is so, so too is the rule on lying down during the day. Indeed, because of not getting up and because of not securing the door, this also originates from non-action.” And this appears to be reasonable; it should be accepted after investigation.

“Uparimatalena [M 2.0006] saddhiṃ asambaddhabhittikassā”ti idaṃ sambaddhabhittike vattabbameva natthīti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Uparimatale sayitassa saṅkā eva natthīti “heṭṭhāpāsāde”tiādi vuttaṃ. Nānūpacāreti bahi nisseṇiyā ārohaṇīye.

The phrase “of one with a wall not connected with the upper floor” is stated to show that in the case of a connected wall, there is nothing at all to be said. For one sleeping on the upper floor, there is no doubt at all; therefore, “in the lower storey of the mansion,” etc., is stated. By “of different precincts” is meant: in a storey that is to be ascended by an external staircase.

Sabhāsaṅkhepenāti [V 2.0006] sabhākārena. “Aḍḍhakuṭṭake”ti iminā saṇṭhānaṃ dasseti. Yattha tīsu dvīsu vā passesu bhittiyo baddhā, chadanaṃ vā asampattā aḍḍhabhitti, idaṃ aḍḍhakuṭṭakaṃ nāma. Vāḷasaṅghāṭo nāma parikkhepassa anto thambhādīnaṃ upari vāḷarūpehi katasaṅghāṭo. Parikkhepassa bahigateti ettha yasmiṃ passe parikkhepo natthi, tattha sace bhūmito vatthu uccaṃ hoti, ubhato uccavatthuto heṭṭhā bhūmiyaṃ nibbakosabbhantarepi anāpatti eva tattha senāsanavohārābhāvato. Atha vatthu nīcaṃ bhūmisamameva senāsanassa heṭṭhimatale tiṭṭhati, tattha parikkheparahitadisāya nibbakosabbhantare sabbattha āpatti hoti, paricchedābhāvato parikkhepassa bahi eva anāpattīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Parimaṇḍalaṃ vātiādi majjhe udakapatanatthāya ākāsaṅgaṇavantaṃ senāsanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tattha aparicchinnagabbhūpacāreti ekekagabbhassa dvīsu passesu pamukhena gamanaṃ paricchinditvā diyaḍḍhahatthubbedhato anūnaṃ kuṭṭaṃ katvā ākāsaṅgaṇena pavesaṃ karonti, evaṃ akatoti attho. Gabbhaparikkhepoti caturassapāsādādīsu samantā ṭhitagabbhabhittiyo sandhāya vuttaṃ.

By “in the shape of an assembly hall” is meant: in the manner of an assembly hall. By “in a half-walled dwelling,” it indicates the structure. Wherein walls are constructed on three or on two sides, or a half-wall does not reach the roof, this is called a “half-walled dwelling.” What is called a “beam with figures of beasts of prey” is a beam made with figures of beasts of prey above pillars and so on within an enclosure. Regarding “gone outside the enclosure”: wherein on a certain side there is no enclosure, if the foundation is high from the ground, there is no offense even within the area of the eavesdrip below the high foundation on the ground on both sides, because there is no designation of “lodging” there. If, however, the foundation is not built up but stands level with the ground on the lower floor of the lodging, there is an offense everywhere within the area of the eavesdrip on the side without an enclosure, because of the lack of a boundary. It should be understood that there is no offense only outside the enclosure. The phrase “circular, or...” and so on is stated with reference to a lodging that has an open courtyard in the middle for rainwater to fall. Therein, by “in a dwelling with an unpartitioned precinct for the inner chambers” is meant: a chamber not made in this way: for each inner chamber, on two sides, having partitioned off the passage with an antechamber by making a wall not less than one and a half cubits in height, they make an entrance through the open courtyard. By “the enclosure of the inner chambers” is meant the walls of the inner chambers standing all around in a four-cornered mansion and so on.

Pāṭekkasannivesāti ekekadisāya gabbhapāḷiyo itaradisāsu gabbhapāḷīnaṃ abhāvena, bhāvepi vā aññamaññabhitticchadanehi asambandhatāya pāṭekkasannivesā nāma vuccati. Taṃ…pe… sandhāya vuttanti tattha pācittiyena anāpattīti vuttaṃ, na dukkaṭena. Tādisāya hi gabbhapāḷiyā pamukhaṃ tīsu disāsu bhittīnaṃ abhāvena ekadisāya gabbhabhittimattena sabbacchannaṃ cūḷaparicchannaṃ nāma hoti. Tasmā dukkaṭameva. Yadi pana tassa pamukhassa itaradisāsupi ekissaṃ, sabbāsu vā bhittiṃ karonti, tadā sabbacchannaupaḍḍhaparicchannādibhāvato pācittiyameva hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Bhūmiyaṃ vinā jagatiyā pamukhaṃ sandhāyāti ettha uccavatthuṃ akatvā bhūmiyaṃ katagehassa pamukhaṃ sandhāya aparikkhitte pācittiyena anāpattīti idaṃ kathitaṃ[M 2.0007]. Uccavatthukaṃ ce pamukhaṃ hoti, tena vatthunā parikkhittasaṅkhyameva pamukhaṃ gacchatīti adhippāyo. Tatthāti andhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ. Jagatiyā pamāṇaṃ vatvāti pakatibhūmiyā nipanno yathā jagatiyā upari sayitaṃ na passati, evaṃ uccātiuccavatthussa ubbedhappamāṇaṃ vatvā. Ekadisāya ujukameva dīghaṃ katvā sannivesito pāsādo ekasālasanniveso. Dvīsu, tīsu vā catūsupi vā disāsu siṅghāṭakasaṇṭhānādivasena katā dvisālādisannivesā veditabbā. Sālappabhedadīpanameva cettha purimato visesoti. Parikkhepo viddhastoti pamukhassa parikkhepaṃ sandhāya vadati.

A 'separate establishment' is so called because there are rows of chambers on one side, and on the other sides there are no rows of chambers, or even if there are, they are not connected by mutual walls and roofs. It is stated with reference to that... Therein, it is said there is no offense of pācittiya; it is not that there is no offense of dukkaṭa. Indeed, the antechamber of such a row of chambers, due to the absence of walls on three sides and having only the wall of the inner chamber on one side, is called 'fully roofed and slightly enclosed.' Therefore, there is only an offense of dukkaṭa. But if they make a wall for that antechamber on the other sides as well, on one or on all, then it should be understood that because it becomes 'fully roofed and half-enclosed,' and so on, there is only an offense of pācittiya. Regarding 'with reference to an antechamber on a terrace, not on the ground': here, with reference to the antechamber of a house built on the ground without making a high foundation, it is stated that in an unenclosed space there is no offense of pācittiya. If the antechamber has a high foundation, the meaning is that by that foundation the antechamber is counted as enclosed. 'Therein' means in the Andhakaṭṭhakathā. 'Having stated the measure of the terrace' means: having stated the measure of the height of a high foundation such that a person lying on the natural ground cannot see a person sleeping on top of the terrace. A mansion established by being made long and straight on one side is a 'single-hall establishment.' Those made on two, three, or even four sides in the manner of a crossroads shape, etc., should be known as 'two-hall establishments,' etc. The distinction here from the former is only the elucidation of the different kinds of halls. The statement 'the enclosure is destroyed' is said with reference to the enclosure of the antechamber.

53. Upaḍḍhacchannaupaḍḍhaparicchannaṃ senāsanaṃ dukkaṭassa ādiṃ vatvā pāḷiyaṃ dassitattā tato [V 2.0007] adhikaṃ sabbacchannaupaḍḍhaparicchannādikampi sabbaṃ pāḷiyaṃ avuttampi pācittiyasseva vatthubhāvena dassitaṃ sikkhāpadassa paṇṇattivajjattā, garuke ṭhātabbato cāti veditabbaṃ. Satta pācittiyānīti pāḷiyaṃ vuttapācittiyadvayaṃ sāmaññato ekattena gahetvā vuttaṃ.

53. Since it is shown in the Pāḷi, having stated at the beginning that a half-covered and half-enclosed lodging entails a dukkaṭa offense, anything more than that—such as a lodging that is fully covered and half-enclosed, etc.—even if not mentioned in the Pāḷi, is shown to be the basis for a pācittiya offense only. This should be understood because the training rule is a prescribed offense and because it should be placed in the serious category. The statement 'seven pācittiya offenses' is said by taking the two pācittiyas mentioned in the Pāḷi generally as one.

54. Pāḷiyaṃ “tatiyāya rattiyā purāruṇā nikkhamitvā puna vasatī”ti idaṃ ukkaṭṭhavasena vuttaṃ, anikkhamitvā pana purāruṇā uṭṭhahitvā antochadane nisinnassāpi punadivase sahaseyyena anāpatti eva. Senambamaṇḍapavaṇṇaṃ hotīti sīhaḷadīpe kira uccavatthuko sabbacchanno sabbaaparicchanno evaṃnāmako sannipātamaṇḍapo atthi, taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Ettha catutthabhāgo cūḷakaṃ, dve bhāgā upaḍḍhaṃ, tīsu bhāgesu dve bhāgā yebhuyyanti iminā nayena cūḷakacchannaparicchannatādīni veditabbāni. Pācittiyavatthukasenāsanaṃ, tattha anupasampannena saha nipajjanaṃ, catutthadivase sūriyatthaṅgamananti imānettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

54. In the Pāḷi, the statement 'on the third night, having gone out before dawn and then lying down again' is said in the ultimate sense. However, if one does not go out but rises before dawn and sits under a roof, there is no offense for sleeping together on a subsequent day. The statement 'it is like the Senamba pavilion' is said in reference to an assembly hall of that name on the island of Sri Lanka, which is said to have a high foundation, be fully covered, and be fully unenclosed. Here, one-fourth is 'minor,' two parts are 'half,' and two parts out of three are 'the majority'; by this method, the states of being slightly covered, slightly enclosed, and so on should be understood. A lodging that is a basis for a pācittiya offense, lying down there together with an unordained person, and the setting of the sun on the fourth day—these are the three factors in this case.

Sahaseyyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on sleeping together is concluded.

6. Dutiyasahaseyyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

6. Explanation of the Second Training Rule on Sleeping Together

55. Chaṭṭhe mātugāmena saddhiṃ catutthadivase sayantassāpi iminā sikkhāpadena ekāva āpatti. Keci pana purimasikkhāpadenāpīti dve āpattiyo vadanti, taṃ na yuttaṃ “anupasampannenā”ti anitthiliṅgena vuttattā napuṃsakena [M 2.0008] pana catutthadivase sayantassa sadukkaṭapācittiyaṃ vattuṃ yuttaṃ. Kiñcāpettha pāḷiyaṃ paṇḍakavaseneva dukkaṭaṃ vuttaṃ, tadanulomikā pana purisaubhatobyañjanakena saha sayantassa iminā dukkaṭaṃ, purimena catutthadivase sadukkaṭapācittiyaṃ. Itthiubhatobyañjanako itthigatikovāti ayaṃ amhākaṃ khanti. Matitthiyā anāpattīti vadanti. Pācittiyavatthukasenāsanaṃ, tattha mātugāmena saddhiṃ nipajjanaṃ, sūriyatthaṅgamananti imānettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

55. In the sixth rule, even for one who sleeps with a woman on the fourth day, there is only one offense by this training rule. Some, however, say there are two offenses, one also by the previous training rule, but that is not correct, because 'with an unordained person' is stated in the non-feminine gender. But for one sleeping with a neuter person on the fourth day, it is proper to state a pācittiya together with a dukkaṭa. Although in the Pāḷi a dukkaṭa is stated only by way of a eunuch, by analogy, for one sleeping with a male who has both sexual characteristics, there is a dukkaṭa by this rule, and by the previous rule, on the fourth day, a pācittiya together with a dukkaṭa. A female who has both sexual characteristics is just like a woman—this is our opinion. They say there is no offense with a dead woman. A lodging that is a basis for a pācittiya offense, lying down there together with a woman, and the setting of the sun—these are the three factors in this case.

Dutiyasahaseyyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Second Training Rule on Sleeping Together is concluded.

7. Dhammadesanāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

7. Explanation of the Training Rule on Teaching the Dhamma

60. Sattame na yakkhenātiādīnaṃ “aññatra viññunā”ti iminā sambandho. Aññatra viññunā [V 2.0008] purisaviggahena, na yakkhādināpīti evamattho gahetabboti adhippāyo. Tādisenapi hi saha ṭhitāya desetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Taṃtaṃdesabhāsāya atthaṃ yathāruci vaṭṭati eva.

60. In the seventh training rule, the words beginning with 'na yakkhena' are connected with this phrase: 'aññatra viññunā' (except with an intelligent person). The meaning should be understood thus: 'except with an intelligent male person', not with a yakkha or the like—this is the intention. For indeed, it is not proper to teach a woman who is standing together even with such a being. It is indeed proper to teach the meaning in the language of that particular country as one wishes.

Iriyāpathāparivattanaṃ, purisaṃ vā dvādasahatthūpacāre apakkosāpanaṃ ettha akiriyā. Vuttalakkhaṇassa dhammassa channaṃ vācānaṃ upari desanā, vuttalakkhaṇo mātugāmo, iriyāpathapaavattanābhāvo, viññūpurisābhāvo, apañhavissajjanāti imānettha pañca aṅgāni.

Not changing posture, or not calling a man into the vicinity of twelve cubits, is non-action here. These five are the factors here: teaching more than six words of the Dhamma which has the aforementioned characteristics; a woman with the aforementioned characteristics; the absence of a change in posture; the absence of an intelligent man; and the teaching not being an answer to a question.

Dhammadesanāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on teaching the Dhamma is concluded.

8. Bhūtārocanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

8. Explanation of the Training Rule on Declaring a True Superhuman State

77. Aṭṭhame antarāti parinibbānakālato pubbepi. Atikaḍḍhiyamānenāti “vadatha, bhante, kiṃ tumhehi adhigata”nti evaṃ nippīḷiyamānena atibaddhiyamānena. Tathārūpe paccaye sati vattabbameva. Sutapariyattisīlaguṇanti ettha atthakusalatā sutaguṇo, pāḷipāṭhakusalatā pariyattiguṇoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Cittakkhepassa vā abhāvā”ti iminā khittacittavedanāṭṭatāpi ariyānaṃ natthīti dasseti.

77. In the eighth training rule, 'antarā' (in between) means even before the time of Parinibbāna. 'Atikaḍḍhiyamānena' (being excessively drawn out) means being greatly pressed and constrained, as in, 'Speak, venerable sir, what have you attained?' When such a condition is present, it should indeed be spoken. In the phrase 'sutapariyattisīlaguṇa' (the qualities of learning, scripture, and virtue), it should be understood that skill in the meaning is the quality of learning (sutaguṇa), and skill in the Pāḷi text is the quality of scriptural learning (pariyattiguṇa). By the phrase 'or because of the absence of mental distraction', it is shown that for noble ones there is no state of a distracted mind nor of being afflicted by feeling.

Pubbe [M 2.0009] avuttehīti catutthapārājike avuttehi. Idañca sikkhāpadaṃ paṇṇattiajaānanavasena ekantato acittakasamuṭṭhānameva hoti ariyānaṃ paṇṇattivītikkamābhāvā. Jhānalābhīnañca satthu āṇāvītikkamapaṭighacittassa jhānaparihānato bhūtārocanaṃ na sambhavati. Uttarimanussadhammassa bhūtatā, anupasampannassa ārocanaṃ, taṅkhaṇavijānanā, anaññāpadesoti imānettha cattāri aṅgāni.

'Pubbe avuttehi' (by those previously unspoken) means by the origins not spoken of in the fourth pārājika. And this training rule is exclusively of unintentional origin, arising through ignorance of the precept, because for noble ones there is no transgression of the precept. And for those who have attained jhāna, a true declaration does not occur, because the mind of aversion that transgresses the Teacher's command is eliminated by jhāna. These four are the factors here: the actuality of the superhuman state; the declaration to one who is not fully ordained; the knowledge at that very moment; and it not being an indirect reference.

Bhūtārocanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on declaring a true superhuman state is concluded.

9. Duṭṭhullārocanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

9. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Divulging a Gross Offense

78. Navame tattha bhaveyyāti tattha kassaci mati evaṃ bhaveyya. Aṭṭhakathāvacanameva upapattito daḷhaṃ katvā patiṭṭhapento “imināpi ceta”ntiādimāha.

78. In the ninth training rule, as to 'tattha bhaveyya' (there it might be): this means, in that matter, someone's thought might be thus. Wishing to establish the word of the commentary firmly by way of reason, he said the words beginning with 'imināpi cetaṃ'.

82. Ādito pañca sikkhāpadānīti pāṇātipātādīni pañca. Sesānīti vikālabhojanādīni[V 2.0009]. Sukkavissaṭṭhiādi ajjhācārova. Antimavatthuṃ anajjhāpannassa bhikkhuno savatthuko saṅghādiseso, anupasampannassa ārocanaṃ, bhikkhusammutiyā abhāvoti imānettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

82. 'Ādito pañca sikkhāpadāni' (the first five training rules) means the five beginning with taking life. 'Sesāni' (the remaining ones) means those beginning with eating at the wrong time. Emission of semen and so on is indeed a transgression. For a bhikkhu who has not committed the final offense (pārājika), these three are the factors here: a saṅghādisesa offense that has a basis; informing one who is not fully ordained; and the absence of authorization by the bhikkhus.

Duṭṭhullārocanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on divulging a gross offense is concluded.

10. Pathavīkhaṇanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

10. Explanation of the Training Rule on Digging the Earth

86. Dasame appapaṃsumattikāya pathaviyā anāpattivatthubhāvena vuttattā upaḍḍhapaṃsumattikāyapi pācittiyamevāti gahetabbaṃ. Na hetaṃ dukkaṭavatthūti sakkā vattuṃ jātājātavinimuttāya tatiyapathaviyā abhāvato.

86. In the tenth training rule, since it is stated that earth with little dust or soil is a case of no offense, it should be understood that even with earth that is half dust or soil, it is indeed a pācittiya offense. For it is not possible to say that this is a case for a dukkaṭa offense, because of the non-existence of a third kind of earth that is free from being jāta (natural) or ajāta (not natural).

Vaṭṭatīti imasmiṃ ṭhāne pokkharaṇiṃ khaṇāti okāsassa aniyamitattā vaṭṭati. Imaṃ valliṃ khaṇāti pathavīkhaṇanaṃ sandhāya vuttattā imināva sikkhāpadena āpatti, na bhūtagāmasikkhāpadena. Ubhayampi [M 2.0010] sandhāya vutte pana dvepi pācittiyā honti. Udakapappaṭakoti udake antobhūmiyaṃ paviṭṭhe tassa uparibhāgaṃ chādetvā tanukapaṃsu vā mattikā vā paṭalaṃ hutvā patamānā tiṭṭhati, tasmiṃ udake sukkhepi taṃ paṭalaṃ vātena calamānā tiṭṭhati, taṃ udakapappaṭako nāma.

As for 'It is allowable': when it is said, 'Dig a pond in this place,' because the location is not specified, it is allowable. When it is said, 'Dig this creeper,' since this is said with reference to digging the earth, an offense is incurred under this very training rule, not under the training rule on vegetation. If, however, it is said with reference to both, two pācittiya offenses are incurred. As for udakapappaṭaka (water-crust): when water has entered into the ground, a thin layer of dust or soil, having covered its upper part, remains floating as a film. Even when that water dries up, that film remains, moving with the wind. That is called udakapappaṭaka.

Akatapabbhāreti avaḷañjanaṭṭhānadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tādise eva hi vammikassa sambhavoti. Mūsikukkaraṃ nāma mūsikāhi khanitvā bahi katapaṃsurāsi. Acchadanantiādivuttattā ujukaṃ ākāsato patitavassodakena ovaṭṭhameva jātapathavī hoti, na chadanādīsu patitvā tato pavattaudakena tintanti veditabbaṃ. Maṇḍapatthambhanti sākhāmaṇḍapatthambhaṃ. Uccāletvāti ukkhipitvā. Tatoti purāṇasenāsanato.

The phrase 'akatapabbhāre' is said to show a place that is not used. For indeed, it is only in such a place that an anthill arises. Mūsikukkara is a pile of earth dug up by mice and made outside. Because it is said 'uncovered,' etc., it should be understood that only earth soaked by rainwater fallen directly from the sky is jāta-pathavī (natural earth), not earth soaked by water that has fallen on a roof or the like and then flowed from there. Maṇḍapatthambha is a pillar of a pavilion made of branches. Uccāletvā is 'having lifted up.' Tato is 'from the old dwelling.'

88. Mahāmattikanti bhittilepanaṃ. Jātapathavitā, tathāsaññitā, khaṇanakhaṇāpanānaṃ aññataranti imānettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

88. Mahāmattika is plaster for a wall. The state of being natural earth, the perception of it as such, and one of the acts of digging or causing to dig—these are the three factors in this case.

Pathavīkhaṇanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on digging the earth is concluded.

Niṭṭhito musāvādavaggo paṭhamo.

The first chapter, on false speech, is concluded.

2. Bhūtagāmavaggo

2. The Chapter on Vegetation

1. Bhūtagāmasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Training Rule on Vegetation

89. Dutiyavaggassa [V 2.0010] paṭhame niggahetuṃ asakkontoti sākhaṭṭhakavimāne sākhāya chijjamānāya chijjante tattha achedanatthāya devatāya upanītaṃ puttaṃ disvāpi kuṭhārinikkhepavegaṃ nivattetuṃ asakkontoti attho. Rukkhadhammeti rukkhassa pavattiyaṃ. Rukkhānaṃ viya chedanādīsu akuppanañhi rukkhadhammo nāma.

89. In the first training rule of the second chapter, 'unable to restrain' has this meaning: even after seeing the son brought by the deity to prevent the cutting, as the celestial mansion abiding on the branch was about to be destroyed when the branch was being cut, he was unable to stop the momentum of the axe's downswing. As for rukkhadhamma (tree-nature): it is in the nature of a tree. Indeed, just as trees do not get angry when they are being cut and so on, the non-anger of the deity is called rukkhadhamma.

Uppatitanti uppannaṃ. Bhantanti dhāvantaṃ. Vārayeti niggaṇheyya. Itaroti uppannaṃ kodhaṃ aniggaṇhanto rājauparājādīnaṃ rasmimattaggāhakajano viya na uttamasārathīti attho. Visaṭaṃ sappavisanti sarīre dāṭhāvaṇānusārena vitthiṇṇaṃ byāpetvā ṭhitaṃ kaṇhasappavisaṃ viya. Jahāti orapāranti pañcorambhāgiyasaññojanāni tatiyamaggena jahāti. “Orapāra”nti hi orimatīraṃ vuccati[M 2.0011]. Atha vā soti tatiyamaggena kodhaṃ vinetvā ṭhito bhikkhu arahattamaggena orapāraṃ jahātīti attho. Tattha oraṃ nāma sakattabhāvo, ajjhattikāni vā āyatanāni. Pāraṃ nāma paraattabhāvo, bāhirāni vā āyatanāni. Tadubhaye pana chandarāgaṃ jahanto “jahāti orimapāra”nti vuccati.

Uppatita means 'arisen.' Bhanta means 'running.' Vāraye means 'one should restrain.' Itaro (the other) has this meaning: one who does not restrain arisen anger is like a mere rein-holder for a king, crown prince, or the like, not a supreme charioteer. Visaṭaṃ sappavisaṃ is like the poison of a black cobra that has spread and established itself, pervading the body along the track of the fang marks. Jahāti orapāraṃ (he abandons the near and far shore) means he abandons the five lower fetters with the third path. For 'orapāra' is called the 'near shore.' Alternatively, so (he) has this meaning: the monk who stands having removed anger with the third path abandons the 'near and far shore' with the path of Arahantship. Therein, ora (near) is one's own being or the internal sense-bases. Pāra (far) is another's being or the external sense-bases. One who abandons sensual passion for both of these is said to 'abandon the near and far shore.'

90. Bhavantīti vaḍḍhanti. Ahuvuntīti babhūvu. Tenāha “jātā vaḍḍhitā”ti. Bhūtānaṃ gāmoti mahābhūtānaṃ haritatiṇādibhāvena samaggānaṃ samūho. Tabbinimuttassa gāmassa abhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “bhūtā eva vā gāmo”ti vuttaṃ. Pātabya-saddassa pā pāneti dhātvatthaṃ sandhāyāha “paribhuñjitabbatā”ti. Sā ca pātabyatā chedanādi eva hotīti āha “tassā…pe… bhūtagāmassa jātā chedanādipaccayā”ti.

90. Bhavanti means 'they increase.' Ahuvu means 'they have become many.' Therefore, he said, 'born and increased.' Bhūtānaṃ gāma (a group of beings) is a collection of many plants that are united in the state of green grass and so on. To show the non-existence of a 'group' apart from that, it was said, 'or the beings themselves are the group.' With reference to the root meaning of the word pātabya—that the root pā is in the sense of 'to consume'—he said, 'because it is fit to be consumed.' And that fitness for consumption is precisely cutting and so on; therefore, he said, 'of that... vegetation... born from causes such as cutting...'

91. Jāta-saddo ettha vijātapariyāyoti “puttaṃ vijātā itthī”tiādīsu viya pasūtavacanoti āha “pasūtānī”ti, nibbattapaṇṇamūlānīti attho.

91. Here, the word jāta is a synonym for vijāta. Thus, just as in such phrases as 'puttaṃ vijātā itthī' (a woman who has given birth to a son), it has the meaning of 'given birth.' Therefore, he said 'pasūtāni' (produced). The meaning is: 'those that have produced leaves and roots.'

Tāni [V 2.0011] dassentoti tāni bījāni dassento. Kāriyadassanamukheneva kāraṇañca gahitanti āha “bījato nibbattena bījaṃ dassita”nti.

Tāni dassento means 'showing those seeds.' Because by way of showing the effect the cause is also grasped, he said, 'The seed is shown by that which is produced from the seed.'

92. “Bījato sambhūto bhūtagāmo bīja”nti iminā uttarapadalopena “padumagacchato nibbattaṃ pupphaṃ paduma”ntiādīsu viyāyaṃ vohāroti dasseti. Yaṃ bījaṃ bhūtagāmo nāma hotīti nibbattapaṇṇamūlaṃ sandhāya vadati. Yathārutanti yathāpāṭhaṃ.

92. By the phrase, 'Vegetation arisen from a seed is a seed,' it shows that this is a conventional usage through the elision of the latter word, just as in such cases as, 'A flower produced from a lotus plant is a lotus.' The statement, 'Whatever seed is called vegetation,' is said with reference to a seed that has produced leaves and roots. Yathāruta means 'according to the text.'

“Sañciccā”ti vuttattā sarīre laggabhāvaṃ ñatvāpi uṭṭhahati, “taṃ uddharissāmī”tisaññāya abhāvato vaṭṭati. Anantaka-ggahaṇena sāsapamattikā gahitā, nāmañhetaṃ tassā sevālajātiyā. Mūlapaṇṇānaṃ abhāvena “asampuṇṇabhūtagāmo nāmā”ti vuttaṃ. So bījagāmena saṅgahitoti. Avaḍḍhamānepi bhūtagāmamūlakattā vuttaṃ “amūlakabhūtagāme saṅgahaṃ gacchatī”ti. Nāḷikerassa āveṇikaṃ katvā vadati.

Because it is said, 'Intentionally,' even if one gets up knowing that it is stuck to the body, it is allowable due to the absence of the perception, 'I will remove it.' By the mention of anantaka, algae the size of a mustard seed is included, for this is the name of that species of algae. Due to the absence of roots and leaves, it is called 'incomplete vegetation.' It is included in the seed-group. Even though it does not grow, because its origin is vegetation, it is said, 'it is included in the category of rootless vegetation.' He speaks having made the coconut a special case.

Seleyyakaṃ [M 2.0012] nāma silāya sambhūtā ekā gandhajāti. Pupphitakālato paṭṭhāyāti vikasitakālato pabhuti. Chattakaṃ gaṇhantoti vikasitaṃ gaṇhanto. Makuḷaṃ pana rukkhattacaṃ akopentenapi gahetuṃ na vaṭṭati, phullaṃ vaṭṭati. Hatthakukkuccenāti hatthacāpallena.

Seleyyaka is a species of fragrant substance that arises on rock. 'From the time of flowering onwards' means from the time of blossoming onwards. 'Taking a mushroom' means taking a blossomed one. A bud, however, is not allowable to take even without damaging the tree bark; a blossomed one is allowable. 'Due to unsteadiness of the hand' means due to restlessness of the hand.

“Pānīyaṃ na vāsetabba”nti idaṃ attano pivanapānīyaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, aññesaṃ pana vaṭṭati anuggahitattā. Tenāha “attanā khāditukāmenā”ti. Yesaṃ rukkhānaṃ sākhā ruhatīti mūlaṃ anotāretvā paṇṇamattaniggamanamattenapi vaḍḍhati. Tattha kappiyampi akaronto chinnanāḷikeraveḷudaṇḍādayo kopetuṃ vaṭṭati.

This statement, 'Drinking water should not be perfumed,' is said with reference to one's own drinking water; but for others, it is allowable, as it was not taken for oneself. Therefore, He said, 'by one wishing to eat it oneself.' As for 'of which trees the branches grow,' it grows even by the mere measure of a leaf emerging, without the root being sent down. In that case, even without performing the act of making it allowable, it is allowable to destroy things like cut coconut palms, bamboo poles, and so on.

“Caṅkamitaṭṭhānaṃ dassessāmī”ti vuttattā kevalaṃ caṅkamanādhippāyena vā maggagamanādhippāyena vā akkamantassa, tiṇānaṃ upari nisīdanādhippāyena nisīdantassa ca doso natthi.

Because it was said, 'I will show the walking place,' there is no fault for one who treads merely with the intention of walking back and forth or with the intention of going along a path, nor for one who sits on the grass with the intention of sitting.

Samaṇakappehīti samaṇānaṃ kappiyavohārehi, abījanibbaṭṭabījānipi kappiyabhāvato “samaṇakappānī”ti vuttāni. Abījaṃ nāma taruṇaambaphalādīni. Nibbaṭṭetabbaṃ viyojetabbaṃ bījaṃ yasmiṃ, taṃ panasādi nibbaṭṭabījaṃ nāma. Kappiyanti vatvāvāti pubbakālakiriyāvasena vuttepi vacanakkhaṇeva aggisatthādinā bījagāme vaṇaṃ kātabbanti vacanato pana pubbe kātuṃ na vaṭṭati, tañca dvidhā akatvā chedanabhedanameva dassetabbaṃ. Karontena ca bhikkhunā “kappiyaṃ karohī”ti [V 2.0012] yāya kāyaci bhāsāya vutteyeva kātabbaṃ. Bījagāmaparimocanatthaṃ puna kappiyaṃ kāretabbanti kārāpanassa paṭhamameva adhikatattā. “Kaṭāhepi kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vuttattā kaṭāhato nīhatāya miñjāya vā bīje vā yattha katthaci vijjhituṃ vaṭṭati eva. Bhūtagāmo, bhūtagāmasaññitā, vikopanaṃ vā vikopāpanaṃ vāti imānettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

'By what is allowable for recluses' means by the allowable expressions of recluses. Even fruits without seeds and fruits with removable seeds are called 'allowable for recluses' because of their allowable nature. 'Without seed' refers to things like young mango fruits. That in which the seed is to be removed or separated, such as jackfruit, is called 'having a removable seed.' Regarding 'having said, "It is allowable,"' even though it is said by way of a past-time action, a wound must be made on the seed-group with fire, a knife, or the like at the very moment of speaking. But it is not allowable to do it beforehand, and that should be presented only by cutting or splitting, not by making it into two parts. And it should be done by the one performing the action only when it is said in any language by a monk, 'Make it allowable.' This is because the causing to be done was established from the very beginning for the purpose of freeing from the seed-group. Because it was said, 'It is allowable to do it even in the husk,' it is indeed allowable to pierce it anywhere, whether on the kernel or on the seed taken out from the husk. The vegetation-group, the perception of it as a vegetation-group, and destroying or causing it to be destroyed—these are the three factors here.

Bhūtagāmasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule regarding the vegetation-group is concluded.

2. Aññavādakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Evasive Speech

94. Dutiye aññaṃ vacananti yaṃ dosavibhāvanatthaṃ parehi vuttavacanaṃ taṃ tassa ananucchavikena aññena vacanena paṭicarati.

94. In the second training rule, as for 'another statement': whatever statement has been said by others for the purpose of making a fault clear, he covers that over with another, unsuitable statement.

98. Yadetaṃ [M 2.0013] aññenaññaṃ paṭicaraṇavasena pavattavacanaṃ, tadeva pucchitamatthaṃ ṭhapetvā aññaṃ vadati pakāsetīti aññavādakanti āha “aññenaññaṃ paṭicaraṇassetaṃ nāma”nti. Tuṇhībhūtassetaṃ nāmanti tuṇhībhāvassetaṃ nāmaṃ, ayameva vā pāṭho. Aññavādakaṃ āropetunti aññavāde āropetuṃ. Vihesakanti vihesakattaṃ.

98. That statement which occurs by way of covering one thing with another—that is, setting aside the meaning that was asked and speaking of or explaining another thing—is called 'evasive speech.' Thus, He said, 'This is the name for covering one thing with another.' As for 'this is the name for one who has become silent,' this is the name for the state of silence, or this is the very reading. 'To impose evasive speech' means to impose the charge of evasive speech. 'Vexation' means the state of vexation.

99. Pāḷiyaṃ na ugghāṭetukāmoti paṭicchādetukāmo.

99. In the Pāḷi, 'not wishing to reveal' means wishing to conceal.

100. Anāropite aññavādaketi vuttadukkaṭaṃ pāḷiyaṃ āgataaññenaññapaṭicaraṇavasena yujjati, aṭṭhakathāyaṃ āgatanayena pana musāvādena aññenaññaṃ paṭicarantassa pācittiyena saddhiṃ dukkaṭaṃ, āropite imināva pācittiyaṃ. Keci pana “musāvādapācittiyena saddhiṃ pācittiyadvaya”nti vadanti, vīmaṃsitabbaṃ. Ādikammikassapi musāvāde imināva anāpattīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Dhammakammena āropitatā, āpattiyā vā vatthunā vā anuyuñjiyamānatā, chādetukāmatāya aññenaññaṃ paṭicaraṇaṃ, tuṇhībhāvo cāti imānettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

100. The dukkaṭa offense spoken of for 'when evasive speech has not been imposed' is applicable by way of covering one thing with another as it appears in the Pāḷi. However, according to the method found in the commentary, for one who covers one thing with another by means of false speech, there is a dukkaṭa offense together with a pācittiya offense. When one has been charged, there is a pācittiya offense by this very rule. Some, however, say, 'a pair of pācittiya offenses together with the pācittiya for false speech'; this should be investigated. It should be understood that even for a first-time offender, in the case of evading with false speech, there is no offense under this very rule. Being charged by a formal act of the Dhamma; being questioned about the offense or the matter; and covering one thing with another out of a desire to conceal, or being silent—these are the three factors here.

Aññavādakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning evasive speech is concluded.

3. Ujjhāpanakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Causing Complaint

103. Tatiye [V 2.0013] cintāyanatthassa jhe-dhātussa anekatthatāya olokanatthasambhavato vuttaṃ “olokāpentī”ti. Chandāyāti liṅgavipallāsoti āha “chandenā”ti.

103. In the third training rule: Of the root 'jhe', which is established in the meaning of 'thinking', because it has many meanings, and because the meaning of 'looking' is possible, it was said, 'olokāpentī'. The word 'chandāya' is a transposition of gender; therefore, he said, 'chandena'.

105. Bhikkhuṃ lāmakato cintāpanatthaṃ aññesaṃ taṃ avaṇṇakathanaṃ ujjhāpanaṃ nāma. Aññesaṃ pana avatvā aññamaññaṃ samullapanavasena bhikkhuno dosappakāsanaṃ khiyyanaṃ nāmāti ayametesaṃ bhedo.

105. Speaking dispraise of that bhikkhu to others for the purpose of causing him to be thought of lowly is called 'ujjhāpana'. Not speaking to others, but revealing a bhikkhu's fault by way of mutual conversation is called 'khiyyana'. This is the distinction between them.

106. Aññaṃ anupasampannaṃ ujjhāpetīti aññena anupasampannena ujjhāpeti. Tassa vā taṃ santiketi tassa anupasampannassa santike taṃ saṅghena sammataṃ upasampannaṃ khiyyati. Idhāpi musāvādena ujjhāpanādīnaṃ sambhavato dukkaṭaṭṭhānāni ca ādikammikassa anāpatti ca iminā eva sikkhāpadena vuttāti [M 2.0014] veditabbaṃ sabbattha musāvādapācittiyassa anivattito. Dhammakammena sammatatā, upasampannatā, agatigamanābhāvo, tassa avaṇṇakāmatā, yassa santike vadati. Tassa upasampannatā, ujjhāpanaṃ vā khiyyanaṃ vāti imānettha cha aṅgāni.

106. 'He causes another unordained person to complain' means: he causes a bhikkhu to be disparaged by another unordained person. 'Or in his presence' means: in the presence of that unordained person, that ordained one who is authorized by the Saṅgha is disparaged. Herein also, because causing complaint and so on through false speech is possible, the instances of a dukkaṭa offense and the non-offense for the first offender are said to be by this very training rule. This should be understood as being because the pācittiya for false speech is not superseded anywhere. Herein, these are the six factors: (1) being authorized by a formal act of the Dhamma, (2) being fully ordained, (3) the absence of following a wrong course, (4) the desire for that person's dispraise, (5) the one in whose presence he speaks is fully ordained, and (6) the act of causing complaint or disparagement.

Ujjhāpanakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning causing complaint is concluded.

4. Paṭhamasenāsanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the First Training Rule Concerning Lodgings

110. Catutthe apaññāteti appasiddhe. Imaṃ pana aṭṭha māse maṇḍapādīsu ṭhapanasaṅkhātaṃ atthavisesaṃ gahetvā bhagavatā paṭhamameva sikkhāpadaṃ paññattanti adhippāyaṃ “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, aṭṭhamāse”tiādivacanena anupaññattisadisena pakāsetvā visuṃ anupaññatti na vuttā. Parivāre panetaṃ anujānanavacanaṃ anupaññattiṭṭhānanti “ekā anupaññattī”ti (pari. 65-67) vuttaṃ.

110. In the fourth: 'apaññāte' means when the rainy season is not apparent. Taking this special meaning, defined as 'placing in pavilions and so on for eight months', the Blessed One laid down this training rule at the very beginning. Having explained this intention with a statement similar to a subsequent allowance, a separate subsequent allowance was not stated. But in the Parivāra, this statement of permission stands in the place of a subsequent allowance; therefore, it is said, 'one subsequent allowance'.

Navavāyimoti adhunā suttena vītakacchena paliveṭhitamañco. Onaddhoti kappiyacammena onaddho. Te hi vassena sīghaṃ na nassanti. “Ukkaṭṭhaabbhokāsiko”ti idaṃ tassa sukhapaṭipattidassanamattaṃ, ukkaṭṭhassāpi pana cīvarakuṭi vaṭṭateva. Kāyānugatikattāti bhikkhuno tattheva nisīdanabhāvaṃ dīpeti, tena ca vassabhayena sayaṃ aññattha gacchantassa āpattīti dasseti[V 2.0014]. Abbhokāsikānaṃ temanatthāya niyametvā dāyakehi dinnampi attānaṃ rakkhantena rakkhitabbameva.

'Navavāyimo' means a bedstead wrapped with webbing newly woven with thread. 'Onaddho' means a bedstead interlaced with suitable leather. For they are not quickly destroyed by the rain. The phrase 'a strict open-air dweller' is merely to show his comfortable practice; however, even for a strict practitioner, a robe-hut is allowable. 'Because it follows the body' indicates the fact that the bhikkhu sits right there, and by that, it shows that there is an offense for one who, out of fear of the rain, goes elsewhere himself. Even that which is given by donors, designated for open-air dwellers for the purpose of getting wet, must be protected by one who is protecting himself.

“Valāhakānaṃ anuṭṭhitabhāvaṃ sallakkhetvā”ti iminā gimhānepi meghe uṭṭhite abbhokāse nikkhipituṃ na vaṭṭatīti dīpeti. Tatra tatrāti cetiyaṅgaṇādike tasmiṃ tasmiṃ abbhokāse niyametvā nikkhittā. Majjhato paṭṭhāya pādaṭṭhānābhimukhāti yattha samantato sammajjitvā aṅgaṇamajjhe sabbadā kacavarassa saṅkaḍḍhanena majjhe vālikā sañcitā hoti. Tattha kattabbavidhidassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Uccavatthupādaṭṭhānābhimukhaṃ vā vālikā haritabbā. Yattha vā pana koṇesu vālikā sañcitā, tattha tato paṭṭhāya aparadisābhimukhā haritabbāti keci atthaṃ vadanti. Keci pana “sammaṭṭhaṭṭhānassa [M 2.0015] padavaḷañjena avikopanatthāya sayaṃ asammaṭṭhaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā attano pādābhimukhaṃ vālikā haritabbāti vutta”nti vadanti, tattha “majjhato paṭṭhāyā”ti vacanassa payojanaṃ na dissati.

By 'having observed the non-arising of clouds', it is shown that even in the hot season, if clouds have arisen, it is not allowable to place it in the open. 'Here and there' means it was placed after designating in this or that open space, such as a stupa courtyard. As for 'starting from the middle, facing the base': this is said to show the method to be performed where sand is piled up in the middle because rubbish is always gathered in the center of the courtyard after sweeping all around. The sand should be carried facing the base of an elevated place or facing the base of a wall. But some say that where sand is piled in the corners, it should be carried from there facing another direction. Others, however, say: 'It is said that to avoid spoiling the swept area with footprints, one should stand on an unswept area and carry the sand towards one's own feet.' In that case, the purpose of the phrase 'starting from the middle' is not apparent.

111. Vaṅkapādatāmattena kuḷīrapādakassa sesehi viseso, na aṭanīsu pādappavesanavisesenāti dassetuṃ “yo vā pana kocī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tassāti upasampannasseva.

111. A crab-foot bedstead is distinct from the others merely by the fact of its legs being crooked, not by a special way of inserting the legs into the frame-rails. To show this, 'or whatever other...' and so on was said. 'Of that one' means: of one who is fully ordained only.

Nisīditvā…pe… pācittiyanti ettha meghuṭṭhānābhāvaṃ ñatvā “pacchā āgantvā uddharissāmī”ti ābhogena gacchantassa anāpatti, tena punāgantabbameva. Kappaṃ labhitvāti “gaccha, mā idha tiṭṭhā”ti vuttavacanaṃ labhitvā.

Herein, in the passage 'Having sat down... (etc.)... a pācittiya offense': knowing there is no arising of clouds, for one who goes with the thought, 'I will come back later and put it away,' there is no offense; he must certainly come back again. 'Having obtained what is suitable' means: having received the spoken words, 'Go, do not stand here'.

Āvāsikānaṃyeva palibodhoti āgantukesu kiñci avatvā nisīditvā “āvāsikā eva uddharissantī”ti gatesupi āvāsikānameva palibodho. Mahāpaccarivāde pana “idaṃ amhāka”nti avatvāpi nisinnānamevāti adhippāyo. “Santharitvā vā santharāpetvā vā”ti vuttattā anāṇattiyā paññāpitattāpi dukkaṭe kāraṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Ussārakoti sarabhāṇako. So hi uddhaṃ uddhaṃ pāḷipāṭhaṃ sāreti pavattetīti ussārakoti vuccati.

'The responsibility is only for the residents' means: even if visiting bhikkhus, without saying anything, sit down and then leave thinking, 'The residents themselves will put it away,' the responsibility is for the residents only. But in the Mahāpaccarī, the intention is that the burden is only on those who sat down, even without saying, 'This is ours.' Because it is said, 'having spread it or having had it spread,' the reason for the dukkaṭa offense is also stated as being because it was laid out without a command. 'Ussārako' is a chanter with a melodious voice. For he makes the Pāli text proceed higher and higher; therefore, he is called 'ussārako'.

112. Vaṇṇānurakkhaṇatthaṃ katāti paṭakhaṇḍādīhi sibbitvā katā. Bhūmiyaṃ attharitabbāti cimilikāya sati tassā upari, asati suddhabhūmiyaṃ attharitabbā. “Sīhacammādīnaṃ pariharaṇeyeva paṭikkhepo”ti iminā mañcapīṭhādīsu attharitvā puna saṃharitvā ṭhapanādivasena [V 2.0015] attano atthāya pariharaṇameva na vaṭṭati, bhūmattharaṇādivasena paribhogo pana attano pariharaṇaṃ na hotīti dasseti. Khandhake hi “antopi mañce paññattāni honti, bahipi mañce paññattāni hontī”ti evaṃ attano attano atthāya mañcādīsu paññapetvā pariharaṇavatthusmiṃ –

112. 'Made for the purpose of protecting the color' means: made by sewing together pieces of cloth and so on. 'To be spread on the ground' means: if there is a coarse rug, on top of it; if there is not, it is to be spread on the bare ground. By 'The prohibition is only on the personal use of lion skins, etc.', it is shown that personal use by way of spreading it on a bedstead, chair, etc., then rolling it up and storing it for one's own sake is not allowable. However, using it by way of a ground-covering is not personal use. For in the Khandhaka, regarding an object for personal use that one has laid out on a bedstead, etc., for one's own sake, it is said: 'They are laid out on bedsteads inside, and they are laid out on bedsteads outside...'

“Na, bhikkhave, mahācammāni dhāretabbāni sīhacammaṃ byagghacammaṃ dīpicammaṃ. Yo dhāreyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 255) –

'Bhikkhus, large hides are not to be used: a lion's skin, a tiger's skin, a leopard's skin. Whoever should use one, commits an offense of dukkaṭa.'

Paṭikkhepo [M 2.0016] kato. Tasmā vuttanayenevettha adhippāyo daṭṭhabbo. Dārumayapīṭhanti phalakamayapīṭhameva. Pādakathalikanti adhotapādaṃ yasmiṃ ghaṃsantā dhovanti, taṃ dāruphalakādi.

The prohibition has been made. Therefore, the intended meaning here should be understood in the way stated. 'A wooden seat' means simply a seat made of wooden planks. 'A foot-scrubbing board' refers to a wooden plank or the like on which one rubs and washes unwashed feet.

113. “Āgantvā uddharissāmīti gacchatī”ti vuttattā aññenapi kāraṇena anotāpentassapi āgamane sāpekkhassa anāpatti. Teneva mātikāṭṭhakathāyaṃ “mañcādīnaṃ saṅghikatā, vuttalakkhaṇe dese santharaṇaṃ vā santharāpanaṃ vā, apalibuddhatā, āpadāya abhāvo, nirapekkhatā, leḍḍupātātikkamo”ti (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. paṭhamasenāsanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) evamettha nirapekkhatāya saddhiṃ cha aṅgāni vuttāni.

113. Because it is said, 'He goes, thinking, "Having come, I will remove it,"' there is no offense for one who is expectant of returning, even if he has spread it for some other reason and not for drying it in the sun. For that very reason, in the Mātikā Commentary, it is said: 'The state of beds, etc., belonging to the Sangha; the spreading or causing to be spread in a place with the stated characteristics; the state of not being obstructed; the absence of danger; the state of not being expectant; the surpassing of a clod's throw'—thus here, together with the state of not being expectant, six factors are stated.

Paṭhamasenāsanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the First Training Rule concerning Lodgings is concluded.

5. Dutiyasenāsanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

5. The Explanation of the Second Training Rule on Lodgings

116. Pañcame pāvāro kojavoti paccattharaṇatthāyeva ṭhapitā uggatalomā attharaṇavisesā. Ettakameva vuttanti aṭṭhakathāsu vuttaṃ. Senāsanatoti sabbapacchimasenāsanato.

116. In the fifth [rule], 'pāvāra' or 'kojava' are special kinds of spreads with upright wool, set aside only for the purpose of a covering. 'Only this much is stated' means it is so stated in the commentaries. 'From the lodging' means from the very last lodging.

117. Kurundaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttamevatthaṃ savisesaṃ katvā dassetuṃ “kiñcāpi vutto”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Vattabbaṃ natthīti rukkhamūlassa pākaṭattā vuttaṃ. Palujjatīti vinassati.

117. In order to show with specifics the very meaning stated in the Kurundaṭṭhakathā, the passage beginning 'kiñcāpi vutto' was undertaken. 'There is nothing to be said' was stated because of the obviousness of the root of a tree. 'Palujjati' means it is destroyed.

118. Yena mañcaṃ vā pīṭhaṃ vā vīnanti, taṃ mañcapīṭhakavānaṃ. Siluccayaleṇanti pabbataguhā. “Āpucchanaṃ pana vatta”nti iminā āpatti natthīti dasseti. Vuttalakkhaṇaseyyā, tassā [V 2.0016] saṅghikatā, vuttalakkhaṇe vihāre santharaṇaṃ vā santharāpanaṃ vā, apalibuddhatā, āpadāya abhāvo, anapekkhassa disāpakkamanaṃ, upacārasīmātikkamoti imānettha satta aṅgāni.

118. That with which they bind or cover a couch or a chair is 'mañcapīṭhakavāna'. 'Siluccayaleṇa' means a mountain cave. By this text, 'But asking permission is the practice,' it shows that there is no offense. The following are the seven factors here: a sleeping place with the stated characteristics; its state of belonging to the Sangha; spreading or causing to be spread in a monastery with the stated characteristics; the state of not being obstructed; the absence of danger; the departure to another region of one who is not expectant; and the surpassing of the precinct boundary.

Dutiyasenāsanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Second Training Rule on Lodgings is concluded.

6. Anupakhajjasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Training Rule on Encroaching

119. Chaṭṭhe [M 2.0017] anupavisitvāti samīpaṃ pavisitvā.

119. In the sixth rule, 'anupavisitvā' means having entered near.

122. Upacāraṃ ṭhapetvāti diyaḍḍhahatthūpacāraṃ ṭhapetvā. Saṅghikavihāratā, anuṭṭhāpanīyabhāvajānanaṃ, sambādhetukāmatā, upacāre nisīdanaṃ vā nipajjanaṃ vāti imānettha cattāri aṅgāni.

122. 'Having set aside the precinct' means having set aside a precinct of one and a half cubits. The following are the four factors here: the state of being a Sangha monastery; knowing that the other monk is not one to be made to get up; the desire to cause crowding; and sitting or lying down within the precinct.

Anupakhajjasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule on Encroaching is concluded.

7. Nikkaḍḍhanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Training Rule on Expulsion

126. Sattame koṭṭhakānīti dvārakoṭṭhakāni.

126. In the seventh training rule, 'koṭṭhakāni' means door-gatehouses.

128. “Sakalasaṅghārāmato nikkaḍḍhituṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti idaṃ ananurūpato vuttaṃ. Pāpagarahitāya hi akupitacittena nikkaḍḍhāpentassa iminā sikkhāpadena āpatti natthi “kupito anattamano”ti vuttattā. Aññāpekkhā āpatti na dissati. Pāḷiyaṃ “alajjiṃ nikkaḍḍhatī”tiādīsu cittassa lahuparivattitāya antarantarā kope uppannepi anāpatti alajjitādipaccayeneva nikkaḍḍhanassa āraddhattā. Saṅghikavihāro, upasampannassa bhaṇḍanakārakabhāvādivinimuttatā, kopena nikkaḍḍhanaṃ vā nikkaḍḍhāpanaṃ vāti imānettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

128. The statement, 'It is not proper to expel from the entire monastery of the Saṅgha,' is said on account of being unsuitable. Indeed, for one who expels with an un-angered mind because of being one who censures evil, there is no offense by this training rule, because of it being stated, 'angry, displeased.' An offense dependent on another reason is not seen. In the Pāḷi, in such cases as 'expels a shameless one,' even if anger arises intermittently due to the mind's quality of changing quickly, there is no offense, because the expulsion was undertaken solely on account of the condition of shamelessness, etc. A monastery belonging to the Saṅgha; the state of a fully ordained one being free from the state of being a maker of quarrels and so on; and expelling or causing to be expelled out of anger—these three are the factors here.

Nikkaḍḍhanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule on Expulsion is finished.

8. Vehāsakuṭisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Training Rule on the Lofty Hut

129. Aṭṭhamaṃ [V 2.0017] uttānameva. Saṅghiko vihāro, asīsaghaṭṭavehāsakuṭi, heṭṭhāparibhogatā, apaṭāṇidinne āhaccapādake nisīdanaṃ vā nipajjanaṃ vāti imānettha cattāri aṅgāni.

129. The eighth training rule is self-evident. A monastery belonging to the Saṅgha; a lofty hut high enough not to touch the head; the state of its lower part being suitable for use; and sitting or lying down on a bed with removable legs that has not been fixed with pins—these four are the factors here.

Vehāsakuṭisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule on the Lofty Hut is finished.

9. Mahallakavihārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Training Rule on the Large Dwelling

135. Navame [M 2.0018] “mahallako nāma vihāro sassāmiko”ti vuttattā saññācikāya kuṭiyā anāpattīti vadanti. Yassāti vihārassa. Sā aparipūrūpacārāpi hotīti vivariyamānaṃ kavāṭaṃ yaṃ bhittiṃ āhanati, sā sāmantā kavāṭavitthārappamāṇā upacārarahitāpi hotīti attho. Ālokaṃ vātapānaṃ sandheti ghaṭayatīti ālokasandhīti kavāṭaṃ vuccati. Dvāravātapānūpacārato aññattha punappunaṃ limpanādiṃ karontassa piṇḍagaṇanāya pācittiyaṃ.

135. In the ninth training rule, because of it being stated, 'A dwelling called "large" has an owner,' they say there is no offense for a hut built by solicitation. 'Yassa' means 'of the dwelling.' As for the phrase 'sā aparipūrūpacārāpi hoti' (its precinct is incomplete), the meaning is this: whatever wall a door-leaf being opened strikes, that wall, for a surrounding area the size of the door-leaf's breadth, is also without a precinct. Because it connects, it joins the light-window, therefore a door-leaf is called 'ālokasandhi'. For a bhikkhu who repeatedly does plastering and so on in a place other than the precinct of the door and window, there is a pācittiya offense for each lump of plaster.

Keci pana “pāḷiyaṃ pācittiyassa avuttattā dukkaṭa”nti vadanti. Adhiṭṭhātabbanti saṃvidhātabbaṃ. Harite ṭhito adhiṭṭhāti. Āpatti dukkaṭassāti haritayutte khette ṭhatvā chādentassa dukkaṭanti attho. Keci pana “tādise khette vihāraṃ karontassa dukkaṭa”nti vadanti, taṃ pāḷiyā na sameti.

Some teachers, however, say, 'Because a pācittiya is not stated in the Pāḷi, it is a dukkaṭa.' 'Adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ' means it should be arranged. The meaning of 'Harite ṭhito adhiṭṭhāti, āpatti dukkaṭassa' (Standing on greenery, one determines; there is an offense of wrong-doing) is this: for a bhikkhu who roofs while standing in a field endowed with greenery, it is a dukkaṭa. Some teachers, however, say, 'For a bhikkhu who makes a dwelling in such a field, it is a dukkaṭa'; that statement does not agree with the Pāḷi.

136. Ujukameva chādananti chādanamukhavaṭṭito paṭṭhāya yāva piṭṭhivaṃsakūṭāgārakaṇṇikādi, tāva iṭṭhakādīhi ujukaṃ chādanaṃ. Iminā pana yena sabbasmiṃ vihāre ekavāraṃ chādite taṃ chādanaṃ ekamagganti gahetvā pāḷiyaṃ “dve magge”tiādi vuttaṃ. Pariyāyena chādanampi imināva nayena yojetabbanti vadanti, taṃ “punappunaṃ chādāpesī”ti imāya pāḷiyā ca “sabbampi cetaṃ chadanaṃ chadanūpari veditabba”nti iminā aṭṭhakathāvacanena ca sameti.

136. 'Ujukameva chādanaṃ' (roofing straight) is roofing straight with bricks, etc., starting from the eaves-board up to wherever there is a ridge-pole, pinnacle, cornice, etc. By this method, when the entire dwelling has been roofed once, taking that roofing as one course, in the Pāḷi it is said, 'two courses,' etc. They say that roofing in layers of grass or thatch should also be connected by this same method. That statement agrees with this Pāḷi passage, 'He had it roofed again and again,' and with this commentary statement, 'And all this roofing should be known as being upon roofing.'

Pāḷiyaṃ “maggena chādentassa pariyāyena chādentassā”ti idañca iṭṭhakādīhi, tiṇapaṇṇehi ca chādanappakārabhedadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Keci pana “pantiyā chāditassa chadanassa upari chadanamukhavaṭṭito paṭṭhāya uddhaṃ ujukameva ekavāraṃ chādanaṃ ekamagganti gahetvā ‘dve magge’tiādi [V 2.0018] vuttaṃ, na pana sakalavihārachādanaṃ. Esa nayo pariyāyena chādanepī”ti vadanti, taṃ pāḷiaṭṭhakathāhi na sameti.

In the Pāḷi, this statement, 'of one who roofs by course, of one who roofs in layers,' is said in order to show the difference in the manner of roofing with bricks, etc., and with grass and leaves. Some teachers, however, say, 'Taking one instance of roofing straight up, starting from the eaves-board on top of a roof that was roofed in rows, as one course, it is said, "two courses," etc.; it is not said taking the roofing of the entire dwelling. This is the method also in roofing in layers.' That statement does not agree with the Pāḷi and Aṭṭhakathā.

Tatiyāya magganti ettha tatiyāyāti upayogatthe sampadānavacanaṃ, tatiyaṃ magganti attho. Ayameva vā pāṭho. Tiṇapaṇṇehi labbhatīti tiṇapaṇṇehi chādetvā upari ullittāvalittakaraṇaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Kevalaṃ [M 2.0019] tiṇakuṭiyā hi anāpatti vuttā. Tiṇṇaṃ maggānanti maggavasena chāditānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ chadanānaṃ. Tiṇṇaṃ pariyāyānanti etthāpi eseva nayo. Mahallakavihāratā, attano vāsāgāratā, uttari adhiṭṭhānanti imānettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

Here in 'tatiyāya magga', the word 'tatiyāya' is a dative case ending in the sense of the accusative; the meaning is this: 'tatiyaṃ maggaṃ' (the third course). Or, this itself is the original reading. The statement 'tiṇapaṇṇehi labbhati' (it is allowable with grass and leaves) is said with reference to roofing with grass and leaves and then doing the inner and outer plastering on top. Indeed, for a mere grass hut, 'no offense' is stated. 'Tiṇṇaṃ maggānaṃ' means 'of three roofings that have been roofed by way of courses.' Here too in 'tiṇṇaṃ pariyāyānaṃ', this is the same method. The state of being a large dwelling; the state of being one's own residence; and determining beyond two or three layers—these three are the factors here.

Mahallakavihārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule on the Large Dwelling is finished.

10. Sappāṇakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Training Rule on Living Beings

140. Dasame mātikāyaṃ sappāṇakaudakaṃ tiṇena vā mattikāya vā siñceyya, chaḍḍeyyāti attho. Atha vā udakaṃ gahetvā bahi siñceyya, tasmiñca udake tiṇaṃ vā mattikaṃ vā āharitvā pakkhipeyyāti ajjhāharitvā attho veditabbo. Tenāha “sakaṭabhāramattañcepī”tiādi. Idanti tiṇamattikapakkhipanavidhānaṃ. Vuttanti mātikāyaṃ “tiṇaṃ vā mattikaṃ vā”ti evaṃ vuttaṃ, aṭṭhakathāsu vā vuttaṃ.

140. In the tenth training rule, in the Mātikā, the meaning is: one should pour water containing living beings onto grass or clay, or one should discard it. Alternatively, having taken water, one should pour it outside, and having brought grass or clay to that water, one should put it in; this is the meaning to be understood by supplying the words. Therefore, it is said, 'even as much as a cartload,' etc. 'This' refers to the method of putting in grass or clay. 'Stated' means it is stated thus in the Mātikā: 'grass or clay,' or it is stated in the commentaries.

Idañca sikkhāpadaṃ bāhiraparibhogaṃ sandhāya vatthuvasena vuttaṃ abbhantaraparibhogassa visuṃ vakkhamānattā. Tadubhayampi “sappāṇaka”nti katvā vadhakacittaṃ vināva siñcane paññattattā “paṇṇattivajja”nti vuttaṃ. Vadhakacitte pana sati sikkhāpadantareneva pācittiyaṃ, na imināti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Udakassa sappāṇakatā, “siñcanena pāṇakā marissantī”ti jānanaṃ, tādisameva ca udakaṃ vinā vadhakacetanāya kenacideva karaṇīyena tiṇādīnaṃ siñcananti imānettha cattāri aṅgāni.

And this training rule was stated with reference to external use, by way of the story, because internal use will be spoken of separately. Both of these are called a 'prescribed fault' because, being considered as 'containing living beings,' it was prescribed for pouring even without an intention to kill. But if there is an intention to kill, it should be known that the pācittiya is by another training rule, not by this one. Herein, these are the three factors: the water's state of containing living beings; knowing that 'by pouring, the living beings will die'; and the pouring of that very same water onto grass, etc., for some purpose, but without an intention to kill.

Sappāṇakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Water with Living Beings is finished.

Niṭṭhito senāsanavaggo dutiyo.

The second chapter on lodgings is finished.

“Bhūtagāmavaggo”tipi etasseva nāmaṃ.

'The Chapter on Plant Life' is also its name.

3. Ovādavaggo

3. The Chapter on Admonition

1. Ovādasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Training Rule on Admonition

144. Tatiyavaggassa [M 2.0020][V 2.0019] paṭhame tiracchānabhūtanti tirokaraṇabhūtaṃ, bāhirabhūtanti attho. Samiddhoti paripuṇṇo. Sahitattho atthayutto. Atthagambhīratādinā gambhīro.

144. In the first rule of the third chapter, `tiracchānabhūta` means 'become transverse,' that is, 'become external.' `Samiddha` means 'complete.' `Sahitattha` means 'endowed with meaning.' It is 'profound' due to profundity of meaning and so on.

145-147. Paratoti uttari. Karontovāti paribāhire karonto. Vibhaṅgeti jhānavibhaṅge. Caraṇanti nibbānagamanāya pādaṃ.

`Parato` means 'further.' `Karonto vā` means 'acting externally.' `Vibhaṅge` means in the Analysis of Jhāna. `Caraṇa` means a 'foot' for going to Nibbāna.

Yadassāti yaṃ assa. Dhāretīti avinassamānaṃ dhāreti. Parikathanatthanti pakiṇṇakakathāvasena paricchinnadhammakathanatthaṃ. Tisso anumodanāti saṅghabhattādīsu dānānisaṃsappaṭisaṃyuttā nidhikuṇḍasuttādi (khu. pā. 8.1 ādayo) -anumodanā, gehappavesamaṅgalādīsu maṅgalasuttādi (khu. pā. 5.1 ādayo; su. ni. maṅgalasutta) -anumodanā, matakabhattādiamaṅgalesu tirokuṭṭādi (khu. pā. 7.1 ādayo; pe. va. 14 ādayo) -anumodanāti imā tisso anumodanā. Kammākammavinicchayoti parivārāvasāne kammavagge (pari. 482 ādayo) vuttavinicchayo. Samādhivasenāti samathapubbakavasena. Vipassanāvasena vāti diṭṭhivisuddhiādikāya sukkhavipassanāya vasena. Attano sīlarakkhaṇatthaṃ aparānapekkhatāya yena kāmaṃ gantuṃ catasso disā arahati, assa vā santi, tāsu vā sādhūti cātuddiso.

`Yadassa` is `yaṃ assa`. `Dhāreti` means he maintains it undiminished. `Parikathanatthaṃ` means for the purpose of explaining a specific teaching by way of miscellaneous talk. The three kinds of blessings (`anumodanā`) are: blessings connected with the benefits of giving at events such as a meal for the Saṅgha, like the Nidhikaṇḍa Sutta, etc.; blessings at auspicious events such as house-entering ceremonies, like the Maṅgala Sutta, etc.; and blessings at inauspicious events such as funeral meals, like the Tirokuṭṭa Sutta, etc.—these are the three kinds of blessings. `Kammākammavinicchayo` is the determination stated in the Kammavagga at the end of the Parivāra. `Samādhivasena` means by way of insight preceded by serenity. `Vipassanāvasena vā` means by way of dry insight, such as purification of view and so on. For the sake of protecting his own virtue, without regard for others, he is worthy (`arahati`) to go wherever he wishes in the four (`catasso`) directions (`disā`); or, the four directions exist (`santi`) for him (`assa`); or, it is good (`sādhu`) for him in them (`tāsu`). Therefore, he is called `cātuddiso`.

Abhivinayeti pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṅkhāte saṃvaravinaye, tappakāsake vā vinayapiṭake. Vinetunti sikkhāpetuṃ pakāsetuṃ. Paguṇā vācuggatāti pāṭhato ca atthato ca paguṇā mukhe sannidhāpanavasena vācuggatā kātabbā. Atthamattavasenapettha yojanaṃ karonti. Abhidhammeti lakkhaṇarasādivasena paricchinne nāmarūpadhamme. Pubbe kira mahātherā pariyattianantaradhānāya ekekassa gaṇassa dīghanikāyādiekekadhammakoṭṭhāsaṃ niyyātentā “tumhe etaṃ pāḷito ca aṭṭhakathāto ca pariharatha, sakkontā uttaripi uggaṇhathā”ti evaṃ sakaladhammaṃ ganthavasena niyyātenti, tattha te ca bhikkhū ganthanāmena dīghabhāṇakā majjhimabhāṇakāti voharīyanti, te ca [V 2.0020] attano bhārabhūtaṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ pariccajitvā aññaṃ [M 2.0021] uggahetuṃ na labhanti. Taṃ sandhāyāha “sace majjhimabhāṇako hotī”tiādi.

`Abhivinaye` means in the discipline of restraint called the Pātimokkha-restraint, or in the Vinaya Piṭaka which explains it. `Vinetuṃ` means to train, to explain. `Paguṇā vācuggatā` means that it should be made fluent and memorized both in text and in meaning, made so by being established in the mouth. Here, they also make the connection by way of the meaning alone. `Abhidhamme` means in the mental and material phenomena which are defined by way of characteristic, function, and so on. It is said that in the past, the great elders, to prevent the disappearance of the scriptural learning, would assign to each group of monks a single portion of the Dhamma, such as the Dīgha Nikāya, saying: 'You should master this in both its Pāli text and its commentary. If you are able, you should learn even more.' In this way, they handed down the entire Dhamma by way of textual divisions. And those monks were known by the name of the text, as Dīgha-reciters, Majjhima-reciters, and so on. And they were not allowed to set aside the portion that was their responsibility and learn another. It was with reference to this that it was said, 'If one is a Majjhima-reciter,' and so on.

Tattha heṭṭhimā vā tayo vaggāti mahāvaggato heṭṭhimā sagāthakavaggo (saṃ. ni. 1.1 ādayo), nidānavaggo (saṃ. ni. 2.1 ādayo), khandhavaggoti (saṃ. ni. 3.1 ādiyo) ime tayo vaggā. Tikanipātato paṭṭhāya heṭṭhāti ekakanipātadukanipāte sandhāya vuttaṃ. Dhammapadampi saha vatthunā jātakabhāṇakena attano jātakena saddhiṃ uggahetabbaṃ. Tato oraṃ na vaṭṭatīti mahāpaccarivādassa adhippāyo. Tato tatoti dīghanikāyādito. Uccinitvā uggahitaṃ saddhammassa ṭhitiyā, bhikkhunopi pubbāparānusandhiādikusalatāya ca na hotīti “taṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti paṭikkhittaṃ. Abhidhamme kiñci uggahetabbanti na vuttanti ettha yasmā vinaye kusalattikādivibhāgo, suttantesu samathavipassanāmaggo ca abhidhammapāṭhaṃ vinā na viññāyati, andhakāre paviṭṭhakālo viya hoti, tasmā suttavinayānaṃ gahaṇavasena abhidhammaggahaṇaṃ vuttamevāti visuṃ na vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Yathā “bhojanaṃ bhuñjitabba”nti vutte “byañjanaṃ khāditabba”nti avuttampi vuttameva hoti tadavinābhāvato, evaṃsampadamidaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Therein, 'the three lower chapters' means these three chapters below the Mahāvagga: the Sagāthakavagga, the Nidānavagga, and the Khandhavagga. 'Lower, starting from the Tikanipāta' is said with reference to the Ekakanipāta and the Dukanipāta. The Dhammapada, along with its stories, should be learned by a Jātaka-reciter together with his own Jātaka. 'Less than that is not permissible'—this is the opinion of the Mahāpaccarī school. `Tato tato` means from here and there, from the Dīghanikāya and so on. Learning by picking and choosing is not conducive to the stability of the good Dhamma, nor to a monk's skill in connecting the preceding and subsequent context; therefore, it is rejected with the words 'that is not permissible.' Regarding the statement, 'It is not said that anything should be learned in the Abhidhamma,' this is because the division into wholesome triads, etc., in the Vinaya, and the path of serenity and insight in the Suttas, cannot be understood without the Abhidhamma text; it would be like a time of entering into darkness. Therefore, it should be understood that the learning of the Abhidhamma is indeed stated by way of learning the Suttas and Vinaya, and thus it is not stated separately. Just as when it is said, 'Rice should be eaten,' it is understood that 'curry should be eaten' even if not explicitly stated, due to their inseparability; in such a way should this example be understood.

Parimaṇḍalapadabyañjanāyāti parimaṇḍalāni paripuṇṇāni padesu sithiladhanitādibyañjanāni yassaṃ, tāya. Purassa esāti porī, nagaravāsīnaṃ kathāti attho. Anelagaḷāyāti ettha elāti kheḷaṃ taggaḷanavirahitāya. Kalyāṇavākkaraṇoti ettha vācā eva vākkaraṇaṃ, udāharaṇaghoso. Kalyāṇaṃ madhuraṃ vākkaraṇamassāti kalyāṇavākkaraṇo. Upasampannāya methuneneva abhabbo hoti, na sikkhamānāsāmaṇerīsūti āha “bhikkhuniyā kāyasaṃsaggaṃ vā”tiādi.

As for `parimaṇḍalapadabyañjanāya`: by that speech in which the sounds, such as lax and aspirated, in the words are rounded and complete. `Purassa esā`'ti `porī` means: this is the speech of a person of the city, therefore it is called `porī`; the meaning is, the speech of city-dwellers. In `anelagaḷāya`, `elā` is saliva; it means free from the dripping of that saliva. In `kalyāṇavākkaraṇo`, speech itself is `vākkaraṇa`, the sound of utterance. One is called `kalyāṇavākkaraṇo` because that monk has a beautiful, sweet utterance. He becomes unfit only through sexual intercourse with an ordained nun, not in the case of a probationer or a female novice; therefore, he said, 'bodily contact with a bhikkhunī,' and so on.

148. Garukehīti garukabhaṇḍehi. Ekatoupasampannāyāti upayogatthe bhummavacanaṃ. Bhikkhūnaṃ santike upasampannā nāma parivattaliṅgā vā pañcasatasākiyāniyo vā. Etā pana ekatoupasampannā ovadantassa pācittiyameva.

148. `Garukehi` means: like heavy goods. The word `ekatoupasampannāya` is a term in the locative case used in the sense of the accusative. Those ordained in the presence of monks refers to either those who have changed their gender or the five hundred Sākiyan women. As for these, even though they are ordained on one side only, for a monk who admonishes them, it is only a pācittiya offense.

149. Na nimantitā hutvā gantukāmāti nimantitā hutvā bhojanapariyosāne gantukāmā na honti, tattheva vasitukāmā hontīti [M 2.0022] attho. Yatoti bhikkhunupassayato. Yācitvāti “tumhehi ānītaovādeneva mayampi vasissāmā”ti yācitvā. Tatthāti tasmiṃ bhikkhunupassaye. Abhikkhukāvāse vassaṃ vasantiyā pācittiyaṃ, apagacchantiyā dukkaṭaṃ.

149. Na nimantitā hutvā gantukāmā means: having been invited, at the end of the meal, they do not wish to go; they wish to stay right there. This is the meaning. Yato means: from the bhikkhunī monastery. Yācitvā means: having requested, “We too will dwell only with the admonition brought by you.” Tattha means: in that bhikkhunī monastery. For a bhikkhunī spending the rains-residence in a dwelling without monks, there is a pācittiya offense; for one who departs, there is a dukkaṭa offense.

Imāsu [V 2.0021] katarāpatti pariharitabbāti codanaṃ pariharanto āha “sā rakkhitabbā”ti. Sā vassānugamanamūlikā āpatti rakkhitabbā, itarāya anāpattikāraṇaṃ atthīti adhippāyo. Tenāha “āpadāsu hī”tiādi.

Refuting the charge, “Among these two offenses, which offense should be avoided?” he said, “That one should be guarded against.” That offense rooted in not undertaking the rains-residence should be guarded against; for the other offense, there is a reason for there being no offense. This is the intention. Therefore, he said, “Indeed, in dangers,” and so on.

Ovādatthāyāti ovāde yācanatthāya. Dve tissoti dvīhi tīhi, karaṇatthe cetaṃ paccattavacanaṃ. Pāsādikenāti pasādajanakena kāyakammādinā. Sampādetūti tividhaṃ sikkhaṃ sampādetu. Asammatatā, bhikkhuniyā paripuṇṇūpasampannatā, ovādavasena aṭṭhagarudhammadānanti imānettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

Ovādatthāya means: for the purpose of requesting admonition. Dve tisso means: by two or three. This is a nominative expression used in the sense of the instrumental. Pāsādikena means: by that which inspires confidence, such as bodily action. Sampādetu means: let him fulfill the threefold training. Not being appointed, the bhikkhunī’s having been fully ordained, and the giving of the eight weighty rules by way of admonition—these are the three factors here.

Ovādasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on admonition is concluded.

2. Atthaṅgatasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Sunset

153. Dutiye kokanadanti padumavisesaṃ, taṃ kira bahupattaṃ vaṇṇasampannaṃ. Ayañhettha attho – yathā kokanadasaṅkhātaṃ padumaṃ, evaṃ phullamukhapadumaṃ avītaguṇagandhaṃ nimmale antalikkhe ādiccaṃ viya ca attano tejasā tapantaṃ tato eva virocamānaṃ aṅgehi niccharaṇakajutiyā aṅgīrasaṃ sammāsambuddhaṃ passāti. Rajoharaṇanti sarīre rajaṃ puñchatīti rajoharaṇanti puñchanacoḷassa nāmaṃ. Obhāsavissajjanapubbakā bhāsitagāthā obhāsagāthā nāma. Visuddhimaggādīsu (visuddhi. 2.386) pana “rāgo rajo na ca pana reṇu vuccatī”tiādi obhāsagāthā vuttā, na panesā “adhicetaso”ti gāthā. Ayañca cūḷapanthakattherassa udānagāthāti udānapāḷiyaṃ natthi, ekudāniyattherassa (theragā. 1.67 ekudāniyattheragāthāvaṇṇanā) nāyaṃ udānagāthāti tattha vuttaṃ. Idha pana pāḷiyā eva vuttattā therassāpi udānagāthāti gahetabbaṃ. Idha ca agarudhammenāpi ovadato [M 2.0023] pācittiyameva. Atthaṅgatasūriyatā, paripuṇṇūpasampannatā, ovadananti imānettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

153. In the second training rule, kokanada is a special kind of lotus; it is said to have many petals and be endowed with color. Herein, this is the meaning: just as one might see the lotus called kokanada, so should you see the Perfectly Enlightened One, the Aṅgīrasa, whose face is like a blooming lotus, whose fragrance of virtue has not faded, who blazes with his own splendor like the sun in a clear sky, and who is therefore radiant, shining with the light emanating from his limbs. Rajoharaṇa means: it wipes dust from the body, therefore rajoharaṇa is the name for a wiping-cloth. A verse spoken, being preceded by the emission of radiance, is called an obhāsagāthā. In the Visuddhimagga and other texts, the verse beginning “Lust is dust, but it is not called powder…” is called an obhāsagāthā, but this verse beginning “Of a mind uplifted…” is not. And the statement that this is the inspired utterance of the Elder Cūḷapanthaka is not found in the Udāna Pāḷi; rather, it is stated there that this is the inspired utterance of the Elder Ekudāniya. But here, since it is stated in the Pāḷi itself, it should be taken as the Elder’s inspired utterance. And here, for one who admonishes even without the weighty rules, there is only a pācittiya offense. The setting of the sun, the bhikkhunī’s having been fully ordained, and the admonition—these are the three factors here.

Atthaṅgatasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on sunset is concluded.

3. Bhikkhunupassayasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

3. The Explanation of the Training Rule on a Bhikkhunī’s Dwelling

162. Tatiyaṃ [V 2.0022] uttānameva. Upassayūpagamanaṃ, paripuṇṇūpasampannatā, samayābhāvo, garudhammehi ovadananti imānettha cattāri aṅgāni.

162. The third training rule is self-evident. Approaching a bhikkhunī’s dwelling, the state of being fully ordained, the absence of an occasion, and instructing with the weighty principles—these are the four factors here.

Bhikkhunupassayasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on a Bhikkhunī’s Dwelling is concluded.

4. Āmisasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

4. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Material Gain

164. Catutthe āmisanirapekkhampi āmisahetu ovadatītisaññāya bhaṇantassapi anāpatti sacittakattā sikkhāpadassa. Sesamettha uttānameva. Upasampannatā, dhammena laddhasammutitā, anāmisantaratā, avaṇṇakāmatāya evaṃ bhaṇananti imānettha cattāri aṅgāni.

164. In the fourth, for one who speaks with the perception, ‘He instructs for the sake of material gain,’ even if the instructor is unconcerned with material gain, there is no offense, because the training rule is intentional. The rest here is self-evident. The state of being ordained, the state of having received authorization according to the Dhamma, the state of not being concerned with material gain, and speaking thus from a desire to disparage—these are the four factors here.

Āmisasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on Material Gain is concluded.

169. Pañcamaṃ cīvaradānasikkhāpadaṃ uttānameva.

169. The fifth training rule on giving a robe is self-evident.

6. Cīvarasibbanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

6. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Sewing a Robe

176. Chaṭṭhe kathinavattanti kathinamāse cīvaraṃ karontānaṃ sabrahmacārīnaṃ sahāyabhāvūpagamanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Vañcetvāti “tava ñātikāyā”ti avatvā “ekissā bhikkhuniyā”ti ettakameva vatvā “ekissā bhikkhuniyā”ti sutvā te aññātikasaññino ahesunti āha “akappiye niyojitattā”ti. Aññātikāya bhikkhuniyā santakatā, nivāsanapārupanūpagatā, vuttanayena sibbanaṃ vā sibbāpanaṃ vāti imānettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

176. In the sixth, kathinavattaṃ is said in reference to becoming a helper for fellow practitioners who are making robes in the Kathina month. Vañcetvā means: not saying, ‘It is the robe of your relative bhikkhunī,’ but saying only this much, ‘It is the robe of a certain bhikkhunī.’ Having heard, ‘It is the robe of a certain bhikkhunī,’ they perceived her as unrelated. Therefore, it is said, ‘because of being engaged in what is improper.’ The state of being the property of an unrelated bhikkhunī, being suitable for an under-robe or an outer-robe, and sewing or causing it to be sewn in the manner described—these are the three factors here.

Cīvarasibbanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on Sewing a Robe is concluded.

7. Saṃvidhānasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

7. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Arrangement

183. Sattame [M 2.0024] pāḷiyaṃ gacchāma bhagini gacchāmāyyāti bhikkhupubbakaṃ saṃvidhānaṃ, itaraṃ bhikkhunipubbakaṃ[V 2.0023]. Ekaddhānamagganti ekato addhānasaṅkhātaṃ maggaṃ. Hiyyoti suve. Pareti tatiye divase.

7. In the seventh, in the Pāḷi text, ‘Let us go, sister; let us go, venerable lady’ is an arrangement preceded by a bhikkhu; the other is one preceded by a bhikkhunī. Ekaddhānamaggaṃ means a road reckoned as one journey together. Hiyyo means tomorrow (suve). Pare means on the third day.

Dvidhā vuttappakāroti pādagamane pakkhagamaneti dvidhā vuttappakāro. Upacāro na labbhatīti yo parikkhittādigāmassa ekaleḍḍupātādiupacāro vutto, so idha na labbhati āsannattā. Etena ca antaraghareyevettha gāmoti adhippeto, na sakalaṃ gāmakhettaṃ. Tatthāpi yattha upacāro labbhati, tattha upacārokkamane eva āpattīti dasseti. Tenāha “ratanamattantaro”tiādi. Upacārokkamanañcettha upacārabbhantare pavisanameva hoti. Tattha appavisitvāpi upacārato bahi addhayojanabbhantaragatena maggena gacchantopi maggassa dvīsu passesu addhayojanabbhantaragataṃ gāmūpacāraṃ sabbaṃ okkamitvā gacchaticceva vuccati. Addhayojanato bahi gatena maggena gacchanto na gāmūpacāragaṇanāya kāretabbo, addhayojanagaṇanāyeva kāretabbo. Evañca sati anantarasikkhāpade nāvāyeva gāmatīrapassena gacchantassa gāmūpacāragaṇanāya āpatti samatthitā hoti. Na hi sakkā nāvāya gāmūpacārabbhantare pavisituṃ. Tiṇṇaṃ maggānaṃ sambandhaṭṭhānaṃ siṅghāṭakaṃ. Etthantare saṃvidahiteti ettha na kevalaṃ yathāvuttarathikādīsu eva saṃvidahane dukkaṭaṃ, antarāmaggepīti adhippāyo.

`Dvidhā vuttappakāro` means the kind spoken of in two ways: traveling on foot and traveling by wing. `Upacāro na labbhati` means that the proximity, such as a single clod-throw, which is spoken of for a village with a surrounding wall, is not obtained here because of nearness. And by this, it is intended that 'village' here is only what is within the houses, not the entire village-field. Even there, where proximity is obtained, it shows that there is an offense only upon entering the proximity. Therefore, he said, 'a distance of one `ratana` apart,' etc. And entering the proximity here is just entering within the proximity. Even without entering there, one who is traveling on a path that is within half a yojana outside of the proximity is said to be traveling having entered all the village proximity that is within half a yojana on both sides of the path. One traveling on a path that is outside half a yojana should not be determined by the count of village proximity; he should be determined only by the count of half a yojana. And this being so, in the immediately following training rule, for one traveling by boat along the side of the village bank, the offense is established by the measure of village proximity. For it is not possible to enter within the village proximity by boat. The place where three roads connect is a crossroads. Here, in `etthantare saṃvidahite`, the intention is this: a `dukkaṭa` offense occurs not only for arranging in the aforementioned main roads, etc., but also for arranging on the road in between.

Addhayojanaṃ atikkamantassāti asati gāme addhayojanaṃ atikkamantassa. Yasmiñhi gāmakhettabhūtepi araññe addhayojanabbhantare gāmo na hoti, tampi idha agāmakaṃ araññanti adhippetaṃ, na viñjhāṭavādayo.

`Addhayojanaṃ atikkamantassa` means for one who transgresses half a yojana when there is no village. For in whatever wilderness, even if it is village-land, there is no village within half a yojana, that too is intended here as a 'villageless wilderness,' not the Vindhya forest and so on.

185. Raṭṭhabhedeti raṭṭhavilope. Cakkasamāruḷhāti iriyāpathacakkaṃ, sakaṭacakkaṃ vā samāruḷhā. Dvinnampi saṃvidahitvā maggappaṭipatti, avisaṅketaṃ, samayābhāvo, anāpadā, gāmantarokkamanaṃ vā addhayojanātikkamo vāti imānettha pañca aṅgāni. Ekatoupasampannādīhi saddhiṃ saṃvidhāya gacchantassa pana mātugāmasikkhāpadena āpatti.

185. `Raṭṭhabhede` means during the destruction of the country. `Cakkasamāruḷhā` means mounted on the wheel of postures or mounted on a cartwheel. For both: having arranged and proceeding on the path; not missing the appointment; the absence of an exceptional occasion; the absence of danger; and entering another village or transgressing half a yojana—these are the five factors here. However, for one who travels having arranged with one ordained on one side, etc., there is an offense under the training rule concerning women.

Saṃvidhānasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on Arrangement is concluded.

8. Nāvābhiruhanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Embarking on a Boat
