189. Aṭṭhame [M 2.0025] ekaṃ tīraṃ…pe… nirantaranti nadito addhayojanabbhantare padese niviṭṭhagāmehi [V 2.0024] nirantaratā vuttā. Ekaṃ agāmakaṃ araññanti tathā niviṭṭhagāmābhāvena vuttaṃ. Agāmakatīrapassenātiādi pana atirekaaddhayojanavitthataṃ nadiṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tato ūnavitthārāya hi nadiyā majjhenāpi gamane tīradvayassāpi addhayojanabbhantare gatattā gāmantaragaṇanāya, addhayojanagaṇanāya ca āpattiyo paricchinditabbā. Teneva “yojanavitthatā…pe… addhayojanagaṇanāya pācittiyānī”ti vuttaṃ. Teneva hi yojanato ūnāya nadiyā addhayojanabbhantaragatatīravaseneva āpattigaṇanaṃ vuttameva hoti. “Sabbaaṭṭhakathāsū”tiādinā vuttamevatthaṃ samattheti. Tattha kiñcāpi samuddataḷākādīsu pācittiyaṃ na vuttaṃ, tathāpi kīḷāpurekkhārassa tattha dukkaṭamevāti gahetabbaṃ, paṭhamaṃ kīḷāpurekkhārassāpi pacchā nāvāya niddupagatassa, yoniso vā manasi karontassa gāmantarokkamanādīsupi āpattisambhavato paṇṇattivajjatā, ticittatā cassa sikkhāpadassa vuttāti veditabbaṃ. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

189. In the eighth [training rule], regarding `ekaṃ tīraṃ... nirantaraṃ`: the state of being uninterrupted is stated because of the villages established in a place within half a yojana from the river. 'One uninhabited wilderness' is stated due to the absence of villages established in that way. However, the words beginning with 'agāmakatīrapassenā' are stated with reference to a river that is wider than half a yojana. Indeed, for a river of lesser width than that, even when going through the middle, because both banks are within half a yojana, the offenses should be determined by the count of intervening villages and by the count of half-yojanas. For that very reason, it is stated: 'A yojana in width... by the count of half-yojanas, there are pācittiya offenses.' Indeed, for a river less than a yojana [wide], the counting of offenses is not stated solely by the power of the bank being within half a yojana. By the words beginning with 'in all commentaries,' it confirms the meaning that has been stated. In that statement, although a pācittiya offense is not stated for seas, lakes, and so on, it should be understood that for a monk who has playfulness as his foremost intention, there is only a dukkaṭa offense. Because an offense can occur even in entering another village and so on, for a monk who initially has playfulness as his foremost intention but later falls asleep on the boat, or for one who gives proper attention, it should be known that for this training rule, the quality of being an offense by formulation (paṇṇattivajja) and the quality of having three mental states (ticittatā) are stated. The rest is easily understood.

Nāvābhiruhanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Embarking on a Boat is concluded.

9. Paripācitasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Having Food Cooked

197. Navame pāḷiyaṃ “sikkhamānā…pe… pañca bhojanāni ṭhapetvā sabbattha anāpattī”ti idaṃ iminā sikkhāpadena anāpattiṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Pañcahi sahadhammikehi kataviññattiparikathādīhi uppannaṃ paribhuñjantassa dukkaṭameva. Bhikkhuniyā paripācitatā, tathā jānanaṃ, gihisamārambhābhāvo, bhojanatā, tassa ajjhoharaṇanti imānettha pañca aṅgāni.

197. In the ninth [training rule], in the Pāḷi, this statement: 'A female trainee... except for the five kinds of food, there is no offense in all cases,' is stated with reference to the non-offense in regard to this training rule. For one who consumes what has arisen from requests, related talk, and so on, made by the five fellow practitioners, there is only a dukkaṭa offense. Here, these are the five factors: (1) the state of having been caused to be cooked by a bhikkhunī, (2) knowing it as such, (3) the absence of instigation by a layperson, (4) the state of being food, and (5) the swallowing of it.

Paripācitasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Having Food Cooked is concluded.

10. Rahonisajjasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Sitting in a Secluded Place

198. Dasame [M 2.0026] upanandassa catutthasikkhāpadenāti mātugāmena rahonisajjasikkhāpadaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, taṃ pana acelakavagge pañcamampi upanandaṃ ārabbha paññattesu catutthattā evaṃ vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

198. In the tenth [training rule], the phrase 'by the fourth training rule of Upananda' is stated with reference to the training rule about sitting in a secluded place with a woman. It should be understood that although that [rule] is the fifth in the Acelakavagga, it is stated thus because it is the fourth among the training rules laid down on account of Upananda.

Rahonisajjasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Sitting in a Secluded Place is concluded.

Niṭṭhito ovādavaggo tatiyo.

The third, the Bhikkhunivagga, is concluded.

4. Bhojanavaggo

4. The Section on Food

1. Āvasathapiṇḍasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Almsfood from a Rest House

206. Catutthavaggassa [V 2.0025] paṭhame imesaṃyevāti imesaṃ pāsaṇḍānaṃyeva. Ettakānanti imasmiṃ pāsaṇḍe ettakānaṃ.

206. In the first [training rule] of the fourth section, ‘just of these’ (imesaṃyeva) means ‘just of these sectarians.’ ‘This many’ (ettakānaṃ) means ‘this many in this sect.’

208. “Gacchanto vā āgacchanto vā”ti idaṃ addhayojanavasena gahetabbaṃ. Aññe uddissa paññattañca bhikkhūsu appasannehi titthiyehi sāmaññatopi paññattampi bhikkhūnaṃ na vaṭṭati eva. Āvasathapiṇḍatā, agilānatā, anuvasitvā bhojananti imānettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

208. This phrase, ‘going or coming,’ should be understood in terms of half a yojana. Food prepared with other sectarians in mind, and also food prepared in general by sectarians who are displeased with the bhikkhus, is not allowable for bhikkhus at all. Here, these are the three factors: the state of being almsfood from a rest house, the state of not being ill, and eating after having stayed in residence.

Āvasathapiṇḍasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Almsfood from a Rest House is concluded.

2. Gaṇabhojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Group Meals

209. Dutiye abhimāreti abhibhavitvā bhagavantaṃ māraṇatthāya payojite dhanudhare. Nanu “rājānampi mārāpesī”ti vacanato idaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ ajātasattuno kāle paññattanti siddhaṃ, evañca sati pāḷiyaṃ “tena kho pana samayena rañño māgadhassa…pe… ñātisālohito ājīvakesu pabbajito hoti…pe… bimbisāraṃ etadavocā”tiādi virujjhatīti? Na virujjhati. So kira ājīvako bimbisārakālato pabhuti antarantarā bhikkhū nimantetvā dānaṃ dento ajātasattukālepi sikkhāpade paññattepi bhikkhūnaṃ santike dūtaṃ pāhesi, bhikkhū ca kukkuccāyantā nivāresuṃ. Tasmā ādito paṭṭhāya taṃ vatthu dassitanti veditabbaṃ.

209. In the second [rule], as for `abhimāreti`: [it refers to] having overpowered the Blessed One, [and to] the archers employed for the purpose of killing [him]. Is it not established, from the saying ‘He even had the king killed,’ that this training rule was laid down in the time of Ajātasattu? And if this is so, does it not contradict the Pāḷi which states: ‘Now at that time, a blood relative of the Magadhan king…pe… had gone forth among the Ājīvakas…pe… he said this to Bimbisāra,’ and so on? It does not contradict. That Ājīvaka, it seems, starting from the time of Bimbisāra, would intermittently invite the bhikkhus and give alms. Even in the time of Ajātasattu, when the training rule was laid down, he sent a messenger to the bhikkhus, and the bhikkhus, being scrupulous, refused. Therefore, it should be understood that the story is shown from its beginning.

215. Aññamaññaṃ [M 2.0027] visadisaṃ rajjaṃ virajjaṃ, virajjato āgatā verajjakā. Te ca yasmā jātigottādito nānāvidhā, tasmā nānāverajjaketipi attho.

215. A kingdom dissimilar from another is a `virajja`. Those who have come from a `virajja` are `verajjakā`. And because they are of various kinds with respect to birth, lineage, and so on, therefore the meaning is also ‘of various different regions’ (`nānāverajjake`).

217-8. Imassa sikkhāpadassa vatthuvaseneva viññattito gaṇabhojanatthatā siddhāti taṃ avatvā padabhājane asiddhameva nimantanato gaṇabhojanaṃ dassitanti veditabbaṃ. Tenāha “dvīhākārehī”tiādi. [V 2.0026] “Yena kenaci vevacanenā”ti vuttattā “bhojanaṃ gaṇhathā”tiādisāmaññanāmenāpi gaṇabhojanaṃ hoti. Yaṃ pana pāḷiyaṃ addhānagamanādivatthūsu “idheva bhuñjathā”ti vuttavacanassa kukkuccāyanaṃ, tampi odanādināmaṃ gahetvā vuttattā eva katanti veditabbaṃ. Ekato gaṇhantīti aññamaññassa dvādasahatthaṃ amuñcitvā ekato ṭhatvā gaṇhanti.

For this training rule, the state of being a group meal is established by the power of the story itself, from the request. Therefore, it should be understood that, without stating this, a group meal [arising] from an invitation, which is not [otherwise] established, is shown in the word-analysis. For that reason, he said, ‘in two ways,’ etc. Because it is said, ‘by whatever expression,’ it becomes a group meal even by a general name such as, ‘Take the meal.’ As for the scruple in the Pāḷi regarding the words, ‘Eat right here,’ in the stories about journeying and so on, that too, it should be understood, was done precisely because a name such as ‘cooked rice’ was used when speaking. ‘They receive together’ means they stand together and receive, without leaving the twelve-cubit proximity of one another.

“Amhākaṃ catunnampi bhattaṃ dehī”ti vuttattā pāḷi (vaṇṇanā) yaṃ “tvaṃ ekassa bhikkhuno bhattaṃ dehī”tiādino vuttattā ca bhojananāmena viññattameva gaṇabhojanaṃ hoti, tañca aññena viññattampi ekato gaṇhantānaṃ sabbesampi hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Visuṃ gahitaṃ pana viññattaṃ bhuñjato paṇītabhojanādisikkhāpadehi āpatti eva.

Because it is said, ‘Give food to all four of us,’ and because it is said in the Pāḷi commentary, ‘You give food to one bhikkhu,’ and so on, only food requested by the name of ‘food’ becomes a group meal. And it should be understood that this applies to all who receive it together, even if it was requested by another. However, for one who eats what was requested and received separately, there is certainly an offense according to the training rules on fine foods and so on.

Āgantukapaṭṭanti acchinditvā anvādhiṃ āropetvā karaṇacīvaraṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Ṭhapetīti ekaṃ antaṃ cīvare bandhanavasena ṭhapeti. Paccāgataṃ sibbatīti tasseva dutiyaantaṃ parivattitvā āhataṃ sibbati. Āgantukapaṭṭaṃ bandhatīti cīvarena laggaṃ karonto punappunaṃ tattha tattha suttena bandhati. Ghaṭṭetīti pamāṇena gahetvā daṇḍādīhi ghaṭṭeti. Suttaṃ karotīti guṇādibhāvena vaṭṭeti. Valetīti anekaguṇasuttaṃ hatthena vā cakkadaṇḍena vā vaṭṭeti ekattaṃ karoti. Parivattanaṃ karotīti parivattanadaṇḍayantakaṃ karoti, yasmiṃ suttaguḷaṃ pavesetvā veḷunāḷikādīsu ṭhapetvā paribbhamāpetvā suttakoṭito paṭṭhāya ākaḍḍhanti.

As for `āgantukapaṭṭa` (guest strip): it is said with reference to a robe being made by placing a border on it without cutting it. As for `ṭhapeti` (he places): he places one end by way of binding it on the robe. As for `paccāgataṃ sibbati` (he sews the returned part): he sews the second end of that same border, which has been brought around. As for `āgantukapaṭṭaṃ bandhati` (he binds the guest strip): making it adhere to the robe, he binds it with thread again and again in various places. As for `ghaṭṭeti` (he strikes/presses): having taken it according to measure, he strikes it with a wooden block, etc. As for `suttaṃ karoti` (he makes thread): he twists it into the state of a strand, etc. As for `valeti` (he twists): he twists a multi-stranded thread by hand or with a spinning rod, making it one. As for `parivattanaṃ karoti` (he makes a revolving thing): he makes a revolving rod-mechanism, into which he inserts a ball of thread, places it in a bamboo tube, etc., makes it revolve, and draws the thread starting from its end.

220. Animantitacatutthanti animantito catuttho yassa bhikkhucatukkassa, taṃ animantitacatutthaṃ. Evaṃ sesesupi. Tenāha “pañcannaṃ catukkāna”nti. Sampavesetvāti tehi yojetvā. Gaṇo bhijjatīti nimantitasaṅgho na hotīti attho.

220. As for `animantitacatuttha` (a group of four with an uninvited fourth): a group of four bhikkhus of which the fourth member is uninvited; that is called an `animantitacatuttha`. It is the same for the remaining cases as well. For that reason, he said, ‘of the five groups of four.’ As for `sampavesetvā` (having caused to enter): having joined with them. As for `gaṇo bhijjati` (the group is broken): the meaning is that it is not an invited Saṅgha.

Adhivāsetvā [M 2.0028] gatesūti ettha akappiyanimantanādhivāsanakkhaṇe pubbapayoge dukkaṭampi natthi, viññattito pasavane pana viññattikkhaṇe itarasikkhāpadehi dukkaṭaṃ hotīti gahetabbaṃ. Nimantanaṃ sādiyathāti nimantanabhattaṃ paṭiggaṇhatha. Tāni cāti kummāsādīni ca tehi bhikkhūhi ekena pacchā gahitattā ekato na gahitāni.

Here, in the phrase ‘when they had departed after accepting,’ at the moment of accepting an improper invitation, there is not even a `dukkaṭa` offense in the preliminary act. However, in the case of a group meal that arises from a request, it should be understood that a `dukkaṭa` offense occurs at the moment of the request, in accordance with other training rules. ‘Accept the invitation’ (`nimantanaṃ sādiyatha`) means ‘Receive the invitation meal.’ ‘And those things’ (`tāni ca`) means that the barley-meal and so on were not received together because they were received later, one by one, by those bhikkhus.

“Bhattuddesakena paṇḍitena bhavitabbaṃ…pe… mocetabbā”ti etena bhattuddesakena akappiyanimantane sādite sabbesampi sāditaṃ hoti. Ekato gaṇhantānaṃ gaṇabhojanāpatti ca hotīti [V 2.0027] dasseti. Dūtassa dvāre āgantvā puna “bhattaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vacanabhayena “gāmadvāre aṭṭhatvā”ti vuttaṃ. Gaṇabhojanatā, samayābhāvo, ajjhoharaṇanti imānettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

By this [passage], ‘The meal-assigner should be skilled…pe… should be released,’ [it is shown that] when an improper invitation is accepted by the meal-assigner, it is accepted by all. It shows that for those who receive together, there is also the offense of a group meal. It was said, ‘having stood at the village gate,’ out of fear that the words, ‘Take the meal,’ would be said again after coming to the messenger’s door. Here, in this training rule, these are the three factors: the state of being a group meal, the absence of an [allowable] occasion, and consuming.

Gaṇabhojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Group Meals is concluded.

3. Paramparabhojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

3. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Eating in Succession

221. Tatiye pāḷiyaṃ bhattapaṭipāṭi aṭṭhitāti kulapaṭipāṭiyā dātabbā bhattapaṭipāṭi aṭṭhitā na ṭhitā, abbocchinnā nirantarappavattāti attho. Badaraphalāni pakkhipitvā pakkayāguādikaṃ “badarasāḷava”nti vuccati.

221. In the third training rule, in the Pāḷi, as for the phrase `bhattapaṭipāṭi aṭṭhitā` (the order of meals is not established): the order of meals to be given according to the order of families is not established, not fixed; it is uninterrupted and continuously occurring. This is the meaning. Cooked gruel and so forth, into which jujube fruits have been put, is called `badarasāḷava`.

Pāḷiyaṃ paramparabhojaneti yena paṭhamaṃ nimantito, tassa bhojanato parassa bhojanassa bhuñjane. Vikappanāva idha anupaññattivasena mātikāyaṃ anāropitāpi parivāre “catasso anupaññattiyo”ti (pari. 86) anupaññattiyaṃ gaṇitā. Tattha kiñcāpi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ mahāpaccarivādassa pacchā kathanena parammukhāvikappanā patiṭṭhapitā, tathāpi sammukhāvikappanāpi gahetabbāva. Teneva mātikāṭṭhakathāyampi “yo bhikkhu pañcasu sahadhammikesu aññatarassa ‘mayhaṃ bhattapaccāsaṃ tuyhaṃ dammī’ti vā ‘vikappemī’ti vā evaṃ sammukhā”tiādi (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. paramparabhojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) vuttaṃ.

In the Pāḷi, `paramparabhojane` is on account of eating another's meal, apart from the meal of the one by whom one was first invited. Although `vikappanā` (formal transfer) itself, in this training rule, by way of a supplementary ruling, was not included in the `mātikā`, it is counted among the supplementary rulings in the Parivāra as “four supplementary rulings.” Therein, although in the commentary `parammukhāvikappanā` (transfer in absence) was established by the later mention of the Mahāpaccarī view, nevertheless, `sammukhāvikappanā` (transfer in presence) should also be accepted. For that very reason, in the commentary on the Mātikā as well, it is said: “A bhikkhu who, in the presence of one of five co-religionists, says, ‘I give you my expectation of food,’ or ‘I formally transfer it,’ thus in person…” and so forth.

229. Khīraṃ vā rasaṃ vāti pañcabhojanāmisaṃ bhattato upari ṭhitaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tañhi abhojanattā uppaṭipāṭiyā pivatopi anāpatti. Tenāha “bhuñjantenā”tiādi.

229. “Milk or juice” (`khīraṃ vā rasaṃ vā`) is said with reference to what is not mixed with the five kinds of food and is placed on top of the staple food. Indeed, since that is not food, there is no offense even for one who drinks it out of order. Therefore, he said, “while eating…” and so forth.

Vikappanāya [M 2.0029] akaraṇato akiriyāvasena idaṃ vācāyapi samuṭṭhitanti āha “vacīkamma”nti. Paramparabhojanatā, samayābhāvo, ajjhoharaṇanti imānettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

Due to not performing `vikappanā`, by way of omission, this offense also arises from speech; therefore, he said, 'verbal action' (`vacīkamma`). The state of eating in succession, the absence of the proper occasion, and swallowing—these are the three factors herein.

Paramparabhojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on Eating in Succession is concluded.

4. Kāṇamātāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

4. The Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning Kāṇamātā

231. Catutthe pāḷiyaṃ paṭiyālokanti pacchimadisaṃ, pacchādisanti attho. Apātheyyādiatthāya [V 2.0028] paṭiyāditantisaññāya gaṇhantassāpi āpatti eva acittakattā sikkhāpadassa. Attano atthāya “imassa hatthe dehī”ti vacanenāpi āpajjanato “vacīkamma”nti vuttaṃ. Vuttalakkhaṇapūvamanthatā, asesakatā, appaṭippassaddhagamanatā, aññātakāditā, atirekapaṭiggahaṇanti imānettha pañca aṅgāni.

231. In the fourth training rule, in the Pāḷi, `paṭiyālokaṃ` means the western direction, that is, the direction behind. Even for one who receives it with the perception that it is prepared for a purpose other than provisions, there is indeed an offense because the training rule is not dependent on intention. Because one falls into an offense even by the words, “Give into this one’s hand,” for one’s own sake, it is called ‘verbal action.’ The state of being cakes or lumps with the stated characteristics, the state of there being no remainder, the non-cessation of the journey, the state of not being a relative, etc., and receiving in excess—these five are the factors herein.

Kāṇamātāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule Concerning Kāṇamātā is concluded.

5. Paṭhamapavāraṇāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

5. The Explanation of the First Pavāraṇā Training Rule

237. Pañcame “ti-kāraṃ avatvā”ti iminā kātabbasaddasāmatthiyā laddhaṃ iti-padaṃ katakāle na vattabbanti dasseti. Idha pana ajānantehi iti-sadde payuttepi atirittaṃ katameva hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

237. In the fifth training rule, by the text 'without saying the syllable ‘ti’,' it shows that the word ‘iti,’ which is found at the end of a meaningful phrase, should not be uttered at the time of a Vinaya transaction. However, it should be understood that here, even if the word ‘iti’ is used by those who do not know, it simply becomes superfluous.

238-9. “Pavārito”ti idañca kattuatthe nipphannanti dassetuṃ “katapavāraṇo”tiādi vuttaṃ. Bhuttāvī-padassa niratthakabhāvameva sādhetuṃ “vuttampi ceta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tāhīti puthukāhi. Sattumodakoti sattuṃ temetvā kato apakko. Sattuṃ pana pisitvā piṭṭhaṃ katvā temetvā pūvaṃ katvā pacanti, taṃ na pavāreti. “Paṭikkhipitabbaṭṭhāne ṭhitameva paṭikkhipati nāmā”ti vuttattā yaṃ yaṃ alajjisantakaṃ vā attano apāpuṇakasaṅghikādiṃ vā paṭikkhepato pavāraṇā na hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

To show that this word 'pavārito' is formed in the agent sense, 'katapavāraṇo,' etc., is said. To establish the very meaninglessness of the word 'bhuttāvī,' 'vuttampi cetaṃ,' etc., is said. 'Tāhi' means with parched rice flakes. 'Sattumodako' is an uncooked sweetmeat made by moistening roasted grain flour. However, when they grind roasted grain flour, make it into a paste, moisten it, form a cake, and cook it, that does not cause pavāraṇā. Because it is said, 'One refuses only that which is in a position to be refused,' it should be understood that pavāraṇā does not occur by refusing whatever belongs to a shameless person, or communal property, etc., that has not reached oneself.

Āsannataraṃ aṅganti hatthapāsato bahi ṭhatvā onamitvā dentassa sīsaṃ āsannataraṃ hoti, tassa orimantena paricchinditabbaṃ.

'The closer part' (`āsannataraṃ aṅgaṃ`) means that when one stands outside arm's reach and bends down to give, the head becomes closer. The boundary should be determined by its near side.

Apanāmetvāti [M 2.0030] abhimukhaṃ haritvā. “Imaṃ bhattaṃ gaṇhā”ti vadatīti kiñci anāmetvā vadati. Kevalaṃ vācābhihārassa anadhippetattā gaṇhathāti gahetuṃ āraddhaṃ kaṭacchunā anukkhittampi pubbepi evaṃ abhihaṭattā pavāraṇā hotīti “abhihaṭāva hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Uddhaṭamatteti bhājanato viyojitamatte. Dvinnaṃ samabhārepīti parivesakassa ca aññassa ca bhattapacchibhājanavahane samakepīti attho.

'Apanāmetvā' means having brought it forward. 'Saying, "Take this food"' means one speaks without bending anything towards the recipient. Because a mere verbal offering is not intended, when one has initiated the act of taking after being told, 'Take it,' even if it has not been lifted with a ladle, pavāraṇā occurs because it has been brought forward in this way before. Therefore, it is said, 'It has indeed been brought forward.' 'Merely lifted' means merely separated from the container. 'In the case of an equal burden for two' means even when the server and another are carrying the burden of the food basket together.

Rasaṃ gaṇhathāti ettha kevalaṃ maṃsarasassa apavāraṇājanakassa nāmena vuttattā paṭikkhipato [V 2.0029] pavāraṇā na hoti. Maccharasantiādīsu maccho ca rasañcāti atthassa sambhavato vatthunopi tādisattā pavāraṇā hoti, “idaṃ gaṇhathā”tipi avatvā tuṇhībhāvena abhihaṭaṃ paṭikkhipatopi hoti eva. Karambakoti missakādhivacanametaṃ. Yañhi bahūhi missetvā karonti, so “karambako”ti vuccati.

Here, in the phrase 'Take the soup,' because it is referred to by the name of mere meat soup, which does not cause pavāraṇā, pavāraṇā does not occur for one who refuses it. In cases like 'fish soup,' etc., because the meaning 'fish and soup' is possible, and also because the substance itself is of such a nature, pavāraṇā occurs. Even without saying, 'Take this,' it still occurs for one who refuses what is brought forward in silence. 'Karambaka' is a term for a mixed dish. For whatever they make by mixing it with many things—such as fish, meat, and vegetables—is called 'karambaka'.

“Uddissa kata”nti maññamānoti ettha vatthuno kappiyattā “pavāritova hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Tañce uddissa katameva hoti, paṭikkhepo natthi. Ayamettha adhippāyoti “yenāpucchito”tiādinā vuttamevatthaṃ sandhāya vadati. Kāraṇaṃ panettha duddasanti bhattassa bahutarabhāvena pavāraṇāsambhavakāraṇaṃ duddasaṃ, aññathā karambakepi macchādibahubhāve pavāraṇā bhaveyyāti adhippāyo. Yathā cettha kāraṇaṃ duddasaṃ, evaṃ parato “missakaṃ gaṇhathā”ti etthāpi kāraṇaṃ duddasamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yañca “idaṃ pana bhattamissakamevā”tiādi kāraṇaṃ vuttaṃ, tampi “appataraṃ na pavāretī”ti vacanena na sameti. Visuṃ katvā detīti “rasaṃ gaṇhathā”tiādinā vācāya visuṃ katvā detīti attho gahetabbo. Na pana kāyena rasādiṃ viyojetvāti. Tathā aviyojitepi paṭikkhipato pavāraṇāya asambhavato appavāraṇāpahoṇakassa nāmena vuttattā bhattamissakayāguṃ āharitvā “yāguṃ gaṇhathā”ti vuttaṭṭhānādīsu viya, aññathā vā ettha yathā pubbāparaṃ na virujjhati, tathā adhippāyo gahetabbo.

Here, in 'thinking, "It was made specifically,"' because the substance is allowable, it is said, 'He is indeed considered to have been satisfied (pavārita).' If it was indeed made specifically for him, pavāraṇā does not occur. 'This is the intention here' refers to and states the very meaning that was spoken of in 'by whom it was asked,' etc. 'The reason here is difficult to see' means that because the rice is the greater part, the reason for the possibility of pavāraṇā is difficult to see. Otherwise, if there were a large amount of fish, etc., in the mixed dish (karambaka), pavāraṇā would occur—this is the intention. Just as the reason here is difficult to see, so too it should be understood that later, in the case of 'Take the mixed dish,' the reason is also difficult to see. And the reason that was given, 'But this is just mixed with rice,' etc., also does not accord with the statement, 'A lesser part does not cause pavāraṇā.' 'Gives having made it separate' should be understood to mean that one gives having made it separate by speech with words such as, 'Take the soup.' It should not be understood as physically separating the soup, etc. Why? Because even when it is not physically separated, pavāraṇā is impossible for one who refuses it. The impossibility of pavāraṇā occurs because it is referred to by the name of the mixed item which is insufficient for pavāraṇā, as in instances such as bringing gruel mixed with rice and saying, 'Take the gruel.' Alternatively, the intention here should be understood in such a way that there is no contradiction between what precedes and what follows.

Nāvā vā setu vātiādimhi nāvādiabhiruhanādikkhaṇe kiñci ṭhatvāpi abhiruhanādikātabbattepi gamanatapparatāya ṭhānaṃ nāma na hoti, janasammaddena pana anokāsādibhāvena kātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Acāletvāti vuttaṭṭhānato [M 2.0031] aññasmimpi padese vā uddhaṃ vā apesetvā tasmiṃ eva pana ṭhāne parivattetuṃ labhati. Tenāha “yena passenā”tiādi.

In the text beginning 'a boat or a bridge,' at the moment of boarding a boat or the like, even if one stands for a little while and even though the act of boarding, etc., must be done, it is not called 'standing' because one is intent on going. However, due to a crowd of people, lack of space, and so on, it is not allowable to stand. 'Without moving' (`acāletvā`) means without pushing it from its place to another area or upwards; but one is allowed to turn it around in that very place. Therefore, he said, 'by which pushing,' etc.

Akappiyabhojanaṃ vāti kuladūsanādinā uppannaṃ, taṃ “akappiya”nti iminā tena missaṃ odanādi atirittaṃ hoti evāti dasseti. Tasmā yaṃ tattha akappakataṃ kandaphalādi, taṃ apanetvā sesaṃ bhuñjitabbameva.

'Or unallowable food' means food that has arisen through corrupting families, etc. By this word 'unallowable,' it shows that rice and so on mixed with that certainly becomes leftover food. Therefore, whatever tubers, fruits, etc., in that bowl have not been made allowable, one should remove them and may certainly eat the remainder.

So puna kātuṃ na labhatīti tasmiññeva bhājane kariyamānaṃ paṭhamakatena saddhiṃ kataṃ hotīti puna so eva kātuṃ na labhati, añño labhati. Aññena hi katato añño puna kātuṃ [V 2.0030] labhati. Aññasmiṃ pana bhājane tena vā aññena vā kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Tenāha “yena akataṃ, tena kātabbaṃ, yañca akataṃ, taṃ kātabba”nti. Evaṃ katanti aññasmiṃ bhājane kataṃ. Sace pana āmisasaṃsaṭṭhānīti ettha mukhādīsu laggampi āmisaṃ sodhetvāva atirittaṃ bhuñjitabbanti veditabbaṃ.

'He is not allowed to do it again' means that when it is being done in that very same vessel, it is considered done together with what was done first. Therefore, that same monk is not allowed to do it again, but another is allowed. Indeed, another is allowed to do again what has been done by another. But in another vessel, it is allowable for it to be done either by him or by another. Therefore, He said: 'By whom it was not done, by him it should be done; and that which was not done, that should be done.' 'Done thus' means done in another vessel. Here, in 'but if they are mixed with food,' it should be known that one should eat the leftover food only after cleaning even the food adhering to the mouth and so on.

241. Vācāya āṇāpetvā atirittaṃ akārāpanato akiriyasamuṭṭhānanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Pavāritabhāvo, āmisassa anatirittatā, kāle ajjhoharaṇanti imānettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

241. It should be understood that this offense originates from inaction because, having given an order by speech, one does not cause leftover food to be made. Here, there are three factors: the state of having been satisfied, the food not having been made leftover, and swallowing it within the proper time.

Paṭhamapavāraṇāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the First Pavāraṇā Training Rule is concluded.

6. Dutiyapavāraṇāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Second Training Rule Concerning Invitation

243. Chaṭṭhe “bhuttasmi”nti mātikāyaṃ vuttattā bhojanapariyosāne pācittiyaṃ. Pavāritatā, tathāsaññitā, āsādanāpekkhatā, anatirittena abhihaṭapavāraṇā, bhojanapaayosānanti imānettha pañca aṅgāni.

243. In the sixth training rule, because it is stated in the Mātikā as 'bhuttasmiṃ,' a pācittiya offense is incurred at the conclusion of the meal. Herein, these are the five factors: the state of having refused further food, the perception of it as such, the desire to find fault, an invitation by bringing forward food that is not leftover, and the conclusion of the meal.

Dutiyapavāraṇāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Second Training Rule Concerning Invitation is concluded.

7. Vikālabhojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Eating at the Wrong Time

247. Sattame naṭānaṃ nāṭakāti naṭanāṭakā, sītāharaṇādīni.

247. In the seventh training rule: The acts of dancers are 'naṭanāṭaka'; for example, the abduction of Sītā and so forth.

248-9. Khādanīye khādanīyatthanti pūvādikhādanīye vijjamānakhādanīyakiccaṃ khādanīyehi kātabbaṃ jighacchāharaṇasaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ payojanaṃ neva pharanti [M 2.0032] na nipphādenti. Ekasmiṃ dese āhārakiccaṃ sādhentaṃ vā aññasmiṃ dese uṭṭhitabhūmirasādibhedena āhārakiccaṃ asādhentampi vā sambhaveyyāti āha “tesu tesu janapadesū”tiādi. Keci pana “ekasmiṃ janapade āhārakiccaṃ sādhentaṃ sesajanapadesupi vikāle na kappati evāti dassanatthaṃ idaṃ vutta”ntipi (sārattha. ṭī. pācittiyakaṇḍa 3.248-249) vadanti. Pakatiāhāravasenāti aññehi yāvakālikehi ayojitaṃ attano pakatiyāva āhārakiccakaraṇavasena. Sammohoyeva hotīti [V 2.0031] anekatthānaṃ nāmānaṃ, appasiddhānañca sambhavato sammoho eva siyā. Tenevettha mayampi mūlakamūlādīnaṃ pariyāyantaradassanena adassanaṃ karimha upadesatova gahetabbato.

Regarding 'the purpose of an edible in what is edible': They do not fulfill or accomplish the function of an edible that exists in edibles such as cakes, which is the purpose and benefit known as the removal of hunger that is to be accomplished by edibles. He said, 'in those various regions,' and so on, because it is possible that in one region a substance may accomplish the function of food, while in another region, due to differences in the taste of the soil that has arisen and so forth, it may not accomplish the function of food. Some, however, also say: 'This was said to show that if in one region it accomplishes the function of food, it is not allowable at the wrong time in other regions either.' 'By way of natural food' means by way of performing the function of food by its own nature, not combined with other yāvakālika items. 'There would indeed be confusion' means that because of the possibility of names with various meanings and of obscure names, there would indeed be confusion. For that very reason, herein we also have not shown alternative synonyms for radish-root and so forth, because it is to be grasped only through instruction.

Yanti vaṭṭakandaṃ. Muḷālanti thūlataruṇamūlameva, rukkhavalliādīnaṃ matthakoti heṭṭhā vuttameva sampiṇḍetvā vuttaṃ. Acchivādīnaṃ aparipakkāneva phalāni yāvajīvikānīti dassetuṃ “aparipakkānī”ti vuttaṃ. Harītakādīnaṃ aṭṭhīnīti ettha miñjaṃ yāvakālikanti keci vadanti, taṃ na yuttaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ avuttattā.

'Yaṃ' is a round tuber. 'Muḷāla' is just a large, young root; the phrase 'the top of trees, vines, and so forth' was said as a summary referring to the sprout mentioned below. To show that only the unripe fruits of the acchivā plant and so forth are allowable for life, the word 'unripe' was stated. Herein, regarding 'the stones of the harītakā fruit and so forth,' some say that the kernel is yāvakālika, but that is not correct, as it is not stated in the Aṭṭhakathā.

Hiṅgurukkhato paggharitaniyyāso hiṅgu nāma. Hiṅgujatuādayo ca hiṅguvikatiyova. Tattha hiṅgujatu nāma hiṅgurukkhassa daṇḍapattāni pacitvā kataniyyāso. Hiṅgusipāṭikā nāma hiṅgupattāni pacitvā kataniyyāso. Aññena missetvā katotipi vadanti. Takanti aggakoṭiyā nikkhantasileso. Takapattinti pattato nikkhantasileso. Takapaṇṇinti palāse bhajjitvā katasileso. Daṇḍato nikkhantasilesotipi vadanti. Vikālatā, yāvakālikatā, ajjhoharaṇanti imānettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

The resin that exudes from the hiṅgu tree is called hiṅgu. Hiṅgujatu and so forth are just varieties of hiṅgu. Among them, hiṅgujatu is the resin made by cooking the stems and leaves of the hiṅgu tree. Hiṅgusipāṭikā is the resin made by cooking the hiṅgu leaves. They also say it is made by mixing it with something else. 'Taka' is the gum that exudes from the tip. 'Takapatti' is the gum that exudes from the leaf. 'Takapaṇṇi' is the gum made by roasting the leaves. They also say it is the gum that exudes from the stem. Herein, these are the three factors: the state of being the wrong time, the state of being a yāvakālika item, and the act of swallowing.

Vikālabhojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Eating at the Wrong Time is concluded.

8. Sannidhikārakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Storing

252-3. Aṭṭhame tādisanti asūpabyañjanaṃ. Yāvakālikaṃ vā yāmakālikaṃ vā…pe… pācittiyanti ettha kiñcāpi pāḷiyaṃ khādanīyabhojanīyapadehi yāvakālikameva saṅgahitaṃ, na yāmakālikaṃ. Tathāpi “anāpatti yāmakālikaṃ yāme nidahitvā bhuñjatī”ti idha ceva –

In the eighth training rule, `tādisaṃ` means food without soup or curry. Herein, regarding the text, 'Whether a yāvakālika item or a yāmakālika item... and so on... entails a pācittiya offense,' although in the Pāḷi text only the yāvakālika is included by the terms `khādanīya` and `bhojanīya`, and the yāmakālika is not included, nevertheless, because it is stated both here in this training rule, 'There is no offense for one who eats a yāmakālika item, having stored it within the watch'—

“Yāmakālikena[M 2.0033], bhikkhave, sattāhakālikaṃ…pe… yāvajīvikaṃ tadahupaṭiggahitaṃ yāme kappati, yāmātikkante na kappatī”ti (mahāva. 305) –

and, 'O monks, a sattāhakālika item... and so on... or a yāvajīvika item, received on that same day, is allowable with a yāmakālika item within the watch; it is not allowable when the watch has passed' (Mahāvagga 305)—

Aññattha ca vuttattā, “yāmakālika”nti vacanasāmatthiyato ca bhagavato adhippāyaññūhi aṭṭhakathācariyehi yāmakālikaṃ sannidhikārakakataṃ pācittiyavatthumeva vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yanti pattaṃ, ghaṃsanakiriyāpekkhāya cetaṃ upayogavacanaṃ. Aṅgulilekhā paññāyatīti sinehābhāvepi pattassa succhavitāya paññāyati. Yanti yāvakālikaṃ, yāmakālikañca. Apariccattamevāti nirapekkhatāya [V 2.0032] anupasampannassa adinnaṃ, apariccattañca yāvakālikādivatthumeva sandhāya vadati, na pana taggatapaṭiggahaṇaṃ. Na hi vatthuṃ apariccajitvā tatthagatapaṭiggahaṇaṃ pariccajituṃ sakkā, na ca tādisaṃ vacanamatthi. Yadi bhaveyya, “sace patto duddhoto hoti…pe… bhuñjantassa pācittiya”nti vacanaṃ virujjheyya. Na hi dhovanena āmisaṃ apanetuṃ vāyamantassa paṭiggahaṇe apekkhā vattati. Yena punadivase bhuñjato pācittiyaṃ janeyya, patte pana vattamānā apekkhā taggatike āmisepi vattati evanāmāti āmise anapekkhatā ettha na labbhati, tato āmise avijahitapaṭiggahaṇaṃ punadivase pācittiyaṃ janetīti idaṃ vuttaṃ. Atha mataṃ “yadaggenettha āmisānapekkhatā na labbhati. Tadaggena paṭiggahaṇānapekkhāpi na labbhatī”ti. Tathā sati yattha āmisāpekkhā atthi, tattha paṭiggahaṇāpekkhāpi na vigacchatīti āpannaṃ, evañca paṭiggahaṇe anapekkhavissajjanaṃ visuṃ na vattabbaṃ siyā. Aṭṭhakathāyañcetampi paṭiggahaṇavijahanakāraṇattena abhimataṃ siyā, idaṃ suṭṭhutaraṃ katvā visuṃ vattabbaṃ cīvarāpekkhāya vattamānāyapi paccuddhārena adhiṭṭhānavijahanaṃ viya. Etasmiñca upāye sati gaṇṭhikāhatapattesu avaṭṭanatā nāma na siyāti vuttovāyamattho. Tasmā yaṃ vuttaṃ sāratthadīpaniyaṃ “yaṃ parassa pariccajitvā adinnampi sace paṭiggahaṇe nirapekkhanissajjanena vijahitapaṭiggahaṇaṃ hoti, tampi dutiyadivase vaṭṭatī”tiādi (sārattha. ṭī. pācittiyakaṇḍa 3.252-253), taṃ na sārato paccetabbaṃ.

And because it was stated elsewhere, and also by the power of the word ‘yāmakālika,’ it should be understood that the commentary masters, who know the Blessed One’s intention, have stated that a yāmakālika item that has been stored is solely a ground for a pācittiya offense. ‘Yaṃ’ means the bowl; and this is a word in the accusative case, used in relation to the action of scraping. As for ‘aṅgulilekhā paññāyati’ (a finger-mark is discernible): it is discernible due to the fine surface of the bowl, even in the absence of grease. ‘Yaṃ’ refers to a yāvakālika item and a yāmakālika item. As for ‘apariccattameva’ (not relinquished at all): this is said referring only to the yāvakālika object itself—which has not been relinquished and, out of lack of concern, has not been given to an unordained person—and not referring to the receiving of it. For it is not possible to relinquish the receiving connected with an object without relinquishing the object, nor is there any such statement. If there were, the statement, ‘If the bowl is badly washed… for one who eats, there is a pācittiya offense,’ would be contradicted. For indeed, for one who is striving to remove the food-remains by washing, there is no concern for the receiving by which a pācittiya offense would be generated for one eating on the next day. However, the concern existing for the bowl also applies indeed to the food-remains in it. Thus, a lack of concern for the food-remains is not found here. Therefore, the food-remains for which the receiving has not been abandoned generate a pācittiya offense on the next day. Thus, this was said. Now, if it is held: ‘Insofar as a lack of concern for the food-remains is not obtained here, to that extent a lack of concern for the receiving is also not obtained.’ That being so, it follows that where there is concern for the food-remains, the concern for the receiving also does not cease. And thus, the relinquishing of the receiving without concern should not have to be stated separately. And if this were intended in the commentary as a reason for abandoning the receiving, this should be stated separately and more clearly, like the abandoning of a determination by means of revocation even while concern for the robe exists. And if this method existed, there would be no such thing as something not being allowable in the case of damaged bowls. This meaning has already been stated. Therefore, the statement made in the Sāratthadīpanī, namely: ‘Whatever item, though relinquished for another person, is not given, if its receiving is abandoned by relinquishing it without concern for the receiving, that too is allowable on the second day,’ and so on, should not be trusted in its essence.

Pakatiāmiseti odanādikappiyayāvakālike. Dveti purebhattaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ yāmakālikaṃ purebhattaṃ sāmisena mukhena bhuñjato sannidhipaccayā ekaṃ, yāmakālikasaṃsaṭṭhatāya yāvakālikattabhajanena anatirittapaccayā [M 2.0034] ekanti dve pācittiyāni. Vikappadvayeti sāmisanirāmisapakkhadvaye. Thullaccayañca dukkaṭañcāti manussamaṃse thullaccayaṃ, sesesu dukkaṭaṃ. Yāvakālikayāmakālikatā, sannidhibhāvo, tassa ajjhoharaṇanti imānettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

As for ‘pakatiāmise’ (in the case of ordinary food-remains): this refers to an allowable yāvakālika item such as cooked rice. As for ‘dve’ (two): for one who, in the forenoon, eats a yāmakālika item received in the forenoon with a mouth containing food-remains, there is one pācittiya offense due to the factor of storing; and because it becomes a yāvakālika item by being mixed with a yāvakālika item, there is one pācittiya offense due to the factor of it not being leftover food. Thus, there are two pācittiya offenses. As for ‘vikappadvaye’ (in the two alternatives): this refers to the two cases of sāmisa (with food-remains) and nirāmisa (without food-remains). As for ‘thullaccayañca dukkaṭañca’ (both a thullaccaya and a dukkaṭa): for human flesh, there is a thullaccaya offense; for the remaining kinds of flesh, a dukkaṭa offense. Being a yāvakālika or yāmakālika item, the state of being stored, and the swallowing of it—these are the three factors herein.

Sannidhikārakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Storing is concluded.

9. Paṇītabhojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Choice Foods

259. Navame paṇītasaṃsaṭṭhāni bhojanāni paṇītabhojanānīti pāḷiyaṃ pana bhojanāni pubbe vuttattā pākaṭānīti adassitāni, tādisehi paṇītehi missattā paṇītabhojanāni nāma honti. Tesaṃ pabhedadassanatthaṃ “seyyathidaṃ sappi navanīta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Sappibhattanti ettha kiñcāpi [V 2.0033] sappinā saṃsaṭṭhaṃ bhattaṃ, sappi ca bhattañcātipi attho viññāyati, aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “sālibhattaṃ viya sappibhattaṃ nāma natthī”tiādinā vuttattā na sakkā aññaṃ vatthuṃ. Aṭṭhakathācariyā eva hi īdisesu ṭhānesu pamāṇaṃ.

259. In the ninth training rule, ‘paṇītabhojanāni’ is a compound meaning ‘foods mixed with delicacies’ (‘paṇītasaṃsaṭṭhāni bhojanāni’). However, in the Pāḷi text, because ‘foods’ (‘bhojanāni’) has been mentioned previously, it is clear, and thus not shown. They are called ‘choice foods’ (‘paṇītabhojanāni’) because they are mixed with such delicacies. In order to show their varieties, the passage beginning, “That is to say, ghee, fresh butter,” was spoken. Here, regarding ‘sappibhattaṃ’ (ghee-rice), although the meaning can be understood as ‘rice mixed with ghee’ or ‘ghee and rice,’ because it is stated in the Commentary, “There is no such thing as ‘ghee-rice’ in the way there is ‘fine rice’ (‘sālibhattaṃ’),” and so on, it is not possible to state another meaning. Indeed, the Commentary Masters are the authority in such matters.

Mūlanti kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ vuttaṃ. Tasmā anāpattīti ettha visaṅketena pācittiyābhāvepi sūpodanadukkaṭā na muccatīti vadanti. “Kappiyasappinā, akappiyasappinā”ti ca idaṃ kappiyākappiyamaṃsasattānaṃ vasena vuttaṃ.

‘Mūla’ is said to be allowable goods. Therefore, here in the phrase ‘no offense,’ although there is no pācittiya offense due to a mistake, they say one is not free from the dukkaṭa offense related to soup and rice. And this phrase, “With allowable ghee, with unallowable ghee,” is spoken with reference to beings whose flesh is allowable and unallowable.

261. Mahānāmasikkhāpadaṃ nāma upari cātumāsapaccayapavāraṇāsikkhāpadaṃ (pāci. 303 ādayo). Agilāno hi appavāritaṭṭhāne viññāpentopi kālaparicchedaṃ, bhesajjaparicchedaṃ vā katvā saṅghavasena pavāritaṭṭhānato taduttari viññāpentena, paricchedabbhantarepi na bhesajjakaraṇīyena rogena bhesajjaṃ viññāpentena ca samo hotīti “mahānāmasikkhāpadena kāretabbo”ti vuttaṃ. Paṇītabhojanatā, agilānatā, akataviññattiyā paṭilābho, ajjhoharaṇanti imānettha cattāri aṅgāni.

261. The training rule called the Mahānāma Sikkhāpada is the training rule concerning the four-month invitation for requisites, which appears later. Indeed, a monk who is not ill is the same as one who requests in a place where he has not been invited; or who, having set a limit on time or medicine, requests beyond that, having been invited by the Saṅgha; or who, even within the limit, requests medicine when there is no illness that requires medicine. Therefore, it is said, “He should be dealt with according to the Mahānāma Sikkhāpada.” The four factors here are: (1) its being a choice food, (2) the state of not being ill, (3) obtaining it through an improper request, and (4) consuming it.

Paṇītabhojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning choice foods is concluded.

10. Dantaponasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Tooth-Sticks

263. Dasame [M 2.0035] ghanabaddhoti ghanamaṃsena sambaddho, kathinasaṃhatasarīroti attho.

263. In the tenth training rule, ‘ghanabaddho’ means connected with dense flesh; the meaning is having a firm, compact body.

264. Mukhadvāranti mukhato heṭṭhā dvāraṃ mukhadvāraṃ, galanāḷikanti attho. Evañca nāsikāya paviṭṭhampi mukhadvāraṃ paviṭṭhameva hoti, mukhe pakkhittamattañca appaviṭṭhaṃ. Āhāranti ajjhoharitabbaṃ kālikaṃ adhippetaṃ, na udakaṃ. Tañhi bhesajjasaṅgahitampi akālikameva paṭiggahitasseva kālikattā. Udake hi paṭiggahaṇaṃ na ruhati. Teneva bhikkhunā tāpitena udakena cirapaṭiggahitena ca akappiyakuṭiyaṃ vutthena ca saha āmisaṃ bhuñjantassāpi sāmapākādidoso na hoti. Vakkhati hi “bhikkhu yāguatthāya…pe… udakaṃ tāpeti, vaṭṭatī”tiādi (pāci. aṭṭha. 265). Bhikkhū pana etaṃ adhippāyaṃ tadā na jāniṃsu. Tenāha “sammā atthaṃ asallakkhetvā”tiādi.

264. Mukhadvāra means the opening below the mouth; the meaning is the throat-passage. And so, even what has entered through the nose is considered to have entered the mouth-door, whereas what is merely placed in the mouth has not entered. By āhāra is intended a kālika item that is to be consumed, not water. For water, even if included among medicines, is timeless, because only what has been formally received is subject to time-limits. Indeed, formal reception does not apply to water. For that very reason, even for a monk who consumes solid food together with water that he has heated, or with water that was formally received long ago, or with water that has been stored in an improper dwelling, the offense of cooking for oneself, and so on, does not occur. For it will be said: “A monk heats water for the purpose of gruel… it is allowable,” and so on. However, the monks at that time did not know this intended meaning. Therefore, he said the passage beginning, “Not having properly marked the meaning…”

265. Rathareṇumpīti [V 2.0034] rathe gacchante uṭṭhahanareṇusadisareṇuṃ. Tena tato sukhumaṃ ākāse paribbhamanakaṃ dissamānampi abbohārikanti dasseti. Akallakoti gilāno.

265. ‘Even the dust of a chariot’ means dust similar to the dust raised when a chariot is moving. By this, it is shown that even dust more subtle than that, appearing to whirl in the sky, is not reckonable. Akallako means a sick monk.

“Gahetuṃ vā…pe… tassa orimantenā”ti iminā ākāse ujuṃ ṭhatvā parena ukkhittaṃ gaṇhantassāpi āsannaṅgabhūtapādatalato paṭṭhāya hatthapāso paricchinditabbo, na pana sīsantato paṭṭhāyāti dasseti. Tattha “orimantenā”ti imassa heṭṭhimantenāti attho gahetabbo.

By the passage beginning, “To take… from its near side,” it is shown that even for one who is standing upright in the air and taking something thrown up by another, the hand-reach should be delimited starting from the sole of the foot, which is the limb that has become the nearest, and not starting from the top of the head. There, the meaning of orimantena should be taken as heṭṭhimantena (from the lower edge).

Ettha ca pavāraṇāsikkhāpadaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “sace bhikkhu nisinno hoti, āsanassa pacchimantato paṭṭhāyā”tiādinā (pāci. aṭṭha. 238-239) paṭiggāhakānaṃ āsannaṅgassa pārimantato paṭṭhāya paricchedassa dassitattā idhāpi ākāse ṭhitassa paṭiggāhakassa āsannaṅgabhūtapādaṅgulassa pārimantabhūtato paṇhipariyantassa heṭṭhimatalato paṭṭhāya, dāyakassa pana orimantabhūtato pādaṅgulassa heṭṭhimatalato paṭṭhāya hatthapāso paricchinditabboti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Imināva nayena bhūmiyaṃ nipajjitvā ussīse nisinnassa hatthato paṭiggaṇhantassapi āsannasīsaṅgassa pārimantabhūtato gīvantato paṭṭhāyeva [M 2.0036] hatthapāso minitabbo, na pādatalato paṭṭhāya. Evaṃ nipajjitvā dānepi yathānurūpaṃ veditabbaṃ. “Yaṃ āsannataraṃ aṅga”nti hi vuttaṃ.

And here, because in the Commentary on the Pavāraṇā training rule it is shown that the delimitation for receivers begins from the far-side extremity of the nearest limb—as in the passage beginning, “If a monk is seated, starting from the back edge of the seat…”—so too here it should be understood that for a receiver standing in the air, the hand-reach should be delimited starting from the lower surface of the end of the heel, which is the far-side extremity; but for the giver, it should be delimited starting from the lower surface of the toe, which is the near-side extremity. By this same method, for one who is lying on the ground and receiving from the hand of a person sitting at his head-end, the hand-reach should be measured starting only from the neck, which is the far-side extremity of the nearest head-limb, not starting from the sole of the foot. Similarly, when giving while lying down, it should be understood as is appropriate. For it has been said: “Whichever limb is nearer.”

Paṭiggahaṇasaññāyāti “mañcādinā paṭiggahessāmī”ti uppāditasaññāya. Iminā “paṭiggaṇhāmī”ti vācāya vattabbakiccaṃ natthīti dasseti. Katthaci aṭṭhakathāsu, padesesu vā. Asaṃhārime phalaketi thāmamajjhimena purisena asaṃhāriye. Puñchitvā paṭiggahetvāti puñchitepi rajanacuṇṇasaṅkāya sati paṭiggahaṇatthāya vuttaṃ, nāsati. Taṃ panāti patitarajaṃ appaṭiggahetvā upari gahitapiṇḍapātaṃ. Anāpattīti durupaciṇṇādidoso natthi. “Anupasampannassa dassāmī”tiādipi vinayadukkaṭaparihārāya vuttaṃ. Tathā akatvā gahitepi paṭiggahetvā paribhuñjato anāpatti eva. “Anupasampannassa datvā”ti idampi purimābhogānuguṇatāya vuttaṃ.

‘By the perception of receiving’ means by the perception that has arisen with the thought, “I will receive it with a couch, etc.” This shows that there is no need to say verbally, “I receive.” In some commentaries or in some places: ‘On an immovable plank’ means on a plank that cannot be moved by a man of moderate strength. The phrase ‘having wiped and received’ is spoken for the sake of receiving when there is a suspicion of dye-powder even after wiping, but not when there is no such suspicion. ‘But that’ refers to almsfood taken from on top without having formally received the dust that has fallen on it. ‘No offense’ means there is no fault of misconduct (durupaciṇṇa) or the like. The phrase beginning, “I will give it to one who is not fully ordained,” is also spoken in order to avoid a dukkaṭa offense against the Vinaya. Even if one takes it without having formed such an intention, for one who formally receives and consumes it, there is no offense. This phrase, “having given it to one who is not fully ordained,” is also spoken in accordance with the prior intention.

Carukenāti khuddakabhājanena. Abhihaṭattāti diyyamānakkhaṇaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Datvā apanayanakāle pana chārikā vā bindūni vā patanti, puna paṭiggahetabbaṃ abhihārassa vigatattāti vadanti. Taṃ yathā na patati, tathā apanessāmīti pariharante yujjati. Pakatisaññāya apanente abhihāro na chijjati, taṃ paṭiggahitameva hoti. Mukhavaṭṭiyāpi gahetuṃ [V 2.0035] vaṭṭatīti abhihariyamānassa pattassa mukhavaṭṭiyā uparibhāge hatthaṃ pasāretvā phusituṃ vaṭṭati.

Carukena means with a small bowl. Abhihaṭattā is said with reference to the moment of giving. However, if ashes or drops fall at the time of taking it away after giving, some say it should be received again because the act of bringing forward has ceased. That statement is appropriate when one handles it with the thought, ‘I will take it away in such a way that it does not fall.’ When one takes it away with normal perception, the act of bringing forward is not interrupted; it remains as having been received. ‘It is permissible to take it even by the rim’ means that of a bowl that is being brought forward, it is permissible to extend a hand over the upper part of its rim and touch it.

Pādena pelletvāti “pādena paṭiggahessāmī”tisaññāya akkamitvā. Kecīti abhayagirivāsino. Vacanamattamevāti paṭibaddhappaṭibaddhanti saddamattameva nānaṃ, kāyapaṭibaddhameva hoti. Tasmā tesaṃ vacanaṃ na gahetabbanti adhippāyo.

Pādena pelletvā means having stepped on it with the perception, ‘I will receive it with the foot.’ Keci means the residents of Abhayagiri. Vacanamattameva means that the term paṭibaddha-paṭibaddha is merely a different sound; it is in fact kāyapaṭibaddha (connected to the body). Therefore, their words should not be accepted—this is the intended meaning.

Tena āharāpetunti yassa bhikkhuno santikaṃ gataṃ, taṃ idha ānehīti āṇāpetvā tena āharāpetuṃ itarassa vaṭṭatīti attho. Na tato paranti tadaheva sāmaṃ appaṭiggahitaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tadaheva paṭiggahitaṃ pana punadivasādīsu appaṭiggahetvāpi paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭatīti vadanti.

Tena āharāpetuṃ means: concerning an item that has gone to a certain bhikkhu, it is permissible for the other bhikkhu to have it brought by that first bhikkhu, having commanded him, ‘Bring that here.’ This is the meaning. Na tato paraṃ is said with reference to something not received by oneself on that very day. However, regarding something that was received on that very day, some say it is permissible to consume it on subsequent days and so on, even without receiving it again.

Khiyyantīti khayaṃ gacchanti, tesaṃ cuṇṇehi thullaccayaappaṭiggahaṇāpattiyo na hontīti adhippāyo. “Navasamuṭṭhita”nti eteneva ucchuādīsu [M 2.0037] abhinavalaggattā abbohārikaṃ na hotīti dasseti. Eseva nayoti sannidhidosādiṃ sandhāya vadati. Tenāha “na hī”tiādi. Tena ca paṭiggahaṇaṅgesu pañcasupi samiddhesu ajjhoharitukāmatāya gahitameva paṭiggahitaṃ nāma hoti ajjhoharitabbesu eva paṭiggahaṇassa anuññātattāti dasseti. Tathā bāhiraparibhogatthāya gahetvā ṭhapitatelādiṃ ajjhoharitukāmatāya sati paṭiggahetvā paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati.

Khiyyanti means they go to destruction. The intended meaning is that due to their powders, offenses of thullaccaya and the pācittiya for not receiving do not occur. By this very term navasamuṭṭhita, it is shown that in the case of sugarcane and so on, because it is newly attached, it is not abbohārika (not reckonable). Eseva nayo (this is the principle): he speaks with reference to the fault of storing (sannidhi), and so on. Therefore, he said, na hi, etc. And by that, it is shown that even when the five factors of receiving are complete, only that which is taken with the desire to swallow is called ‘received,’ because receiving is permitted only for things that are to be swallowed. Similarly, regarding oil, etc., taken and set aside for external use, if there is a desire to swallow it, it is permissible to receive it and consume it.

Kesañcītiādīsu anupasampannānaṃ atthāya katthaci ṭhapiyamānampi hatthato muttamatte eva paṭiggahaṇaṃ na vijahati, atha kho bhājane patitameva paṭiggahaṇaṃ vijahati. Bhājanañca bhikkhunā punadivasatthāya apekkhitamevāti taggatampi āmisaṃ duddhotapattagataṃ viya paṭiggahaṇaṃ na vijahatīti āsaṅkāya “sāmaṇerassa hatthe pakkhipitabba”nti vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Īdisesu hi yutti na gavesitabbā, vuttanayeneva paṭipajjitabbaṃ. “Pattagatā yāgū”ti iminā pattamukhavaṭṭiyā phuṭṭhepi kūṭe yāgu paṭiggahitā, uggahitā vā na hoti bhikkhuno anicchāya phuṭṭhattāti dasseti. Āropetīti hatthaṃ phusāpeti. Paṭiggahaṇūpagaṃ bhāraṃ nāma majjhimassa purisassa ukkhepārahaṃ. Na pidahitabbanti hatthato muttaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, hatthagataṃ pana itarena hatthena pidahato, hatthato muttampi vā aphusitvā uparipidhānaṃ pātentassa na doso.

In 'kesañci,' etc.: even when something is being placed somewhere for the sake of the unordained, the state of having been received is not relinquished merely upon being released from the hand; rather, it is relinquished only when it has fallen into a vessel. And because the vessel is one that the bhikkhu has regard for, for the next day's use, due to the concern that the food in it, like food in an improperly washed bowl, does not relinquish its received state, it should be understood that it was said, 'It should be placed in the novice's hand.' Indeed, in such cases, reasoning should not be sought; one should practice only according to the stated method. By 'pattagatā yāgū,' it is shown that even when the pot touches the rim of the bowl, the gruel is neither received nor is its received state broken, because it was touched without the bhikkhu's intention. 'Āropeti' means he causes the hand to touch. A 'load suitable for receiving' is what a man of average strength is able to lift. 'Na pidahitabbaṃ' is said with reference to what has been released from the hand. However, there is no fault for one who covers what is in his hand with the other hand, or for one who drops a lid from above without touching the pot, even when it has been released from the hand.

Paṭiggaṇhātīti [V 2.0036] chāyatthāya upari dhārayamānā mahāsākhā yena kenaci chijjeyya, tattha laggarajaṃ mukhe pāteyya cāti kappiyaṃ kārāpetvā paṭiggaṇhāti. Kuṇḍaketi mahāghaṭe. Tasmimpīti cāṭighaṭepi. Gāhāpetvāti appaṭiggahitaṃ kālikaṃ gāhāpetvā.

'Paṭiggaṇhāti': A large branch being held overhead for the sake of shade might break for some reason, and the dust clinging to it might fall into the mouth; therefore, having had it made allowable, he receives it. 'Kuṇḍake' means in a large pot. 'Tasmimpi' means even in a large pot or jar. 'Gāhāpetvā' means having had an unreceived temporal item taken.

Dutiyattherassāti “therassa pattaṃ mayhaṃ dethā”ti tena attano pariccajāpetvā dutiyattherassa deti. Ettha panāti pattaparivattane. Kāraṇanti ettha yathā “sāmaṇerā ito amhākampi dentī”ti vitakko uppajjati, na tathāti kāraṇaṃ vadanti, tañca yuttaṃ. Yassa pana tādiso vitakko natthi, tena aparivattetvāpi bhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati.

'Dutiyattherassa': Having made that elder relinquish his bowl to oneself by saying, 'Give the elder's bowl to me,' he gives it to the second elder. 'Ettha pana' refers to the exchange of bowls. Regarding 'kāraṇaṃ': they state the reason that just as the thought, 'The novices give to us also from this,' arises, it is not so here, and that is proper. But for one for whom such a thought does not exist, it is permissible to consume it even without exchanging.

Niccāletunti [M 2.0038] cāletvā pāsāṇasakkharādiapanayaṃ kātuṃ. Uddhanaṃ āropetabbanti anaggikaṃ uddhanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Uddhane paccamānassa āluḷane upari apakkataṇḍulā heṭṭhā pavisitvā paccatīti āha “sāmaṃpākañceva hotī”ti.

'Niccāletuṃ' means to shake in order to remove stones, gravel, and so on. 'Uddhanaṃ āropetabbaṃ' is said with reference to a hearth without fire. When what is being cooked on the hearth is stirred, the uncooked rice grains on top go underneath and are cooked; therefore, it was said, 'It becomes evenly cooked.'

Ādhārake patto ṭhapitoti appaṭiggahitāmiso patto puna paṭiggahaṇatthāya ṭhapito. Ekaggahaṇenevāti sāmaṇerānaṃ gahitassa puna acchaḍḍanavasena gahaṇena. Bhuñjituṃ vaṭṭatīti dhūmavaṭṭiyā tadahupaṭiggahitattā vuttaṃ. Bhattuggārotiādi abbohārikappasaṅgena vikālabhojanavinicchayadassanaṃ. Samuddodakenāti appaṭiggahitena. Himakarakā nāma kadāci vassodakena saha patanakā pāsāṇalekhā viya ghanībhūtaudakavisesā, tesu paṭiggahaṇakiccaṃ natthi. Tenāha “udakagatikā evā”ti. Purebhattameva vaṭṭatīti appaṭiggahitāpattīhi abbohārikampi vikālabhojanāpattīhi sabbohārikanti dasseti.

'Ādhārake patto ṭhapito' means a bowl with unreceived food is placed for the purpose of receiving it again. 'Ekaggahaṇeneva' means by the act of receiving of the novices, which is a receiving again without having discarded what was taken. 'Bhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati' is said because the smoke-stick was received on that day. 'Bhattuggāro,' etc., is the showing of the decision on untimely eating in connection with what is non-reckonable. 'Samuddodakena' means with unreceived sea water. 'Himakarakā' are a special kind of solidified water, like streaks on stone, that sometimes fall together with rain; for them, there is no duty of receiving. Therefore, he said, 'They are just included under water.' By 'purebhattameva vaṭṭati,' it is shown that although it is non-reckonable regarding the offenses for not receiving, it is reckonable regarding the offenses for untimely eating.

Laggatīti mukhe ca hatthe ca mattikāvaṇṇaṃ dasseti. Bahalanti hatthamukhesu alagganakampi paṭiggahetabbaṃ. Vāsamattanti reṇukhīrābhāvaṃ dasseti. Ākirati paṭiggahetabbanti puppharasassa paññāyanato vuttaṃ.

By 'laggati,' it shows the appearance of the color of clay on the mouth and hand. 'Bahalaṃ' means that even what does not stick to the hands and mouth should be received. By 'vāsamattaṃ,' it shows the absence of pollen and nectar. The statement 'ākirati paṭiggahetabbaṃ' was said because the flower juice is apparent.

Mahābhūtesūti pāṇasarīrasannissitesu pathavīādimahābhūtesu. Sabbaṃ vaṭṭatīti attano, paresañca sarīranissitaṃ sabbaṃ vaṭṭati. Akappiyamaṃsānulomatāya thullaccayādiṃ na janetīti adhippāyo. Patatīti attano sarīrato vicchinditvā patati. “Rukkhato chinditvā”ti vuttattā mattikatthāya pathaviṃ khaṇituṃ, aññampi yaṃkiñci mūlapaṇṇādivisabhesajjaṃ chinditvā chārikaṃ [V 2.0037] akatvāpi appaṭiggahitampi paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Appaṭiggahitatā, ananuññātatā, dhūmādiabbohārikatābhāvo, ajjhoharaṇanti imānettha cattāri aṅgāni.

'In the great elements' (mahābhūtesu): in the great elements such as earth, which are dependent on the bodies of living beings. 'Everything is permissible' (sabbaṃ vaṭṭati): everything dependent on one's own or others' bodies, such as tears and saliva, is permissible. The meaning is that it does not give rise to a thullaccaya offense or the like, by way of being in conformity with what is unallowable meat. 'It falls' (patati): it falls, having been severed from one's own body. Because it is said, 'having cut it from a tree,' it should be understood that it is permissible to dig the earth for clay, and to cut any other medicinal substance such as roots, leaves, etc., and consume it even without making it into ash and even if it has not been formally received. The state of not having been formally received, the state of not being a permitted item, the absence of the state of being non-consumable such as smoke, and the act of swallowing—these are the four factors here.

Dantaponasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning water and tooth-sticks is concluded.

Niṭṭhito bhojanavaggo catuttho.

The Bhojanavagga, the fourth chapter, is concluded.

5. Acelakavaggo

5. The Acelaka Chapter

1. Acelakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning a Naked Ascetic

273. Pañcamavaggassa [M 2.0039] paṭhame mayhaṃ nāmāti bhikkhunā bhūmiyaṃ ṭhapetvā dinnampi sandhāya vadati. Aññatitthiyatā, ananuññātatā, ajjhoharaṇīyatā, ajjhoharaṇatthāya sahatthā anikkhittabhājane dānanti imānettha cattāri aṅgāni.

273. In the first training rule of the fifth chapter, the phrase 'for me' (mayhaṃ nāma) is spoken in reference to food that has also been given by a bhikkhu after placing it on the ground. The state of being an adherent of another sect, the state of not being permitted, the state of being a food that can be swallowed, and the act of giving with one's own hand into a vessel that has not been set down for the purpose of swallowing—these are the four factors here.

Acelakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Acelaka training rule is concluded.

2. Uyyojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Dismissal

274. Dutiye anācāraṃ ācaritukāmatā, tadatthameva upasampannassa uyyojanā, tassa upacārātikkamoti imānettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

274. In the second training rule, these are the three factors here: the desire to practice improper conduct, the dismissal of an ordained person for that very purpose, and the transgression of the boundary by that person.

Uyyojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning dismissal is concluded.

3. Sabhojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning a Family Meal

281. Tatiye pāḷiyaṃ khuddake ghareti ettha khuddakaṃ gharaṃ nāma pañcahatthato ūnakavitthāraṃ adhippetaṃ. Tattha ca piṭṭhasaṅghāṭato hatthapāse avijahitepi piṭṭhivaṃsātikkamo hotīti āha “piṭṭhivaṃsaṃ atikkamitvā”ti. Yathā tathā vā katassāti piṭṭhivaṃsaṃ āropetvā vā anāropetvā vā katassa.

281. In the third training rule, regarding the phrase 'in a small house' (khuddake ghare) in the Pāli text, a 'small house' is intended to mean one with a width of less than five cubits. And there, even if one has not left the vicinity of a hand's reach from the door-panel, there is the transgression of the ridge-pole; thus, it is said, 'having transgressed the ridge-pole.' As for 'of one made in whatever way,' it means of a house made either with a ridge-pole placed on it or without a ridge-pole placed on it.

283. Pāḷiyaṃ [V 2.0038] vītarāgāti apariyuṭṭhitarāgānaṃ, anāgāmīnañca saṅgaho. Sacittakanti anupavisitvā nisīdanacittena sacittakaṃ. Pariyuṭṭhitarāgajāyampatikānaṃ sannihitatā, sayanigharatā, dutiyassa bhikkhuno abhāvo, anupakhajja nisīdananti imānettha cattāri aṅgāni.

283. In the Pāli text, 'free from lust' (vītarāgā) is an inclusion of those whose lust is not aroused and also of non-returners. As for 'with intention' (sacittakaṃ), it is 'with intention' by the thought of sitting down after having approached. The presence of a husband and wife whose lust is aroused, the state of it being a bedroom, the absence of a second bhikkhu, and sitting close together—these are the four factors here.

Sabhojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning a family meal is concluded.

284-289. Catutthapañcamāni vuttatthāni.

The fourth and fifth training rules have their meanings already stated.

6. Cārittasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Training Rule on Conduct

298. Chaṭṭhe [M 2.0040] “pariyesitvā ārocanakiccaṃ nāma natthī”ti vuttattā yo apariyesitabbo upasaṅkamituṃ yuttaṭṭhāne dissati, so sacepi pakativacanassa savanūpacāraṃ atikkamma ṭhito upagantvā āpucchitabbo. Tenāha “api ca…pe… yaṃ passati, so āpucchitabbo”tiādi.

298. In the sixth training rule, because it is said, “There is no duty of informing after searching,” a bhikkhu who is not to be sought out, if he is seen in a suitable place to approach, should be approached and asked permission, even if he is standing beyond the range of hearing of normal speech. Therefore, it is said, “Moreover…pe… Whomever one sees, he should be asked permission,” and so on.

302. Anāpattivāre cettha antarārāmādīnaññeva vuttattā vihārato gāmavīthiṃ anuññātakāraṇaṃ vinā atikkamantassāpi āpatti hoti, na pana gharūpacāraṃ atikkamantasseva.

302. Here, in the section on non-offenses, because only monasteries within a village and so on are mentioned, an offense is incurred even by a bhikkhu who crosses from the monastery to the village street without a permitted reason; it is not that an offense is incurred only by one who crosses the precincts of a house.

Yaṃ pana pāḷiyaṃ “aññassa gharūpacāraṃ okkamantassa…pe… paṭhamaṃ pādaṃ ummāraṃ atikkāmetī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Taṃ gāme paviṭṭhaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, tathāpi aññassa gharūpacāraṃ anokkamitvā vīthimajjheneva gantvā icchiticchitagharadvārābhimukhe ṭhatvā manusse oloketvā gacchantassāpi pācittiyameva. Tattha keci “vīthiyaṃ atikkamantassa gharūpacāragaṇanāya āpattiyo”ti vadanti. Aññe pana “yāni kulāni uddissa gato, tesaṃ gaṇanāyā”ti. Pañcannaṃ bhojanānaṃ aññatarena nimantanasādiyanaṃ, santaṃ bhikkhuṃ anāpucchanā, bhattiyagharato aññagharūpasaṅkamanaṃ, majjhanhikānatikkamo, samayāpadānaṃ abhāvoti imānettha pañca aṅgāni.

As for what is stated in the Pāḷi, “When one enters another’s house-precincts…pe… one makes the first foot cross the threshold,” etc., that is said in reference to a house established in a village. Even so, for a bhikkhu who, without entering another’s house-precincts, goes only along the middle of the street, stands facing the door of a desired house, and proceeds while looking at people, it is indeed a pācittiya offense. Regarding this, some teachers say: “For a bhikkhu who transgresses on the street, there are pācittiya offenses according to the count of house-precincts.” But other teachers say: “The offenses occur according to the count of those families for which one has gone.” The five factors here are: (1) delighting in an invitation with one of the five kinds of food, (2) not asking permission from a present bhikkhu, (3) approaching another house from the house of the meal invitation, (4) the time being before midday, and (5) the absence of a special occasion or danger.

Cārittasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule on conduct is concluded.

7. Mahānāmasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Mahānāma Training Rule

303. Sattame [V 2.0039] mahānāmoti sukkodanassa putto anuruddhattherassa, satthu ca jeṭṭhabhātā. Ānandatthero amitodanassa putto, nandatthero pana suddhodanasseva.

303. In the seventh training rule, Mahānāma is the son of Sukkodana, and the elder brother of both the Elder Anuruddha and the Teacher. The Elder Ānanda is the son of Amitodana, while the Elder Nanda is the son of Suddhodana himself.

305. Pāḷiyaṃ kālaṃ āharissathāti ajjatanaṃ kālaṃ vītināmessatha, sve bhesajjaṃ harissathāti vā attho. “Atthi pavāraṇā bhesajjapariyantā ca rattipariyantā cā”ti tatiyakoṭṭhāse niyamitameva bhesajjaṃ niyamitakālantareyeva gahetabbaṃ, na tato bahi. Itarathā [M 2.0041] visuṃ payojanaṃ natthīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sapariyantā saṅghapavāraṇā, taduttari bhesajjaviññatti, agilānatāti imānettha tīṇi aṅgāni.

305. In the Pāḷi, the phrase ‘kālaṃ āharissatha’ means ‘you will let today’s time pass,’ or ‘you will bring medicine tomorrow’; this is the meaning. In the third section, which says, “There is an invitation limited by medicine and limited by night,” a specified medicine should be taken only within a specified period of time, not outside of it. It should be understood that if the meaning is taken otherwise, there is no separate purpose. The three factors here are: (1) an invitation to the Saṅgha that has a limit, (2) requesting medicine beyond that limit, and (3) not being ill.

Mahānāmasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Mahānāma training rule is concluded.

8. Uyyuttasenāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning a Deployed Army

315. Aṭṭhame ekamekanti ettha duvaṅginīpi tivaṅginīpi senā saṅgayhati. Uyyuttacaturaṅgasenādassanāya tathārūpapaccayādiṃ vinā gamanaṃ, ananuññātokāse dassananti imānettha dve aṅgāni.

315. In the eighth training rule, in the phrase `ekamekaṃ`, an army of two components and an army of three components are included. The two factors here are: (1) going to see a deployed four-component army without a suitable reason, and (2) viewing it in an unpermitted place.

Uyyuttasenāsikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning a deployed army is concluded.

9. Senāvāsasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Staying with an Army

319. Navame senāya catuttho sūriyatthaṅgamo, agilānatāti imānettha dve aṅgāni.

319. In the ninth training rule, the two factors are: (1) the fourth sunset while with the army, and (2) not being ill.

Senāvāsasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning staying with an army is concluded.

10. Uyyodhikasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning a Mock Battle

322. Dasame pāḷiyaṃ kati te lakkhāni laddhānīti kittakā tayā laddhāti attho. Uyyodhikādidassanāya [V 2.0040] tathārūpapaccayaṃ vinā gamanaṃ, ananuññātokāse dassananti imānettha dve aṅgāni.

322. In the tenth training rule, in the Pāḷi, the phrase `kati te lakkhāni laddhāni` means: ‘How many targets were hit by you?’ The two factors here are: (1) going to see a mock battle and so forth without a suitable reason, and (2) viewing it in an unpermitted place.

Uyyodhikasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning a mock battle is concluded.

Niṭṭhito acelakavaggo pañcamo.

The fifth chapter, the Acelakavagga, is concluded.

6. Surāpānavaggo

6. The Surāpāna Chapter

1. Surāpānasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Drinking Intoxicants

328. Chaṭṭhavaggassa [M 2.0042] paṭhame pāḷiyaṃ kiṇṇapakkhittāti piṭṭhapūvādiṃ apakkhipitvā kiṇṇasaṅkhātaṃ dhaññaṅkurādisurābījaṃ pakkhipitvā katā. Sambhārasaṃyuttāti sāsapādianekasambhārehi saññuttā.

328. In the first training rule of the sixth chapter, in the Pāḷi, `kiṇṇapakkhittā` refers to an intoxicant made by adding the seed of intoxicants, such as grain sprouts, known as `kiṇṇa` (leaven), without adding flour, cakes, or the like. `Sambhārasaṃyuttā` refers to an intoxicant combined with many ingredients such as mustard and so on.

Madhukatālanāḷikerādipupphādiraso ciraparivāsito pupphāsavo nāma. Tathā panasādi phalāsavo. Muddikaraso madhvāsavo. Ucchuraso guḷāsavo. Tiphalatikaṭukādinānāsambhārānaṃ raso ciraparivāsito sambhārasaṃyutto. Bījato paṭṭhāyāti yathāvuttānaṃ piṭṭhādīnaṃ majjatthāya bhājane pakkhittakālato paṭṭhāya.

The juice of flowers such as madhuka, palmyra, and coconut, having been steeped for a long time, is called `pupphāsava` (flower liquor). Similarly, from fruits such as jackfruit, there is `phalāsava` (fruit liquor). Grape juice is `madhvāsavo` (grape liquor). Sugarcane juice is `guḷāsavo` (molasses liquor). The juice of various ingredients such as triphala, trikaṭuka, and so on, having been steeped for a long time, is `sambhārasaṃyutta` (liquor from mixed ingredients). The phrase `bījato paṭṭhāya` means: starting from the time that the aforementioned flour and so on are placed in a vessel for the purpose of making an intoxicant.

329. Loṇasovīrakaṃ suttañca anekehi dabbasambhārehi abhisaṅkhato bhesajjaviseso. Uyyuttasikkhāpadānaṃ acittakalokavajjesu lokavajjatā pubbe vuttanayāvāti tattha kiñcipi avatvā idha tehi asādhāraṇavatthuvisesasiddhāya acittakapakkhepi akusalacittatāya taṃ lokavajjatādivisesaṃ dassetumeva “vatthuajānanatāya cetthā”tiādinā vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ paṭhamapārājikavaṇṇanāyaṃ vitthārato sāratthadīpaniyaṃ viraddhaṭṭhānavisodhanavasena vuttanti tattheva gahetabbaṃ. Majjabhāvo, tassa pānañcāti imānettha dve aṅgāni.

329. `Loṇasovīraka` and `sutta` are a special kind of medicine prepared with many material ingredients. Since the worldly blameworthiness of the `Uyyutta` training rules, in cases of mindless worldly faults, is in the manner previously stated, nothing is said about them in that context. It should be understood that here, in this training rule, the passage beginning `vatthuajānanatāya cettha` was stated only to show the special quality of worldly blameworthiness, etc., which is established by the special case not shared with those rules and by the presence of an unwholesome mind even in the mindless aspect. Whatever should be said on this matter has been stated in detail in the commentary on the first Pārājika, in the Sāratthadīpanī, by way of clarifying contradictory points; therefore, it should be taken from there. The two factors here are: (1) the substance being an intoxicant, and (2) the act of drinking it.

Surāpānasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule concerning drinking intoxicants is concluded.

2. Aṅgulipatodakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Training Rule on Tickling

330. Dutiye [V 2.0041] hasādhippāyatā, upasampannassa kāyena kāyāmasananti imānettha dve aṅgāni.

330. In the second training rule, the two factors are: (1) the intention to jest, and (2) touching the body of an ordained person with one's own body.

Aṅgulipatodakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the training rule on tickling is concluded.

3. Hasadhammasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Training Rule on Playing in the Water

338. Tatiye [M 2.0043] pāḷiyaṃ hasadhamme hasadhammasaññītiādīsu uplavādimattaṃ kiṃ hasadhammo hotīti gahaṇavasena sati karaṇīye kariyamānaṃ hasadhammaṃ hasadhammoti gahaṇavasena attho veditabbo. Ussārentoti udake ṭhitaṃ nāvaṃ tīre āropento.

338. In the third training rule, in the Pāḷi, in phrases such as `hasadhamme hasadhammasaññī`, the meaning should be understood by way of taking it as, 'How is the mere act of diving and surfacing playful conduct?'; and also by way of taking it that when there is a task to be done, the act of diving and surfacing being performed is considered 'playful conduct'. As for `ussārento`, it means one who is bringing a boat that is in the water onto the shore.

Patanuppatanavāresūti udakassa uparitale maṇḍūkagatiyā patanuppatanavasena gamanatthaṃ khittāya ekissā kathalāya vasena vuttaṃ. Udakassa uparigopphakatā, hasādhippāyena kīḷananti dve aṅgāni.

As for `patanuppatanavāresu`: this is said with reference to a single potsherd thrown for the purpose of moving on the surface of the water by way of falling and rising, like the movement of a frog. The water being above the ankle, and playing with the intention to jest—these two are the factors here.

Hasadhammasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on playful conduct is concluded.

4. Anādariyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

4. Explanation of the Training Rule on Disrespect

344. Catutthe suttānulomanti mahāpadesā. Aṭṭhakathātipi vadanti. Upasampannassa paññattena vacanaṃ, anādariyakaraṇanti dve aṅgāni.

344. In the fourth [training rule], as for `suttānuloma`, it means the great references. They also call them the commentaries. A statement to an ordained person concerning what is prescribed, and the act of showing disrespect—these two are the factors here.

Anādariyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on disrespect is concluded.

5. Bhiṃsāpanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

5. Explanation of the Training Rule on Frightening

345. Pañcame upasampannatā, tassa dassanasavanavisaye bhiṃsāpetukāmatāya vāyamananti dve aṅgāni.

345. In the fifth [training rule]: the state of the other being an ordained person, and making an effort with the desire to frighten that person within the range of sight and hearing—these two are the factors.

Bhiṃsāpanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on frightening is concluded.

6. Jotisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

6. Explanation of the Training Rule on Fire

354. Chaṭṭhe [V 2.0042] alātaṃ patitanti aggikapālato bahi patitaṃ. Vijjhātanti vijjhātaṃ alātaṃ kapālaggimhi pakkhipitvā jālentassa pācittiyaṃ, tathā kevalaṃ indhanaṃ pātentassapi vijjhātaṃ kapālaggiṃ mukhavātādinā ujjālentassapi. Gilānatādikāraṇābhāvo, visibbetukāmatā, samādahananti tīṇi aṅgāni.

354. In the sixth [training rule], as for `alātaṃ patitaṃ`, it means a firebrand fallen outside from the mass of fire. As for `vijjhātaṃ`: for a monk who places an extinguished firebrand in a fire-pot and kindles it, there is a pācittiya offense; similarly, for one who merely drops fuel in, and for one who causes an extinguished fire in a pot to blaze with mouth-wind and so forth. The absence of a reason such as being ill, the desire to warm oneself or bake something, and the act of kindling—these three are the factors.

Jotisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the training rule on fire is concluded.

7. Nahānasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

7. Explanation of the Training Rule on Bathing

357. Sattame [M 2.0044] pāḷiyaṃ nagare thakiteti ettha raññā ciraṃ nahāyitukāmena “ahaṃ bahi uyyāne katārakkho vasissāmi, nagaraṃ thaketvā gopethā”ti anuññātā, te thakiṃsūti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Asambhinnenāti anaṭṭhena, taṃ divasaṃ puna aggahitālaṅkārena pabuddhamattenāti adhippāyo. Majjhimadese ūnakaddhamāsanahānaṃ, samayādīnaṃ abhāvoti dve aṅgāni.

357. In the seventh [training rule], in the Pāḷi, regarding the phrase `nagare thakite`, it should be understood thus: when permission was given by the king, who wished to bathe for a long time, saying, “I will dwell outside in the guarded park; close the city and protect it,” they closed it. As for `asambhinnena`: it means with unbroken fragrant paste; the intention is that on that day, just upon waking, one has not yet taken up adornment.
