Pāḷiyaṃ “ehi bhikkhunīti bhikkhunī, tīhi saraṇagamanehi upasampannāti bhikkhunī”ti idaṃ bhikkhuvibhaṅgapāḷiyā samadassanatthaṃ aṭṭhagarudhammappaṭiggahaṇena laddhūpasampadaṃ mahāpajāpatigotamiñceva tāya saha nikkhantā bhagavato āṇāya bhikkhūnaññeva santike ekatoupasampannā pañcasatasākiyāniyo ca sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tā hi bhagavatā ānandattherassa yācanāya pabbajjaṃ anujānantena “etha bhikkhuniyo, mama sāsane tumhepi pavisathā”ti vuttā viya jātā. Sākiyāniyo eva saraṇasīlāni datvā kammavācāya upasampāditattā “tīhi saraṇagamanehi upasampannā”ti vuttā. Na hi etāhi aññā ehibhikkhunibhāvādinā upasampannā nāma santi. Yaṃ pana therīgāthāsu bhaddāya kuṇḍalakesiyā –

1. In the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga, `migāramātuyā` means of Visākhā, whom the wealthy Migāra placed in the position of a mother; this is the meaning. In the Pāli, this statement, “a bhikkhunī is one ordained by the words ‘Come, bhikkhunī’; a bhikkhunī is one ordained by the three refuges,” was said in reference to Mahāpajāpati Gotamī, who had obtained ordination by accepting the eight weighty rules, and the five hundred Sakyan women who went forth together with her and were ordained together in the presence of only the bhikkhus by the command of the Blessed One, in order to show conformity with the Bhikkhuvibhaṅga Pāli. Indeed, they became as if they were told by the Blessed One, when he permitted the going forth at the request of the Elder Ānanda, “Come, bhikkhunīs, you too enter my dispensation.” Because the Sakyan women themselves were ordained by means of a formal act after being given the refuges and precepts, they were called “ordained by the three refuges.” Indeed, apart from these, there are no others named as having been ordained by the state of ‘ehi bhikkhunī’ and so on. However, that which is in the Therīgāthā, concerning Bhaddā Kuṇḍalakesī—

“Nihacca [V 2.0065] jāṇuṃ vanditvā, sammukhā añjaliṃ akaṃ;

‘Ehi bhadde’ti maṃ avoca, sā me āsūpasampadā”ti. (therīgā. 109) –

656. “Having placed down my knee and paid homage, I made the gesture of reverence in his presence. ‘Come, Bhaddā,’ he said to me; that was my ordination.”

Vuttaṃ. Yañca apadānepi –

It was said. And that which was said in the Apadāna also—

“Āyācito tadā āha, ‘ehi bhadde’ti nāyako;

Tadāhaṃ upasampannā, parittaṃ toyamaddasa”nti. (apa. therī 2.3.44) –

“Then the Leader, having been requested, said, ‘Come, Bhaddā’; at that time I was ordained and saw a small amount of water.”

Vuttaṃ. Tampi “ehi tvaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ santike pabbajjaṃ, upasampadañca gaṇhāhī”ti bhagavato āṇā upasampadāya kāraṇattā upasampadā ahosīti imamatthaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tathā hi vuttaṃ therīgāthāṭṭhakathāyaṃ “ehi bhadde, bhikkhunupassayaṃ [M 2.0068] gantvā bhikkhunīnaṃ santike pabbajja upasampajjassūti maṃ avaca āṇāpesi, sā satthu āṇā mayhaṃ upasampadāya kāraṇattā upasampadā āsi ahosī”ti (therīgā. aṭṭha. 111).

That statement also was said in reference to this meaning: the Blessed One’s command, “Come, you, take the going forth and the ordination in the presence of the bhikkhunīs,” was the ordination because it was the cause of the ordination. For thus it is said in the Therīgāthā Commentary: “He spoke to me and commanded, ‘Come, Bhaddā, having gone to the bhikkhunīs’ residence, go forth and receive ordination in the presence of the bhikkhunīs.’ That command of the Teacher, because it was the cause of my ordination, was my ordination.”

657. Sādhāraṇapārājikehīti methunādīhi catūhi. Tāni, pana aññāni ca sādhāraṇasikkhāpadāni yasmā bhikkhuvibhaṅge vuttanidānavatthādīsu eva sādhāraṇavasena paññattāni, pacchā pana tāni bhikkhunīnaṃ pātimokkhuddesaṃ anujānantena bhagavatā tāsaṃ sikkhāpaccakkhānābhāvena “yā pana bhikkhunī chandaso methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭiseveyyā”tiādinā tadanurūpavasena parivattetvā asādhāraṇasikkhāpadehi saddhiṃ saṃsandetvā bhikkhunipātimokkhuddesavasena ekato saṅgahitāni. Yasmā ca nesaṃ bhikkhuvibhaṅge (pārā. 44 ādayo) vuttanayeneva sabbopi vinicchayo sakkā ñātuṃ, tasmā tāni vajjetvā asādhāraṇānaṃ eva idha vibhaṅgo vuttoti veditabbaṃ.

657. By `sādhāraṇapārājikehi` is meant the four offenses beginning with sexual intercourse. Since those and other common training rules were laid down by way of being common only in the stated origins, stories, and so on in the Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga, but later, when the Blessed One permitted the recitation of the Pātimokkha for the bhikkhunīs, because there was no renunciation of the training for them, those rules were adapted in a corresponding manner with, “Whatever bhikkhunī should by choice engage in the act of sexual intercourse…” and so on, and having been connected with the non-common training rules, they were included together by way of the recitation of the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha. And since their entire analysis can be known by the very method stated in the Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga, therefore it should be understood that, having excluded those, the analysis of only the non-common rules is stated here.

659. Bhikkhūnaṃ “kāyasaṃsaggaṃ sādiyeyyā”ti avatvā “samāpajjeyyā”ti vuttattā “bhikkhu āpattiyā na kāretabbo”ti vuttaṃ. Tabbahulanayenāti kiriyāsamuṭṭhānasseva bahulabhāvato, etena akiriyāsamuṭṭhānāpi ayaṃ āpatti hotīti dasseti. Kiñcāpi dasseti, mayaṃ panettha evaṃ takkayāma “kāyasaṃsaggakkhaṇe sādiyantiyā kiriyāya abhāvepi tato pubbe pavattitānaṃ paṭicchannaṭṭhānagamanaiṅgitākāradassanādikiriyānaṃ vaseneva kiriyāsamauṭṭhānameva, parehi magge kariyamānupakkamena niccalassa sādiyato sukkavissaṭṭhi viya pubbapayogābhāvepi [V 2.0066] vā tasmiññeva khaṇe parūpakkamena janiyamānāya attano kāyacalanādisaṅkhātāya kiriyāya, sā hi sādiyamānena tassā cittenāpi samuṭṭhitā kiriyā nāma hoti avāyamitvā parūpakkamena methunasādiyane viya, bhikkhūnaṃ pana parūpakkamajanitaṃ kiriyaṃ abbohārikaṃ katvā attanā kariyamānapayogavaseneva ‘kāyasaṃsaggaṃ samāpajjeyyā’ti evaṃ visesetvāva sikkhāpadassa paññattattā sādiyamānepi na doso. Itarathā hi tabbahulanayenettha kiriyatte gayhamāne aññesampi kiriyākiriyasikkhāpadānaṃ kiriyattaggahaṇappasaṅgo siyā”ti. Tasmā [M 2.0069] vīmaṃsitvā gahetabbaṃ. Sāti kiriyāsamuṭṭhānatā. Tathevāti kāyasaṃsaggarāgī eva.

659. Because for bhikkhus it was said “should engage in” (`samāpajjeyyā`) physical contact, and not “should consent to” (`sādiyeyyā`), it was stated, “a bhikkhu is not to be made to fall into an offense.” By `tabbahulanayena` (“by way of its prevalence”) is meant because of the prevalence of its arising from action; by this, it shows that this offense can also arise from non-action. Although it shows this, we reason thus in this matter: “Even if there is no action on the part of one who is consenting at the moment of physical contact, it is solely an arising from action by the power of actions performed beforehand, such as going to a secluded place, showing signs by winking, making expressions, and so on—just like the emission of semen of one who, being still, consents to the effort made by another on the path. Or, even if there is no prior effort, because of consenting in that very moment to the action called one's own bodily movement and so on, which is generated by the effort of another—for that offense, having arisen also from her mind as she consents, is called ‘action’—just as in the case of consenting to sexual intercourse, etc., by another’s effort without exerting oneself. However, for bhikkhus, having treated the action generated by another’s effort as non-determinative, and because the training rule was laid down specifically as ‘should engage in physical contact’ solely by the power of the effort made by oneself, there is no fault even in consenting. Otherwise, if the nature of ‘action’ were to be taken here according to the `tabbahulanayena` principle, there would be the consequence of taking other action/non-action training rules as being of the nature of ‘action’.” Therefore, it should be taken after investigation. `Sā` refers to the state of arising from action. `Tatheva` means only being one with lust for physical contact.

Ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalikasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning an Act Above the Kneecap is concluded.

2. Vajjapaṭicchādikasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Concealing a Transgression

666. Dutiye purimenātiādi sundarīnandāya vajjapaṭicchādane paññattataṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. “Aṭṭhanna”nti vuttattā vajjapaṭicchādanassāpi paṭicchādane pārājikamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Dhuraṃ nikkhittamatte”ti vuttattā paṇṇattiṃ ajānantiyāpi “idaṃ vajjaṃ na pakāsessāmī”ti chandena dhuraṃ nikkhepakkhaṇe pārājikanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Taṃ pana paṭicchādanaṃ yasmā “pesalā ñatvā garahissantī”ti bhayeneva hoti, bhayañca kodhacittasampayuttaṃ, tasmā idaṃ “dukkhavedana”nti vuttaṃ. Yaṃ pana sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. pārājikakaṇḍa 3.666) “kiñcāpi vajjapaṭicchādanaṃ pemavasena hoti, tathāpi sikkhāpadavītikkamacittaṃ domanassitameva hotī”ti evaṃ paṇṇattivītikkamacitteneva chādanaṃ domanassatte kāraṇaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ akāraṇaṃ paṇṇattivijānanaṃ vināpi āpajjitabbatova.

666. In the second training rule, the words beginning with 'purimena' are stated with reference to the regulation being laid down concerning Sundarīnandā's concealment of a transgression. Since it is said 'of eight,' it should be understood that for concealing one who has concealed a transgression, it is indeed a pārājika offense. Because it is said 'just upon laying down the burden,' it should be understood that even for one who does not know the regulation, if one lays down the burden with the intention 'I will not reveal this transgression,' a pārājika is incurred at that moment of laying down the burden. And since that concealment arises solely from the fear that 'the virtuous will know and censure me,' and fear is associated with a mind rooted in aversion, therefore this is called 'painful feeling.' But as for what is said in the Sāratthadīpanī: 'Although the concealment of a transgression may arise out of affection, still, the mind that transgresses the training rule is indeed accompanied by displeasure'—thus stating that concealment by a mind that transgresses the regulation is the cause for displeasure—that is not the cause, for the offense must be incurred even without knowing the regulation.

Vajjapaṭicchādikasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on Concealing a Transgression is concluded.

669. Tatiyaṃ uttānameva.

669. The third is self-evident.

4. Aṭṭhavatthukasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

4. The Explanation of the Training Rule on the Eight Grounds

675. Catutthe [V 2.0067] lokassādasaṅkhātaṃ mittehi aññamaññaṃ kātabbaṃ santhavaṃ. Vuttamevatthaṃ pariyāyantarena dassetuṃ “kāyasaṃsaggarāgenā”ti vuttaṃ.

675. In the fourth, santhava is the association to be made mutually by friends, which is called worldly delight. To show the very meaning already stated by another method, it is said, 'due to lust for bodily contact.'

Tissitthiyo methunaṃ taṃ na seveti yā tisso itthiyo, tāsu vuttaṃ taṃ methunaṃ na seveyya. Anariyapaṇḍaketi tayo anariye, tayo paṇḍake ca upasaṅkamitvā methunaṃ na seveti attho. Anariyāti [M 2.0070] cettha ubhatobyañjanakā adhippetā. Byañjanasminti attano vaccamukhamaggepi. Chedo eva chejjaṃ, pārājikaṃ.

'One should not engage in that sexual intercourse with the three women': Whatever three women there are, one should not engage in that sexual intercourse which has been mentioned concerning them. 'With anariyas and paṇḍakas': The meaning is that having approached three anariyas and three paṇḍakas, one should not engage in sexual intercourse. Here, by 'anariyas' is meant hermaphrodites. 'In the organ' means even in one's own anus or mouth. An act of penetration is indeed what is meant by 'deserving expulsion'; it is a pārājika.

Vaṇṇāvaṇṇoti dvīhi sukkavissaṭṭhi vuttā. Gamanuppādananti sañcarittaṃ. “Methunadhammassa pubbabhāgattā paccayo hotī”ti iminā kāriyopacārena kāyasaṃsaggo methunadhammoti vuttoti dasseti. Sabbapadesūti saṅghāṭikaṇṇaggahaṇādipadesu. Kāyasaṃsaggarāgo, saussāhatā, aṭṭhamavatthussa pūraṇanti tīṇettha aṅgāni.

By the two words 'vaṇṇāvaṇṇa', emission of semen is stated. By 'gamanuppādanaṃ', acting as a go-between is stated. By this phrase, 'because it is a preliminary part of the sexual act, it is a condition,' it is shown that by way of metaphorical usage regarding the result, bodily contact is called 'the sexual act'. 'In all instances' means in instances such as grasping the corner of the outer robe, and so on. Lust for bodily contact, effortfulness, and the completion of the eighth ground—these three are the factors here.

Aṭṭhavatthukasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Training Rule on the Eight Grounds is concluded.

Pārājikavaṇṇanānayo niṭṭhito.

The exposition of the Pārājika is concluded.

2. Saṅghādisesakaṇḍaṃ

2. The Saṅghādisesa Section

1. Paṭhamasaṅghādisesasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. The Explanation of the First Saṅghādisesa Training Rule

679. Saṅghādisesakaṇḍe [M 2.0071][V 2.0068] “dutiyassa ārocetī”ti etthāpi dvīsupi aḍḍakārakesu yassa kassaci dutiyassa kathaṃ yo koci ārocetīti evamattho gahetabboti āha “eseva nayo”ti.

679. In the Saṅghādisesa section, regarding the phrase 'informs a second,' here too, among the two litigants, the meaning should be understood thus: 'whoever informs any second person of the matter.' Therefore, he said, 'This is the very method.'

Gatigatanti cirakālappavattaṃ. Āpattīti āpajjanaṃ. “Nissāraṇīya”nti idaṃ kattuatthe siddhanti āha “nissāretī”ti. Āpannaṃ bhikkhuniṃ saṅghato viyojeti, viyojanahetu hotīti attho.

'Gatigata' means that which has occurred for a long time. 'Āpatti' means the incurring. This word 'nissāraṇīya' is established in the agent sense; therefore, he said, 'nissāreti' (he expels). It separates a bhikkhunī who has incurred an offense from the Saṅgha; the meaning is that it is the cause for separation.

Gīvāyevāti āṇattiyā abhāvato. Tesaṃ anatthakāmatāyāti “coro”ti vuttaṃ mama vacanaṃ sutvā keci daṇḍissanti jīvitā voropessantīti evaṃ saññāya. Etena kevalaṃ bhayena vā parikkhāraggahaṇatthaṃ vā sahasā “coro”ti vutte daṇḍitepi na dosoti dasseti. Rājapurisānañhi “coro aya”nti uddissa kathane eva gīvā, bhikkhūnaṃ, pana ārāmikādīnaṃ vā sammukhā “asuko coro evamakāsī”ti kenaci vuttavacanaṃ nissāya ārāmikādīsu rājapurisānaṃ vatvā daṇḍāpentesupi bhikkhussa na gīvā rājapurisānaṃ avuttattā. Yesañca vuttaṃ, tehi sayaṃ corassa adaṇḍitattāti gahetabbaṃ. “Tvaṃ etassa santakaṃ acchindā”ti āṇattopi hi sace aññena acchindāpeti, āṇāpakassa anāpatti visaṅketattā. “Attano vacanakara”nti idaṃ sāmīcivasena vuttaṃ. Vacanaṃ akarontānaṃ rājapurisānampi “iminā gahitaparikkhāraṃ āharāpehi, mā cassa daṇḍaṃ karohī”ti uddissa vadantassāpi daṇḍe gahitepi na gīvā eva daṇḍaggahaṇassa paṭikkhittattā, “asukabhaṇḍaṃ avaharā”ti āṇāpetvā vippaṭisāre uppanne puna paṭikkhipane (pārā. 121) viya.

'Gīvāyeva' is due to the absence of a command. 'Tesaṃ anatthakāmatāya' is with the perception that, 'Having heard my words, "thief," some will impose a fine or deprive him of life.' By this, it is shown that even if a fine is imposed when one has hastily said 'thief' merely out of fear or for the purpose of having requisites taken, there is no fault. Indeed, for royal officials, it is a capital offense only in the case of speaking while pointing out, 'This is a thief.' However, if, in the presence of monks or monastery attendants and so on, relying on the words spoken by some monk, 'Such-and-such is a thief; he did thus,' the monastery attendants and so on, having told the royal officials, cause a fine to be imposed, it is not a capital offense for the monk, because it was not said to the royal officials. And it should be understood that those to whom it was said did not themselves impose the fine on the thief. Indeed, even if one who was commanded, 'You, seize his property,' causes another to seize it, for the one who gave the command there is no offense, due to the discrepancy. This phrase 'one who does one's bidding' is said by way of propriety. Even for royal officials who do not follow the instruction, and even if a fine is taken when one says, pointing out, 'Have him bring the requisites seized by this person, and do not impose a fine on him,' it is still not a capital offense, because the taking of the fine was forbidden, just as in the case of forbidding it again after regret has arisen, having commanded, 'Steal such-and-such goods.'

Dāsādīnaṃ [V 2.0069] sampaṭicchane viya tadatthāya aḍḍakaraṇe bhikkhūnampi dukkaṭanti āha “akappiyaaḍḍo nāma na vaṭṭatī”ti. Kenaci pana bhikkhunā khettādiatthāya vohārikānaṃ santikaṃ gantvā aḍḍe katepi taṃ khettādisampaṭicchane viya sabbesaṃ akappiyaṃ na hoti pubbe eva saṅghassa santakattā[M 2.0072], bhikkhusseva pana payogavasena āpattiyo honti. Dāsādīnampi pana atthāya rakkhaṃ yācituṃ vohārikena puṭṭhena saṅghassa uppannaṃ kappiyakkamaṃ vattuṃ, ārāmikādīhi ca aḍḍaṃ kārāpetuñca vaṭṭati eva. Vihāravatthādikappiyaaḍḍaṃ pana bhikkhuno sayampi kātuṃ vaṭṭati.

Just as in accepting slaves and so on, so too in engaging in litigation for their sake, it is a dukkaṭa for monks. Therefore, he said, 'An improper legal dispute, indeed, is not allowable.' Some, however, say: even if a monk, having gone to judges for the sake of fields and so on, engages in litigation, it is not improper for all, as in the case of accepting those fields and so on, because it was already the property of the Saṅgha beforehand. But for that monk, offenses arise by way of his effort. However, for the sake of slaves and so on, it is indeed allowable to ask for protection; and for a monk who is asked by a judge to state the proper procedure that has arisen for the Saṅgha; and to cause monastery attendants and so on to engage in litigation. Moreover, it is allowable for a monk to personally conduct a proper legal dispute concerning monastery land and so forth.

Bhikkhunīnaṃ vuttoti rakkhaṃ yācantīnaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ vutto uddissaanuddissavasena rakkhāyācanavinicchayo, na sabbo sikkhāpadavinicchayo asādhāraṇattā sikkhāpadassa. Tenāha “bhikkhunopī”tiādi. Anākaḍḍhitāya aḍḍakaraṇaṃ, aḍḍapariyosānanti dve aṅgāni.

‘Bhikkhunīnaṃ vutto’ means the legal decision on asking for protection, spoken concerning bhikkhunīs who ask for protection, by way of specific and non-specific reference; it is not the legal decision for the entire training rule, because the training rule is not common to both. Therefore, he said the words beginning with ‘bhikkhunopi.’ Engaging in a legal proceeding without being summoned and the completion of the legal proceeding—these are the two factors.

Paṭhamasaṅghādisesasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the First Saṅghādisesa Training Rule is concluded.

2. Dutiyasaṅghādisesasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Second Saṅghādisesa Training Rule

683. Pāḷiyaṃ dutiye mallagaṇabhaṭiputtagaṇādikantiādīsu mallarājūnaṃ gaṇo mallagaṇo. Bhaṭiputtā nāma keci gaṇarājāno, tesaṃ gaṇo. Keci pana “nārāyanabhattiko puññakāragaṇo mallagaṇo. Tathā kumārabhattiko ca gaṇo bhaṭiputtagaṇo”tipi (sārattha. ṭī. saṃghādisesakaṇḍa 3.683) vadanti. Dhammagaṇoti sāsane, loke vā anekappakārapuññakārako gaṇo. Gandhavikatikārako gaṇo gandhikaseṇī. Pesakārādigaṇo dussikaseṇī. Kappagatikanti kappiyabhāvagataṃ, pabbajitapubbanti attho.

In the Pāḷi, in the second training rule, in the texts beginning with 'the group of Mallas, the group of Bhaṭiputtas, and so on,' the group of Malla kings is the Mallagaṇa. The Bhaṭiputtas are certain group-kings; their group is the Bhaṭiputtagaṇa. Some, however, also say: 'The group that makes offerings to Nārāyaṇa, a merit-making group, is the Mallagaṇa. Similarly, the group that makes offerings to Kumāra is the Bhaṭiputtagaṇa.' The Dhammagaṇa is a group in the Dispensation or in the world that performs meritorious deeds of many kinds. The group that makes special perfumes is the Gandhikaseṇī. The group of weavers and so on is the Dussikaseṇī. As for 'Kappagatikaṃ,' the meaning is: having reached a state of suitability, previously ordained.

685. Pāḷiyaṃ vuṭṭhāpetīti upasampādeti. Akappagatampi pabbājentiyā dukkaṭanti vadanti. Khīṇāsavāyapi āpajjitabbato “ticitta”nti vuttaṃ. Coritā, taṃ ñatvā ananuññātakāraṇā vuṭṭhāpananti dve aṅgāni.

2. In the Pāḷi, 'vuṭṭhāpeti' means to confer the higher ordination. They say there is a dukkaṭa offense for a bhikkhunī who ordains even a woman who has not reached a state of suitability. Because it is fit to be incurred even by one whose cankers are destroyed, it is said to be 'ticittaṃ.' The two factors are: the state of being a thief, and knowing her to be such, conferring the higher ordination without a permitted reason.

Dutiyasaṅghādisesasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

683. The Explanation of the Second Saṅghādisesa Training Rule is concluded.

3. Tatiyasaṅghādisesasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

685. Explanation of the Third Saṅghādisesa Training Rule

692. Tatiye [M 2.0073][V 2.0070] parikkhepaṃ atikkāmentiyāti gāmantarassa parikkhepaṃ atikkāmentiyā. “Gāmantaraṃ gaccheyyā”ti hi vuttaṃ. Vikālagāmappavesanasikkhāpade viya “aparikkhittassa upacāraṃ okkamantiyā”ti avatvā “atikkāmentiyā”ti pāḷiyaṃ vuttattā gāmaṃ pavisantiyā gharūpacāre ṭhitassa dutiyaleḍḍupātasaṅkhātassa upacārassa atikkamo nāma paṭhamaleḍḍupātaṭṭhānasaṅkhātassa parikkhepārahaṭṭhānassa atikkamo evāti āha “parikkhepārahaṭṭhānaṃ ekena pādena atikkamatī”ti.

In the third training rule, 'crossing the boundary' means for a bhikkhunī who crosses the boundary of another village. For it was said, 'One may go to another village.' Because it is said 'crossing' in the Pāḷi—unlike in the training rule on entering a village at the wrong time, where it does not say 'entering the vicinity of an unenclosed area'—for a bhikkhunī entering a village, the crossing of the vicinity known as the second clod-throw from one standing in the vicinity of a house, is precisely the crossing of the place suitable for a boundary, known as the place of the first clod-throw. Therefore, it is said: 'she crosses the place suitable for a boundary with one foot.'

Majjheti gāmamajjhe. Pacchāti aparakāle. “Catugāmasādhāraṇattā”ti iminā vihārato catūsu gāmesu yattha katthaci pavisituṃ vaṭṭatīti ettha kāraṇamāha.

3. 'Majjhe' means in the middle of the village. 'Pacchā' means at a later time. By 'because it is common to four villages,' he states the reason here for the statement that 'it is allowable to enter any of the four villages from the monastery.'

Paratīrameva akkamantiyāti nadiṃ anotaritvā orimatīrato laṅghitvā vā ākāsādinā vā paratīrameva atikkāmentiyā. Orimatīrameva āgacchati, āpattīti pāragamanāya otiṇṇattā vuttaṃ.

692. 'Paratīrameva akkamantiyā' means for a bhikkhunī who steps only on the far bank without descending into the river, either by leaping from the near bank or by the sky, and so on. The statement, 'If she returns only to the near bank, there is an offense,' is said because she had descended in order to go to the far bank.

Tādise araññeti indakhīlato bahibhāvalakkhaṇe araññe. “Tenevā”tiādinā dassanūpacāre virahite savanūpacārassa vijjamānattepi āpatti hotīti dasseti. Aññaṃ maggaṃ gaṇhātīti maggamūḷhattā gaṇhāti, na dutiyikaṃ ohiyituṃ. Tasmā anāpatti. Anantarāyena ekabhāvo, anāpadāya gāmantaragamanādīsu ekanti dve aṅgāni.

'Such a wilderness' means a wilderness characterized by being outside the boundary post. With 'Teneva,' and so on, it shows that there is an offense even when the range of sight is absent, as long as the range of hearing is present. 'Taking another path' means she takes it because she is lost on the path; she does not take it in order to abandon her companion. Therefore, there is no offense. The two factors are: being alone without danger, and one among the acts of going to another village, and so on, without calamity.

Tatiyasaṅghādisesasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Third Saṅghādisesa Training Rule is concluded.

4. Catutthasaṅghādisesasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Fourth Saṅghādisesa Training Rule

694. Catutthe kārakagaṇassāti imassa kammaṃ kātabbanti yehi sanniṭṭhānaṃ kataṃ, te sandhāya vuttaṃ. Kammavācakkhaṇe sahaṭhiteti keci. Netthāravatteti nittharaṇahetumhi vatte.

694. In the fourth [training rule]: As for 'of the acting group,' it is said referring to those by whom the decision was made, 'An act should be done for this one.' And it is said referring to those standing together at the moment of the formal act. Thus some say. As for 'netthāravatte,' it means: in a matter that is a cause for overcoming.

698. Pāḷiyaṃ [M 2.0074] asante kārakasaṅgheti ettha vijjamānaṃ sudūrampi gantvā āpucchitabbaṃ[V 2.0071]. Antarāye pana sati sammā vattantaṃ osāretuṃ vaṭṭatīti. Dhammakammena ukkhittatā, ananuññātakāraṇā osāraṇanti dve aṅgāni.

698. In the Pāḷi, regarding the phrase 'when the acting group is not present': the existing group, even if very far away, should be gone to and consulted. However, if there is an obstacle, it is allowable to reinstate one who is practicing well. The state of having been suspended by a formal act according to the Dhamma, and reinstatement for an unpermitted reason—these are the two factors.

Catutthasaṅghādisesasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Fourth Saṅghādisesa Training Rule is concluded.

5. Pañcamasaṅghādisesasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Fifth Saṅghādisesa Training Rule

701. Pañcame tanti mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ avacanaṃ “anavassutoti jānantī paṭiggaṇhātī”tiādi pāḷiyā sameti. Ubhato avassutabhāvo, udakadantaponato aññaṃ sahatthā gahetvā ajjhoharaṇanti dve aṅgāni.

701. In the fifth [training rule]: For that non-mention in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā agrees with the Pāḷi beginning with 'knowing him to be lustful, she accepts.' The state of being lustful on both sides, and taking with one's own hand and consuming an edible or food other than water and a tooth-cleaner—these are the two factors.

Pañcamasaṅghādisesasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Fifth Saṅghādisesa Training Rule is concluded.

6. Chaṭṭhasaṅghādisesasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Sixth Saṅghādisesa Training Rule

705. Chaṭṭhe paṭiggaho tena na vijjatīti teneva “na detī”ti vuttakāraṇena uyyojitāya hatthato itarāya paṭiggahopi natthi. Paribhogapaccayāti uyyojitāya bhojanapariyosānapaccayāti attho. Manussapurisassa avassutatā, taṃ ñatvā ananuññātakāraṇā uyyojanā, tena itarissā gahetvā bhojanapariyosānanti tīṇi aṅgāni.

705. In the sixth [training rule]: As for 'there is no acceptance because of that,' it means that precisely by the stated reason 'he does not give,' there is also no acceptance by the other from the hand of the one instigated for. As for 'due to the condition of using,' the meaning is 'due to the condition of the one instigated for finishing the meal.' The state of a human male being lustful; knowing that, instigating without a permitted reason; and because of that, the other's taking and finishing the meal—these are the three factors.

Chaṭṭhasaṅghādisesasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Sixth Saṅghādisesa Training Rule is concluded.

709-727. Sattamato yāvadasamapariyosānāni uttānāneva.

The training rules from the seventh up to the end of the tenth are indeed clear.

Saṅghādisesavaṇṇanānayo niṭṭhito.

The method for the commentary on the Saṅghādisesa is concluded.

3. Nissaggiyakaṇḍaṃ

3. The Section on Offenses Entailing Forfeiture

2. Dutiyanissaggiyādipācittiyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Nissaggiya Pācittiya Training Rules Beginning with the Second

733. Nissaggiyesupi [M 2.0075][V 2.0072] paṭhamaṃ uttānameva.

733. Even among the Nissaggiya rules, the first is straightforward.

740. Dutiye ayyāya dammīti evaṃ paṭiladdhanti nissaṭṭhapaṭiladdhaṃ, nissaṭṭhaṃ paṭilabhitvāpi yaṃ uddissa dāyakehi dinnaṃ, tattheva dātabbaṃ. Tenāha “yathādāneyeva upanetabba”nti. Akālacīvaratā, taṃ ñatvā kālacīvaranti lesena bhājāpanaṃ, paṭilābhoti tīṇi aṅgāni.

740. In the second [training rule]: As for 'obtained thus: "I will give to the venerable lady,"' it is what was forfeited being obtained again. Even having obtained again what was forfeited, for whomever it was intended and given by the donors, to that very one it must be given. Therefore, it is said: 'It should be presented just as it was given.' Being an out-of-season robe; knowing it to be so, causing it to be distributed with the pretext that 'it is a season-robe'; and the receiving—these are the three factors.

743. Tatiye metanti mamevetaṃ cīvaraṃ. Upasampannatā, parivattitavikappanupagacīvarassa sakasaññāya acchindanādīti dve aṅgāni.

743. In the third [training rule]: As for 'metaṃ,' it means 'this robe is mine.' Being fully ordained, and the snatching, etc., with the perception that it is one's own, of a robe that has been exchanged and is suitable for formal designation—these are the two factors.

748-752. Catutthe āhaṭasappiṃ datvāti attano datvā. Yamakaṃ pacitabbanti sappiñca telañca ekato pacitabbaṃ. Lesena gahetukāmatā, aññassa viññatti, paṭilābhoti tīṇi aṅgāni.

In the fourth [training rule]: As for 'having given brought ghee,' it means having given to oneself. As for 'a pair should be cooked,' it means ghee and oil should be cooked together. The desire to take by means of a pretext; requesting from another; and the receiving—these are the three factors.

753. Pañcame sāti thullanandā. Ayanti sikkhamānā. Cetāpetvāti jānāpetvāti idha vuttaṃ, mātikāṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “attano kappiyabhaṇḍena ‘idaṃ nāma āharā’ti aññaṃ parivattāpetvā”ti (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. aññacetāpanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) vuttaṃ.

753. In the fifth [training rule]: 'She' means Thullanandā. 'This one' means the female probationer. As for 'cetāpetvā' (having caused to be exchanged), it is said here to mean 'jānāpetvā' (having made known). But in the Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā, it is said: 'Having caused another to exchange by means of one's own allowable goods, saying, "Bring this particular thing."'.

758. Chaṭṭhe pāvārikassāti dussavāṇijakassa.

758. In the sixth [training rule], 'of a weaver' means of a cloth merchant.

764. Sattame [V 2.0073] saññācitakenāti sayaṃ yācitakenapīti attho.

764. In the seventh [training rule], 'with what was requested by hint' means 'even with what was requested by oneself'; this is the meaning.

769-789. Aṭṭhamato yāvadvādasamā uttānameva.

From the eighth up to the twelfth [training rules], they are indeed clear.

Nissaggiyavaṇṇanānayo niṭṭhito.

The method for the commentary on the Nissaggiya is concluded.

4. Pācittiyakaṇḍaṃ

4. The Pācittiya Section

1. Lasuṇavaggo

1. The Garlic Chapter

1. Paṭhamalasuṇādisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the First Training Rule on Garlic, etc.

797. Pācittiyesu [M 2.0076][V 2.0074] lasuṇavaggassa paṭhame badarasāḷavaṃ nāma badaraphalāni sukkhāpetvā tehi kattabbabyañjanavikati. Āmakamāgadhalasuṇañceva, ajjhoharaṇañcāti dve aṅgāni.

797. In the Pācittiyas, in the first [training rule] of the Lasuṇavagga: `badarasāḷavaṃ` is a special dish to be made with jujube fruits after having them dried. Raw Māgadha garlic and swallowing—these are the two factors.

799-812. Dutiyādīni uttānatthāni.

The second and subsequent [rules] are of plain meaning.

815. Chaṭṭhe pāḷiyaṃ āsumbhitvāti pātetvā.

815. In the sixth [training rule], in the Pāḷi, `āsumbhitvā` means having dropped.

817. Dadhimatthūti dadhimhi pasannodakaṃ. Rasakhīrādīnanti maṃsarasakhīrādīnaṃ. Bhuñjantassa bhikkhuno hatthapāse ṭhānaṃ, pānīyassa vā vidhūpanassa vā gahaṇanti dve aṅgāni.

817. `Dadhimatthu` is the clear water in curds. `Rasakhīrādīnaṃ` means of meat broth, milk-broth, etc. The standing [of a person] within hand's reach of an eating monk, and the taking of drinking water or a fan—these are the two factors.

822. Sattame aviññattiyā laddhanti attano viññattiṃ vinā laddhaṃ. Pubbāparaviruddhanti sayaṃ karaṇe pācittiyanti idaṃ kārāpane dukkaṭavacanena virujjhanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tenāha “na hī”tiādi, “aviññattiyā laddha”ntiādivacanena vā virujjhanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Aññāya viññattipi hi imissā aviññattiyā laddhamevāti. Āmakadhaññaviññāpanādi, taṃ bhajjanādinā ajjhoharaṇanti dve aṅgāni.

822. In the seventh [training rule], `aviññattiyā laddhaṃ` means obtained without one's own request. The statement `pubbāparaviruddhaṃ` is said with reference to the contradiction of the statement `sayaṃ karaṇe pācittiyaṃ` with the statement of a `dukkaṭa` for causing it to be done. Therefore, he says 'na hi', etc.; or, it is said with reference to the contradiction with the statement beginning 'obtained without request'. For, even if requested by another bhikkhunī, for this bhikkhunī it is indeed obtained without her own request. Requesting raw grain, etc., and swallowing it after roasting, etc.—these are the two factors.

824. Aṭṭhame nibbiṭṭhoti laddho. Keṇīti rañño dātabbo āyo, āyuppattiṭṭhānanti attho[V 2.0075]. Tenāha “ekaṃ ṭhānantara”ntiādi. Ṭhānantaranti ca gāmajanapadāṇāyattaṃ. Vaḷañjiyamānatirokuṭṭāditā, anapaloketvā uccārādīnaṃ chaḍḍanādīti dve aṅgāni.

824. In the eighth [training rule], `nibbiṭṭho` means obtained. `Keṇī` means revenue to be given to the king, that is, a place where revenue arises. Therefore, it is said, `ekaṃ ṭhānantaraṃ`, etc. And `ṭhānantaraṃ` is the state of being a chief of a village, district, etc. The state of being a place used that is beyond a wall, etc., and the disposing of excrement, etc., without asking permission—these are the two factors.

830. Navame “matthakacchinnanāḷikerampī”ti vuttattā haritūpari chaḍḍanameva paṭikkhittaṃ. Tenāha “anikkhittabījesū”tiādi. Yattha ca chaḍḍetuṃ vaṭṭati, tattha harite vaccādiṃ kātumpi vaṭṭati eva. Sabbesanti bhikkhubhikkhunīnaṃ.

830. In the ninth [training rule], because it is said, 'even a coconut with its head cut off,' only discarding upon living green [plants] is prohibited. Therefore, it is said, `anikkhittabījesu`, etc. And where it is allowable to discard, it is also allowable to pass excrement, etc., on what is green. `Sabbesaṃ` means for monks and nuns.

836-7. Dasame [M 2.0077] tesaṃyevāti yesaṃ niccaṃ passati. Ārāme ṭhatvāti ṭhitanisannaṭṭhāne eva ṭhatvā samantato gīvaṃ parivattetvāpi passati, anāpatti. Ṭhitaṭṭhānato gantvā passituṃ na vaṭṭati. Keci pana “vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti. Taṃ pana “dassanāya gaccheyya, pācittiya”nti sāmaññato gamanassa paṭikkhittattā, anāpattiyampi gamanāya avuttattā ca na gahetabbaṃ. Naccāditā, ananuññātakāraṇā gamanaṃ, dassanādi cāti tīṇi aṅgāni.

836-7. In the tenth [training rule], tesaṃyeva means: of those whose dancing one sees. Ārāme ṭhatvā means: if one sees by turning the neck all around while remaining in one's standing or sitting place, there is no offense. It is not allowable to go from the place where one is standing in order to see. But some say it is allowable. That, however, should not be accepted, because going is generally prohibited by [the rule], 'Should one go to see, it is a pācittiya,' and because going is not mentioned in the non-offense clause. Dancing, etc.; going without a permitted reason; and seeing, etc.—these are the three factors.

Niṭṭhito lasuṇavaggo paṭhamo.

The first chapter, the Lasuṇavagga, is finished.

2. Andhakāravaggo

2. The Chapter on Darkness

1. Paṭhamādisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the First Training Rule and so forth

841. Dutiyavaggassa paṭhame dāne vāti dānanimittaṃ. Rattandhakāre purisassa hatthapāse ṭhānādi, rahopekkhā, sahāyābhāvoti tīṇi aṅgāni.

841. In the first [training rule] of the second chapter, the phrase dāne vā means: on account of giving. The three factors are: standing, etc., within arm's reach of a man in the darkness of night; seeking a secluded place; and the absence of a companion.

842-850. Dutiyādīni uttānāni.

842-850. The second and the following are clear.

854. Pañcame pallaṅkassa anokāseti ūrubaddhāsanassa appahonake. Purebhattaṃ antaraghare pallaṅkappahonakāsane nisajjā, ananuññātakāraṇā anāpucchā vuttaparicchedātikkamoti dve aṅgāni.

854. In the fifth [training rule], the phrase pallaṅkassa anokāse means: in a place insufficient for sitting with thighs bound (cross-legged). The two factors are: sitting before the meal inside a house on a seat that is sufficient for sitting cross-legged; and, without a permitted reason and without asking, transgressing the stated limit.

860-879. Chaṭṭhādīni [V 2.0076] uttānāni.

860-879. The sixth and the following are clear.

Niṭṭhito andhakāravaggo dutiyo.

The second chapter, the Andhakāravagga, is concluded.

3. Naggavaggo

3. The Chapter on Nakedness

1. Paṭhamādisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the First Training Rule and so forth

883-887. Tatiyavaggassa paṭhamadutiyāni uttānāni.

883-887. The first and second [training rules] of the third chapter are clear.

893. Tatiye visibbetvāti vijaṭetvā. Dhuraṃ nikkhittamatteti visibbanadivasato pañca divase atikkāmetvā dhuraṃ nikkhittamatte. Antopañcāhe pana dhuranikkhepepi anāpatti eva “aññatra catūhapañcāhā”ti vuttattā[M 2.0078]. Upasampannāya cīvaraṃ sibbanatthāya visibbetvā pañcahātikkamo, ananuññātakāraṇā dhuranikkhepoti dve aṅgāni.

893. In the third [training rule], the phrase visibbetvā means: having unraveled. The phrase dhuraṃ nikkhittamatta means: just at the point of laying down the burden after letting five days pass from the day of unraveling. However, even if the burden is laid down within five days, there is no offense, because it is said, ‘except for four or five days.’ The two factors are: for a fully ordained nun, having unraveled a robe for the purpose of sewing, the transgression of five days; and laying down the burden without a permitted reason.

900. Catutthe pañcannaṃ cīvarānaṃ aparivattanaṃ, ananuññātakāraṇā pañcāhātikkamoti dve aṅgāni.

900. In the fourth [training rule], the two factors are: not exchanging the five robes; and the transgression of five days without a permitted reason.

903. Pañcamaṃ uttānameva.

903. The fifth [training rule] is clear.

909. Chaṭṭhe vikappanupagassa saṅghe pariṇatatā, vinā ānisaṃsadassanena antarāyakaraṇanti dve aṅgāni.

909. In the sixth [training rule], the two factors are: a robe suitable for formal determination being designated for the Saṅgha; and causing an obstruction without showing the benefits.

911. Sattamaṃ uttānameva.

911. The seventh [training rule] is clear.

916. Aṭṭhame kumbhathūṇaṃ nāma kumbhasaddo, tena kīḷantīti kumbhathūṇikā. Tenāha “ghaṭakena kīḷanakā”ti. Dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “caturassaambaṇakatāḷa”nti vuttaṃ. Tañhi rukkhasārādimayaṃ antochiddaṃ catūsu passesu cammonaddhaṃ vāditabhaṇḍaṃ, yaṃ “bimbisaka”ntipi vuccati, taṃ vādentāpi kumbhathūṇikā. Tenāha “bimbisakavāditakātipi vadantī”ti.

916. In the eighth [training rule], the term kumbhathūṇa refers to a drum with a sound like a broken pot; because they play with it, they are called kumbhathūṇikā. Therefore, it is said, ‘players with a small pot.’ However, in the commentary to the Dīgha Nikāya, it is stated as ‘the striking of a four-sided drum.’ That, indeed, is a musical instrument made of wood core and other materials, hollow inside, covered with leather on four sides, which is also called bimbisaka; those who play it are also called kumbhathūṇikā. Hence, it is said, ‘they are also called players of the bimbisaka.’

918. Pāḷiyaṃ [V 2.0077] kappakatanti kappakataṃ nivāsanapārupanūpagaṃ. Samaṇacīvaratā, ananuññātānaṃ dānanti dve aṅgāni.

918. In the Pāḷi, the term kappakataṃ refers to a robe suitable for wearing and covering that has been made allowable. The two factors are: its state as a monastic robe; and the giving of it to those who are not permitted.

921-931. Navamadasamāni uttānāneva.

921-931. The ninth and tenth [training rules] are clear.

Niṭṭhito naggavaggo tatiyo.

The third chapter, the Naggavagga, is concluded.

4. Tuvaṭṭavaggo

4. The Tuvaṭṭa Chapter

10. Dasamasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Tenth Training Rule

976. Tuvaṭṭavaggassa dasame cārikāya apakkamanaṃ paṇṇattivajjameva. Paṇṇattivijānanacittena sacittakataṃ sandhāya panettha “lokavajja”nti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānameva.

976. In the tenth [training rule] of the Tuvaṭṭa Chapter, not departing on a journey is only an offense by designation. However, with reference to it being done intentionally with a mind that knows the designation, here it should be understood as a 'worldly offense'. The rest is clear everywhere.

Niṭṭhito tuvaṭṭavaggo catuttho.

The fourth, the Tuvaṭṭa Chapter, is concluded.

5. Cittāgāravaggo

5. The Cittāgāra Chapter

1. Paṭhamādisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the First Training Rule and so forth

978. Cittāgāravaggassa [M 2.0079] paṭhame pāṭekkā āpattiyoti gīvāya parivattanappayogagaṇanāya.

978. In the first [training rule] of the Cittāgāra Chapter, 'separate offenses' [are incurred] according to the count of the applications of turning the neck.

1015. Navame hatthiādīsu sippa-saddo paccekaṃ yojetabbo, tathā āthabbaṇādīsu manta-saddo. Tattha āthabbaṇamanto nāma āthabbaṇavedavihito parūpaghātakaro manto. Khīlanamanto nāma verimāraṇatthāya sāradārumayaṃ khīlaṃ mantetvā pathaviyaṃ ākoṭanamanto. Agadappayogo visappayojanaṃ. Nāgamaṇḍalanti sappānaṃ pavesanivāraṇatthaṃ maṇḍalabandhamanto. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānameva.

1015. In the ninth [training rule], the word 'craft' should be applied individually to 'elephants' and so on, and similarly, the word 'spell' to 'āthabbaṇa' and so on. Therein, an 'āthabbaṇa spell' is a spell prescribed in the Atharva Veda that harms others. A 'khīlana spell' is a spell for striking a stake made of hardwood into the ground, having enchanted it for the purpose of killing an enemy. Agadappayoga is the application of poison. 'Nāgamaṇḍala' is a spell for binding a circle to prevent the entry of snakes. The rest is clear everywhere.

Niṭṭhito cittāgāravaggo pañcamo.

The fifth, the Cittāgāra Chapter, is concluded.

1025-1116. Ārāmavagge[V 2.0078], gabbhinivagge ca sabbaṃ uttānameva.

1025-1116. In the Ārāma Chapter and in the Gabbhinī Chapter, everything is clear.

8. Kumāribhūtavaggo

8. The Kumāribhūta Chapter

1. Paṭhamādisikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the First Training Rule and so forth

1119. Aṭṭhamavaggassa paṭhame sabbapaṭhamā dve mahāsikkhamānāti gabbhinivagge (pāci. 1067 ādayo) sabbapaṭhamaṃ vuttā dve. Sikkhamānā icceva vattabbāti sammutikammādīsu aññathā vutte kammaṃ kuppatīti adhippāyo.

1119. In the first [training rule] of the eighth chapter, 'the very first two great sikkhamānās' means the two spoken of first of all in the Gabbhinī Chapter. 'They should be called only "sikkhamānā"'—this is the meaning: if it is stated otherwise in formal acts and so on, the act becomes invalid.

1167. Ekādasame pārivāsiyena chandadānenāti parivutthena navikappavutthena vigatena chandadānenāti attho, chandavissajjanamattena vā.

1167. In the eleventh [training rule], 'by the giving of consent by one on probation' means: by the giving of consent by one who has completed probation, who has completed a special period, who is free [from the offense]; this is the meaning. Or, it means merely by the relinquishing of consent.

1168. “Vuṭṭhitāyā”ti etena “idāni kammaṃ na karissāmā”ti dhuraṃ nikkhipitvā kāyena avuṭṭhahitvā nisinnāyapi parisāya kammaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭatīti dasseti. Tenāha “chandaṃ avissajjetvā avuṭṭhitāyā”ti. Pāḷiyaṃ pana “anāpatti avuṭṭhitāya parisāyā”ti sāmaññato vuttattā[M 2.0080], uposathakkhandhake ca “na, bhikkhave, pārivāsikapārisuddhidānena uposatho kātabbo aññatra avuṭṭhitāya parisāyā”ti (mahāva. 183) vuttattā, tadaṭṭhakathāyampi “pārivāsiyapārisuddhidānaṃ nāma parisāya vuṭṭhitakālato paṭṭhāya na vaṭṭati, avuṭṭhitāya pana vaṭṭatī”ti (mahāva. aṭṭha. 183) vuttattā ca “kammaṃ na karissāmī”ti dhuraṃ nikkhipitvā nisinnāyapi kammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatīti gahetabbaṃ. Sesaṃ uttānameva.

1168. By this [word] vuṭṭhitāyā (of one who has risen), it is shown that it is not allowable to perform a formal act for an assembly that remains seated without having risen up physically, having laid down the responsibility, thinking, 'We will not perform the act now.' Therefore, it is said, 'of one who has not risen without relinquishing consent.' However, since it is stated generally in the Pāḷi, 'There is no offense for an assembly that has not risen'; and since it is stated in the Uposathakkhandhaka, 'Bhikkhus, the Uposatha should not be performed by giving the purity of one on probation, except for an assembly that has not risen'; and since it is also stated in its commentary, 'The giving of the purity of one on probation is not allowable from the time the assembly has risen, but it is allowable for one that has not risen'; therefore, it should be understood that it is allowable to perform a formal act even for an assembly that remains seated having laid down the responsibility, thinking, 'I will not perform the act.' The rest is clear.

Niṭṭhito kumāribhūtavaggo aṭṭhamo.

The eighth, the Kumāribhūta Chapter, is concluded.

1181. Chattavaggo uttāno eva.

1181. The Chatta Chapter is clear indeed.

Khuddakavaṇṇanānayo niṭṭhito.

The method of commenting on the Khuddaka [section] is concluded.

5. Pāṭidesanīyakaṇḍaṃ

5. The Section on Offenses to be Confessed

Pāṭidesanīyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Training Rules on Offenses to be Confessed

1228. Pāṭidesanīyādīsu [M 2.0081][V 2.0079] pāḷivinimuttakesūti pāḷiyaṃ anāgatesu sappiādīsu.

1228. In the Pāṭidesanīya and so forth, ‘pāḷivinimuttakesu’ means: concerning ghee and so forth that have not come in the Pāḷi.

Sattādhikaraṇavhayāti sattādhikaraṇasamathanāmakā. Taṃ atthavinicchayaṃ tādisaṃyeva yasmā vidū vadantīti attho. Yathā niṭṭhitāti sambandho. Sabbāsavapahanti sabbāsavavighātakaṃ arahattamaggaṃ. Passantu nibbutinti maggañāṇena nibbānaṃ sacchikarontu, pappontūti vā pāṭho. Tattha nibbutinti khandhaparinibbānaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

‘Named the seven settlements of legal questions’ means the training rules named the seven settlements of legal questions. Because the wise state that determination of meaning is just so, this is the meaning. The connection is: ‘as it is concluded.’ ‘The dispelling of all cankers’ means the path of Arahantship, which destroys all cankers. ‘May they see Nibbāna’ means may they realize Nibbāna with path-knowledge; or, the reading is also ‘may they attain.’ Therein, by the word ‘Nibbāna,’ the final passing away of the aggregates should be understood.

Iti samantapāsādikāya vinayaṭṭhakathāya vimativinodaniyaṃ

Thus in the Vimativinodanī, the sub-commentary to the Vinaya commentary, the Samantapāsādikā.

Bhikkhunīvibhaṅgavaṇṇanānayo niṭṭhito.

The method of explaining the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga is concluded.

Ubhatovibhaṅgaṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the commentary on the Ubhatovibhaṅga is concluded.

Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Mahāvaggavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Mahāvagga

1. Mahākhandhako

1. The Great Section

Bodhikathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on Enlightenment

Mahāvagge [M 2.0083][V 2.0081] ubhinnaṃ pātimokkhānanti ubhinnaṃ pātimokkhavibhaṅgānaṃ. Yaṃ khandhakaṃ saṅgāyiṃsūti sambandho. Khandhānaṃ samūho, khandhānaṃ vā pakāsanato khandhako. Khandhāti cettha pabbajjādicārittavārittasikkhāpadapaññattisamūho adhippeto. Padabhājanīye yesaṃ padānaṃ atthā yehi aṭṭhakathānayehi pakāsitāti yojanā. Atha vā ye atthāti yojetabbaṃ. Hi-saddo cettha padapūraṇe daṭṭhabbo.

In the Mahāvagga, ‘of the two Pātimokkhas’ means of the two Pātimokkha-Vibhaṅgas. The connection is with ‘which section they recited.’ A section (khandhaka) is a collection of sections (khandhas); or, it is a section because it explains the sections. And here, by the word ‘khandha,’ the collection of prescribed training rules on conduct and restraint concerning such things as the going forth is intended. In the word-analysis, the construction is: ‘the meanings of which words were explained by which commentarial methods.’ Alternatively, it should be construed as ‘which meanings.’ And here, the particle ‘hi’ should be seen as a mere expletive.

1. Visesakāraṇanti “yena samayena āyasmato sāriputtattherassa sikkhāpadapaññattiyācanahetubhūto [V 2.0082] parivitakko udapādi, tena samayenā”tiādinā vuttakāraṇaṃ viya visesakāraṇaṃ bhummavacananivattanakakāraṇanti attho. Etassāti abhisambodhito paṭṭhāya satthu cariyāvibhāvanassa vinayapaññattiyaṃ kiṃ payojanaṃ? Yadi visesakāraṇaṃ natthīti adhippāyo. Nidānadassanaṃ payojananti yojanā. Nidānanticettha sikkhāpadapaññattihetubhūtaṃ vatthupuggalādikāraṇaṃ adhippetaṃ, na paññattiṭṭhānameva. Tenāha “yā hī”tiādi.

1. ‘A special reason’ means a special reason like the reason stated in such passages as, ‘At the time when a reflection that was the cause for requesting the prescription of a training rule arose in the venerable Elder Sāriputta, at that time…’; the meaning is that it is a reason that displaces the locative case. Regarding this, if there is no special reason, what is the purpose in the Vinaya prescription for the statement that explains the Teacher’s conduct beginning from his full enlightenment? This is the intended question. The construction is that the purpose is the showing of the origin. And here, by ‘origin,’ the cause that is the basis for prescribing a training rule, such as the story, the person, and so on, is intended, not merely the place of the prescription. Therefore, he said, ‘For which…’ and so on.

Uruvelāyanti ettha uru-saddo mahantavācī. Velā-saddo tīrapariyāyo. Unnatattādinā velā viya velā. Uru mahantī velā uruvelā, tassaṃ. Tenāha “mahāvelāya”ntiādi. Mariyādāti sīlādiguṇasīmā. Pattapuṭenāti tālādīnaṃ paṇṇapuṭena.

Regarding ‘at Uruvelā,’ here the word ‘uru’ means ‘great.’ The word ‘velā’ is a synonym for ‘bank.’ Because of being elevated and so on, it is a ‘velā’ like a bank. A great, high bank is Uruvelā; at that. Therefore, he said, ‘at the great bank,’ and so on. ‘Boundary’ means the boundary of virtues such as moral conduct. ‘With a leaf-container’ means with a container woven from the leaves of palm trees and so on.

“Paṭhamābhisambuddho”ti anunāsikalopenāyaṃ niddesoti āha “paṭhamaṃ abhisambuddho”ti. Paṭhamanti ca bhāvanapuṃsakaniddeso. Tasmā abhisambuddho [M 2.0084] hutvā sabbapaṭhamaṃ bodhirukkhamūle viharatīti yojanā daṭṭhabbā.

The designation ‘paṭhamābhisambuddho’ is made by eliding the nasal; therefore, he said, ‘paṭhamaṃ abhisambuddho.’ And ‘paṭhamaṃ’ is a neuter designation indicating an adverbial sense. Therefore, the construction should be understood as: having become fully enlightened, he dwells first of all at the root of the Bodhi tree.

Pāḷiyaṃ atha khoti ettha athāti etasmiṃ samayeti attho anekatthattā nipātānaṃ. Sattāhanti accantasaṃyoge etaṃ upayogavacanaṃ. Atha khoti adhikārantaradassane nipāto. Tena vimuttisukhapaṭisaṃvedanaṃ pahāya paṭiccasamuppādamanasikāre adhikatabhāvaṃ dasseti. Paṭiccāti paṭimukhaṃ gantvā, aññamaññaṃ apekkhitvāti attho. Etena kāraṇabahutā dassitā. Sahiteti kāriyabahutā. Anulomanti bhāvanapuṃsakaniddeso. Svevāti so eva paccayākāro. Purimanayena vā vuttoti “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”tiādinā nayena vutto paccayākāro. Pavattiyāti saṃsārappavattiyā.

In the Pāḷi, regarding ‘atha kho,’ here ‘atha’ has the meaning ‘at one time,’ because particles have many meanings. ‘For seven days’ is a word in the accusative case in the sense of continuous duration. ‘Atha kho’ is a particle indicating a change of topic. By this, it shows the state of having undertaken the contemplation of dependent origination after abandoning the experience of the bliss of liberation. ‘Paṭicca’ means ‘having gone towards’ or ‘depending on one another.’ By this, the multiplicity of causes is shown. By ‘sahite,’ the multiplicity of effects is shown. ‘Anulomaṃ’ is a neuter designation indicating an adverbial sense. ‘Sveva’ means that very conditional structure. ‘Or stated by the previous method’ means the conditional structure stated by the method of ‘with ignorance as condition, formations,’ and so on. ‘For the process’ means for the process of saṃsāra.

Pāḷiyaṃ “avijjāpaccayā”tiādīsu dukkhādīsu aññāṇaṃ avijjā. Lokiyakusalākusalacetanā saṅkhārā. Lokiyavipākameva viññāṇaṃ. Lokiyavedanādikkhandhattayaṃ nāmaṃ, bhūtupādāyabhedaṃ rūpaṃ. Pasādaviññāṇabhedaṃ saḷāyatanaṃ. Vipākabhūto sabbo phasso, vedanā ca. Rāgo taṇhā. Balavarāgo, tividhā ca diṭṭhi upādānaṃ. Bhavo pana duvidho kammabhavo, upapattibhavo ca. Tattha kammabhavo sāsavakusalākusalacetanāva, upapattibhavo upādinnakakkhandhā. Tesaṃ upapatti jāti. Pāko jarā. Bhedo maraṇaṃ. Te eva nissāya socanaṃ soko. Kandanaṃ paridevo. Dukkhaṃ kāyikaṃ. Domanassaṃ cetasikaṃ. Ativiya soko upāyāso.

In the Pāḷi, in ‘with ignorance as condition’ and so on, ignorance is the lack of knowledge regarding suffering and so forth. Formations are worldly wholesome and unwholesome volitions. Consciousness is only worldly resultant consciousness. Name is the three worldly aggregates beginning with feeling. Form is that which is divided into primary elements and derived matter. The sixfold sense base is that which is divided into sense-sensitivity and consciousness. Contact is all that has come to be as a result, and so too is feeling. Craving is weak lust. Clinging is strong lust and the three kinds of wrong view. Existence, however, is twofold: kamma-existence and rebirth-existence. Therein, kamma-existence is only wholesome and unwholesome volitions connected with the cankers. Rebirth-existence is the aggregates that are the object of clinging. Their arising is birth. Ripening is aging. Breaking up is death. Dependent on these very things, sorrowing is sorrow. Lamenting is lamentation. Bodily suffering is suffering. Mental suffering is displeasure. Extreme sorrow is despair.

Paccekañca [V 2.0083] sambhavati-saddo yojetabbo. Tenāha “iminā nayenā”tiādi. “Dukkharāsissā”ti iminā na sattassa. Nāpi subhasukhādīnanti dasseti.

And the word ‘arises’ should be connected with each one. Therefore, he said, ‘by this method,’ and so on. By ‘of this mass of suffering,’ he shows that this is not the arising of a being, nor is it the arising of beauty, happiness, and so on.

Haveti byattanti imasmiṃ atthe nipāto. “Anulomapaccayākārapaṭivedhasādhakā bodhipakkhiyadhammā”ti idaṃ paṭhamavāre kiñcāpi “avijjāyatveva asesavirāganirodhā”tiādinā paṭilomapaccayākāropi āgato, tathāpi “yato pajānāti sahetudhamma”nti anulomapaccayākārapaṭivedhasseva kāraṇattena vuttanti. Yathā cettha, evaṃ dutiyavārepi “yato khayaṃ paccayānaṃ avedī”ti gāthāya vuttattā “paccayānaṃ khayasaṅkhāta”ntiādi [M 2.0085] vuttanti veditabbaṃ. No kallo pañhoti ayutto na byākātabbo, avijjamānaṃ attānaṃ siddhaṃ katvā “ko phusatī”ti tassa kiriyāya puṭṭhattā “ko vañjhāputto phusatī”tiādi viyāti adhippāyo. Soḷasa kaṅkhāti “ahosiṃ nu kho ahamatītamaddhānaṃ, nanu kho ahosiṃ, kiṃ nu kho ahosiṃ, kathaṃ nu kho ahosiṃ, kiṃ hutvā kiṃ ahosiṃ nu kho ahamatītamaddhānaṃ, bhavissāmi nu kho ahaṃ anāgatamaddhānaṃ, nanu kho bhavissāmi, kiṃ nu kho bhavissāmi, kathaṃ nu kho bhavissāmi, kiṃ hutvā kiṃ bhavissāmi nu kho ahaṃ anāgatamaddhānaṃ, ahaṃ nu khosmi, no nu khosmi, kiṃ nu khosmi, kathaṃ nu khosmi, ayaṃ nu kho satto kuto āgato, so kuhiṃ gāmī bhavissatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.18; saṃ. ni. 2.20) evaṃ āgatā atīte pañca, anāgate pañca, paccuppanne chāti soḷasavidhā kaṅkhā.

‘Haveti’ is a particle in the sense of ‘clearly.’ Regarding ‘the factors of enlightenment that accomplish the penetration of the dependent origination pattern in the forward order’—although in the first instance the reverse order of dependent origination is also mentioned, such as ‘with the complete fading away and cessation of ignorance,’ nevertheless, it is said to be the cause of penetrating the forward order of dependent origination, as in ‘when one understands the causally arisen phenomena.’ As it is here, so too in the second instance, because it is said in the verse, ‘when one knew the destruction of conditions,’ it should be understood that ‘what is called the destruction of conditions’ and so on is said. ‘The question is not proper’ means it is unsuitable, not to be answered. The intention is that, having posited a non-existent self as established and asked about its action with ‘who makes contact?’, it is like asking, ‘who is the son of a barren woman that makes contact?’ The sixteen doubts are: ‘Did I exist in the past? Did I not exist in the past? What was I in the past? How was I in the past? Having been what, what did I become in the past? Will I exist in the future? Will I not exist in the future? What will I be in the future? How will I be in the future? Having been what, what will I become in the future? Am I? Am I not? What am I? How am I? From where has this being come? Where will this being go?’ Thus, the sixteen kinds of doubt are the five concerning the past, five concerning the future, and six concerning the present.

Tattha kiṃ nu khoti manussadevādīsu, khattiyādīsu vā aññataraṃ nissāya kaṅkhati. Kathaṃ nu khoti pana saṇṭhānākārādīsu issarādijanakaṃ, kāraṇaṃ vā nissāya. Kiṃ hutvā kiṃ ahosinti ca manussādīsu paṭhamaṃ kiṃ hutvā pacchā kiṃ ahosinti kaṅkhati. Ahaṃ nu khosmītiādi idāni attano vijjamānāvijjamānataṃ, sarūpapakārādikañca kaṅkhati. Vapayantīti viapayanti byapagacchanti. Tenāha “apagacchanti nirujjhantī”ti.

Therein, regarding ‘what indeed?’, one doubts with reference to one or another among humans, devas, etc., or among khattiyas, etc. Regarding ‘how indeed?’, one doubts with reference to shape, appearance, etc., or a cause that produces sovereignty, etc. Regarding ‘Having been what, what did one become?’, one doubts thus: among humans, etc., having been what first, what did one become afterwards? Regarding ‘Am I?’, etc., one now doubts about one's own existence and non-existence, and one's own nature, variety, etc. ‘Vapayanti’ means they are removed, they depart. For that reason, it is said: ‘they depart, they cease.’

3. Tassa vasenāti tassa paccayākārapajānanassa, paccayakkhayādhigamassa ca vasena. Ekekameva koṭṭhāsanti anulomapaṭilomato ekekameva koṭṭhāsaṃ. Pāṭipadarattiyā evaṃ manasākāsīti rattiyā tīsupi yāmesu evaṃ idha khandhakapāḷiyā āgatanayena anulomapaṭilomaṃyeva manasākāsi.

3. ‘By means of that’ refers to by means of his understanding of the pattern of conditions and his attainment of the exhaustion of conditions. ‘Each single portion’ means each single portion in forward and reverse order. ‘On the first night of the lunar fortnight, he attended thus’ means that during all three watches of the night, he attended thus, only to the forward and reverse order, according to the method that came in the Khandhaka-pāḷi.

Ajapālakathāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Ajapāla Story

4. Tassa [V 2.0084] sattāhassa accayenāti pallaṅkasattāhassa apagamanena. Tamhā samādhimhāti arahattaphalasamāpattisamādhimhā. Antarantarā eva hi paccayākāramanasikāro. Avasesakālaṃ pana sabbaṃ bhagavā phalasamāpattiyāpi vītināmesi. Taṃ sandhāya “tamhā samādhimhā”ti vuttaṃ. Ratanacaṅkameti [M 2.0086] bhagavato ciraṃ ṭhitassa caṅkamanādhippāyaṃ ñatvā devatāhi māpite ratanacaṅkame. Ratanagharanti bhagavato nisīdanādhippāyaṃ ñatvā devatāhi māpitaṃ ratanamayaṃ gehaṃ.

4. ‘At the end of that week’ means by the passing of the week spent in the cross-legged posture. ‘From that concentration’ means from the concentration which is the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship. For indeed, attention to the pattern of conditions occurs only intermittently. But the Blessed One passed all the remaining time in the attainment of fruition itself. With reference to that, it is said, ‘from that concentration.’ ‘The Jeweled Promenade’ refers to the jeweled promenade created by the deities, who knew the Blessed One’s intention to walk after having stood for a long time. ‘The Jeweled House’ refers to the jeweled house created by the deities, who knew the Blessed One’s intention to sit.

Tatrāpīti na kevalaṃ ratanaghareyeva. Tatrāpi ajapālanigrodhamūlepi abhidhammaṃ vicinanto eva antarantarā vimuttisukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedentoti attho. Tatthāpi hi anantanayasamantapaṭṭhānaṃ sammasato sammāsambuddhassa pītisamuṭṭhitā chabbaṇṇā buddharasmiyo ratanaghare viya nicchariṃsu eva. “Huṃhu”nti karontoti “sabbe hīnajātikā maṃ mā upagacchantū”ti mānavasena, samīpaṃ upagatesu kodhavasena ca “apethā”ti adhippāyanicchāritaṃ huṃhuṃkāraṃ karonto.

‘There too’ means not only in the Jeweled House. The meaning is that there too, at the foot of the Ajapāla banyan tree, while investigating the Abhidhamma, he intermittently experienced the bliss of liberation. For there too, as the Perfectly Enlightened One was contemplating the Samantapaṭṭhāna with its infinite methods, the six-colored Buddha-rays, arisen from rapture, streamed forth just as in the Jeweled House. ‘Making the “huṃ huṃ” sound’ means making the “huṃ huṃ” sound to express the intention ‘Go away!’, both through the power of conceit with the thought ‘Let no one of low birth approach me,’ and through the power of anger towards those who came near.

Brahmaññanti brāhmaṇattaṃ. Antanti nibbānaṃ. Devānaṃ vā antanti maggañāṇānaṃ vā antabhūtaṃ arahattaphalaṃ.

‘Brahmañña’ means the state of being a brahmin. ‘The end’ means Nibbāna. Or, ‘the end of the vedas’ means the fruit of Arahantship, which is the culmination of the path-knowledges.

Mucalindakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Account of Mucalinda

5. Mucalindamūleti ettha ca mucalindo vuccati nīparukkho, yo “niculo”tipi vuccati. Uppannameghoti sakalacakkavāḷagabbhaṃ pūretvā uppanno mahāmegho. Vaddalikāti vuṭṭhiyā eva itthiliṅgavasena nāmaṃ. Yā ca sattāhaṃ pavattattā sattāhavaddalikāti vuttāti āha “sattāhaṃ avicchinnavuṭṭhikā ahosī”ti. Sītavātena dūsitaṃ dinametissā vaddalikāyāti sītavātaduddinīti āha “udakaphusitasammissenā”tiādi. Ubbiddhatā nāma dūrabhāvena upaṭṭhānanti āha “meghavigamena dūrībhūta”nti. Indanīlamaṇi viya dibbati jotetīti devo, ākāso.

5. Here, in the phrase ‘at the root of the Mucalinda,’ the nīpa tree is called ‘mucalinda,’ which is also called ‘nicula.’ ‘A cloud had arisen’ means a great cloud that arose, filling the entire Cakkavāḷa-sphere. ‘Vaddalikā’ is a name for rain, by way of the feminine gender. And because it continued for seven days, it is called ‘sattāhavaddalikā’ (a seven-day rain-shower); therefore, it is said, “There was continuous rain for seven days.” A day of this rain-shower afflicted by a cold wind is a ‘sītavātaduddinī’ (a dark day with a cold wind); therefore, it is said, “mixed with sprinkles of water,” etc. ‘Ubbiddhatā’ means presence by way of being far; therefore, it is said, “become distant by the departure of the cloud.” Because it shines and illuminates like an Indanīla gem (sapphire), the sky is called ‘deva.’

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti vivekassa sukhabhāvaṃ viditvā. Sabbaso asantuṭṭhisamucchedakattā maggañāṇānaṃ “catumaggañāṇasantosenā”ti vuttaṃ. Akuppanabhāvoti akujjhanasabhāvo.

‘Having understood this matter’ means having understood the blissful nature of seclusion. Because the path-knowledges utterly cut off dissatisfaction, it is said, “by the contentment of the four path-knowledges.” ‘The unshakeable state’ means the nature of not being angered.

Rājāyatanakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Account of the Rājāyatana

6. Paccaggheti [V 2.0085] abhinave. Ayameva attho pasattho, na purimo. Na hi buddhā mahagghaṃ pattaṃ paribhuñjanti.

6. ‘Paccagghe’ means brand new. This very meaning is praised, not the former. For indeed, Buddhas do not use a bowl of great value.

Brahmayācanakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Account of Brahmā's Entreaty

7. Ālīyanti [M 2.0087] sevīyantīti ālayā. Pañca kāmaguṇāti āha “sattā…pe… vuccantī”ti. Suṭṭhu muditāti ativiya pamuditā. Ṭhānaṃ sandhāyāti ṭhāna-saddaṃ apekkhitvā. Imesanti saṅkhārādīnaṃ phalānaṃ. Pāḷiyaṃ sabbasaṅkhārasamathotiādīni nibbānavevacanāni. Apissūti sampiṇḍanatthe nipāto. Na kevalaṃ etadahosi, imāpi gāthā paṭibhaṃsūti attho.

7. Because they are clung to and resorted to, they are called ‘ālayā’ (attachments). The five strands of sensual pleasure are ‘ālayā.’ Therefore, he said: “beings… etc. … are called…” ‘Suṭṭhu muditā’ means exceedingly delighted. ‘Ṭhānaṃ sandhāya’ means having regard for the word ‘ṭhāna.’ ‘Imesaṃ’ means ‘of these fruits, namely formations and so on.’ In the Pāḷi, the phrases beginning with ‘the stilling of all formations’ are synonyms for Nibbāna. ‘Apissū’ is a particle in the sense of aggregation. The meaning is: “Not only did this thought occur, but these verses also appeared.”

Kicchena me adhigatanti pāramipūraṇaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, na dukkhāpaṭipadaṃ. Buddhānañhi cattāro maggā sukhāpaṭipadāva honti. Ha-iti byattaṃ, ekaṃsanti dvīsu atthesu nipāto, byattaṃ, ekaṃsena vā alanti viyojenti. Halanti vā eko nipāto.

“With difficulty was it attained by me” was said with reference to the fulfillment of the perfections, not with reference to the painful practice. For indeed, the four paths of the Buddhas are only of pleasant practice. The particle ‘ha’ occurs in two meanings: ‘byattaṃ’ (clearly) and ‘ekaṃsaṃ’ (certainly). ‘Alaṃ’ means useless. Alternatively, ‘halaṃ’ is a single particle.

8. Pāḷiyaṃ sahampatissāti so kira kassapassa bhagavato sāsane sahako nāma thero paṭhamajjhānabhūmiyaṃ brahmapati hutvā nibbatto, tena naṃ “sahampatī”ti sañjāniṃsu. Assavanatāti assavanatāya, assavanenāti attho. Savanameva hi savanatā yathā devatāti.

8. In the Pāḷi, regarding ‘sahampatissa’: it is said that in the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, a thera named Sahaka was reborn in the first jhāna realm, having become a lord of Brahmās; therefore, they knew him as ‘Sahampati.’ ‘Assavanatā’ means ‘due to not hearing’ or ‘by not hearing’; this is the meaning. For hearing itself is ‘savanatā,’ just as in the case of ‘devatā.’

Dhammo asuddhoti micchādiṭṭhidhammo. Samalehīti pūraṇakassapādīhi chahi satthārehi. Apāpurāti desanāhatthena vivara. Dvāranti ariyamaggaṃ sandhāya vadati.

‘The Dhamma is impure’ means the Dhamma of wrong view. ‘By the stained ones’ means by the six teachers beginning with Pūraṇa Kassapa. ‘Apāpura’ means: open with the hand that is teaching. As for ‘dvāraṃ’ (door), he says it with reference to the noble path.

Seleti ghanasilāmaye. Tathūpamanti ettha tathā-saddo taṃ-saddatthe daṭṭhabbo. Tena so selapabbato upamā yassa. Taṃ tathūpamanti attho. Tena vā pabbatādinā pakārena upamā assātipi attho. Dhammamayanti lokuttaradhammabhūtaṃ. Uṭṭhāhīti dhammadesanatthāya cārikacaraṇatthaṃ imamhā āsanā kāyena, appossukkabhāvato vā cittena uṭṭhehi, ayameva vā pāṭho. Teneva “vicara, desassū”ti duvidhepi kāyacittapayoge niyojesi. Vīrātiādi cattāri thutivasena sambodhanāni.

‘Sele’ means made of solid rock. Here, in ‘tathūpamaṃ,’ the word ‘tathā’ should be seen in the meaning of the word ‘taṃ.’ Therefore, the meaning is: that Dhamma which has that rock mountain as its simile is ‘tathūpamaṃ.’ Alternatively, the meaning is also: for this Dhamma, there is a simile in the manner of that mountain, etc. ‘Dhammamayaṃ’ means consisting of the supramundane Dhamma. ‘Uṭṭhāhi’ (Arise) means: for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma and for the purpose of wandering on tour, arise from this seat with the body, or from the state of being without concern with the mind. Or, this is the very reading. For that very reason, with “wander, teach,” he urged both kinds of application: of body and of mind. The four terms beginning with ‘vīra’ are vocatives by way of praise.

9. Buddhacakkhunāti [V 2.0086] indriyaparopariyattañāṇena, āsayānusayañāṇena ca. Imesañhi dvinnaṃ “buddhacakkhū”ti nāmaṃ. Svākārāti saddhindriyādayova ākārā [M 2.0088] sundarā yesaṃ, te svākārā, suviññāpayā, paralokañca vajjañca bhayato dassanasīlā cāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Uppalāni ettha santīti uppalinīti gacchalatāpi pokkharaṇīpi vuccati. Idha pana pokkharaṇī. Evamitaresupi. Udakānuggatānīti udakato anuggatāni. Anto nimuggāneva hutvā pusanti vaḍḍhanti, tāni antonimuggaposīni. Accuggammāti udakaṃ atikkamanavasena uggantvā.

9. ‘With the Buddha-eye’ means with the knowledge of the maturity and immaturity of faculties and with the knowledge of dispositions and underlying tendencies. Indeed, the name of these two is “the Buddha's eye.” ‘Svākārā’ means: they whose characteristics, namely the faith faculty and so on, are beautiful, they are ‘svākārā’; they are also easy to instruct and are disposed to see the next world and faults as fearful—thus it should be understood. Because water lilies are here (‘ettha santi’), it is an ‘uppalinī’; both a bush and a pond are so called. But here, it is a pond. Thus also in the other cases. ‘Udakānuggatāni’ means not having emerged from the water. Having remained submerged within, they are nourished and grow; they are ‘antonimuggaposīni’ (nourished while submerged within). ‘Accuggamma’ means having ascended by way of surpassing the water.

Apārutāti vivaṭā. Tesanti saupanissayānaṃ sattānaṃ. Dvārāti ariyamaggadvārāni. Idañca attano sayambhuñāṇena saupanissayānaṃ tesaṃ magguppattidiṭṭhataṃ sandhāya vadati. Vihiṃsasaññītiādīsu evamattho daṭṭhabbo – “ahañhi attano paguṇaṃ suppavattitampi imaṃ paṇītaṃ dhammaṃ ajānantesu manujesu desanāya vihiṃsā kāyavācākilamatho hotī”ti evaṃ vihiṃsasaññī hutvā na bhāsiṃ bhāsituṃ na icchiṃ. Idāni pana hetusampannā attano saddhābhājanaṃ vivarantu, pūressāmi nesaṃ saṅkappanti.

‘Apārutā’ means opened. ‘Tesaṃ’ means for beings who have a supporting condition. ‘Dvārā’ means the doors of the noble path. And this he says with reference to his having seen, with his own self-become knowledge, the arising of the path for those beings with a supporting condition. In the phrases beginning with ‘vihiṃsasaññī,’ the meaning should be seen thus: “For me, by teaching this sublime Dhamma, even though well-practiced and well-mastered by myself, to humans who do not know it, there would be vexation, a weariness of body and speech.” Thus, having had the perception of vexation, I did not speak; I did not wish to speak. But now, let those endowed with the necessary conditions open the vessel of their faith; I will fulfill their intention.

Pañcavaggiyakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse concerning the Group of Five

10. Āḷāroti nāmaṃ. Kālāmoti gottaṃ. Bhagavatopi kho ñāṇaṃ udapādīti kiṃ idāneva udapādi, nanu bodhimūle tekālikā, kālavinimuttā ca sabbe dhammā sabbākārato diṭṭhāti? Saccaṃ diṭṭhā, tathāpi nāmādivasena avikappitā ekacittakkhaṇikattā sabbaññutaññāṇassa. Na hi ekena cittena sabbadhammānaṃ nāmajātiādikaṃ paccekaṃ anantaṃ vibhāgaṃ vikappetuṃ sakkā vikappānaṃ viruddhānaṃ sahānuppattito, sabbavikappārahadhammadassanameva panānena sakkā kātuṃ. Yathā diṭṭhesu pana yathicchitākāraṃ ārabbha vikappo uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇena diṭṭhe cittapaṭe viya. Idhāpi āḷāraṃ nissāya āvajjanānantarameva sabbākārañāṇaṃ udapādi. Na kevalañca taṃ, atha kho pañcavaggiyā eva paṭhamaṃ dhammaṃ jānissanti, tappamukhā ca devatā, āḷāro kālaṃ katvā ākiñcaññāyatane, udako ca nevasaññānāsaññāyatane nibbattoti evamādikaṃ sabbampi nissāya ñāṇaṃ uppajjati eva. Taṃ pana khaṇasampattiyā dullabhabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ kamena oloketvā devatāya vutte ñāṇaṃ viya katvā [M 2.0089] vuttaṃ. Saddagatiyā hi bandhattā ekena ñāṇena ñātampi vuccamānaṃ kamena ñātaṃ viya paṭibhāti, devatāpi ca bhagavatā ñātamevatthaṃ ārocesi. Teneva “bhagavatopi kho ñāṇaṃ udapādī”ti vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evamaññatthāpi īdisesu “lokaṃ volokento asukaṃ addasa, tattha [V 2.0087] mayi gate kiṃ bhavissatī”ti evamādinā satthu hitesitāsandassanavasappavattesu. Sabbattha vacanagatiyaṃ kamavuttite paññāyamānepi ekeneva ñāṇena sakalāvabodho veditabbo. Bahukārā kho me pañcavaggiyāti upakārassāpi vijjamānataṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, na pana dhammadesanāya kāraṇattena anupakārānampi desanato.

10. ‘Āḷāra’ is the name. ‘Kālāma’ is the clan. Regarding the phrase, ‘And in the Blessed One, too, knowledge arose’: Did knowledge arise just now? Was it not at the root of the Bodhi tree that all phenomena—those of the three times and those free from time—were seen in every aspect? Truly, they were seen. Even so, they were not differentiated by way of name and so on, because of the single-mind-moment nature of omniscience-knowledge. For it is not possible with one mind to individually differentiate the infinite classifications, such as name and origin, of all phenomena, due to the non-co-arising of conflicting differentiations. However, by this knowledge, it is possible only to see all phenomena that are free from differentiation. But with regard to things that have been seen, differentiation arises, taking as its object the desired aspect, like differentiation arising in regard to an intricate cloth seen by eye-consciousness. Here too, based on Āḷāra, immediately after adverting, the knowledge of all aspects arose. And it did not arise based only on him, but in fact, knowledge arose based on all such things as: ‘The group of five will be the first to know the Dhamma, and the deities headed by them will also know’; and ‘Āḷāra, having passed away, has been reborn in the sphere of nothingness, and Udaka in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.’ But that statement was made by the Elder Upāli, who wished to show the rarity of the attainment of the opportune moment, making it seem as if the knowledge arose only after a deity spoke, having considered the matter. For, being bound by the way of speech, even what is known by a single knowledge, when spoken of, appears as if known sequentially. And the deity, too, reports a matter already known by the Blessed One. Therefore, it should be understood that it was said, ‘And in the Blessed One, too, knowledge arose.’ So it is also in other similar instances, in all places where the Teacher's words proceed from his demonstration of a search for the welfare of beings, such as, ‘Surveying the world, he saw so-and-so; what will happen when I go there?’ Even though the way of speech appears to be sequential, the complete understanding should be known to be by a single knowledge. The statement, ‘The group of five were very helpful to me,’ was said with reference to the existence of their help, but not as the reason for teaching the Dhamma, because He also taught those who were not helpful.

11. Antarā ca gayaṃ antarā ca bodhinti gayāya, bodhissa ca antare tigāvute ṭhāne.

11. ‘Between Gayā and between Bodhi’ means: in a place three gāvutas between Gayā and the Bodhi tree.

Sabbābhibhūti sabbaṃ tebhūmakadhammaṃ abhibhavitvā ṭhito. Anūpalittoti kilesalepena alitto. Tato eva sabbañjaho. Taṇhakkhaye vimuttoti taṇhakkhaye nibbāne ārammaṇakaraṇavasaena vimutto. Evaṃ sayaṃ sabbadhamme attanāva jānitvā. Kamuddiseyyanti kaṃ aññaṃ “ayaṃ me ācariyo”ti uddiseyyaṃ.

As for 'All-conquering' (Sabbābhibhū): He stands having overcome all phenomena of the three realms. As for 'Unstained' (Anūpalitta): He is unstained by the stain of defilements. For that very reason, he is the 'Abandoner of all' (Sabbañjaho). As for 'Liberated in the destruction of craving' (Taṇhakkhaye vimutto): He is liberated by way of taking as object Nibbāna, which is the destruction of craving. Thus, having known all phenomena by myself, on my own. As for 'Whom should I point out?' (Kamuddiseyyaṃ): Whom else should I point out, saying, 'This is my teacher'?

Kāsinaṃ puranti bārāṇasiṃ. Āhañchanti āhanissāmi. Amatādhigamāya ugghosanato amatadundubhinti satthu dhammadesanā vuttā, “amatabheriṃ paharissāmī”ti gacchāmīti attho.

As for 'the city of the Kāsis' (Kāsinaṃ puraṃ): it means Bārāṇasī. As for 'I shall strike' (Āhañchaṃ): it means 'I shall beat'. Because it proclaims the attainment of the Deathless, the Teacher's Dhamma teaching is called the 'Drum of the Deathless' (amatadundubhi). The meaning is: 'I go to beat the drum of the Deathless'.

Arahasi anantajinoti anantajinopi bhavituṃ yuttoti attho. Anantañāṇatāya ananto jino ca, anantena vā ñāṇena, anantaṃ vā dosaṃ jitavā, uppādavayantarahitatāya vā anantaṃ nibbānaṃ ajini kilesārayo madditvā gaṇhītipi anantajino.

As for 'You are worthy, O Infinite Conqueror' (Arahasi anantajino): the meaning is, 'You are worthy to be an Infinite Conqueror.' Because of having infinite knowledge, he is 'Infinite' (Ananta), and he is a 'Conqueror' (Jina). Or, he has conquered with infinite knowledge. Or, he has conquered infinite faults. Or, because it is free from the limits of arising and ceasing, he has conquered the infinite Nibbāna. Also, because he has crushed and seized the enemies that are the defilements, he is called 'Infinite Conqueror' (Anantajino).

Hupeyyāpīti evampi bhaveyya, evaṃvidhe rūpakāyaratane īdisena ñāṇena bhavitabbanti adhippāyo. Evaṃ nāma kathanañhissa upanissayasampannassa aparakāle dukkhappattassa bhagavantaṃ upagamma pabbajitvā maggaphalapaṭivedhāya paccayo jāto. Tathāhesa bhagavā tena samāgamatthaṃ padasāva maggaṃ paṭipajji.

As for 'It could be so' (Hupeyyāpi): it means 'It might be so.' The intention is this: 'In such a jewel of a physical body, such a knowledge should exist.' Thus, this speaking of the name became a supporting condition for that Upaka—who was endowed with supporting conditions and in a later time met with suffering—to approach the Blessed One, go forth, and realize the path and its fruit. For that very reason, the Blessed One traveled that path on foot in order to meet him.

12. Bāhullikoti [M 2.0090] paccayabāhulliko. Padhānavibbhantoti padhānato dukkaracaraṇato parihīno. Natthi ettha agāriyaṃ, agārassa hitaṃ kasigorakkhādikammanti anagāriyā, pabbajjā, taṃ anagāriyaṃ. Pabbajantīti upagacchanti. Tadanuttaranti taṃ anuttaraṃ. Brahmacariyapariyosānanti maggabrahmacariyassa pariyosānaṃ, arahattaphalanti attho. Tassa hi atthāya kulaputtā pabbajanti. Diṭṭheva dhammeti imasmiṃ paccakkhe attabhāve. Sayanti aparappaccayā[V 2.0088]. Abhiññā sacchikatvāti attanova ñāṇena paccakkhaṃ katvā. Upasampajjāti pāpuṇitvā.

12. As for 'living in abundance' (Bāhulliko): it means abundant in requisites. As for 'fallen away from striving' (Padhānavibbhanto): it means fallen away from striving, from the practice of austerities. Herein there is no 'household life' (agāriyaṃ)—work for the benefit of a house such as ploughing, tending cattle, etc.—therefore, the going forth is called 'homelessness' (anagāriyā). As for 'they go forth' (pabbajanti): it means they approach. As for 'that unsurpassed' (tadanuttaraṃ): it means that which is unsurpassed. As for 'the culmination of the holy life' (brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ): the meaning is the fruit of Arahantship, which is the culmination of the holy life that is the path. For it is for the sake of this that clansmen go forth. As for 'in this very life' (diṭṭheva dhamme): it means in this present existence. As for 'by oneself' (sayaṃ): it means not relying on another. As for 'having realized for oneself through direct knowledge' (abhiññā sacchikatvā): it means having made it manifest with one's own knowledge. As for 'having attained' (upasampajja): it means having reached.

Iriyāyāti dukkarairiyāya. Uttarimanussadhammātiādīsu manussadhammato lokiyañāṇato upari ariyaṃ kātuṃ alaṃ samattho alamariyo. Ñāṇadassanavisesoti sabbaññutaññāṇassa pubbabhāgaṃ adhippetaṃ. Noti nu. Bhāsitametanti evarūpametaṃ vākyabhedanti attho. Te ca “yadi esa padhānakāle ‘ahaṃ arahā’ti vadeyya, mayañca saddahāma, na cānena tadā vuttaṃ. Idāni pana vijjamānameva guṇaṃ vadatī”ti ekapadena satiṃ labhitvā “buddho jāto”ti uppannagāravā āvusovādaṃ pahāya “no hetaṃ, bhante”ti āhaṃsu. Aññā cittanti aññāya arahattappattiyā cittaṃ.

As for 'by conduct' (iriyāya): it means by difficult conduct. In phrases such as 'superhuman states' (uttarimanussadhammā): it means what is above the human state, that is, worldly knowledge; it is capable of making one noble (ariya), hence 'alamariya' (sufficient for making one noble). As for 'the distinction of knowledge and vision' (ñāṇadassanaviseso): the preliminary stage of omniscience-knowledge is intended. The word 'no' has the same meaning as 'nu'. As for 'this was spoken' (bhāsitametaṃ): the meaning is 'this statement is of such a kind'. And they, having regained mindfulness with a single word, thinking, 'If, during the time of his striving, he had said, "I am an Arahant," we would have believed him, but he did not say so then. Now, however, he speaks of a quality that is actually present,' and with reverence arisen, thinking, 'A Buddha has arisen!', they abandoned addressing him as 'friend' (āvuso) and said, 'Not so, venerable sir' (no hetaṃ, bhante).
