As for 'the mind for final knowledge' (aññā cittaṃ): it means the mind for the attainment of Arahantship through final knowledge.

13. Antāti koṭṭhāsā dve bhāgā. Kāmesu kāmasukhallikānuyogoti vatthukāmesu kilesakāmasukhassa anubhavo. Kilesakāmā eva vā āmisasukhena allīyanato kāmasukhallikāti vuttāti daṭṭhabbā. Gammoti gāmavāsīnaṃ santako. Attakilamathānuyogoti attano kilamathassa kaṇṭakaseyyādidukkhassa anuyogo. Ubho anteti yathāvutte lobho vā sassato vā eko anto, doso vā ucchedo vā ekoti veditabbo.

13. As for 'extremes' (antā): they are portions, two parts. As for 'the pursuit of indulgence in sensual pleasures' (kāmesu kāmasukhallikānuyogo): it is the enjoyment of the pleasure of defiled sensuality in regard to sensual objects. Or, it should be understood that defiled sensual desires themselves, because they cling through material pleasure, are called 'indulgence in sensual pleasure' (kāmasukhallikā). As for 'low' (gammo): it means belonging to villagers. As for 'the pursuit of self-mortification' (attakilamathānuyogo): it is the practice of one's own exhaustion, of suffering such as sleeping on a bed of thorns. As for 'both extremes' (ubho ante): it should be understood thus: greed or eternalism is one extreme; hatred or annihilationism is the other extreme.

Cakkhukaraṇītiādīsu attanā sampayuttañāṇacakkhuṃ karotīti cakkhukaraṇī. Dutiyaṃ tasseva vevacanaṃ. Upasamoti kilesupasamo. Abhiññā, sambodho ca catusaccapaṭivedhova. Nibbānaṃ asaṅkhatadhātu. Etesampi atthāya saṃvattatīti paṭipadaṃ thometi. Sammādiṭṭhīti ñāṇaṃ. Sammāsaṅkappoti vitakko. Sesaṃ dhammato suviññeyyameva.

In the terms beginning with 'vision-producing' (cakkhukaraṇī): because it produces the eye of knowledge associated with oneself, it is called 'vision-producing'. The second term is a synonym for that very one. As for 'calming' (upasamo), it is the calming of the defilements. 'Higher knowledge' (abhiññā) and 'full enlightenment' (sambodho) are indeed the penetration of the Four Truths. Nibbāna is the unconditioned element. 'It conduces to the benefit of these as well'—thus it praises the path. As for 'right view' (sammādiṭṭhi), it is knowledge. As for 'right thought' (sammāsaṅkappo), it is thought. The remainder is indeed easy to understand in terms of its intrinsic nature.

14. Evaṃ [M 2.0091] cattāropi magge ekato dassetvā idāni tehi maggehi paṭivijjhitabbāni cattāri ariyasaccāni dassetuṃ “idaṃ kho pana, bhikkhave”tiādimāha. Jātipi dukkhātiādīsu tattha tattha bhave nibbattamānānaṃ sattānaṃ sabbapaṭhamaṃ rūpārūpadhammappavatti idha jāti nāma, sā ca tattha tattha bhavesu upalabbhamānānaṃ dukkhādīnaṃ vatthubhāvato dukkhā, evaṃ jarādīsu dukkhavatthukatāya dukkhatā veditabbā. Pañcupādānakkhandhā pana dukkhadukkhavipariṇāmadukkhasaṅkhāradukkhavasena dukkhā eva. Ponobhavikāti punabbhavakaraṇaṃ punabbhavo uttarapadalopena, punabbhavo sīlametissāti ponobhavikā. Nandirāgasahagatāti ettha rūpādīsu nandati piyāyatīti nandī, sā eva rāgoti nandirāgoti bhāvappadhānoyaṃ niddeso, nandirāgattanti [V 2.0089] attho. Tena sahagatāni nandirāgasahagatā. Tatra tatrāti tasmiṃ tasmiṃ bhave. Rūpādīsu chasu ārammaṇesu kāmassādanavasena pavattā kāmataṇhā nāma. Sassatadiṭṭhiyā saha pavattā bhavataṇhā. Ucchedadiṭṭhiyā saha pavattā vibhavataṇhā. Asesavirāganirodhotiādinā nibbānameva vuccati. Tattha virajjanaṃ vigamanaṃ virāgo. Nirujjhanaṃ nirodho. Ubhayenāpi suṭṭhu vigamova vuccati. Asesāyapi taṇhāya virāgo, nirodho ca yena hoti, so asesavirāganirodho, nibbānameva. Yasmā ca taṃ āgamma taṇhaṃ, vaṭṭañca cajanti paṭinissajjanti vimuccanti na allīyanti, tasmā cāgo paṭinissaggo mutti anālayoti vuccati.

14. Having thus shown the four paths together, now, in order to show the Four Noble Truths that are to be penetrated by those paths, he spoke the words beginning with, 'Now this, O monks...'. In the phrases beginning with 'birth is suffering': here, for beings being born in this or that existence, the very first arising of material and immaterial phenomena is called 'birth'. And that birth is 'suffering' because it is the basis for the various kinds of suffering found in those various existences. In the same way, in the case of aging and so on, their nature as suffering should be understood from their being a basis for suffering. As for the five aggregates of clinging, they are indeed suffering by way of being suffering-as-suffering, suffering-due-to-change, and suffering-due-to-formations. As for ponobhavikā: punabbhavakaraṇaṃ (the making of a new existence) becomes punabbhavo by the elision of the latter word. Because its nature (sīla) is renewed existence (punabbhavo), it is called ponobhavikā. In the phrase nandirāgasahagatā: 'it delights, it holds dear in regard to forms, etc.'—thus it is nandī. That very thing is lust (rāgo)—thus it is nandirāgo. This is an explanation where the abstract noun is primary; the meaning is 'the state of delight-lust'. Accompanied by that, it is nandirāgasahagatā. As for tatra tatra: in this or that existence. Craving that arises in the six sense objects, such as forms, by way of enjoying sensual pleasures, is called craving for sensual pleasures (kāmataṇhā). Craving that arises together with the eternalist view is craving for existence (bhavataṇhā). Craving that arises together with the annihilationist view is craving for non-existence (vibhavataṇhā). By the words beginning with asesavirāganirodho, Nibbāna itself is spoken of. Therein, fading away, departing, is virāgo. Ceasing is nirodho. By both terms, a complete departure is spoken of. That by which there is the remainderless fading away and cessation of all craving is asesavirāganirodho; this is Nibbāna itself. And because, having come to that, they abandon and relinquish craving and the round of existence, are liberated, and do not cling, it is therefore called cāgo (abandonment), paṭinissaggo (relinquishment), vimutti (liberation), and anālayo (non-reliance).

15. Cakkhuntiādīni ñāṇavevacanāneva.

15. The terms beginning with cakkhu are indeed synonyms for knowledge.

16. Yāvakīvañcāti yattakaṃ kālaṃ. Tiparivaṭṭanti saccañāṇa, kiccañāṇa, katañāṇasaṅkhātānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ parivaṭṭānaṃ vasena tiparivaṭṭaṃ ñāṇadassanaṃ. Ettha ca “idaṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ, idaṃ dukkhasamudaya”nti evaṃ catūsu saccesu yathābhūtañāṇaṃ saccañāṇaṃ nāma. Tesu eva “pariññeyyaṃ pahātabbaṃ sacchikātabbaṃ bhāvetabba”nti evaṃ kattabbakiccajānanañāṇaṃ kiccañāṇaṃ nāma. “Pariññātaṃ pahīnaṃ sacchikataṃ bhāvita”nti tassa kiccassa katabhāvajānanañāṇaṃ katañāṇaṃ nāma. Dvādasākāranti tesameva ekekasmiṃ sacce tiṇṇaṃ tiṇṇaṃ ākārānaṃ vasena dvādasākāraṃ.

16. As for yāvakīvañca, it means: for whatever length of time. As for tiparivaṭṭaṃ (of three cycles): it is the knowledge and vision with three cycles by way of the three cycles known as knowledge of the truth (saccañāṇa), knowledge of the function (kiccañāṇa), and knowledge of the accomplishment (katañāṇa). And here, the knowledge of things as they truly are regarding the Four Truths—thus, 'This is the Noble Truth of Suffering,' 'This is the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering,' and so on—is called knowledge of the truth. Regarding those same truths, the knowledge of knowing the task to be done—thus, 'it should be fully understood,' 'it should be abandoned,' 'it should be realized,' 'it should be developed'—is called knowledge of the function. The knowledge of knowing the state of that task having been accomplished—thus, 'it has been fully understood,' 'it has been abandoned,' 'it has been realized,' 'it has been developed'—is called knowledge of the accomplishment. As for dvādasākāraṃ (of twelve aspects): it has twelve aspects by way of three aspects in each single truth among those very truths.

Abhisambuddhoti paccaññāsinti abhisambuddho arahattaṃ pattoti evaṃ na paṭijāniṃ. Yato ca khoti yato bodhimūle nisinnakālato paṭṭhāya[M 2.0092]. Athāhanti tato paraṃ ahaṃ. Ñāṇañca pana meti paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ sandhāya vadati. Akuppā metiādi tassa pavattiākāradassanaṃ. Tattha akuppā me vimuttīti arahattaphalaṃ tassa maggasaṅkhātakāraṇato ca ārammaṇato ca akuppatā veditabbā.

Regarding the claim to be fully enlightened (abhisambuddhoti paccaññāsiṃ), the meaning is: I did not claim, 'I am fully enlightened; I have attained Arahantship.' As for yato ca kho: from the time of sitting at the root of the Bodhi tree onwards. As for athāhaṃ: thereafter, I. As for ñāṇañca pana me, he speaks referring to the reviewing knowledge. The words beginning with akuppā me are a demonstration of the manner of its arising. Therein, as for akuppā me vimutti (my liberation is unshakeable), this is the fruit of Arahantship. Its unshakeable nature should be understood by way of its cause, known as the path, and by way of its object.

Imasmiṃ pana veyyākaraṇasminti niggāthasutte. Bhaññamāneti bhaṇiyamāne. Dhammacakkhunti idha catusaccadhammesu cakkhukiccakaraṇato sotāpattimaggo adhippeto. Yaṃ kiñcītiādi nibbānārammaṇattepi kiccavasena asammohato pavattidassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ.

As for imasmiṃ pana veyyākaraṇasmiṃ: in the discourse without verses. As for bhaññamāne: while it was being spoken. As for dhammacakkhu: here, the path of stream-entry is intended, because it performs the function of an eye in regard to the phenomena of the Four Truths. The words beginning with yaṃ kiñci were said in order to show its arising through non-delusion by way of its function, even though it has Nibbāna as its object.

17. Dhammacakkanti paṭivedhañāṇadhammañceva desanāñāṇadhammañca pavattanaṭṭhena cakkanti dhammacakkaṃ[V 2.0090]. Obhāsoti sabbaññutaññāṇānubhāvena pavatto cittapaccayautusamuṭṭhāno dasasahassilokadhātuṃ pharitvā ṭhito obhāso.

17. As for dhammacakkaṃ: both the Dhamma which is the knowledge of penetration and the Dhamma which is the knowledge of teaching are a 'wheel' (cakka) in the sense of setting in motion; therefore, it is the dhammacakka. As for obhāso: it is the radiance, arisen through the power of the knowledge of omniscience and produced by temperature which has mind as its condition, that stood pervading the ten-thousandfold world-system.

18. Diṭṭho ariyasaccadhammo etenāti diṭṭhadhammo. Esa nayo sesesupi. Attano paccakkhato adhigatattā na paraṃ pacceti, parassa saddhāya ettha na pavattatīti aparappaccayo. Ehi bhikkhūti ettake vuttamatte pabbajjā, upasampadā ca sijjhati, teneva tattha iti-saddena paricchedo dassitoti vadanti. Keci pana “sammā dukkhassa antakiriyāyāti vacanapariyosāne eva upasampadā sijjhati, aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana ‘ehi bhikkhūti bhagavato vacanenā’ti idaṃ ehibhikkhusaddopalakkhitavacanaṃ ehibhikkhuvacanantiādipadavasena vuttaṃ musāvādavaggotiādīsu viyā”ti vadanti, tadetaṃ paṭhamapārājikaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “bhagavā hi…pe… ehi bhikkhu, cara brahmacariyaṃ sammā dukkhassa antakiriyāyā”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.45 bhikkhūpadabhājanīyavaṇṇanā) iminā vacanena sameti. Yattakañhi bhagavatā niyamena vuccati, tattakaṃ sabbampi aṅgameva. Sekkhaputhujjanānañhi etaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ vuccati, asekkhānaṃ pana “cara brahmacariya”nti pariyosānanti daṭṭhabbaṃ sikkhattayasamiddhito. Lokiyasampadāhi uparibhūtā seṭṭhabhūtā sampadāti upasampadā.

18. ‘The Dhamma of the Noble Truths is seen by this one,’ thus he is called ‘one who has seen the Dhamma’ (diṭṭhadhamma). This is the method for the remaining terms as well. Because it is realized by one's own direct experience, one does not rely on another; one does not proceed in this matter by faith in another—thus, one is ‘not reliant on another’ (aparappaccayo). They say that with just the words, “Come, bhikkhu,” both the going forth and the higher ordination are accomplished; therefore, the word iti is used there to show a delimitation. Some, however, say that the higher ordination is accomplished only at the conclusion of the statement, “for the right ending of suffering.” But in the commentary, this phrase, “by the Blessed One’s words, ‘Come, bhikkhu,’” is said by way of being the initial phrase indicating the utterance that begins with the words “Come, bhikkhu,” as in the sections on the Musāvāda Vagga and so on. This agrees with the statement in the commentary on the first Pārājika: “For the Blessed One… (etc.)… ‘Come, bhikkhu, live the holy life for the right ending of suffering.’” For whatever is spoken definitively by the Blessed One, all of that is a component. For trainees and worldlings, this is spoken in full. But for the Asekhas (those beyond training), it should be understood that the conclusion is “live the holy life,” because they are endowed with the threefold training. An accomplishment that is higher and more excellent than worldly accomplishments is called ‘higher ordination’ (upasampadā).

19-21. Nīhārabhattoti bhikkhūhi gāmato nīharitvā dinnabhatto. Kallaṃ nūti yuttaṃ nu. Etaṃ mamātiādi yathākkamaṃ taṇhāmānadiṭṭhigāhānaṃ dassanaṃ.

Nīhārabhatta is food brought out from the village by monks and then given. ‘Kallaṃ nu’ means ‘Is it fitting?’ ‘This is mine,’ and so forth, demonstrates the grasping of craving, conceit, and views, respectively.

22-23. Tasmā [M 2.0093] tihāti ettha tihāti nipātamattaṃ, tasmāti attho. Nibbindatīti vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanāvasena ukkaṇṭhati. Virajjatīti catunnaṃ maggānaṃ vasena na rajjati. Vimuccatīti phalavasena vimuccati. Vimuttasmintiādi paccavekkhaṇañāṇadassanaṃ. Brahmacariyanti maggabrahmacariyaṃ. Karaṇīyaṃ catūsu saccesu catūhi maggehi paccekaṃ kattabbaṃ pariññādivasena soḷasavidhaṃ kiccaṃ. Nāparaṃ itthattāyāti itthabhāvāya soḷasakiccabhāvāya, kilesakkhayāya vā aparaṃ puna maggabhāvanākiccaṃ me natthīti pajānāti. Atha vā itthattāyāti itthabhāvato vattamānakkhandhasantānato aparaṃ khandhasantānaṃ mayhaṃ na bhavissatīti attho.

22-23. Here, in ‘tasmā tihā,’ ‘tiha’ is merely a particle; the meaning is ‘therefore.’ ‘He becomes disenchanted’ means he feels revulsion by way of insight leading to emergence. ‘He becomes dispassionate’ means he is not impassioned by way of the four paths. ‘He is liberated’ means he is liberated by way of fruition. ‘When liberated,’ and so forth, demonstrates the knowledge of reviewing. ‘The holy life’ means the holy life of the path. ‘What was to be done’ is the sixteenfold task to be performed individually for the four truths by the four paths, by way of full understanding, and so forth. ‘There is nothing further for this state’ means he understands thus: “For me there is no other task of developing the path again for the sake of this state—that is, for the sixteenfold task—or for the destruction of defilements.” Alternatively, ‘for this state’ means: from this present continuum of aggregates, another continuum of aggregates will not arise for me.

Pabbajjākathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse of the Going Forth

15. Āḷambaranti paṇavaṃ. Vikesikanti vippakiṇṇakesaṃ. Vikkheḷikanti vissandamānalālaṃ[V 2.0091]. Susānaṃ maññeti susānaṃ viya addasa sakaṃ parijananti sambandho. Udānaṃ udānesīti saṃvegavasappavattaṃ vacanaṃ nicchāresi. Upassaṭṭhanti dukkhena sammissaṃ, dukkhotiṇṇaṃ sabbasattakāyajātanti attho.

15. ‘Āḷambara’ means a tabor. ‘Vikesika’ means one with disheveled hair. ‘Vikkheḷika’ means one with flowing saliva. ‘He thought it a charnel ground’: the connection is that he saw his own retinue as if it were a charnel ground. ‘He uttered an inspired utterance’ means he voiced words that arose through the power of spiritual urgency. ‘Afflicted’ means the entire host of beings is entangled with suffering, filled with suffering.

26. Idaṃ kho yasāti bhagavā nibbānaṃ sandhāyāha. Anupubbiṃ kathanti anupaṭipāṭikathaṃ. Ādīnavanti dosaṃ. Okāranti nihīnatā nihīnajanasevitattā. Saṃkilesanti tehi sattānaṃ saṃkilesanaṃ, saṃkilesavisayanti vā attho. Kallacittanti arogacittaṃ. Sāmaṃ attanāva ukkaṃso ukkhipanaṃ etissanti sāmukkaṃsikā, saccadesanā. Tassā sarūpadassanaṃ “dukkha”ntiādi.

26. The Blessed One said, “This, Yasa…” with reference to Nibbāna. ‘A gradual discourse’ means a discourse in sequence. ‘Danger’ means a fault. ‘Baseness’ means inferiority, because it is resorted to by base people. ‘Defilement’ means the defiling of beings by those things, or it means being the object of defilements. ‘With a fit mind’ means with a mind free from sickness. Because in this teaching there is an uplifting, an exaltation, by the Buddha himself, this teaching of the truths is called ‘personally exalted’ (sāmukkaṃsikā). The words “suffering,” and so forth, demonstrate its nature.

27. Assadūteti assaāruḷhe dūte. Iddhābhisaṅkhāranti iddhikiriyaṃ. Abhisaṅkharesi akāsi.

27. ‘Horse-messengers’ means messengers riding on horses. ‘Creation of psychic power’ means the act of creation by psychic power. ‘He created’ means he performed.

28. Yathādiṭṭhanti paṭhamamaggena diṭṭhaṃ catussaccabhūmiṃ sesamaggattayena paccavekkhantassa, passantassāti attho. Mātu no jīvitanti ettha noti nipātamattaṃ, mātu jīvitanti attho. Yasassa khīṇāsavattā “ehi bhikkhu, svākkhāto dhammo, cara brahmacariya”nti ettakeneva bhagavā upasampadaṃ adāsi. Khīṇāsavānañhi ettakeneva upasampadā anuññātā pubbeva dukkhassa parikkhīṇattā. Cara brahmacariyanti sāsanabrahmacariyasaṅkhātaṃ sikkhāpadapūraṇaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, na maggabrahmacariyaṃ.

28. ‘As seen’ means for one who sees, who reviews with the remaining three paths, the ground which is the four truths seen by the first path. In ‘Give life to our mother,’ ‘no’ is merely a particle; the meaning is ‘Give life to your mother.’ Because Yasa’s taints were destroyed, the Blessed One gave him the higher ordination with just this: “Come, bhikkhu; the Dhamma is well-proclaimed; live the holy life.” For those whose taints are destroyed, higher ordination is permitted with just this much, because suffering was already destroyed beforehand. “Live the holy life” was said with reference to the fulfillment of the training rules, known as the holy life of the Dispensation; it was not said with reference to the holy life of the path.

30. Seṭṭhānuseṭṭhīnanti [M 2.0094] seṭṭhino ca anuseṭṭhino ca paveṇīvasena āgatā yesaṃ kulānaṃ santi, tesaṃ seṭṭhānuseṭṭhīnaṃ kulānaṃ. Orakoti lāmako.

30. ‘Of treasurers and sub-treasurers’ refers to those families for whom there are treasurers and sub-treasurers who have come by way of lineage. ‘Oraka’ means base.

32-33. Mā ekena dveti ekena maggena dve bhikkhū mā agamittha. Visuddhe satte, guṇe vā māretīti māro. Pāpe niyutto pāpimā.

32-33. ‘Not two by one’ means two bhikkhus should not go by one path. Because he kills purified beings or virtues, he is called Māra. Because he is engaged in evil, he is called Pāpimā, the Evil One.

Sabbapāsehīti sabbakilesapāsehi. Ye dibbā ye ca mānusāti ye dibbakāmaguṇanissitā, mānusakakāmaguṇanissitā ca kilesapāsā nāma atthi, sabbehi tehi. “Tvaṃ buddho”ti devamanussehi kariyamānasakkārasampaṭicchanaṃ sandhāya vadati.

‘By all snares’ means by all the snares of the defilements. ‘Those which are divine and those which are human’ refers to all those snares of defilements that are based on divine sensual pleasures and those based on human sensual pleasures. He says, “You are the Buddha,” with reference to the acceptance of honor made by devas and humans.

Antalikkhe [V 2.0092] carante pañcābhiññepi bandhatīti antalikkhacaro, rāgapāso. Māro pana pāsampi antalikkhacaraṃ maññati. Mānasoti manosampayutto.

Because it binds even those with the five supernormal knowledges who travel in the sky, the snare of lust is called the ‘sky-wanderer’ (antalikkhacaro). But Māra thinks that the snare, too, wanders in the sky. ‘Mānasa’ means associated with the mind.

Jānāti manti so kira “mahānubhāvo añño devaputto nivāretīti bhīto nivattissati nu kho”tisaññāya vatvā “nihato tvamasi antakā”ti vutte “jānāti ma”nti dummano palāyi.

As for ‘He knows me’: Māra, having spoken with the thought, “Will the noble Gotama perhaps turn back, fearing that another devaputta of great power is obstructing him?”—when he was told, “You are defeated, O Ender!”—became dejected and fled, thinking, “He knows me.”

34. Parivitakko udapādīti yasmā ehibhikkhubhāvāya upanissayarahitānampi pabbajitukāmatā uppajjissati, buddhā ca te na pabbājenti, tasmā tesampi pabbajjāvidhiṃ dassento evaṃ parivitakkesīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Upanissayasampannā pana bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā ehibhikkhubhāveneva pabbajanti. Ye paṭikkhittapuggalāti sambandho. Sayaṃ pabbājetabboti ettha “kesamassuṃ ohāretvā”tiādivacanato kesacchedanakāsāyacchādanasaraṇadānāni pabbajjā nāma, tesu pacchimadvayaṃ bhikkhūhi eva kātabbaṃ, kāretabbaṃ vā. “Pabbājehī”ti idaṃ tividhampi sandhāya vuttaṃ. Khaṇḍasīmaṃ netvāti bhaṇḍukammārocanapariharaṇatthaṃ. Bhikkhūnañhi anārocetvā ekasīmāya “etassa kese chindā”ti aññaṃ āṇāpetumpi na vaṭṭati. Pabbājetvāti kesādicchedanameva sandhāya vuttaṃ “kāsāyāni acchādetvā”ti visuṃ vuttattā. Pabbājetuṃ na labhatīti saraṇadānaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, anupasampannena bhikkhuāṇattiyā dinnampi saraṇaṃ na ruhati.

34. As for 'A thought arose': because the desire to go forth will arise even for those who are devoid of the supporting conditions for the 'ehi-bhikkhu' state, and the Buddhas do not ordain them, it should be understood that he reflected thus, showing the procedure of ordination for them as well. Those, however, who are endowed with the supporting conditions, approach the Blessed One and go forth simply by means of the 'ehi-bhikkhu' state. The connection is: 'Which persons are rejected.' In the phrase 'He should be ordained by oneself,' from the statement beginning with 'having shaved off hair and beard,' the cutting of hair, the donning of the ochre robe, and the giving of the refuges are called 'going forth.' Of these, the latter two must be done only by bhikkhus, or they must have it done. The word 'Ordain him' is said with reference to all three aspects in order to avoid announcing the act of shaving. Indeed, it is not proper for bhikkhus, without announcing it, to command another person within the same boundary, saying, 'Cut this one's hair.' 'Having ordained him' is said with reference only to the cutting of hair and so on, because 'having clothed him in ochre robes' is stated separately. 'He is not able to ordain' is said with reference to the giving of the refuges, for a refuge, even if given by one who is not fully ordained by the command of a bhikkhu, is not established.

Yasassīti parivārasampanno. Nijjīvanissattabhāvanti “kesā nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño [M 2.0095] nissatto thaddho pathavīdhātū”tiādinayaṃ saṅgaṇhāti, sabbaṃ visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.311) āgatanayena gahetabbaṃ. Pubbeti pubbabuddhuppādesu. Madditasaṅkhāroti vipassanāvasena vuttaṃ. Bhāvitabhāvanoti samathavasenāpi.

As for 'renowned' (yasassī): he is endowed with a retinue. By the text 'the state of being lifeless and without a soul,' it includes the method beginning: 'Hairs, namely, in this body are a separate part, without consciousness, undeclared, empty, not a being, hard, the earth element.' All should be understood according to the method that comes in the Visuddhimagga. As for 'formerly' (pubbe): in the times of the arising of previous Buddhas. The word 'madditasaṅkhāro' (one who has crushed formations) is said by way of insight. The word 'bhāvitabhāvano' (one who has developed development) is said also by way of serenity.

Kāsāyāni tikkhattuṃ vā…pe… paṭiggāhāpetabboti ettha “sabbadukkhanissaraṇatthāya imaṃ kāsāvaṃ gahetvā”ti vā “taṃ kāsāvaṃ datvā”ti vā vatvā “pabbājetha maṃ, bhante, anukampaṃ upādāyā”ti evaṃ yācanapubbakaṃ cīvaraṃ paṭicchāpeti. Athāpītiādi tikkhattuṃ paṭiggāhāpanato paraṃ kattabbavidhidassanaṃ. Athāpīti tato parampīti attho. Keci pana “cīvaraṃ appaṭiggāhāpetvā pabbajanappakārabhedadassanatthaṃ “athāpī”ti vuttaṃ, athāpīti ca atha vāti attho”ti vadanti. “Adinnaṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti iminā pabbajjā na ruhatīti dasseti.

In the phrase 'The ochre robes should be caused to be accepted three times, or... etc.': having said either, 'For the purpose of realizing Nibbāna, the escape from all suffering, having taken this ochre robe,' or, 'having given that ochre robe,' he has him accept the robe, preceded by the request, 'Venerable sirs, ordain me out of compassion.' The words beginning with 'Then also' are for showing the procedure to be done after having him accept it three times. 'Then also' means 'after that as well.' Some teachers, however, say: 'It is said "then also" for the purpose of showing a different type of ordination procedure without having him accept the robe; and "then also" means "or alternatively."' By this text, 'What is not given is not proper,' it shows that the state of being a novice is not established.

Pāde [V 2.0093] vandāpetvāti pādābhimukhaṃ namāpetvā. Dūre vandantopi hi pāde vandatīti vuccati. Upajjhāyena vāti ettha yassa santike upajjhaṃ gaṇhāti, ayaṃ upajjhāyo. Ābhisamācārikesu vinayanatthaṃ yaṃ ācariyaṃ katvā niyyātenti, ayaṃ ācariyo. Sace pana upajjhāyo sayameva sabbaṃ sikkhāpeti, aññasmiṃ na niyyāteti, upajjhāyovassa ācariyopi hoti, yathā upasampadākāle sayameva kammavācaṃ vācento upajjhāyova kammavācācariyopi hoti.

As for 'having had him pay homage at the feet': having had him bow facing the feet. Indeed, even one who pays homage from afar is said to 'pay homage at the feet.' In the phrase 'By the preceptor or...': the bhikkhu in whose presence one takes the preceptor's guidance, this one is called the preceptor. The one to whom they entrust him, having made him a teacher for the purpose of instruction in the duties of proper conduct, this one is called the teacher. But if the preceptor himself teaches all the duties and does not entrust him to another, his preceptor is also the teacher, just as at the time of higher ordination, the preceptor who himself recites the formal act (kammavācā) is also the teacher of the formal act (kammavācācariya).

Anunāsikantaṃ katvā dānakāle antarā vicchedo na kātabboti āha “ekasambandhānī”ti.

Having made it end with a nasal consonant, a break should not be made in between at the time of giving the refuges; therefore, he said, 'as a single connected phrase.'

“Ābhisamācārikesu vinetabbo”ti iminā sekhiyavattakhandhakavattesu, aññesu

By this text, 'He should be trained in the duties of proper conduct,' it refers to the duties of the Sekhiyas, the duties of the Khandhakas, and in other...

Ca sukkavissaṭṭhiādilokavajjasikkhāpadesu sāmaṇerehi vattitabbaṃ, tattha avattamāno alajjī, daṇḍakammāraho ca hotīti dasseti.

...and in the training rules concerning worldly faults beginning with the emission of semen, it should be practiced by novices. It is shown that a novice who does not practice in accordance with them is shameless and is also deserving of punishment.

Pabbajjākathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the discourse on the going forth is finished.

Dutiyamārakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Second Story of Māra

35. Pāḷiyaṃ [M 2.0096] anuttaraṃ vimuttiṃ anupāpuṇāthāti “khīṇāsavā mayaṃ, kiṃ amhākaṃ padhānenā”ti vāsanādosena vosānaṃ anāpajjitvā pantesu senāsanesu phalasamāpattiyāva vītināmanatthaṃ, taṃ disvā aññesampi diṭṭhānugatisamāpajjanatthañca ovadatīti veditabbaṃ.

35. In the Pāḷi, by the words 'attain the unsurpassed liberation,' He advises so that, through the fault of latent tendencies, they would not come to a conclusion with the thought, 'We are those with taints destroyed; what is the use of striving for us?' but would instead pass the time in secluded dwellings with the attainment of fruition, and also so that others, seeing this, might follow the example they have seen. Thus it should be understood.

Dutiyamārakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Second Story of Māra is concluded.

Bhaddavaggiyakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Story of the Bhaddavaggiyas

36. Idaṃ nesaṃ pubbakammanti tesaṃ tiṃsajanānaṃ ekato abhisamayassa pubbakammaṃ. Aññampi tesaṃ paccekaṃ pubbabuddhuppādesu saddhammassavanasaraṇagamanadānasīlasamādhivipassanāsamāyogavasena bahuṃ vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ kusalaṃ atthevāti gahetabbaṃ. Itarathā hi tadaheva paṭivedho, ehibhikkhubhāvādiviseso ca na sampajjeyya.

36. As for 'This is their past kamma': it is the past kamma of those thirty men for their simultaneous realization. Moreover, it should be understood that for each of them, there was indeed much wholesome kamma that is a supporting condition for liberation, by way of listening to the true Dhamma, going for refuge, giving, observing precepts, and practicing concentration and insight during the time of past Buddhas. Indeed, otherwise, the penetration of the truth and the distinction of becoming an 'ehi-bhikkhu' and so on would not have come to pass.

Bhaddavaggiyakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Story of the Bhaddavaggiyas is concluded.

Uruvelapāṭihāriyakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Story of the Miracle at Uruvelā

37-38. Pāḷiyaṃ [V 2.0094] agarūti bhāriyaṃ na siyāti attho. Ubhinnaṃ sajotibhūtānanti ubhosu sajotibhūtesu. Patte pakkhipīti taṃ nāgaṃ nihatatejaṃ dhammadesanāya santappetvā saraṇasīlāni datvā sakalarattiṃ bhagavantaṃ payirupāsitvā ṭhitaṃ jaṭilānaṃ dassanatthaṃ patte pakkhipi, na ahituṇḍiko viya balakkārenāti veditabbaṃ. Yatra hi nāmāti yo nāma.

In the Pāḷi, as for 'not heavy,' the meaning is 'it should not be burdensome.' As for 'of the two who were ablaze,' it means 'when both were ablaze.' As for 'he placed it in the bowl': having satisfied that nāga—whose power was subdued—with a Dhamma discourse, having given the refuges and precepts, and who stood attending upon the Blessed One for the entire night, he placed him in the bowl for the purpose of showing the matted-hair ascetics. It should be understood that he did not place him by force, like a snake charmer. As for 'yatra hi nāma,' it means 'whichever great monk.'

39. Ajjaṇhoti ajja ekadivasaṃ. Aggisālamhīti agyāgāre. Sumanānaṃ buddhānaṃ manasā sadiso mano assāti sumanamanaso. Adhicittoti mahākaruṇādīhi adhicitto. Udicchareti ullokesuṃ, parivāresunti attho. Anekavaṇṇā acciyoti chabbaṇṇaraṃsiyo vuttā. Ahaṃ te dhuvabhattena paṭimānanaṃ karissāmīti seso.

39. As for 'ajjaṇho,' it means 'today, for one day.' As for 'aggisālamhi,' it means 'in the fire-hut.' He is 'sumanamanaso' because he has a mind similar to the mind of the Buddhas of good mind. As for 'adhicitto,' it means one with a superior mind due to great compassion and so on. As for 'udicchare,' the meaning is 'they looked up' or 'they surrounded.' By 'flames of many colors,' the six-colored rays are meant. 'I will honor you with a constant supply of food' is the remainder of the text.

40. Abhikkantāya [M 2.0097] rattiyāti parikkhīṇāya rattiyā, majjharattisamayeti attho. Abhikkantavaṇṇāti abhirūpacchavivaṇṇā. Kevalakappanti ettha kevala-saddassa anavasesattho, kappa-saddassa samantabhāvo, tasmā anavasesaṃ samantato vanasaṇḍanti attho. Catuddisāti catūsu disāsu. Yatra hi nāmāti yaṃ nāma.

40. As for 'when the night had passed,' it means 'when the night was spent'; the meaning is 'at midnight.' As for 'of excellent appearance,' it means 'having a very beautiful complexion.' In 'kevalakappaṃ,' the word 'kevala' has the meaning 'entire/without remainder,' and the word 'kappa' has the meaning 'all around'; therefore, the meaning is 'the entire forest grove all around.' As for 'the four directions,' it means 'in the four directions.' As for 'yatra hi nāma,' it means 'whichever great monk.'

43. Aṅgamagadhāti aṅgamagadharaṭṭhavāsino. Iddhipāṭihāriyanti abhiññiddhiyeva paṭipakkhānaṃ titthiyānaṃ, veneyyasattagatadosānañca haraṇato apanayanato pāṭihāriyaṃ, taṃ taṃ vā sattahitaṃ paṭicca haritabbaṃ pavattetabbanti paṭihāriyaṃ, tadeva pāṭihāriyaṃ. Iddhi eva pāṭihāriyaṃ iddhipāṭihāriyaṃ.

43. As for 'Aṅga and Magadha,' it means 'the inhabitants of the countries of Aṅga and Magadha.' As for 'the miracle of psychic power': it is the psychic power of higher knowledge itself. It is called a 'pāṭihāriya' (miracle) because it removes and dispels the views of opposing sectarians and the faults found in trainable beings. Alternatively, it is called 'paṭihāriya' because it should be brought about and enacted in consideration of the welfare of various beings. That itself is the miracle. Psychic power itself is the miracle; thus, 'the miracle of psychic power.'

44. Paṃsukūlaṃ uppannaṃ hotīti puṇṇāya dāsiyā sarīraṃ parikkhipitvā chaḍḍitaṃ sāṇamayaṃ kimikulākulaṃ pariyesanavasena uppannaṃ hoti, yaṃ bhagavā bhūmiṃ kampento pārupitvā pacchā mahākassapattherassa adāsi, taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttanti vadanti. Kattha nu khotiādiparivitakko jaṭilānaṃ vividhapāṭihāriyadassanatthaṃ kato. Pāṇinā khaṇanto viya iddhiyā mattikaṃ apanetvā dinnattā vuttaṃ “pāṇinā pokkharaṇiṃ khaṇitvā”ti.

44. As for 'a rag-robe has arisen': a rag-robe made of hemp, infested with a multitude of worms, which had been discarded after wrapping the corpse of the slave-girl Puṇṇā, was obtained by way of searching. They say this was said in reference to that robe, which the Blessed One, causing the earth to shake, wore and later gave to the Elder Mahākassapa. The reflection beginning 'Where now...?' was brought about for the purpose of showing the matted-hair ascetics various miracles. It is said 'having dug a pond with his hand' because, as if digging with his hand, he removed the soil by psychic power and gave it.

46. Phāliyantu, kassapa, kaṭṭhānīti uruvelakassapena nivedite evamavocāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evaṃ sesesupi.

46. It should be understood that he spoke the words, 'Let the logs be split, Kassapa,' when it was reported by Uruvelakassapa. Likewise in the remaining cases.

49. Antaraṭṭhakāsu [V 2.0095] himapātasamayeti ettha māghamāsassa avasāne catasso, phagguṇamāsassa ādimhi catassoti evaṃ ubhinnaṃ māsānaṃ antare aṭṭharattiyo antaraṭṭhakā nāma. Tāsu antaraṭṭhakāsu rattīsu himapātakāle. Ummujjananimujjanampi sahasā tadubhayakaraṇavasena vuttaṃ.

49. Here, in 'during the time of snowfall in the intermediate eight days': four days at the end of the month of Māgha and four days at the beginning of the month of Phagguṇa—thus, the eight nights in between the two months are called 'antaraṭṭhakā.' It means during those 'antaraṭṭhakā' nights, at the time of snowfall. 'Emerging and submerging' is said by way of doing both of those things suddenly.

50. Udakavāhakoti udakogho. Reṇuhatāyāti rajokiṇṇāya, atintāyāti attho. Nāvāyāti kullena. Idaṃ nu tvaṃ mahāsamaṇāti idha nu tvaṃ. Dha-kārassa da-kāraṃ, anusārañca katvā “idaṃ nū”ti vuttaṃ “ekamidāha”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.165, 265) viya. “Imasmiṃ padese tvaṃ nu kho ṭhitosī”ti pucchi. Ayamahamasmīti ayamahaṃ idha ṭhitosmīti attho.

50. As for 'udakavāhako', it means a flood of water. As for 'reṇuhatāya', the meaning is 'covered with dust', 'not wet'. As for 'nāvāya', it means by a raft. As for 'idaṃ nu tvaṃ mahāsamaṇa', this means 'here, are you?'. By making the letter 'dha' into 'da' and adding an anusvāra, 'idaṃ nu' is said, as in 'ekamidāhaṃ' and so on. He asked, 'Are you standing in this place?' As for 'ayamahamasmī', the meaning is 'Here I am, standing in this place'.

51. Cirapaṭikāti [M 2.0098] cirakālato paṭṭhāya. Kesamissaṃ sabbaṃ parikkhāraṃ udake pavāhetvātipi yojetabbaṃ. Araṇikamaṇḍaluādikā tāpasaparikkhārā khārī nāma, taṃharaṇakakājaṃ khārikājaṃ nāma. Aggihutamissanti aggipūjopakaraṇasahitaṃ.

51. As for 'cirapaṭikā', it means 'starting from a long time ago'. It should also be construed as: 'having set adrift in the water all the requisites, including the matted hair'. The ascetic's requisites, such as the fire-stick and water-pot, are called 'khārī'. The carrying-pole for them is called 'khārikāja'. As for 'aggihutamissaṃ', it means 'together with the implements for the fire-sacrifice'.

52-3. Upasaggoti upaddavo. “Aḍḍhuḍḍhāni pāṭihāriyasahassānī”ti idaṃ nāgadamanādīni pannarasa pāṭihāriyāni vajjetvā vuttaṃ appakamadhikaṃ gaṇanūpagaṃ na hotīti.

52-53. As for 'upasaggo', it means 'calamity'. This phrase, 'three and a half thousand miracles,' was said excluding the fifteen miracles beginning with the taming of the nāga. It means that a little more or less does not come into the reckoning.

54. Gayāyanti gayānāmikāya nadiyā adūrabhavattā gāmo itthiliṅgavasena gayā nāma jāto, tassaṃ. Gayāsīseti evaṃnāmake piṭṭhipāsāṇe.

54. As for 'gayāyaṃ': because of its proximity to the river named Gayā, the village came to be called Gayā, by way of the feminine gender; it means 'in that Gayā'. As for 'gayāsīse', it means 'on the rock plateau so named'.

“Yamidaṃ cakkhusamphassapaccayā…pe… sukhaṃ vā”tiādinā cakkhuviññāṇavīthicittesu somanassadomanassaupekkhāvedanāmukhena sesārūpakkhandhānampi ādittataṃ dasseti. Esa nayo sesesupi. Manoti bhavaṅgacittaṃ manodvārassa adhippetattā. Manoviññāṇanti manodvāravīthipaayāpannameva gahitaṃ.

By the text beginning, 'Whatever... conditioned by eye-contact... whether pleasant...', he shows the inflamed nature of the remaining mental aggregates as well, by means of pleasant, painful, and neutral feelings in the mind-states of the eye-consciousness process. This is the method in the remaining cases as well. As for 'mano', it is the life-continuum consciousness (bhavaṅga-citta), because the mind-door is intended. By the word 'manoviññāṇa', only the process-consciousness included in the mind-door process is taken.

Uruvelapāṭihāriyakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Story of the Miracle at Uruvelā is concluded.

Bimbisārasamāgamakathāvaṇṇanā

The Elucidation of the Account of Bimbisāra's Meeting

55. Yaññā [V 2.0096] abhivadantīti yāgahetu ijjhantīti vadanti. Upadhīsūti ettha dukkhasukhādīnaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhena cattāro upadhī kāmakhandhakilesaabhisaṅkhārūpadhīnaṃ vasena. Tesu khandhūpadhi idhādhippetoti āha “khandhūpadhīsu malanti ñatvā”ti. Yaññāti yaññahetu. Yiṭṭheti mahāyāge. Huteti divase divase kattabbe aggiparicaraṇe. Kiṃ vakkhāmīti kathaṃ vakkhāmi.

55. “Yaññā abhivadanti” means they say that one prospers due to sacrifice. In “upadhīsu,” in the sense of being the foundation for suffering, happiness, and so on, the four upadhis are so called by way of the upadhi of sensuality, the upadhi of the aggregates, the upadhi of the defilements, and the upadhi of formations. Among these, the upadhi of the aggregates is intended here; therefore, it is said, “having known the stain in the upadhis of the aggregates.” “Yaññā” means due to the cause which is sacrifice. “Yiṭṭhe” means in the great sacrifice. “Hute” means in the tending of the fire that should be done day by day. “Kiṃ vakkhāmi” means how shall I speak?

57-8. Āsīsanāti manorathā. Siṅgīsuvaṇṇanikkhenāti siṅgīsuvaṇṇassa rāsinā. Suvaṇṇesu hi yuttikataṃ hīnaṃ. Tato rasaviddhaṃ seṭṭhaṃ, tato ākaruppannaṃ seṭṭhaṃ, tato yaṃkiñci dibbasuvaṇṇaṃ seṭṭhaṃ[M 2.0099], tatrāpi cāmīkaraṃ, tato sātakumbhaṃ, tato jambunadaṃ, tatopi siṅgīsuvaṇṇaṃ seṭṭhaṃ. Tassa nikkhaṃ nāma pañcasuvaṇṇaparimāṇaṃ. Aṭṭhasuvaṇṇādibhedaṃ anekavidhampi vadanti. Dasasu ariyavāsesūti –

57–8. “Āsīsanā” means aspirations. “Siṅgīsuvaṇṇanikkhena” means by a heap of Siṅgī gold. Among golds, yuttikata gold is inferior. Superior to that is rasaviddha gold. Superior to that is ākaruppanna gold. Superior to that is any divine gold. Even among that divine gold, cāmīkara gold is superior. Superior to that is sātakumbha gold. Superior to that is jambunada gold. Even superior to that is siṅgī gold. A nikkha of that siṅgī gold has a measure of five suvaṇṇas. They also speak of many kinds with distinctions such as eight suvaṇṇas. As for “in the ten noble dwellings”:

“Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu pañcaṅgavippahīno hoti chaḷaṅgasamannāgato ekārakkho caturāpasseno paṇunnapaccekasacco samavayasaṭṭhesano anāvilasaṅkappo passaddhakāyasaṅkhāro suvimuttacitto suvimuttapañño”ti (dī. ni. 3.348, 360; a. ni. 10.19) –

“Here, monks, a monk is one who has abandoned five factors, is endowed with six factors, has one guard, has four supports, has dispelled the individual truths of views, has abandoned seeking, has undefiled intentions, has tranquilized bodily formations, has a well-liberated mind, and has well-liberated wisdom.”

Evamāgatesu dasasu ariyavāsesu. Tattha pañcaṅgavippahīnoti pañcanīvaraṇehi vippayuttatā vuttā. Chaḷaṅgasamannāgatoti iṭṭhādīsu chasu ārammaṇesu somanassitādipaṭipakkhā chaḷaṅgupekkhā vuttā. Ekārakkhoti upaṭṭhitasatitā. Saṅkhāyasevanā adhivāsanā parivajjanā vinodanāsaṅkhātāni cattāri apassenā nissayā etassāti caturāpasseno, etena ca te nissayā dassitā. Paṇunnāni apanītāni diṭṭhigatikehi paccekaṃ gahitāni diṭṭhisaccāni yassa, so paṇunnapaccekasacco, tena lokiyañāṇena diṭṭhippahānaṃ vuttaṃ. Kāmesanā bhavesanābrahmacariyesanāsaṅkhātā esanā sammadeva avayā anūnā saṭṭhā nisaṭṭhā anenāti samavayasaṭṭhesano. Etena tiṇṇaṃ esanānaṃ abhāvo vutto. “Anāvilasaṅkappo”ti iminā kāmavitakkādīhi anāvilacittatā. “Passaddhakāyasaṅkhāro”ti iminā catutthajjhānasamāyogena vigatadarathatā vuttā. “Suvimuttacitto”ti iminā maggo. “Suvimuttapañño”ti iminā paccavekkhaṇañāṇamukhena phalañāṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Ete hi ariyā vasanti etthāti ariyavāsāti vuccanti[V 2.0097]. Te pana vāsā vutthā vasitā sampāditā yena, so vutthavāso, bhagavā. Dasabaloti dasahi kāyabalehi, ñāṇabalehi ca upeto. Yāni hetāni –

In these ten noble abodes thus stated: By “one who has abandoned five factors,” freedom from the five hindrances is stated. By “endowed with six factors,” the six-factored equanimity, which is the opposite of joy and so on in the six sense objects beginning with the desirable, is stated. By “one guard,” the state of having established mindfulness is stated. He has four supports, called using with reflection, enduring, avoiding, and dispelling; therefore, he is one with four supports, and by this, those supports are shown. He is one for whom the individually-grasped truths of views held by those with wrong views are dispelled; therefore, he is one who has dispelled the individual truths of views. By this, the abandoning of views by mundane knowledge is stated. The quests—called seeking sensual pleasures, seeking existence, and seeking the holy life—have been well and truly abandoned without deficiency by this monk; therefore, he is one who has abandoned seeking. By this, the absence of the three quests is stated. By “undefiled intentions,” the state of having a mind undefiled by sensual thoughts and so on is stated. By “tranquilized bodily formations,” the state of being free from agitation through association with the fourth jhāna is stated. By “well-liberated mind,” the path is stated. By “well-liberated wisdom,” the knowledge of fruition, by means of reviewing knowledge, is stated. Indeed, the noble ones dwell in these, and therefore they are called “noble abodes.” Moreover, those abodes have been dwelt in and accomplished by the Blessed One; therefore, he is called “one who has dwelt the dwelling.” “One of ten powers” means he is endowed with the ten bodily powers and the ten knowledge powers. These are:

“Kāḷāvakañca gaṅgeyyaṃ, paṇḍaraṃ tambapiṅgalaṃ;

Gandhamaṅgalahemañca, uposathachaddantime dasā”ti. (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.148; saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 2.2.22; a. ni. aṭṭha. 3.10.21; vibha. aṭṭha. 760; udā. aṭṭha. 75; bu. va. aṭṭha. 1.39; cūḷani. aṭṭha. 81; paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 2.2.44) –

“Kāḷāvaka and Gaṅgeyya, Paṇḍara, Tamba, and Piṅgala; Gandha, Maṅgala, and Hema, Uposatha and Chaddanta—these are the ten.”

Evaṃ [M 2.0100] vuttāni dasahatthikulāni purimapurimato dasabalaguṇopetāni, tesu sabbajeṭṭhānaṃ dasannaṃ chaddantānaṃ balāni bhagavato kāyassa dasabalāni nāma. Tañca kāḷāvakasaṅkhātānaṃ pakatihatthīnaṃ koṭisahassassa, majjhimapurisānaṃ pana dasannaṃ koṭisahassānañca balaṃ hoti, taṃ “nārāyanasaṅghātabala”ntipi vuccati.

Thus were spoken of the ten elephant clans, each endowed with tenfold the strength of the one preceding it. Among them, the strengths of the ten foremost Chaddanta elephants are called the ten bodily powers of the Blessed One. And that strength is equal to that of a thousand koṭis of ordinary elephants known as Kāḷāvaka, and it is the strength of ten thousand koṭis of middle-sized men. That is also called 'the strength of Nārāyaṇa's host'.

Yāni panetāni pāḷiyaṃ “idha, sāriputta, tathāgato ṭhānañca ṭhānato aṭṭhānañca aṭṭhānato yathābhūtaṃ pajānātī”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.148; a. ni. 10.21; vibha. 760; paṭi. ma. 2.44) vuttāni ṭhānāṭhānañāṇabalaṃ, kammavipākañāṇabalaṃ, sabbatthagāminipaṭipadāñāṇabalaṃ, anekadhātunānādhātulokañāṇabalaṃ, sattānaṃ nānādhimuttikatāñāṇabalaṃ, indriyaparopariyattañāṇabalaṃ, jhānavimokkhasamādhisamāpattīnaṃ saṃkilesavodānavuṭṭhānañāṇabalaṃ, pubbenivāsañāṇabalaṃ, dibbacakkhuñāṇabalaṃ, āsavakkhayañāṇabalanti dasabalañāṇāni, imāni bhagavato dasabalāni nāma. Dasahi asekkhehi aṅgehīti arahattaphalasampayuttehi pāḷiyaṃ “asekkhā sammādiṭṭhi…pe… asekkho sammāsamādhi, asekkhaṃ sammāñāṇaṃ, asekkhā sammāvimuttī”ti (dī. ni. 3.348, 360) evaṃ vuttehi dasahi asekkhadhammehi samannāgato. Ettha ca dassanaṭṭhena vuttā sammādiṭṭhi eva jānanaṭṭhena sammāñāṇantipi vuttā, vuttāvasesā pana phalacittasampayuttā sabbe phassādidhammā sammāvimuttīti vuttāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

And these are the ten powers of knowledge spoken of in the Pāli, beginning with “Here, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata understands as it actually is the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible”: the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible; the power of knowing the results of actions; the power of knowing the path leading to all destinations; the power of knowing the world with its many and varied elements; the power of knowing the diverse inclinations of beings; the power of knowing the superior and inferior faculties of other beings; the power of knowing the defilement, cleansing, and emergence in meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments; the power of remembering past lives; the power of the divine eye; and the power of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. These are called the ten powers of the Blessed One. He is endowed with the ten non-learner's factors, that is, those associated with the fruit of arahantship, as stated in the Pāli: “The non-learner’s right view… the non-learner’s right concentration, the non-learner’s right knowledge, the non-learner’s right liberation.” And here, it should be understood that right view, spoken of in the sense of seeing, is also spoken of as right knowledge in the sense of knowing; and all the remaining factors associated with the fruition-consciousness, beginning with contact, are called right liberation.

Bimbisārasamāgamakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Elucidation of the Account of the Meeting with Bimbisāra is concluded.

Sāriputtamoggallānapabbajjākathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Story of the Going Forth of Sāriputta and Moggallāna

60. Sārībrāhmaṇiyā [V 2.0098] putto sāriputto. Moggalībrāhmaṇiyā putto moggallāno. Channaparibbājakassāti setavatthena hirikopīnaṃ chādetvā vicaraṇakaparibbājakassa, tena “nāyaṃ naggaparibbājako”ti dasseti. “Upaññāta”nti imassa vivaraṇaṃ ñāto cevāti. “Magga”nti imassa vivaraṇaṃ upagato ca maggoti. Tena ca upaññātanti ettha ñāta-saddo ñāṇapariyāyo. Magganti liṅgavipallāsena maggova vutto. Upasaddo ca upagamanattho maggasaddenapi sambandhitabboti dasseti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yasmā [M 2.0101] piṭṭhito piṭṭhito anubandhanaṃ nāma atthikehi upaññātaṃ upagatañāṇañceva hoti, tehi upagato paṭipanno maggo ca, tasmā yaṃnūnāhaṃ anubandheyyanti. Upaññātaṃ nibbānanti upapattiyā anumānena ñātaṃ nibbānaṃ. “Magga”nti imassa vivaraṇaṃ maggantoti, anumānena ñātaṃ paccakkhato dassanatthāya gavesantoti attho.

60. Sāriputta was the son of the brahmin woman Sārī. Moggallāna was the son of the brahmin woman Moggallī. “Of Channa the wanderer”: this refers to a wandering ascetic who covers his private parts with a white cloth, thereby showing that he is not a naked ascetic. The explanation of “upaññāta” is “ñāto ceva” (it is indeed known). The explanation of “maggaṃ” is “upagato ca maggo” (the path that has been approached). And by that, here in “upaññāta,” the word “ñāta” is a synonym for knowledge (ñāṇa). By “maggaṃ,” through a change of gender, only the path is spoken of. And it shows that the prefix “upa-,” having the meaning of approaching, should be connected with the word “magga.” This is what is said: Because following from behind is, for those who desire it, both knowledge that has been approached and the path that has been approached and entered upon by them, therefore, he thought, “Indeed, I should follow.” “Nibbāna is known” (upaññātaṃ nibbānaṃ) means Nibbāna known by inference through reasoning. The explanation of “maggaṃ” is “magganto” (seeking the path); the meaning is seeking to see directly what is known by inference.

Nirodho ca nirodhūpāyo ca ekasesena nirodhoti vuttoti dassento “atha vā”tiādimāha. Paṭipādentoti nigamento.

Showing that cessation and the means to cessation are spoken of as “cessation” by way of ekasesa, he said, “or else,” etc. “Paṭipādento” means “concluding.”

Ito uttarīti ito mayā laddhasotāpattito uttari itaramaggattayaṃ yadipi natthi, tathāpi eso eva mayā gavesito nibbānadhammoti attho.

“From here onwards”: The meaning is, beyond the stream-entry attained by me from this point, even if the other three paths do not yet exist, still, this itself is the Nibbāna-dhamma I have sought.

62-3. Tadārammaṇāyāti nibbānārammaṇāya sotāpattiphalavimuttiyā. Tesaṃ āyasmantānanti saparisānaṃ tesaṃ dvinnaṃ parisānaṃ tasmiṃyeva khaṇe bhagavato dhammaṃ sutvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi, aggasāvakā pana attano ñāṇakiccassa mahantatāya katipāhaccayena. Tenāha “eva”ntiādi. Usūyanakiriyāya kammabhāvaṃ sandhāya “upayogatthevā”ti vuttaṃ.

62-3. “Having that as its object” refers to the liberation of stream-entry fruition, which has Nibbāna as its object. “For those venerable ones” refers to those with their retinue; the retinues of those two attained Arahantship at that very moment upon hearing the Dhamma from the Blessed One. The chief disciples, however, due to the greatness of their task of knowledge, attained it after a few days. Therefore, he said, “evaṃ,” etc. With reference to being the object of the act of envying, it is said “in the sense of application.”

Sāriputtamoggallānapabbajjākathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Story of the Going Forth of Sāriputta and Moggallāna is concluded.

Upajjhāyavattakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Duties toward a Preceptor

64. Vajjāvajjanti khuddakaṃ, mahantañca vajjaṃ. Uttiṭṭhapattanti ettha uttiṭṭhaṃ nāma piṇḍāya caraṇaṃ vuccati “uttiṭṭhe nappamajjeyyā”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 168) viya. Uttiṭṭhatthāya [V 2.0099] gahitaṃ pattaṃ uttiṭṭhapattaṃ, tenāha “piṇḍāya caraṇakapatta”nti. Tassa upanāme ko dosoti āha “tasmiṃ hī”tiādi. Tasmāti yasmā manussā etasmiṃyeva ete bhuñjantīti uttiṭṭhapatte ucchiṭṭhasaññino, tasmā uttiṭṭhapattanti vuttaṃ uttiṭṭha-saddeneva manussānaṃ saññāya ucchiṭṭhatāpi gammatīti. Keci pana “ucchiṭṭhasaddena samānattho uttiṭṭhasaddo”ti vadanti. “Uttiṭṭhā”ti tvāpaccayantopi hotīti āha “uṭṭhahitvā”ti. Upajjhāyaṃ gahetunti upajjhāyattaṃ [M 2.0102] manasā gahetuṃ, yācanavacanena tassa anumatiṃ gahetunti vā attho.

64. “Vajjāvajjaṃ” means a minor and a major fault. “Uttiṭṭhapattaṃ” (alms-round bowl): here “uttiṭṭhaṃ” is said to mean going for alms, as in phrases like “One should arise, not be heedless,” etc. A bowl taken for the purpose of the alms-round is an “uttiṭṭhapattaṃ”; therefore, he said, “a bowl for going for alms.” As to what fault there is in offering that, he said, “For in that…,” etc. “Therefore”: because people perceive an alms-round bowl as containing leftovers, thinking, “they eat from this very bowl,” it is called an “uttiṭṭhapattaṃ.” By the very word “uttiṭṭha,” according to people's perception, the state of being a leftover is also understood. Some, however, say that the word “uttiṭṭha” has the same meaning as “ucchiṭṭha” (leftover). That “uttiṭṭhā” can also be a gerund is why he said “uṭṭhahitvā” (having stood up). “To take a preceptor” means to mentally accept his status as preceptor, or the meaning is to get his consent through a verbal request.

65. Patissayanaṃ patisso, garuṃ nissāya vattanabhāvo, yaṃkiñci gāravanti attho. Saha patissena sappatisso, paraṃ jeṭṭhaṃ katvā tassovāde vattanatāti attho. Tenāha “jeṭṭhakabhāvañca upaṭṭhapetvā”ti. Sāhūti sādhu sundaraṃ. Lahūti agaru, subharatāti attho. Opāyikanti upāyapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ, evaṃ paṭipajjanaṃ nittharaṇūpāyoti attho. Patirūpanti sāmīcikammamidanti attho. Pāsādikenāti pasādāvahena kāyavacīpayogena sampādehīti attho. Kāyenāti etadatthaviññāpakaṃ hatthamuddādiṃ dassento kāyena viññāpeti. Sādhūti sampaṭicchanaṃ sandhāyāti upajjhāyena “sāhū”tiādīsu vuttesu saddhivihārikassa “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchanaṃ vacanaṃ sandhāya “kāyena viññāpetī”tiādi vuttanti adhippāyo. Āyācanadānamattenāti saddhivihārikassa paṭhamaṃ āyācanamattena, tato upajjhāyassa ca “sāhū”tiādinā vacanamattenāti attho.

65. “Patissayana” means “patisso,” the state of living in dependence on a respected one; the meaning is any kind of respect. “Sappatisso” means with respect, respectful; the meaning is regarding another as a superior and conducting oneself according to their instruction. Therefore, he said, “having established the state of seniority.” “Sāhu” means good, beautiful. “Lahu” means not heavy; the meaning is easy to support. “Opāyikaṃ” means connected with a skillful means; the meaning is that such practice is a means to deliverance. “Patirūpaṃ” means “this is an appropriate action.” “Pāsādikena” means: accomplish with bodily and verbal conduct that inspires confidence. “Kāyena” means: he communicates with the body, showing a gesture of the hand or the like that conveys this meaning. With reference to the acceptance 'Sādhu': The meaning is that when the preceptor says 'sāhu' and so on, the phrase 'communicates with the body,' etc., is said with reference to the pupil's verbal acceptance 'sādhu'. “Āyācanadānamattena” means: merely by the pupil’s initial request, and then merely by the preceptor’s utterance of “sāhu” and so on.

66. Assāti saddhivihārikassa. Dve cīvarānīti uttarāsaṅgaṃ, saṅghāṭiñca sandhāya vadati. Ito paṭṭhāyāti “na upajjhāyassa bhaṇamānassā”ti ettha na-kārato paṭṭhāya, tena “nātidūre”tiādīsu na-kārapaṭisiddhesu āpatti natthīti dasseti. Sabbattha dukkaṭāpattīti āpadāummattakhittacittavedanaṭṭatādīhi vinā paṇṇattiṃ ajānitvāpi vadantassa gilānassapi dukkaṭameva. Āpadāsu hi antarantarā kathā vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Evamaññesupi na-kārapaṭisiddhesu īdisesu, itaresu pana gilānopi na muccati. Pāḷiyaṃ “heṭṭhāpīṭhaṃ vā parāmasitvā”ti idaṃ pubbe tattha ṭhapitapattādinā asaṅghaṭṭanatthāya vuttaṃ, cakkhunā oloketvāpi aññesaṃ abhāvaṃ ñatvāpi ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati eva. Āpattiyā āsannanti āpattikaraṇameva.

66. “Assa” refers to the pupil. “Two robes” refers to the upper robe and the outer robe. “From here onwards” means starting from the negative particle “na” in “not while the preceptor is speaking,” thereby showing that in prohibitions with the negative particle “na,” such as “not too far,” there is no offense. “A dukkaṭa offense in all cases” means: apart from cases of danger, insanity, a distracted mind, being afflicted by pain, and so on, for one who speaks without knowing the regulation, and also for a sick person, it is just a dukkaṭa offense. Indeed, in situations of danger, it is allowable to speak intermittently. Similarly, in other such prohibitions with 'na', a sick person is released, but in others, even a sick person is not released. In the Pāḷi, “or having felt underneath the chair or bed” was said to avoid collision with a bowl, etc., previously placed there; however, it is indeed allowable to place it after looking with the eye and knowing of the absence of other things. “Close to an offense” means the very act of committing an offense.

Gāmeti antogāme tādise maṇḍapādimhi. Antaraghareti antogehe. Paṭikkamaneti āsanasālāyaṃ. Dhotavālikāyāti udakena gataṭṭhāne nirajāya parisuddhavālikāya. Niddhūmeti jantāghare jaliyamānaaggidhūmarahite. Jantāgharañhi nāma himapātabahulesu desesu tappaccayarogapīḷādinivāraṇatthaṃ [M 2.0103][V 2.0100] sarīrasedāpanaṭṭhānaṃ. Tattha kira andhakārapaṭicchannatāya bahūpi ekato pavisitvā cīvaraṃ nikkhipitvā aggitāpaparihārāya mattikāya mukhaṃ limpitvā sarīraṃ yāvadatthaṃ sedetvā cuṇṇādīhi ubbaṭṭetvā nahāyanti. Teneva pāḷiyaṃ “cuṇṇaṃ sannetabba”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Ullokanti uddhaṃ olokanaṭṭhānaṃ. Uparibhāganti attho.

Gāme means: in a pavilion or the like of that sort within the village. Antaraghare means: inside a house. Paṭikkamane means: in a sitting hall. Dhotavālikāya means: on purified, dust-free sand in a place where water has flowed. Niddhūme means: in a steam-house, in a place free from the smoke of a burning fire. Indeed, a steam-house is a place in regions with abundant snowfall for inducing sweat in the body to prevent affliction by diseases and so on caused by that. There, it is said, because of being covered in darkness, many monks enter together, put down their robes, smear their faces with clay to ward off the heat of the fire, make the body sweat as much as desired, rub themselves with cleansing powder and so on, and bathe. For that very reason, in the Pāḷi it is said, “Cleansing powder should be prepared,” and so on. Ullokaṃ means: a place to be looked at upwards. The meaning is the upper part.

Aññattha netabboti yattha viharato sāsane anabhirati uppannā, tato aññattha kalyāṇamittādisampattiyuttaṭṭhāne netabbo. Visabhāgapuggalānanti lajjino vā alajjino vā upajjhāyassa avaḍḍhikāme sandhāya vuttaṃ. Sace pana upajjhāyo alajjī ovādampi na gaṇhāti, lajjino ca etassa visabhāgā honti, tattha upajjhāyaṃ vihāya lajjīheva saddhiṃ āmisādiparibhogo kātabbo. Upajjhāyādibhāvo hettha na pamāṇanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Pariveṇaṃ gantvāti upajjhāyassa pariveṇaṃ gantvā. “Na susāna”nti idaṃ upalakkhaṇaṃ, upacārasīmato bahi gantukāmena anāpucchā gantuṃ na vaṭṭati.

Aññattha netabbo means: when discontent with the Dispensation has arisen for a pupil where he is dwelling, he should be taken elsewhere to a place endowed with the accomplishment of good friends and so on. Visabhāgapuggalānaṃ is said with reference to those, whether conscientious or unconscientious, who do not desire the preceptor’s progress. But if the preceptor is unconscientious and does not accept admonition, and the conscientious ones are incompatible with him, then, having abandoned the preceptor, the use of material requisites and so on should be done only together with the conscientious ones. Indeed, in this matter, the status of preceptor and so on should be understood as not being the standard. Pariveṇaṃ gantvā means: having gone to the preceptor’s monastic cell. The phrase ‘na susānaṃ’ is an indication; it is not proper for a pupil who wishes to go outside the vicinity boundary to go without asking permission.

Upajjhāyavattakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Duties Towards the Preceptor is concluded.

Saddhivihārikavattakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Duties of a Pupil

67. Saddhivihārikavattakathāyaṃ saṅgahetabbo anuggahetabbotiādīsu anādariyaṃ paṭicca dhammāmisehi asaṅgaṇhantānaṃ ācariyupajjhāyānaṃ dukkaṭaṃ vattabhedattā. Teneva parivārepi “nadento āpajjatī”ti (pari. 322) vuttaṃ. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

67. In the discourse on the duties of a pupil, regarding such phrases as 'should be supported, should be assisted,' for teachers and preceptors who, on account of disrespect, do not support them with the Dhamma and material things, there is a dukkaṭa offense because of the breach of duty. For that very reason, also in the Parivāra it is said: “Not giving, one incurs an offense.” The rest is indeed easy to understand.

Saddhivihārikavattakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Duties of a Pupil is concluded.

Nasammāvattanādikathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on Not Properly Performing Duties and So Forth

68. Nasammāvattanādikathāyaṃ vattaṃ na pūreyyāti “vattakaraṇakālo”ti vatthuvijānanavasena ñatvā mānakosajjādivasena vā upajjhāyādīsu [M 2.0104] anādarena vā “akātuṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti ajānanatāya vā na kareyya, dukkaṭameva. Asañcicca asatiyātiādīhi ca akarontassa pana anāpatti. Sabbāni hi vattāni sekhiyāneva, tasmā sekhiyesu vuttanayenevettha sabbopi vinicchayo veditabbo. Gehassitapemanti mettāpemaṃ.

68. In the discourse on not properly performing duties and so forth: As for 'one should not fulfill the duty,' if one, knowing 'it is the time for performing the duty' by way of understanding the matter, should not do it due to pride, laziness, and so forth, or with disrespect towards one's preceptor and so forth, or due to not knowing that 'it is not proper not to do it,' it is indeed a dukkaṭa offense. However, for one who does not do it unintentionally, or due to unmindfulness and so forth, there is no offense. Indeed, all duties are sekhiya rules; therefore, in this duty of the Khandhaka, the entire decision should be understood according to the method already stated in the sekhiya rules. As for 'affection connected with the household life,' it is affection of loving-kindness.

Sādiyanaṃ [V 2.0101] vā asādiyanaṃ vā na jānātīti “mayi sādiyante akarontānaṃ āpatti hoti, paṭikkhipitvā asādiyante āpatti na hotī”ti evaṃ na jānātīti attho. “Tesu eko vattasampanno bhikkhu…pe… tesaṃ anāpattī”ti vacanato sace koci “tumhākaṃ saddhivihārike, antevāsike vā gilāne upaṭṭhahissāmi, ovādānusāsaniādikaṃ sabbaṃ kattabbaṃ karissāmī”ti vadati, te vā saddhivihārikādayo “appossukkā hothā”ti vadanti, vattaṃ vā na sādiyanti, ācariyupajjhāyānampi anāpatti.

As for 'does not know whether there is consent or non-consent': this means he does not know thus: 'When I consent, an offense occurs for those who do not perform the duty; when I, having rejected it, do not consent, an offense does not occur.' Because the commentary states, 'Among them, one monk accomplished in duty... for them there is no offense,' if some monk should say, 'I will attend to your sick pupils or resident pupils; I will do all that needs to be done, such as admonition and instruction,' or if those pupils and so forth say, 'Be without concern,' or do not consent to the duty, for the teachers and preceptors also, there is no offense.

Nasammāvattanādikathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on Not Properly Performing Duties and So Forth is concluded.

Rādhabrāhmaṇavatthukathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Story of Rādha the Brahmin

69. Rādhabrāhmaṇavatthusmiṃ pāḷiyaṃ uppaṇḍuppaṇḍukajātoti sakalasarīre sañjātapaṇḍuvaṇṇo. Paṇḍuvaṇṇassa sakalasarīre byāpitabhāvadassanatthañhi vicchāvacanaṃ kataṃ. Adhikāranti upakāraṃ. Katavedinoti attano kataṃ upakāraṃ paṭikiriyāya ñāpakā. Upasampadākammavācāya yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ pariyosāne vakkhāma. Parimaṇḍalehīti paripuṇṇehi.

69. In the story of Rādha the Brahmin, in the Pāḷi: As for uppaṇḍuppaṇḍukajāto, it means 'one in whom a pale color has arisen in the entire body.' Indeed, the repetitive word was used to show the state of the pale color having spread throughout the entire body. As for adhikāraṃ, it means a favor. As for katavedino, they are those who make known the favor done to them by way of reciprocation. Whatever is to be said in the kammavācā for higher ordination, that we shall speak at the end. As for parimaṇḍalehi, it means by complete ones.

71-73. Paṇṇattivītikkamanti sikkhāpadavītikkamaṃ. Pāḷiyaṃ piṇḍiyālopabhojananti jaṅghapiṇḍimaṃsabalena caritvā ālopālopavasena pariyiṭṭhabhojanaṃ. Atirekalābhoti bhikkhāhārato adhikalābho. Saṅghabhattādīnaṃ vibhāgo senāsanakkhandhake āvi bhavissati. Vihāroti tiṇakuṭikādisahito pākāraparicchinno sakalo saṅghārāmo. Aḍḍhayogoti ekasālo dīghapāsādo. Hatthipiṭṭhigaruḷasaṇṭhāno dīghapāsādotipi vadanti. Pāsādoti caturasso ucco [M 2.0105] anekabhūmakapāsādo. Hammiyanti muṇḍacchadano candikaṅgaṇayutto nātiucco pāsādo. Guhāti pabbataguhā. Pūtimuttanti gomuttaṃ.

71-73. As for paṇṇattivītikkamaṃ, it means the transgression of a training rule. In the Pāḷi, as for piṇḍiyālopabhojanaṃ, it is food sought for by way of morsel after morsel, having wandered with the strength of the calf muscle. As for atirekalābho, it is a gain that is more than almsfood. The distribution of communal meals and so forth will become manifest in the Senāsanakkhandhaka. As for vihāro, it is the entire monastic compound, which includes grass huts and so forth, and is enclosed by a wall. As for aḍḍhayogo, it is a long building that is a single hall. They also call a long building shaped like an elephant's back or a garuḷa bird a dīghapāsādo. As for pāsādo, it is a tall, four-sided building with many stories. As for hammiyaṃ, it is a not-too-high building with a flat roof, furnished with a moonlit terrace. As for guhā, it is a mountain cave. As for pūtimuttaṃ, it is the urine of cattle.

Rādhabrāhmaṇavatthukathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Story of Rādha the Brahmin is finished.

Ācariyavattakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discussion of the Duties Towards a Teacher

76. Sahadhammikaṃ vuccamānoti “evaṃ nivāsetabba”ntiādinā sikkhāpadena ovadiyamāno. Vādaṃ āropetvāti “olambitvā nivāsanādīsu ko doso? Yadi doso bhaveyya[V 2.0102], parimaṇḍalanivāsanādīsupi doso siyā”tiādinā niggahaṃ āropetvā. Taṃyeva titthāyatananti diṭṭhisaṅkhātatitthameva āyatanaṃ dukkhuppattiṭṭhānanti titthāyatanaṃ. Āyasmato nissāya vacchāmīti āyasmantaṃ nissāya vasissāmīti attho.

76. `Sahadhammikaṃ vuccamāno` means: being admonished by the training rule beginning with, 'It should be worn thus.' `Vādaṃ āropetvā` means: having established a refutation by saying such things as, 'What fault is there in wearing it hanging down? If there were a fault, there would also be a fault in wearing it evenly all around.' `Taṃyeva titthāyatanaṃ` means: `titthāyatanaṃ` (a ground for views) is so called because the view (`tittha`) itself, designated as wrong view (`diṭṭhi`), is the basis (`āyatanaṃ`), the place of origin for suffering. `Āyasmato nissāya vacchāmi` has the meaning: 'I will dwell depending on the venerable one.'

Ācariyavattakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discussion of the Duties Towards a Teacher is concluded.

Paṇāmanākhamāpanākathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discussion of Bowing and Asking Forgiveness

80. Yaṃ pubbe lakkhaṇaṃ vuttaṃ, teneva lakkhaṇena nissayantevāsikassa āpatti na veditabbāti sambandhayojanā daṭṭhabbā. Potthakesu pana “na teneva lakkhaṇenā”ti ettha na-kāraṃ chaḍḍetvā “teneva lakkhaṇena nissayantevāsikassa āpatti veditabbā”ti likhanti, taṃ pamādalikhitaṃ. Tathā hi teneva lakkhaṇena āpattibhāve gayhamāne nissayamuttakassāpi amuttakassāpi āpatti evāti vuttalakkhaṇena āpattiṃ āpajjeyya. Tathā ca “nissayantevāsikena hi yāva ācariyaṃ nissāya vasati, tāva sabbaṃ ācariyavattaṃ kātabba”nti iminā anantaravacanena virodho siyā. Visuddhimaggepi ca –

80. The connection should be understood thus: by that very characteristic which was stated previously, an offense should not be known for a dependent pupil. However, in the books, having omitted the letter 'na' in the phrase 'na teneva lakkhaṇena,' they write, 'by that very characteristic an offense should be known for a dependent pupil'; that writing is a careless error. For if the state of having an offense were to be taken by that very characteristic, then by the characteristic stated—'for one released from dependence and for one not released, there is an offense indeed'—one would fall into an offense. And if that were so, there would be a contradiction with this immediately following statement: 'For as long as a dependent pupil dwells relying on a teacher, all the duties towards the teacher must be performed.' And also in the Visuddhimagga –

“Nissayācariya, uddesācariya, nissayantevāsika, uddesantevāsika, samānācariyakā pana yāva nissayauddesā anupacchinnā. Tāva paṭijaggitabbā”ti (visuddhi. 1.41) –

“However, the dependence-teacher, the instruction-teacher, the dependence-pupil, the instruction-pupil, and those who share the same teacher should be attended to for as long as dependence and instruction are uninterrupted.”

Vuttaṃ[M 2.0106]. Tasmā vuttanayena idha parigaḷitaṃ na-kāraṃ ānetvā teneva saddhivihārikassa vutteneva lakkhaṇena nissayantevāsikassa āpatti na veditabbāti evamattho gahetabbo.

It is said. Therefore, by the method stated, having brought in the 'na' character that was dropped here, this meaning should be understood: by that very characteristic stated for the co-resident, an offense should not be known for the dependent pupil.

Paṇāmanākhamāpanākathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discussion of Bowing and Asking Forgiveness is concluded.

Nissayapaṭippassaddhikathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discussion of the Cessation of Dependence

83. Nissayapaṭippassaddhikathāyaṃ “yo vā ekasambhogaparibhogo, tassa santike nissayo gahetabbo”ti iminā lajjīsu eva nissayaggahaṇaṃ niyojeti alajjīsu paṭikkhittattā. Ettha ca paribhogasaddena ekakammādiko saṃvāso gahito paccayaparibhogassa sambhoga-saddena gahitattā, etena [V 2.0103] ca sambhogasaṃvāsānaṃ alajjīhi saddhiṃ na kattabbataṃ dasseti. Parihāro natthīti āpattiparihāro natthi. Tādisoti yattha nissayo gahitapubbo, yo ca ekasambhogaparibhogo, tādiso. Tathā vuttanti “lahuṃ āgamissāmī”ti vuttañceti attho. “Cattāri pañca divasānī”ti idaṃ upalakkhaṇamattaṃ. Yadi ekāhadvīhena sabhāgatā paññāyati, ñātadivasena gahetabbova. Athāpi catupañcāhenāpi na paññāyati, yattakehi divasehi paññāyati, tattakāni atikkametabbāni. Sabhāgataṃ olokemīti pana leso na kātabbo.

83. In the discussion on the cessation of dependence, the text 'Or whoever has common partaking and common use, dependence should be taken from him' enjoins the taking of dependence only from the scrupulous, as it is rejected for the unscrupulous. And here, since the use of requisites is understood by the word `sambhoga` (partaking), co-residence involving common acts is understood by the word `paribhoga` (use). By this it is shown that partaking and co-residence should not be done with the unscrupulous. 'There is no dispensation' means there is no protection from an offense. 'Such a one' refers to one from whom dependence was formerly taken, and who has common partaking and use. 'As stated' means when it was said, 'I will return quickly.' The phrase 'four or five days' is merely an indication. If compatibility becomes apparent in one or two days, dependence should be taken on the very day it is known. If it is not apparent even after four or five days, one should wait for as many days as it takes for it to become apparent. But one should not make a pretext, saying, 'I am observing the compatibility.'

Daharā suṇantīti ettha asutvāpi āgamissati, kenaci antarāyena cirāyatīti saññāya sati labbhateva parihāro. Tenāha “idhevāhaṃ vasissāmīti pahiṇati, parihāro natthī”ti.

Regarding 'The young ones hear': here, even without having heard, if there is the perception, 'He will come; he is delayed by some obstacle,' a dispensation is indeed obtained. Therefore, it is said: 'If he sends word, "I will live right here," there is no dispensation.'

Ekadivasampi parihāro natthīti gamane nirussāhaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Saussāhassa pana senāsanapaṭisāmanādivasena katipāhe gatepi na doso.

“Even for a single day, there is no dispensation”—this is said with reference to one who is unenergetic in going. But for one who is energetic, there is no fault even if a few days pass by way of arranging lodging, and so forth.

Tatreva vasitabbanti tatra sabhāgaṭṭhāne eva nissayaṃ gahetvā vasitabbaṃ. “Taṃyeva vihāraṃ…pe… vasituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti iminā upajjhāye saṅgaṇhanteyeva taṃsamodhāne nissayapaṭippassaddhi vuttā, tasmiṃ pana kodhena [M 2.0107] vā gaṇanirapekkhatāya vā asaṅgaṇhante aññesu gahito nissayo na paṭippassambhatīti dasseti.

`Tatreva vasitabbaṃ` (one should reside right there) means: one should live having taken dependence in that very suitable place. By the text, 'That very monastery… it is proper to reside,' the cessation of dependence is said to occur upon meeting with the preceptor only when he is supportive. But it shows that if he is unsupportive due to anger or disregard for the group, the dependence taken from others does not cease.

Ācariyamhā nissayapaṭippassaddhiyaṃ vutto “koci ācariyo”tiādiko nayo upajjhāyapakkamanādīsupi netvā tattha ca vutto idhāpi netvā yathārahaṃ yojetabbo.

In the cessation of dependence from a teacher, the method stated beginning with 'some teacher' should be applied also to cases such as the preceptor's departure, etc., and the method stated there should also be applied here, as is appropriate.

Dve leḍḍupāte atikkamma aññasmiṃ vihāre vasantīti upacārasīmato bahi aññasmiṃ vihāre antevāsikānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānato dve leḍḍupāte atikkamma vasanti. Tena bahiupacārepi antevāsikādīnaṃ vasanaṭṭhānato dvinnaṃ leḍḍupātānaṃ antare āsannapadese vasati, nissayo na paṭippassambhatīti dasseti. Antoupacārasīmāyaṃ pana dve leḍḍupāte atikkamitvā vasato nissayo na paṭippassambhateva.

“Residing in another monastery beyond two clod-throws” refers to residing in another monastery outside the boundary of proximity, having gone beyond two clod-throws from the dwelling place of the resident disciples. Therefore, it is shown that even outside the boundary of proximity, if one dwells in a nearby place within two clod-throws from the dwelling place of the resident disciples, etc., dependence does not cease. However, within the boundary of proximity, for one who resides having gone beyond two clod-throws, dependence certainly does not cease.

Nissayapaṭippassaddhikathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discussion of the Cessation of Dependence is concluded.

Upasampādetabbapañcakakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Fivefold Matter Concerning Those to be Given Higher Ordination

84. Upajjhācariyalakkhaṇakathāyaṃ [V 2.0104] na sāmaṇero upaṭṭhāpetabboti upajjhāyena hutvā na pabbājetabbo. Asekkhassa ayanti asekkho, lokiyalokuttaro sīlakkhandho.

84. In the discussion on the characteristics of a preceptor and teacher: “A novice should not be attended to” means one should not give the going-forth having become a preceptor. “This is of one beyond training” refers to one who is beyond training, the mundane and supramundane aggregate of virtue.

Antaggāhikāyāti sassatucchedakoṭṭhāsaggāhikāya. Pacchimāni dveti appassuto hoti, duppañño hotīti imāni dve aṅgāni. Pacchimāni tīṇīti na paṭibalo uppannaṃ kukkuccaṃ dhammato vinodetuṃ, āpattiṃ na jānāti, āpattiyā vuṭṭhānaṃ na jānātīti imāni tīṇi. Kukkuccassa hi pāḷiaṭṭhakathānayasaṅkhātadhammato vinodetuṃ apaṭibalatā nāma abyattatā eva hotīti sāpi āpattiaṅgameva vuttā.

“Adhering to extremes” means adhering to the divisions of eternalism and annihilationism. “The latter two” refers to “one is unlearned” and “one is unwise”—these are the two factors. “The latter three” refers to “one is incapable of dispelling arisen remorse according to the Dhamma,” “one does not know an offense,” and “one does not know the procedure for emerging from an offense”—these are the three factors. For the inability to dispel remorse according to the Dhamma, which is reckoned as the method of the Pāḷi and commentaries, is indeed incompetence; thus, that too is stated as a factor of an offense.

Abhivisiṭṭho uttamo samācāro ābhisamācāro, vattapaṭivattasīlaṃ. Taṃ ārabbha paññattā khandhakasikkhāpadasaṅkhātā sikkhā ābhisamācārikā. Sikkhāpadampi hi taṃ tattha paṭipūraṇatthikehi uggahaṇādivasena sikkhitabbato “sikkhā”ti vuccati. Maggabrahmacariyassa ādibhūtā kāraṇabhūtāti ādibrahmacariyakā sikkhā, ubhatovibhaṅgapariyāpannasikkhāpadaṃ. Teneva [M 2.0108] visuddhimaggepi “ubhatovibhaṅgapariyāpannasikkhāpadaṃ ādibrahmacariyakaṃ, khandhakavattapaayāpannaṃ ābhisamācārika”nti (visuddhi. 1.11) vuttaṃ. Tasmā sekkhapaṇṇattiya”nti ettha sikkhitabbato sekkhā, bhagavatā paññattattā paṇṇatti. Sabbāpi ubhatovibhaṅgapariyāpannā sikkhāpadapaṇṇatti “sekkhapaṇṇattī”ti vuttāti gahetabbā. Nāmarūpaparicchedeti ettha kusalattikādīhi vuttaṃ jātibhūmipuggalasampayogavatthārammaṇakammadvāralakkhaṇarasādibhedehi vedanākkhandhādicatubbidhaṃ sanibbānaṃ nāmaṃ, bhūtupādāyabhedaṃ rūpañca paricchinditvā jānanapaññā, tappakāsako ca gantho nāmarūpaparicchedo nāma. Iminā abhidhammatthakusalena bhavitabbanti dasseti. Sikkhāpetunti uggaṇhāpetuṃ.

Excellent, supreme conduct is proper conduct (ābhisamācāra), the virtue of duties and practices. Regarding this, the trainings that were prescribed, reckoned as the Khandhaka training rules, are called ābhisamācārikā (pertaining to proper conduct). Indeed, a training rule is also called 'training' because it is to be practiced by way of study, etc., by those who wish to fulfill its meaning. The training that is the beginning and cause of the holy life of the path is called ādibrahmacariyakā (pertaining to the initial holy life), which refers to the training rule included in both Vibhaṅgas. For that very reason, in the Visuddhimagga as well, it is said: 'The training rule included in both Vibhaṅgas is ādibrahmacariyakaṃ, and that included in the Khandhaka duties is ābhisamācārikaṃ.' Therefore, in the term 'sekkhapaṇṇatti', it is 'sekkha' because it is to be learned and practiced, and it is 'paṇṇatti' because it was prescribed by the Blessed One. It should be understood that all training rule regulations included in both Vibhaṅgas are called 'sekkhapaṇṇatti'. Regarding 'delimitation of name and form': here, this term refers to the wisdom that knows by delimiting: (1) name—which is taught by means of the wholesome triad, etc., is distinguished by birth, plane, person, association, basis, object, action, door, characteristic, function, etc., is fourfold beginning with the feeling aggregate, and is together with Nibbāna; and (2) form—which is divided into primary elements and derived matter. The treatise that explains this wisdom is also called 'delimitation of name and form'. By this, it is shown that one should be skilled in the Abhidhamma. 'To train' means to cause to learn.

Upasampādetabbapañcakakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Fivefold Matter Concerning Those to be Given Higher Ordination is concluded.

Aññatitthiyapubbavatthukathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Story of the Former Heretics

86. Titthiyaparivāsakathāyaṃ ājīvakassa vātiādīsu akiriyavādī ājīvako nāma, kiriyavādino pana nigaṇṭhāpi aññepi naggatitthikā acelakapade saṅgahitā. Sabbathā naggasseva [V 2.0105] titthiyaparivāso vihito. So ca teneva naggavesena bhikkhūnaṃ santikaṃ āgatassa, na paṭicchādetvā āgatassāti dassetuṃ “sace sopī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha sopīti ājīvako.

86. In the discourse on the probation for heretics, in the text beginning with 'ājīvakassa vā', an exponent of non-action is called an Ājīvaka. However, the Nigaṇṭhas, who are exponents of action, and other naked heretics are included in the term acelaka (one without clothes). In every case, the probation for heretics is prescribed only for one who is naked. And it is prescribed for one who has come into the presence of the monks in that very state of nakedness; to show that it is not for one who has come having covered himself, the passage beginning with 'sace so pi' (“if he too...”) was spoken. Therein, 'so pi' refers to the Ājīvaka.

Āmisakiñcikkhasampadānaṃ nāma appamattakassa deyyadhammassa anuppadānaṃ. Rūpūpajīvikāti attano rūpameva nissāya jīvantiyo. Vesiyā gocaro bahulaṃ pavattiṭṭhānaṃ assāti vesiyāgocaro. Esa nayo sabbattha. Yobbannātītāti anividdhā eva mahallikabhāvaṃ pattā thullakumārī evāti vuttaṃ. Ādāyassāti ādānassa gahaṇassa.

The giving of a trifle of material things (āmisakiñcikkhasampadāna) is the repeated giving of a small gift-object. Rūpūpajīvikā refers to women who make a living relying solely on their own beauty. One is called vesiyāgocara because a prostitute is his resort (gocara), his place of frequent activity. This is the method in all cases. Yobbannātītā refers to one who has reached mature womanhood without having been penetrated; she is called a thullakumārī (a stout maiden). Ādāyassa means 'of taking,' 'of grasping.'

Aññatitthiyapubbavatthukathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Story of the Former Heretics is finished.

Pañcābādhavatthukathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Story of the Five Diseases

88-9. Pañcābādhādivatthūsu [M 2.0109] pāḷiyaṃ somhi arogo, vibbhamissāmīti so ahaṃ arogo, vibbhamissāmīti attho. Nakhapiṭṭhippamāṇanti kaniṭṭhaṅgulinakhapiṭṭhi adhippetā. “Paṭicchanne ṭhāne nakhapiṭṭhippamāṇaṃ avaḍḍhanakapakkhe ṭhitaṃ hoti, vaṭṭatī”ti vuttattā appaṭicchannaṭṭhāne tādisampi na vaṭṭati, paṭicchannaṭṭhānepi ca vaḍḍhanakapakkhe ṭhitopi na vaṭṭatīti siddhameva hoti.
