The statement 'Stones suitable as boundary markers should be placed' is said because tree markers and so forth are rare in desired locations, and because, by growing, they cause the mingling of two consecrated sīmās, whereas a stone marker lacks that characteristic, and because it is easy to bring them from anywhere and place them. Likewise, also in the phrase 'sīmantarika stones should be placed.' By 'even of four finger-breadths in measure,' it should be understood thus: in such a way that when the boundary marker stones are placed, an area of about four finger-breadths of the stones extends outwards from the boundary of the khaṇḍasīmā all around, while the remaining area of the stones is indeed inside the khaṇḍasīmā. In that way, when those stones are placed, the sīmantarika becomes about four finger-breadths.

Sīmantarikapāsāṇāti [M 2.0144] sīmantarikāya ṭhapitanimittapāsāṇā. Te pana kittentena padakkhiṇato anupariyāyanteneva kittetabbā. Kathaṃ? Khaṇḍasīmato hi pacchimāya disāya puratthābhimukhena ṭhatvā “puratthimāya disāya kiṃ nimitta”nti tattha sabbāni nimittāni anukkamena [V 2.0137] kittetvā tathā uttarāya disāya dakkhiṇābhimukhena ṭhatvā “dakkhiṇāya disāya kiṃ nimitta”nti anukkamena kittetvā tathā puratthimāya disāya pacchimābhimukhena ṭhatvā “pacchimāya disāya kiṃ nimitta”nti anukkamena kittetvā tathā dakkhiṇāya disāya uttarābhimukhena ṭhatvā “uttarāya disāya kiṃ nimitta”nti tattha sabbāni nimittāni anukkamena kittetvā puna pacchimāya disāya puratthābhimukhena ṭhatvā purimakittitaṃ vuttanayena puna kittetabbaṃ. Evaṃ bahūnampi khaṇḍasīmānaṃ sīmantarikapāsāṇā paccekaṃ kittetabbā. Tatoti pacchā. Avasesanimittānīti mahāsīmāya bāhirantaresu avasesanimittāni. Ubhinnampi na kopentīti ubhinnampi kammaṃ na kopenti.

By 'sīmantarikapāsāṇā' is meant the boundary marker stones placed in the sīmantarika. However, they should be announced by one circumambulating them clockwise. How? From the khaṇḍasīmā, standing in the western direction facing east, one should announce, 'What is the boundary marker in the eastern direction?' and announce all the markers there in sequence. Likewise, standing in the northern direction facing south, one should announce, 'What is the boundary marker in the southern direction?' and announce them in sequence. Likewise, standing in the eastern direction facing west, one should announce, 'What is the boundary marker in the western direction?' and announce them in sequence. Likewise, standing in the southern direction facing north, one should announce, 'What is the boundary marker in the northern direction?' and announce all the markers there in sequence. Then, standing again in the western direction facing east, one should again announce the previously announced marker in the manner described. In this way, the sīmantarika stones of even many khaṇḍasīmās should be announced individually. By 'tato' is meant afterwards. By 'avasesanimittāni' is meant the remaining boundary markers at the outer extremities of the mahāsīmā. By 'they do not spoil for both' is meant they do not spoil the formal act of either of the two.

Kuṭigeheti bhūmiyaṃ katatiṇakuṭiyaṃ. Udukkhalanti udukkhalāvāṭasadisakhuddakāvāṭaṃ. Nimittaṃ na kātabbanti taṃ rājiṃ vā udukkhalaṃ vā nimittaṃ na kātabbaṃ. Idañca yathāvuttesu nimittesu anāgatattena na vaṭṭatīti siddhampi avinassakasaññāya koci mohena nimittaṃ kareyyāti dūratopi vipattiparihāratthaṃ vuttaṃ. Evaṃ upari “bhittiṃ akittetvā”tiādīsupi siddhamevatthaṃ punappunaṃ kathane kāraṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sīmāvipatti hi upasampadādisabbakammavipattimūlanti tassā sabbaṃ dvāraṃ sabbathā pidahanavasena vattabbaṃ. Sabbaṃ vatvāva idha ācariyā vinicchayaṃ ṭhapesunti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

By 'kuṭigehe' is meant in a grass hut made on the ground. By 'udukkhalaṃ' is meant a small pit similar to a mortar-pit. By 'nimittaṃ na kātabbaṃ' is meant that that line or that mortar should not be made a boundary marker. And this is said to prevent a fault even from afar because, although it is already established that it is not allowable as it is not included among the eight aforementioned boundary markers, someone might, out of delusion and a perception of it being indestructible, make it a boundary marker. Similarly, above, in passages such as 'without announcing the wall,' the reason for repeatedly stating an already established meaning should be known. For a fault in the sīmā is the root of faults in all formal acts, such as higher ordination. Therefore, it should be understood that the teachers established their ruling here only after having said everything that should be said by way of completely blocking every door to that fault in the sīmā in every way.

Bhittinti iṭṭhakadārumattikāmayaṃ. Silāmayāya pana bhittiyā nimittupagaṃ ekaṃ pāsāṇaṃ taṃtaṃdisāya kittetuṃ vaṭṭati. Anekasilāhi cinitaṃ sakalabhittiṃ kittetuṃ na vaṭṭati “eso pāsāṇo nimitta”nti ekavacanena vattabbato. Antokuṭṭamevāti ettha antokuṭṭepi nimittānaṃ ṭhitokāsato anto eva sīmāti gahetabbaṃ. Pamukhe nimittapāsāṇe ṭhapetvāti gabbhābhimukhepi bahipamukhe gabbhavitthārappamāṇe ṭhāne pāsāṇe ṭhapetvā sammannitabbā. Evañhi gabbhapamukhānaṃ antare ṭhitakuṭṭampi upādāya anto ca bahi ca caturassasaṇṭhānāva sīmā hoti. Bahīti sakalassa kuṭigehassa samantato bahi.

By 'wall' is meant one made of brick, wood, or clay. For a wall made of stone, however, it is permissible to announce a single stone, which is suitable as a marker, in each respective direction. It is not permissible to announce the entire wall built with many stones, because the announcement must be made with the singular form: 'This stone is the marker.' In the phrase 'antokuṭṭameva,' even within the wall, the sīmā should be taken as only the inside from the place where the markers stand. By 'pamukhe nimittapāsāṇe ṭhapetvā' is meant that having placed the stones in a place the size of the inner chamber's width, also at the outer front hall which faces the inner chamber, it should be consecrated. Indeed, when it is consecrated thus, including also the wall standing between the inner chamber and the front hall, the sīmā becomes one of a square shape both inside and outside. By 'bahi' is meant outside, all around the entire hut-dwelling.

Anto [M 2.0145] ca bahi ca sīmā hotīti majjhe ṭhitabhittiyā saha caturassasīmā hoti.

By 'the sīmā is both inside and outside' is meant that it becomes a square sīmā together with the wall standing in the middle.

“Uparipāsādeyeva hotī”ti iminā gabbhassa ca pamukhassa ca antarā ṭhitabhittiyā ekattā tattha ca ekavīsatiyā bhikkhūnaṃ okāsābhāvena heṭṭhā na otarati, uparibhitti pana sīmaṭṭhāva hotīti dasseti. Heṭṭhimatale kuṭṭoti heṭṭhimatale catūsu disāsu ṭhitakuṭṭo. Sace hi [V 2.0138] dvīsu, tīsu vā disāsu eva kuṭṭo tiṭṭheyya, heṭṭhā na otarati. Heṭṭhāpi otaratīti catunnampi bhittīnaṃ anto bhittīhi saha ekavīsatiyā bhikkhūnaṃ pahonakattā vuttaṃ. Otaramānā ca uparisīmappamāṇena otarati, catunnaṃ pana bhittīnaṃ bāhirantaraparicchede heṭṭhābhūmibhāge udakapariyantaṃ katvā otarati. Na pana bhittīnaṃ bahi kesaggamattampi ṭhānaṃ. Pāsādabhittitoti uparitale bhittito. Otaraṇānotaraṇaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbanti uparisīmappamāṇassa antogadhānaṃ heṭṭhimatale catūsu disāsu kuṭṭānaṃ tulārukkhehi ekasambandhataṃ tadanto pacchimasīmappamāṇatādiñca sandhāya vuttaṃ. Kiñcāpettha niyyūhakādayo nimittānaṃ ṭhitokāsatāya bajjhamānakkhaṇe sīmā na honti, baddhāya pana sīmāya sīmaṭṭhāva hontīti daṭṭhabbā. Pariyantathambhānanti nimittagatapāsāṇatthambhe sandhāya vuttaṃ. “Uparimatalena sambaddho hotī”ti idaṃ kuṭṭānaṃ antarā sīmaṭṭhānaṃ thambhānaṃ abhāvato vuttaṃ. Yadi hi bhaveyyuṃ, kuṭṭe uparimatalena asambandhepi sīmaṭṭhatthambhānaṃ upari ṭhito pāsādo sīmaṭṭhova hoti.

By `uparipāsādeyeva hoti`, it is shown that because of the oneness of the wall standing between the inner chamber and the front hall, and because of the lack of space there for twenty-one monks, it does not descend below; but the upper wall is indeed established in the sīmā. By `heṭṭhimatale kuṭṭo` is meant the wall standing on the lower level in the four directions. Indeed, if the wall were to stand in only two or three directions, it does not descend below. The statement `heṭṭhāpi otarati` is said because the inside of the four walls, together with the walls, is sufficient for twenty-one monks. And when descending, it descends with the measure of the upper sīmā. However, in the ground-portion defined by the outer limits of the four walls, it descends down to the water-level. But it does not descend to a place even the size of a hair's tip outside the walls. By `pāsādabhittito` is meant from the wall on the upper level. The statement `otaraṇānotaraṇaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ` is said with reference to the single connection by means of beams and posts of the walls on the lower level in the four directions which are included within the measure of the upper sīmā, and to their interior having the minimum sīmā measure, and so on. It should be understood that although projections and so forth, being places where markers stand, are not the sīmā at the moment of being bound, yet once the sīmā has been bound, they are indeed established in the sīmā. The statement `pariyantathambhānaṃ` is said with reference to the stone pillars that have become markers. This statement `uparimatalena sambaddho hoti` is said because of the absence of pillars established in the sīmā between the walls. Indeed, if there were pillars established in the sīmā, even if the wall were not connected with the upper level, the palace standing above the pillars established in the sīmā would indeed be established in the sīmā.

Sace pana bahūnaṃ thambhapantīnaṃ upari katapāsādassa heṭṭhā pathaviyaṃ sabbabāhirāya thambhapantiyā anto nimittapāsāṇe ṭhapetvā sīmā baddhā hoti, ettha kathanti? Etthāpi yaṃ tāva sīmaṭṭhatthambheheva dhāriyamānānaṃ tulānaṃ uparimatalaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ sīmaṭṭhameva, ettha vivādo natthi. Yaṃ pana sīmaṭṭhatthambhapantiyā, asīmaṭṭhāya bāhiratthambhapantiyā ca samadhuraṃ dhāriyamānānaṃ tulānaṃ uparimatalaṃ, tattha upaḍḍhaṃ sīmāti keci vadanti. Sakalampi gāmasīmāti apare. Baddhasīmā evāti aññe. Tasmā kammaṃ karontehi garuke nirāsaṅkaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā sabbaṃ taṃ āsaṅkaṭṭhānaṃ sodhetvāva kammaṃ kātabbaṃ, sanniṭṭhānakāraṇaṃ vā gavesitvā tadanuguṇaṃ kātabbaṃ.

If a sīmā is bound on the earth below a palace made upon many rows of pillars, having placed the marker stones inside the outermost row of pillars, what of this? This is the objection. Here, whatever upper level of the beams is supported by only the pillars established in the sīmā, all of that is indeed established in the sīmā; there is no dispute here. But as for the upper level of the beams that are supported with equal load by the row of pillars established in the sīmā and by the outer row of pillars not established in the sīmā, some say half of it is sīmā. Others say the whole of it is gāmasīmā. Still others say it is only the bound sīmā. Therefore, those performing a formal act, being scrupulous, should stand in a place free from doubt, and only after clearing that entire doubtful place should the act be performed. Or, having sought the reason for the conclusion, one should act in accordance with it.

Tālamūlakapabbateti [M 2.0146] tālakkhandhamūlasadise heṭṭhā thūlo hutvā kamena kiso hutvā uggato hi tālasadiso nāma hoti. Vitānasaṇṭhānoti ahicchattakasaṇṭhāno. Paṇavasaṇṭhānoti majjhe tanuko heṭṭhā ca upari ca vitthiṇṇo. Heṭṭhā vā majjhe vāti mudiṅgasaṇṭhānassa heṭṭhā, paṇavasaṇṭhānassa majjhe.

By `tālamūlakapabbate` is meant a mountain like the root of a palm trunk. Indeed, a mountain that, being thick below, rises up becoming gradually slender, is called 'palm-like'. By `vitānasaṇṭhāno` is meant mushroom-shaped. By `paṇavasaṇṭhāno` is meant slender in the middle and wide both below and above. By `heṭṭhā vā majjhe vā`: for one of a `mudiṅga`-drum shape, there is no sīmā measure below; for one of a `paṇava`-drum shape, there is no sīmā measure in the middle.

Sappaphaṇasadiso pabbatoti sappaphaṇo viya khujjo, mūlaṭṭhānato aññattha avanatasīsoti attho. Ākāsapabbhāranti bhittiyā aparikkhittapabbhāraṃ. Sīmappamāṇoti antoākāsena saddhiṃ pacchimasīmappamāṇo. “So ca pāsāṇo sīmaṭṭho”ti iminā īdisehi susirapāsāṇaleṇakuṭṭādīhi paricchinne bhūmibhāge eva sīmā patiṭṭhāti, na aparicchinne. Te pana sīmaṭṭhattā sīmā honti, na sarūpena sīmaṭṭhamañcādi viyāti dasseti. Sace pana so susirapāsāṇo [V 2.0139] bhūmiṃ anāhacca ākāsagatova olambati, sīmā na otarati. Susirapāsāṇā pana sayaṃ sīmāpaṭibaddhattā sīmā honti. Kathaṃ pana pacchimappamāṇarahitehi etehi susirapāsāṇādīhi sīmā na otaratīti idaṃ saddhātabbanti? Aṭṭhakathāpamāṇato.

By `sappaphaṇasadiso pabbato` is meant a mountain that is humped like a snake's hood; the meaning is that its peak is bent towards another place from its base. By `ākāsapabbhāraṃ` is meant a mountain slope not enclosed by a wall. By `sīmappamāṇo` is meant a rock having the minimum sīmā measure together with the hollow space inside. By this phrase `so ca pāsāṇo sīmaṭṭho`, it is shown that a sīmā is established only in a portion of ground defined by such things as hollow rocks, caves, walls, and so on; it is not established in an undefined area. But those things are sīmā because they are established in the sīmā; they are not sīmā by their own nature, just like a couch, etc., established in a sīmā. If that hollow rock hangs in the air without touching the ground, the sīmā does not descend. Hollow rocks, however, are sīmā because they themselves are connected to the sīmā. But how is this statement to be believed: that the sīmā descends by means of these hollow rocks and so on, which are devoid of the minimum measure? This is the objection. It should be believed on the authority of the Commentary.

Apicettha susirapāsāṇabhittianusārena mūsikādīnaṃ viya sīmāya heṭṭhimatale otaraṇakiccaṃ natthi. Heṭṭhā pana pacchimasīmappamāṇe ākāse dvaṅgulamattabahalehi pāsāṇabhittiādīhipi uparimatalaṃ āhacca ṭhitehi sabbaso, yebhuyyena vā paricchinne sati upari bajjhamānā sīmā tehi pāsāṇādīhi antaritāya tapparicchinnāya heṭṭhābhūmiyāpi uparimatalena saddhiṃ ekakkhaṇe patiṭṭhāti nadipārasīmā viya nadiantaritesu ubhosu tīresu, leṇādīsu apanītesupi heṭṭhā otiṇṇā sīmā yāva sāsanantaradhānā na vigacchati. Paṭhamaṃ pana upari sīmāya baddhāya pacchā leṇādīsu katesupi heṭṭhābhūmiyaṃ sīmā otarati eva. Keci taṃ na icchanti. Evaṃ ubhayattha patiṭṭhitā ca sā sīmā ekāva hoti gottādijāti viya byattibhedesūti gahetabbaṃ. Sabbā eva hi baddhasīmā, abaddhasīmā ca attano attano pakatinissayabhūte gāmāraññanadiādike khette yathāparicchedaṃ sabbattha sākalyena ekasmiṃ khaṇe byāpinī paramatthato avijjamānāpi te te nissayabhūte paramatthadhamme, taṃ taṃ kiriyāvisesampi vā upādāya lokiyehi, sāsanikehi [M 2.0147] ca yathārahaṃ ekattena paññattatāya nissayekarūpā eva. Tathā hi eko gāmo araññaṃ nadī jātassaro samuddoti evaṃ loke,

Moreover, here, following a hollow stone wall, there is no task for the sīmā to descend to the lower level, as there is for mice and other creatures. However, below, in a space the size of the smallest sīmā, when it is enclosed either entirely or for the most part by stone walls and the like that are about two finger-breadths thick and are established contacting the upper level, the sīmā being bound above is established in a single moment in the lower ground—which is separated and delimited by those stones and the like—together with the upper level. This is like a river-crossing sīmā established on both banks that are separated by a river. Even when caves and the like are removed, a sīmā that has descended below does not disappear until the vanishing of the Dispensation. However, if a sīmā is first bound above, and caves and the like are made afterwards, the sīmā certainly descends to the ground below. Some do not accept this. Thus, it should be understood that the sīmā established in both places is just one, like lineage, caste, and so on, among different individuals. Indeed, every bound sīmā and unbound sīmā, in its own respective natural supporting domain such as a village, forest, river, and so on, is pervasive everywhere completely in a single moment according to its delimitation. Although non-existent in an ultimate sense, based on those respective supporting ultimate realities or on those respective specific activities, it is designated by worldly people and by those of the Dispensation, as appropriate, as being of a single nature by way of its support. Indeed, thus in the world, [there are designations such as] 'one village, a forest, a river, a natural lake, the ocean,'

“Sammatā sā sīmā saṅghena (mahāva. 143). Agāmake ce, bhikkhave, araññe samantā sattabbhantarā, ayaṃ tattha samānasaṃvāsā ekūposathā. Samantā udakukkhepā, ayaṃ tattha samānasaṃvāsā ekūposathā”ti (mahāva. 147) –

'That sīmā is authorized by the Saṅgha... of common communion, of a single Uposatha.'

Ādinā sāsane ca ekavohāro dissati. Na hi paramatthato ekassa anekadhammesu byāpanamatthi. Kasiṇekadesādivikappāsamānatāya ekattahānitoti ayaṃ no mati.

By such [sayings] as these, and in the Dispensation, a single designation is seen. Indeed, in an ultimate sense, there is no pervasion of one thing in many phenomena. There is a loss of oneness due to the non-uniformity of conceptualization regarding parts of a kasiṇa, etc. This is our view.

Assa heṭṭhāti sappaphaṇapabbatassa heṭṭhā ākāsapabbhāre. Leṇassāti leṇañce kataṃ, tassa leṇassāti attho. Tameva puna leṇaṃ pañcahi pakārehi vikappetvā otaraṇānotaraṇavinicchayaṃ dassetuṃ āha “sace pana heṭṭhā”tiādi. Tattha “heṭṭhā”ti imassa “leṇaṃ hotī”ti iminā sambandho. Heṭṭhā leṇañca ekasmiṃ padeseti āha “anto”ti, pabbatassa anto, pabbatamūleti attho. Tameva anto-saddaṃ sīmāparicchedena visesetuṃ “uparimassa sīmāparicchedassa pārato”ti vuttaṃ[V 2.0140]. Pabbatapādaṃ pana apekkhitvā “orato”ti vattabbepi sīmānissayaṃ pabbataggaṃ sandhāya “pārato”ti vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Teneva “bahileṇa”nti ettha bahi-saddaṃ visesento “uparimassa sīmāparicchedassa orato”ti āha. Bahi sīmā na otaratīti ettha bahīti pabbatapāde leṇaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, leṇassa bahibhūte uparisīmāparicchedassa heṭṭhābhāge sīmā na otaratīti attho. Anto sīmāti leṇassa ca pabbatapādassa ca anto attano otaraṇārahaṭṭhāne na otaratīti attho. “Bahi sīmā na otarati, anto sīmā na otaratī”ti cettha attano otaraṇārahaṭṭhāne leṇābhāvena sīmāya sabbathā anotaraṇameva dassitanti gahetabbaṃ. Tatthāpi anotarantī upari eva hotīti. “Bahi patitaṃ asīmā”tiādinā uparipāsādādīsu athiranissayesu ṭhitā sīmāpi tesaṃ vināsena vinassatīti dassitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

The phrase 'below it' means below the mountain that is like a snake's hood, in the open space of the mountain slope. The phrase 'of the cave' means: if a cave is made, it refers to that cave. To show the decision of descending and not descending by differentiating that same cave in five ways, he said the words beginning with 'But if below...'. Therein, the word 'below' has a connection with the words 'there is a cave'. To show that the cave below is in a certain place, he said 'inside'; the meaning is inside the mountain, at the foot of the mountain. To specify that very word 'inside' by the sīmā-delimitation, it is said 'beyond the upper sīmā-delimitation'. However, it should be understood that although 'on this side' should be said with reference to the foot of the mountain, 'beyond' is said with reference to the mountain peak, which is the support of the sīmā. For that very reason, when specifying the word 'outside' in the phrase 'outside the cave', he said 'on this side of the upper sīmā-delimitation'. In the phrase 'the sīmā does not descend outside', 'outside' is said with reference to the cave at the foot of the mountain; the meaning is that the sīmā does not descend to the lower part of the upper sīmā-delimitation, which is outside the cave. The phrase 'inside the sīmā' means: inside both the cave and the foot of the mountain, the sīmā does not descend to its own place suitable for descending. And in the phrase 'The sīmā does not descend outside, the sīmā does not descend inside', it should be understood that it is shown that the sīmā absolutely does not descend, due to the absence of a cave in its own place suitable for descending. Even there, not descending, it is only above. By the text beginning with 'Fallen outside is not sīmā', it is shown that even a sīmā established on unstable supports such as the upper stories of palaces is destroyed by their destruction; this should be understood.

Pokkharaṇiṃ [M 2.0148] khaṇanti, sīmāyevāti ettha sace heṭṭhā umaṅganadisīmappamāṇato anūnā paṭhamameva ca pavattā hoti. Sīmā ca pacchā baddhā nadito upari eva hoti, nadiṃ āhacca pokkharaṇiyā ca khatāya sīmā vinassatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Heṭṭhāpathavitaleti antarā bhūmivivare.

In the phrase 'They dig a pond, it is the sīmā itself': if an underground river, not less than the measure of a sīmā, exists below from the very beginning, and the sīmā is established afterwards, it is only above the river. It should be understood that when the pond is dug, reaching the river, the sīmā is destroyed. The phrase 'below the earth's surface' means in a cavity within the earth.

Sīmāmāḷaketi khaṇḍasīmaṅgaṇe. “Vaṭarukkho”ti idaṃ pārohopatthambhena atidūrampi gantuṃ samatthasākhāsamaṅgitāya vuttaṃ. Sabbarukkhalatādīnampi sambandho na vaṭṭati eva. Teneva nāvārajjusetusambandhopi paṭikkhitto. Tatoti sākhato. Mahāsīmāya pathavitalanti ettha āsannatarampi gāmasīmaṃ aggahetvā baddhasīmāya eva gahitattā gāmasīmābaddhasīmānaṃ aññamaññaṃ rukkhādisambandhepi sambhedadoso natthi, aññamaññaṃ nissayanissitabhāvena pavattitoti gahetabbaṃ. Yadi hi tāsampi sambandhadoso bhaveyya, kathaṃ gāmasīmāya baddhasīmā sammannitabbā siyā? Yassā hi sīmāya saddhiṃ sambandhe doso bhaveyya, sā tattha bandhitumeva na vaṭṭati, baddhasīmāudakukkhepasīmāsu baddhasīmā viya, attano nissayabhūtagāmasīmādīsu udakukkhepasīmā viya ca. Teneva “sace pana rukkhassa sākhā vā tato nikkhantapāroho vā bahinaditīre vihārasīmāya vā gāmasīmāya vā patiṭṭhito”tiādinā (mahāva. aṭṭha. 147) udakukkhepasīmāya attano anissayabhūtagāmasīmādīhi eva sambandhadoso dassito, na nadisīmāyaṃ. Evamidhāpīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ayañcattho upari pākaṭo bhavissati. Āhaccāti phusitvā.

The phrase 'in the sīmā-precinct' means in the courtyard of a partial sīmā. This word 'banyan tree' is said because of its being endowed with branches, supported by aerial roots, that are capable of going even very far. A connection with any trees, creepers, and so on is certainly not allowable. By that very text, a connection by boat, rope, or bridge is also rejected. The word 'from that' means from the branch. In the phrase 'the ground of the great sīmā', because only the established sīmā is taken, without taking even the very near village sīmā, there is no fault of intermingling even in the mutual connection by a tree, etc., of a village sīmā and an established sīmā. It should be understood that this is because they proceed with a mutual relationship of support and supported. For if there were a fault of connection for them, how could an established sīmā be authorized in a village sīmā? For a sīmā which would have a fault through connection with another sīmā is not allowable to be established in that other sīmā, just as an established sīmā is not allowable in an established sīmā or a water-throw sīmā, and just as a water-throw sīmā is not allowable in its own supporting village sīmā, etc. For that very reason, by the text beginning 'But if a branch of a tree or an aerial root extending from it is established on the far bank of a river, within the monastery sīmā or the village sīmā...', the fault of connection is shown only for a water-throw sīmā with a village sīmā, etc., which is not its support; it is not shown with the river sīmā. Thus, it should be understood that here too, a fault is not shown. And this meaning will become clear above. The word 'āhacca' means 'having touched'.

Mahāsīmaṃ vā sodhetvāti mahāsīmāgatānaṃ sabbesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ hatthapāsānayanabahikaraṇādivasena [V 2.0141] sakalaṃ mahāsīmaṃ sodhetvā. Etena sabbavipattiyo mocetvā pubbe suṭṭhu baddhānampi dvinnaṃ baddhasīmānaṃ pacchā rukkhādisambandhena uppajjanako īdiso pāḷimuttako sambhedadoso atthīti dasseti. So ca “na, bhikkhave, sīmāya sīmā sambhinditabbā”tiādinā baddhasīmānaṃ aññamaññaṃ sambhedajjhottharaṇaṃ paṭikkhipitvā “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, sīmaṃ sammannantena sīmantarikaṃ ṭhapetvā sīmaṃ sammannitu”nti ubhinnaṃ (mahāva. 148) baddhasīmānamantarā sīmantarikaṃ ṭhapetvāva bandhituṃ anujānantena sambhedajjhottharaṇaṃ viya tāsaṃ aññamaññaṃ phusitvā tiṭṭhanavasena bandhanampi na vaṭṭatīti siddhattā baddhānampi tāsaṃ pacchā aññamaññaṃ ekarukkhādīhi [M 2.0149] phusitvā ṭhānampi na vaṭṭatīti bhagavato adhippāyaññūhi saṅgītikārakehi niddhārito. Bandhanakāle paṭikkhittassa sambandhadosassa anulomena akappiyānulomattā.

“Having purified the great boundary” means having purified the entire great boundary of all the bhikkhus present within it by means of bringing them into hand's reach, removing [those who are disqualified], and so forth. By this, having been freed from all defects, it is shown that even for two boundaries that were previously well-established, such a fault of connection, which is external to the Pāḷi, can arise later through connection by a tree or the like. And that [fault of connection] was determined by the compilers of the recitals, who knew the intention of the Blessed One. Because the Blessed One rejected the mutual connection and overlapping of established boundaries by means of the text beginning with, “Bhikkhus, a boundary should not be connected with another boundary,” and allowed establishing a boundary only after setting an interstice between two established boundaries with the words, “I allow, bhikkhus, for one establishing a boundary to establish the boundary after setting an interstice,” it is thereby established that just as connection and overlapping are not allowable, so too is establishing them in such a way that they stand touching each other not allowable. Therefore, they concluded that even for boundaries that have already been established, for them to later stand touching each other by means of a single tree or the like is also not allowable. This is because it conforms with what is improper, being in accordance with the fault of connection rejected at the time of establishment.

Ayaṃ pana sambandhadoso – pubbe suṭṭhu baddhānaṃ pacchā sañjātattā bajjhamānakkhaṇe viya asīmattaṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti. Tasmā rukkhādisambandhe apanītamatte tā sīmā pākatikā honti. Yathā cāyaṃ pacchā na vaṭṭati, evaṃ bajjhamānakkhaṇepi tāsaṃ rukkhādisambandhe sati tā bandhituṃ na vaṭṭatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

This fault of connection, however, because it arises later for boundaries that were previously well-established, cannot render them 'not a boundary' as it would at the moment of establishment. Therefore, as soon as the connection by a tree or the like is removed, those boundaries become as they were originally. And just as this connection is not allowable afterwards, so too it should be understood that at the very moment of establishment, if there is a connection to a tree or the like, it is not allowable to establish them.

Keci pana “mahāsīmaṃ vā sodhetvāti ettha mahāsīmāgatā bhikkhū yathā taṃ sākhaṃ vā pārohaṃ vā kāyapaṭibaddhehi na phusanti, evaṃ sodhanameva idhādhippetaṃ, na sakalasīmāsodhana”nti vadanti, taṃ na yuttaṃ aṭṭhakathāya virujjhanato. Tathā hi “mahāsīmāya pathavitalaṃ vā tatthajātarukkhādīni vā āhacca tiṭṭhatī”ti evaṃ sākhāpārohānaṃ mahāsīmaṃ phusitvā ṭhānameva sambandhadose kāraṇattena vuttaṃ, na pana tattha ṭhitabhikkhūhi sākhādīnaṃ phusanaṃ. Yadi hi bhikkhūnaṃ sākhādi phusitvā ṭhānameva kāraṇaṃ siyā, tassa sākhaṃ vā tato niggatapārohaṃ vā mahāsīmāya paviṭṭhaṃ tatraṭṭho koci bhikkhu phusitvā tiṭṭhatīti bhikkhuphusanameva vattabbaṃ siyā. Yañhi tattha mahāsīmāsodhane kāraṇaṃ, tadeva tasmiṃ vākye padhānato dassetabbaṃ. Na hi āhacca ṭhitameva sākhādiṃ phusitvā ṭhito bhikkhu sodhetabbo ākāsaṭṭhasākhādiṃ phusitvā ṭhitassāpi sodhetabbato, kiṃ niratthakena āhaccaṭṭhānavacanena. Ākāsaṭṭhasākhāsu ca bhikkhuno phusanameva kāraṇattena vuttaṃ, sodhanañca tasseva bhikkhussa hatthapāsānayanādivasena sodhanaṃ vuttaṃ. Idha pana “mahāsīmaṃ sodhetvā”ti sakalasīmāsādhāraṇavacanena sodhanaṃ vuttaṃ.

Some, however, say: “Here, in the phrase ‘or having purified the great boundary,’ what is intended is only the purification whereby the bhikkhus who have come to the great boundary do not touch that branch or aerial root with their bodies or things connected to their bodies; the purification of the entire boundary is not intended.” That is not correct, because it contradicts the commentary. For, in the statement, “[A branch] stands touching the ground level of the great boundary or trees, etc., growing there,” it is only the standing of branches and aerial roots touching the great boundary that is stated as the cause in the fault of connection, not the touching of branches, etc., by the bhikkhus standing there. For if the cause were only a bhikkhu standing and touching a branch, etc., it should have been stated only as the touching by a bhikkhu, thus: “Some bhikkhu standing there stands touching its branch that has entered the great boundary, or an aerial root that has emerged from it.” For whatever is the cause for purifying the great boundary there, that very thing should be shown primarily in that sentence. It is not that only a bhikkhu who stands touching a branch, etc., that is itself touching the ground should be purified, because even one who stands touching a branch, etc., that is in the air should be purified. What then is the use of the meaningless expression “standing touching”? And concerning branches in the air, the bhikkhu's touching alone should have been stated as the cause, and the purification should have been stated as the purification of that very bhikkhu by means of bringing him into hand's reach, etc. Here, however, purification is stated with the phrase “having purified the great boundary,” a statement applicable to the entire boundary.

Apica sākhādiṃ phusitvā ṭhitabhikkhumattasodhane abhimate “mahāsīmāya pathavitala”nti visesasīmopādānaṃ [V 2.0142] niratthakaṃ siyā yattha katthaci antamaso ākāsepi ṭhatvā sākhādiṃ phusitvā ṭhitassa visodhetabbato. Chinditvā [M 2.0150] bahiṭṭhakā kātabbāti tattha patiṭṭhitabhāvaviyojanavacanato ca visabhāgasīmānaṃ phusaneneva sakalasīmāsodhanahetuko aṭṭhakathāsiddhoyaṃ eko sambandhadoso atthevāti gahetabbo. Teneva udakukkhepasīmākathāyampi (mahāva. aṭṭha. 147) “vihārasīmāya vā gāmasīmāya vā patiṭṭhito”ti ca “naditīre pana khāṇukaṃ koṭṭetvā tattha baddhanāvāya na vaṭṭatī”ti ca “sace pana setu vā setupādā vā bahitīre patiṭṭhitā, kammaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti ca evaṃ visabhāgāsu gāmasīmāsu sākhādīnaṃ phusanameva saṅkaradosakāraṇattena vuttaṃ, na bhikkhuphusanaṃ. Tathā hi “antonadiyaṃ jātarukkhe bandhitvā kammaṃ kātabba”nti nadiyaṃ nāvābandhanaṃ anuññātaṃ udakukkhepanissayattena nadisīmāya sabhāgattā. Yadi hi bhikkhūnaṃ phusanameva paṭicca sabbattha sambandhadoso vutto siyā, nadiyampi bandhanaṃ paṭikkhipitabbaṃ bhaveyya. Tatthāpi hi bhikkhuphusanaṃ kammakopakāraṇaṃ hoti, tasmā sabhāgasīmāsu pavisitvā bhūmiādiṃ phusitvā vā aphusitvā vā sākhādimhi ṭhite taṃ sākhādiṃ phusantova bhikkhu sodhetabbo. Visabhāgasīmāsu pana sākhādimhi phusitvā ṭhite taṃ sākhādiṃ aphusantāpi sabbe bhikkhū sodhetabbā. Aphusitvā ṭhite pana taṃ sākhādiṃ phusantova bhikkhu sodhetabboti niṭṭhamettha gantabbaṃ.

Moreover, if the purification of only the bhikkhu who stands touching a branch, etc., were intended, the specific mention of the boundary in “the ground level of the great boundary” would be meaningless, because one who stands touching a branch, etc., having stood anywhere at all, even in the air, should be purified. And from the statement, “Having cut it, it should be made to be outside,” which speaks of severing its established state there, it should be understood that this one fault of connection, established by the commentary—which is a cause for purifying the entire boundary—indeed exists merely by the touching of dissimilar boundaries. For that very reason, in the discussion on the water-throwing boundary as well, it is said: “established in a monastery boundary or a village boundary,” and “but on a riverbank, having driven in a stake, a boat tied there is not allowable,” and “but if a bridge or bridge-posts are established on the outer bank, it is not allowable to perform the act.” Thus, in the case of dissimilar boundaries like village boundaries, it is only the touching by branches, etc., that is stated as the cause of the fault of mixture, not the touching by a bhikkhu. For so it is that tying a boat in the river was allowed with the words, “Having tied it to a tree growing within the river, the act should be done,” because the river-boundary is of a similar nature, being dependent on the water-throwing boundary. For if the fault of connection were stated everywhere depending only on the touching by bhikkhus, then tying a boat in the river should also be rejected. For there too, the touching by a bhikkhu is a cause for spoiling the act. Therefore, in similar boundaries, when a branch, etc., has entered and is standing there, whether it is touching the ground, etc., or not, only the bhikkhu who is touching that branch, etc., should be purified. But in dissimilar boundaries, when a branch, etc., is standing there touching it, all the bhikkhus should be purified, even those not touching that branch, etc. But when it is standing there without touching, only the bhikkhu who is touching that branch, etc., should be purified. This is the conclusion to be reached here.

Yaṃ panettha keci “baddhasīmānaṃ dvinnaṃ aññamaññaṃ viya baddhasīmāgāmasīmānampi tadaññāsampi sabbāsaṃ samānasaṃvāsakasīmānaṃ aññamaññaṃ rukkhādisambandhe sati tadubhayampi ekasīmaṃ viya sodhetvā ekattheva kammaṃ kātabbaṃ, aññattha kataṃ kammaṃ vipajjati, natthettha sabhāgavisabhāgabhedo”ti vadanti, taṃ tesaṃ matimattaṃ, sabhāgasīmānaṃ aññamaññaṃ sambhedadosābhāvassa visabhāgasīmānameva tabbhāvassa suttasuttānulomādivinayanayehi siddhattā. Tathā hi “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, sīmaṃ sammannitu”nti gāmasīmāyameva baddhasīmaṃ sammannituṃ anuññātaṃ. Tāsaṃ nissayanissitabhāvena sabhāgatā, sambhedajjhottharaṇādidosābhāvo ca suttatova siddho. Bandhanakāle pana anuññātassa sambandhassa anulomato pacchā sañjātarukkhādisambandhopi tāsaṃ vaṭṭati eva. “Yaṃ, bhikkhave…pe… kappiyaṃ anulometi akappiyaṃ paṭibāhati. Taṃ vo kappatī”ti (mahāva. 305) vuttattā. Evaṃ tāva baddhasīmāgāmasīmānaṃ aññamaññaṃ sabhāgatā, sambhedādidosābhāvo ca [M 2.0151] suttasuttānulomato siddho. Iminā eva nayena araññasīmāsattabbhantarasīmānaṃ, nadiādiudakukkhepasīmānañca suttasuttānulomato aññamaññaṃ sabhāgatā, sambhedādidosābhāvo ca siddhoti veditabbo.

As for the statement that some teachers here make: 'Just as when two consecrated boundaries are mutually connected by trees and so forth, both should be purified as if they were one boundary and the formal act performed in one place only; so too, when a consecrated boundary and a village boundary, or any other boundaries of common communion, are mutually connected by trees and so forth, both should be purified as if they were one boundary and the formal act performed in one place only. A formal act performed elsewhere is invalid. Here, there is no distinction between similar and dissimilar boundaries'—that is merely their opinion. Why? Because it is established by the Vinaya methods, such as the sutta and what is consistent with the sutta, that there is an absence of faults like intermixture between similar boundaries, and that such faults exist only for dissimilar boundaries. Indeed, it was said, 'I allow, monks, to establish a boundary,' and thus it is permitted to establish a consecrated boundary within a village boundary itself. Their similarity, by way of being the support and the supported, and the absence of faults such as intermixture and overlapping, are established by the sutta itself. Furthermore, in accordance with the connection permitted at the time of consecration, even a connection by trees and so forth that arise later is permissible for them. For it is said: 'Monks, whatever... is in conformity with what is allowable and rejects what is not allowable, that is permissible for you.' Thus, firstly, the mutual similarity of a consecrated boundary and a village boundary, and the absence of faults such as intermixture, are established by the sutta and what is consistent with the sutta. By this same method, it should be understood that the mutual similarity of a forest boundary and a seven-abbhantara boundary, and of a river, etc., boundary and a water-throwing boundary, and the absence of faults such as intermixture, are also established by the sutta and what is consistent with the sutta.

Baddhasīmāya [V 2.0143] pana aññāya baddhasīmāya, nadiādisīmāsu ca bandhituṃ paṭikkhepasiddhito ceva udakukkhepasattabbhantarasīmānaṃ nadiādīsu eva kātuṃ niyamanasuttasāmatthiyena baddhasīmāgāmasīmādīsu karaṇapaṭikkhepasiddhito ca tāsaṃ aññamaññaṃ visabhāgatā, uppattikkhaṇe, pacchā ca rukkhādīhi sambhedādidosasambhavo ca vuttanayena suttasuttānulomato ca sijjhanti. Teneva aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (mahāva. aṭṭha. 148) visabhāgasīmānameva vaṭarukkhādivacanehi sambandhadosaṃ dassetvā sabhāgānaṃ baddhasīmāgāmasīmādīnaṃ sambandhadoso na dassito, na kevalañca na dassito, atha kho tāsaṃ sabhāgasīmānaṃ rukkhādisambandhepi dosābhāvo pāḷiaṭṭhakathāsu ñāpito eva. Tathā hi pāḷiyaṃ “pabbatanimittaṃ pāsāṇanimittaṃ vananimittaṃ rukkhanimitta”ntiādinā vaḍḍhanakanimittāni anuññātāni. Tena nesaṃ rukkhādīnaṃ nimittānaṃ vaḍḍhanepi baddhasīmāgāmasīmānaṃ saṅkaradosābhāvo ñāpitova hoti. Dvinnaṃ pana baddhasīmānaṃ īdiso sambandho na vaṭṭati. Vuttañhi “ekarukkhopi ca dvinnaṃ sīmānaṃ nimittaṃ hoti, so pana vaḍḍhanto sīmāsaṅkaraṃ karoti, tasmā na kātabbo”ti “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, tiyojanaparamaṃ sīmaṃ sammannitu”nti vacanatopi cāyaṃ ñāpito. Tiyojanaparamāya hi sīmāya samantā pariyantesu rukkhalatāgumbādīhi baddhasīmāgāmasīmānaṃ niyamena aññamaññaṃ sambandhassa sambhavato “īdisaṃ sambandhanaṃ vināsetvāva sīmā sammannitabbā”ti aṭṭhakathāyampi na vuttaṃ.

Furthermore, because of the established prohibition against consecrating a consecrated boundary within another consecrated boundary or within boundaries such as a river, and by the power of the regulating sutta to establish water-throwing and seven-abbhantara boundaries only in rivers and the like, and because of the established prohibition against establishing them in consecrated boundaries, village boundaries, and so forth—for these reasons, their mutual dissimilarity, and the possibility of faults such as intermixture by trees and so forth arising both at the moment of their origin and later, are established by the aforesaid method and by the sutta and what is consistent with the sutta. For that very reason, in the commentary, having shown the fault of connection with words such as 'banyan tree' only for dissimilar boundaries, the fault of connection for similar boundaries, such as consecrated and village boundaries, was not shown. Not only was it not shown, but indeed, the absence of fault for those similar boundaries even when there is a connection by trees and so forth was made known in the Pāḷi and the commentaries. Indeed, in the Pāḷi, growing markers such as 'a mountain as a landmark, a rock as a landmark, a forest as a landmark, a tree as a landmark' were permitted. By that permission, even with the growth of those markers such as trees, the absence of the fault of intermingling for consecrated and village boundaries is indeed made known. However, for two consecrated boundaries, such a connection is not permissible. For it was said: 'A single tree may be a landmark for two boundaries, but as it grows, it causes intermingling of the boundaries; therefore, it should not be made so.' This meaning is also made known by the statement, 'I allow, monks, to establish a boundary with a maximum extent of three yojanas.' For, with a boundary of a maximum extent of three yojanas, there is necessarily the possibility of mutual connection between consecrated and village boundaries by trees, vines, bushes, and so forth, at the peripheries all around. Yet it is not said in the commentary either that 'a boundary should be established only after having destroyed such a connection.'

Yadi cettha rukkhādisambandhena kammavipatti bhaveyya, avassameva vattabbaṃ siyā. Vipattiparihāratthañhi ācariyā nirāsaṅkaṭṭhānesupi “bhittiṃ akittetvā”tiādinā siddhamevatthaṃ punappunaṃ avocuṃ. Idha pana “vanamajjhe vihāraṃ karonti, vanaṃ na kittetabba”ntiādirukkhalatādīhi nirantare vanamajjhepi sīmābandhanameva avocuṃ. Tathā thambhānaṃ upari katapāsādādīsu heṭṭhā thambhādīhi ekābaddhesu uparimatalādīsu sīmābandhanaṃ bahudhā vuttaṃ. Tasmā baddhasīmāgāmasīmānaṃ rukkhādisambandho tehi mukhatova vihito. Apica gāmasīmānampi pāṭekkaṃ baddhasīmāsadisatāya ekissā gāmasīmāya kammaṃ [M 2.0152] karontehi dabbatiṇamattenāpi sambandhā gāmantaraparamparā araññanadisamuddā ca sodhetabbāti sakaladīpaṃ sodhetvāva kātabbaṃ siyā. Evaṃ pana asodhetvā paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikālato pabhuti katānaṃ upasampadādikammānaṃ, sīmāsammutīnañca vipajjanato sabbesampi bhikkhūnaṃ anupasampannasaṅkāpasaṅgo ca dunnivāro hoti. Na cetaṃ yuttaṃ. Tasmā vuttanayeneva visabhāgasīmānameva rukkhādīhi sambandhadoso, na baddhasīmāgāmasīmādīnaṃ sabhāgasīmānanti gahetabbaṃ.

If, in this matter, an invalidity of a formal act were to occur due to a connection by trees and so forth, it would certainly have to be stated. Indeed, for the purpose of avoiding invalidity, the teachers repeatedly stated an already established meaning even in places free from doubt, with phrases such as 'without announcing the wall.' But here, with phrases such as 'they build a monastery in the middle of a forest, the forest need not be announced,' they spoke only of consecrating the boundary even in the middle of a forest dense with trees, vines, and so forth. Likewise, the consecration of a boundary on upper floors and the like, in mansions and so forth built on top of pillars that are connected as one with the pillars below, has been stated in many ways. Therefore, the connection by trees and so forth of consecrated and village boundaries was directly sanctioned by them. Moreover, since each village boundary is also similar to a consecrated boundary, when performing a formal act in one village boundary, if a connection even by a mere blade of grass were to necessitate purification, then successive other villages, forests, rivers, and oceans would have to be purified. Thus, the formal act would have to be performed only after purifying the entire island. But if it were done without purifying in this way, then due to the invalidity of the formal acts of higher ordination and so forth, and of the boundary establishments, performed from the time of the First Great Council onwards, the suspicion that all monks are not fully ordained would be difficult to prevent. And this is not proper. Therefore, it should be understood in accordance with the aforesaid method that there is a fault of connection with trees and so forth only for dissimilar boundaries, and not for similar boundaries such as consecrated and village boundaries.

Mahāsīmāsodhanassa dukkaratāya khaṇḍasīmāyameva yebhuyyena saṅghakammakaraṇanti āha “sīmāmāḷake”tiādi[V 2.0144]. Mahāsaṅghasannipāte pana khaṇḍasīmāya appahonakatāya mahāsīmāya kamme kariyamānepi ayaṃ nayo gahetabbova.

Due to the difficulty of purifying a great boundary, the Sangha's formal acts are mostly performed within a constituent boundary; thus, he said, 'in the boundary hall,' and so forth. However, in a great assembly of the Sangha, even when a formal act is being performed in the great boundary due to the insufficiency of the constituent boundary, this same method should be adopted.

“Ukkhipāpetvā”ti iminā kāyapaṭibaddhenapi sīmaṃ phusanto sīmaṭṭhova hotīti dasseti. Purimanayepīti khaṇḍasīmato mahāsīmaṃ paviṭṭhasākhānayepi. Sīmaṭṭharukkhasākhāya nisinno sīmaṭṭhova hotīti āha “hatthapāsameva ānetabbo”ti. Ettha ca rukkhasākhādīhi aññamaññaṃ sambandhāsu etāsu khandhasīmāyaṃ tayo bhikkhū, mahāsīmāyaṃ dveti evaṃ dvīsu sīmāsu sīmantarikaṃ aphusitvā, hatthapāsañca avijahitvā ṭhitehi pañcahi bhikkhūhi upasampadādikammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatīti keci vadanti. Taṃ na yuttaṃ “nānāsīmāya ṭhitacatuttho kammaṃ kareyya, akammaṃ, na ca karaṇīya”ntiādi (mahāva. 389) vacanato. Tenevetthāpi mahāsīmaṃ sodhetvā māḷakasīmāyameva kammakaraṇaṃ vihitaṃ. Aññathā bhinnasīmaṭṭhatāya tatraṭṭhassa gaṇapūrakattābhāvā kammakopova hotīti.

By 'ukkhipāpetvā,' it is shown that a monk touching the boundary even with an object connected to his body is indeed one who stands in the boundary. As for 'in the previous method also,' this refers to the method concerning a branch that has entered a great boundary from a constituent boundary. A monk sitting on a tree branch that stands in the boundary is indeed one who stands in the boundary; therefore, it is said, 'he should be brought only within hand's reach.' And here, concerning these boundaries interconnected by tree branches and so on, some say that it is permissible for five monks—three in the constituent boundary and two in the great boundary, thus standing in two boundaries without touching the intervening space and without going out of hand's reach—to perform an act such as ordination. That is not proper, because of the statement beginning, 'If a fourth person standing in a different boundary were to perform the act, it would be a non-act, and it should not be done.' For that very reason, here also, having purified the great boundary, the performance of the act is prescribed only within the māḷaka-sīmā. Otherwise, due to being one who stands in a separate boundary, because the one standing there is not a quorum-filler, the act itself becomes invalidated.

Yadi evaṃ kathaṃ chandapārisuddhiāharaṇavasena mahāsīmāsodhananti? Tampi vinayaññū na icchanti, hatthapāsānayanabahisīmākaraṇavaseneva panettha sodhanaṃ icchanti, dinnassāpi chandassa anāgamanena mahāsīmaṭṭho kammaṃ kopetīti. Yadi cassa chandādi nāgacchati, kathaṃ so kammaṃ kopessatīti? Dvinnaṃ visabhāgasīmānaṃ sambandhadosato. So ca sambandhadoso aṭṭhakathāvacanappamāṇato. Na hi vinaye sabbattha yutti sakkā ñātuṃ buddhagocarattāti veditabbaṃ. Keci pana “sace dvepi sīmāyo pūretvā nirantaraṃ [M 2.0153] ṭhitesu bhikkhūsu kammaṃ karontesu ekissā eva sīmāya gaṇo ca upasampadāpekkho ca anussāvako ca ekato tiṭṭhati, kammaṃ sukatameva hoti. Sace pana kammāraho vā anussāvako vā sīmantaraṭṭho hoti, kammaṃ vipajjatī”ti vadanti, tañca baddhasīmāgāmasīmādisabhāgasīmāsu eva yujjati, yāsu aññamaññaṃ rukkhādisambandhesupi doso natthi. Yāsu pana atthi, na tāsu visabhāgasīmāsu rukkhādisambandhe sati ekattha ṭhito itaraṭṭhānaṃ kammaṃ kopeti eva aṭṭhakathāyaṃ sāmaññato sodhanassa vuttattāti amhākaṃ khanti. Vīmaṃsitvā gahetabbaṃ.

If so, how is there purification of the great boundary by means of bringing consent and purity? The experts in Vinaya do not desire that either; they desire purification here only by means of bringing into hand's reach and making someone be outside the boundary, for because of the non-arrival of consent, even though given, the one standing in the great boundary corrupts the act. If his consent and so forth do not arrive, how will he corrupt the act? Due to the fault of connection between two dissimilar boundaries. And that fault of connection is to be accepted on the authority of the commentary's word. Indeed, it is not possible to know the reason everywhere in the Vinaya, because it is the domain of the Buddha—thus it should be known. Some, however, say: 'If, while the monks are performing an act, having filled both boundaries and standing without interval, the quorum, the ordination candidate, and the announcer stand together in one boundary only, the act is well-done indeed. But if one eligible for the act or the announcer stands in another boundary, the act fails.' And that is proper only in similar boundaries such as a bound boundary, a village boundary, etc., in which there is no fault even in connections with each other by trees and so on. But in those dissimilar boundaries where there is a fault, when there is a connection by trees and so on, one standing in one place does not corrupt the act of those in the other place, because in the commentary, purification is spoken of in a general way. This is our opinion. It should be investigated and accepted.

Na otaratīti paṇavasaṇṭhānapabbatādīsu heṭṭhā pamāṇarahitaṭṭhānaṃ na otarati. Kiñcāpi panettha bajjhamānakkhaṇe uddhampi pamāṇarahitaṃ pabbatādīni nārohati, tathāpi taṃ pacchā sīmaṭṭhatāya sīmā hoti. Heṭṭhā paṇavasaṇṭhānādi pana upari baddhāyapi sīmāya sīmāsaṅkhyaṃ na gacchati, tassa vasena na otaratīti vuttaṃ, itarathā orohaṇārohaṇānaṃ sādhāraṇavasena “na otaratī”tiādinā [V 2.0145] vattabbato. Yaṃ kiñcīti niṭṭhitasīmāya upari jātaṃ vijjamānaṃ pubbe ṭhitaṃ, pacchā sañjātaṃ, paviṭṭhañca yaṃkiñci saviññāṇakāviññāṇakaṃ sabbampīti attho. Antosīmāya hi hatthikkhandhādisaviññāṇakesu nisinnopi bhikkhu sīmaṭṭhova hoti. “Baddhasīmāyā”ti idañca pakaraṇavasena upalakkhaṇato vuttaṃ. Abaddhasīmāsupi sabbāsu ṭhitaṃ taṃ sīmāsaṅkhyameva gacchati.

'It does not descend' means that on a drum-shaped mountain and so on, it does not descend to a place below that is without measure. Although here, at the moment of being bound, it does not ascend to a mountain, etc., that is without measure even above, nevertheless, that later becomes the boundary by virtue of being situated in the boundary. But what is below, such as a drum-shaped mountain, even when a boundary is bound above, does not go into the count of a boundary; it is said 'it does not descend' with reference to that. Otherwise, due to the commonality of descending and ascending, it would have to be said as 'it does not descend,' etc. 'Whatever' means: whatever is above the completed boundary—arisen, existing, previously standing, later come into being, and entered—all of it, whether sentient or insentient. For a monk sitting on a sentient being such as an elephant's back within the boundary is indeed one who stands in the boundary. And this, 'of a bound boundary,' is said by way of indication due to the context. In all unbound boundaries also, that which stands therein goes into the count of a boundary.

Ekasambaddhena gatanti rukkhalatāditatrajātameva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tādisampi “ito gata”nti vattabbataṃ arahati. Yaṃ pana “ito gata”nti vā “tato āgata”nti vā vattuṃ asakkuṇeyyaṃ ubhosu baddhasīmāgāmasīmāsu, udakukkhepanadiādīsu ca tiriyaṃ patitarajjudaṇḍādi, tattha kiṃ kātabbanti? Ettha pana baddhasīmāya patiṭṭhitabhāgo baddhasīmā, abaddhagāmasīmāya patiṭṭhitabhāgo gāmasīmā tadubhayasīmaṭṭhapabbatādi viya. Baddhasīmato uṭṭhitavaṭarukkhassa pārohe, gāmasīmāya gāmasīmato uṭṭhitavaṭarukkhassa pārohe ca baddhasīmāya patiṭṭhitepi eseva nayo. Mūlapatiṭṭhitakālato hi paṭṭhāya “ito gataṃ, tato āgata”nti vattuṃ asakkuṇeyyato so bhāgo yathāpaviṭṭhasīmāsaṅkhyameva gacchati, tesaṃ rukkhapārohānaṃ antarā pana ākāsaṭṭhasākhā bhūmiyaṃ sīmāparicchedappamāṇena [M 2.0154] tadubhayasīmā hotīti keci vadanti. Yasmā panassa sākhāya pāroho paviṭṭhasīmāya pathaviyaṃ mūlehi patiṭṭhahitvāpi yāva sākhaṃ vinā ṭhātuṃ na sakkoti, tāva mūlasīmaṭṭhataṃ na vijahati. Yadā pana vinā ṭhātuṃ sakkoti, tadāpi pārohamattameva paviṭṭhasīmaṭṭhataṃ samupeti. Tasmā sabbopi ākāsaṭṭhasākhābhāgo purimasīmaṭṭhataṃ na vijahati, tato āgatabhāgassa avijahitattāti amhākaṃ khanti. Udakukkhepanadiādīsupi eseva nayo. Tattha ca visabhāgasīmāya evaṃ paviṭṭhe sakalasīmāsodhanaṃ, sabhāgāya paviṭṭhe phusitvā ṭhitamattabhikkhusodhanañca sabbaṃ pubbe vuttanayameva.

'Gone by being connected as one' is said referring only to a tree, vine, and so on, born there. Indeed, such a thing deserves to be called 'gone from here.' But regarding that which is impossible to call either 'gone from here' or 'come from there'—such as a rope, staff, etc., fallen across in both a bound boundary and a village boundary, or in a water-throw boundary, a river boundary, and so on—what is to be done there? Here, the part established in the bound boundary is a bound boundary, and the part established in an unbound village boundary is a village boundary, like a mountain, etc., standing on both those boundaries. This is the same method regarding an aerial root of a banyan tree that has arisen from a bound boundary, even when it is established in a village boundary, and regarding an aerial root of a banyan tree that has arisen from a village boundary, even when it is established in a bound boundary. For, starting from the time it is established by its roots, because it is impossible to say 'gone from here, come from there,' that part goes into the count of the boundary it has entered. Some, however, say that between those aerial roots, the branch standing in the sky becomes both boundaries by the measure of the boundary's demarcation on the ground. But since the aerial root from its branch, even after being established by its roots in the ground of the entered boundary, cannot stand without the branch for as long as it cannot, it does not abandon its state of being in the root-boundary. When, however, it can stand without it, then also only the aerial root itself attains the state of being in the entered boundary. Therefore, the entire part of the branch standing in the sky does not abandon its state of being in the former boundary, because its state of having come from there has not been abandoned. This is our opinion. In a water-throw boundary, a river boundary, and so on, this is the same method. And there, if it has entered a dissimilar boundary in this way, there is purification of the entire boundary; if it has entered a similar boundary, there is purification of only the monk who is standing touching it—all is just as in the method previously stated.

140. Pārayatīti ajjhottharati, nadiyā ubhosu tīresu patiṭṭhamānā sīmā nadiajjhottharā nāma hotīti āha “nadiṃajjhottharamāna”nti. Antonadiyañhi sīmā na otarati. Nadilakkhaṇe pana asati otarati, sā ca tadā nadipārasīmā na hotīti āha “nadiyā lakkhaṇaṃ nadinimitte vuttanayamevā”ti. Assāti bhaveyya. Avassaṃ labbhaneyyā pana dhuvanāvāva hotīti sambandho. “Na nāvāyā”ti iminā nāvaṃ vināpi sīmā baddhā subaddhā eva hoti, āpattiparihāratthā nāvāti dasseti.

140. As for 'pārayati,' it means it overwhelms. A boundary established on both banks of a river is called 'nadiajjhottharā' (river-overwhelming); therefore, it is said, 'nadiṃ ajjhottharamānaṃ' (overwhelming the river). Indeed, the boundary does not descend into the river. But when the characteristics of a river are absent, it does descend, and at that time, it is not a 'nadipārasīmā' (far-shore boundary). Therefore, it is said, 'The characteristics of a river are just as stated in the section on river-signs.' As for 'assā,' it means 'it might be.' The connection is that 'avassaṃ labbhaneyyā' (that which is definitely obtainable) is a permanent boat. By this text, 'na nāvāyā' (not by a boat), it is shown that even without a boat, a boundary, once established, is indeed well-established; the boat is for the purpose of avoiding an offense.

Rukkhasaṅghāṭamayoti [V 2.0146] anekarukkhe ekato ghaṭetvā katasetu. Rukkhaṃ chinditvā katoti pāṭhaseso. “Sabbanimittānaṃ anto ṭhite bhikkhū hatthapāsagate katvā”ti idaṃ ubhinnaṃ tīrānaṃ ekagāmakhettabhāvaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Pabbatasaṇṭhānāti ekato uggatadīpasikharattā vuttaṃ.

As for 'rukkhasaṅghāṭamayo' (made of a raft of trees), it is a bridge made by joining many trees together. The remaining part of the text is 'made by cutting a tree.' This statement, 'having brought the bhikkhus standing within all the signs into hand's reach,' was said with reference to the fact of both banks being a single village-field. The statement 'pabbatasaṇṭhānā' (having the shape of a mountain) was said because of it having the peak of an island rising from one side.

Sīmānujānanakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Authorization of Boundaries is concluded.

Uposathāgārādikathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Uposatha Hall and So Forth

141. Samūhanitvāti vināsetvā, uddharitvāti attho. Idañca āpattiparihāratthaṃ vuttaṃ.

141. As for 'samūhanitvā,' it means 'having destroyed'; the meaning is 'having removed' or 'having revoked.' And this was stated for the purpose of avoiding an offense.

142. Yāni kānicīti idha nimittānaṃ sīmāya pāḷiyaṃ sarūpato avuttattā vuttaṃ.

142. The statement 'yāni kānici' (whatever they may be) was said because here, unlike in the case of a boundary, the signs are not stated in their specific form in the Pāli.

Uposathāgārādikathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Uposatha Hall and So Forth is concluded.

Avippavāsasīmānujānanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Authorization of the Non-separation Boundary

143. Aṭṭhārasāti [M 2.0155] andhakavindavihārampi upādāya vuccati. Nesaṃ sīmāti tesu mahāvihāresu. “Mana”nti imassa vivaraṇaṃ īsakanti, īsakaṃ vuḷhoti attho. Imamevatthaṃ dassetuṃ “appattavuḷhabhāvo ahosī”ti vuttaṃ. Amanasikarontoti iddhiyā anatikkamassa kāraṇaṃ vuttaṃ.

143. The statement 'aṭṭhārasā' (eighteen) is said by including the Andhakavinda monastery. 'Nesaṃ sīmā' (their boundary) refers to those great monasteries. 'Īsakaṃ' is an explanation of the word 'manaṃ'; the meaning is 'a little was carried away.' In order to show this very meaning, it was said, 'there was a state of not being much carried away.' By the text 'amanasikaronto' (not paying attention), the reason for not transgressing by means of psychic power was stated.

144. Soti bhikkhunisaṅgho. Dvepīti dve samānasaṃvāsaavippavāsāyo. Avippavāsasīmāti mahāsīmaṃ sandhāya vadati. Tattheva yebhuyyena avippavāsāti.

144. 'So' refers to the community of bhikkhunīs. 'Dvepi' refers to the two: the common-communion and non-separation boundaries. The statement 'avippavāsasīmā' (non-separation boundary) is said with reference to the great boundary, because for the most part, the designation of non-separation occurs in that very place.

“Avippavāsaṃ ajānantāpī”ti idaṃ mahāsīmāya vijjamānāvijjamānattaṃ, tassā bāhiraparicchedañca ajānantānaṃ vasena vuttaṃ. Evaṃ ajānantehipi antosīmāya ṭhatvā kammavācāya katāya sā sīmā samūhatāva hotīti āha “samūhanituñceva bandhituñca sakkhissantī”ti. Nirāsaṅkaṭṭhāneti khaṇḍasīmārahitaṭṭhāne. Idañca mahāsīmāya vijjamānāyapi kammakaraṇasukhatthaṃ khaṇḍasīmā icchitāti taṃ cetiyaṅgaṇādibahusannipātaṭṭhāne na bandhatīti vuttaṃ. Tatthāpi [V 2.0147] sā baddhā subaddhā eva mahāsīmā viya. “Paṭibandhituṃ pana na sakkhissantevā”ti idaṃ khaṇḍasīmāya asamūhatattā, tassā avijjamānattassa ajānanato ca mahāsīmābandhanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Khaṇḍasīmaṃ pana nirāsaṅkaṭṭhāne bandhituṃ sakkhissanteva. Sīmāsambhedaṃ katvāti khaṇḍasīmāya vijjamānapakkhe sīmāya sīmaṃ ajjhottharaṇasambhedaṃ katvā avijjamānapakkhepi sambhedasaṅkāya anivattanena sambhedasaṅkaṃ katvā. Avihāraṃ kareyyunti saṅghakammānārahaṃ kareyyuṃ. Pubbe hi cetiyaṅgaṇādinirāsaṅkaṭṭhāne kammaṃ kātuṃ sakkā, idāni tampi vināsitanti adhippāyo. Na samūhanitabbāti khaṇḍasīmaṃ ajānantehi na samūhanitabbā. Ubhopi na jānantīti ubhinnaṃ padesaniyamaṃ vā tāsaṃ dvinnampi vā aññatarāya vā vijjamānataṃ vā avijjamānataṃ vā na jānanti, sabbattha saṅkā eva hoti. “Neva samūhanituṃ, na bandhituṃ sakkhissantī”ti idaṃ nirāsaṅkaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā samūhanituṃ sakkontopi mahāsīmaṃ paṭibandhituṃ na sakkontīti imamatthaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. “Na ca sakkā…pe… kammavācaṃ kātu”nti idaṃ sīmābandhanakammavācaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tasmāti yasmā bandhituṃ na sakkā, tasmā na samūhanitabbāti attho.

This statement, 'avippavāsaṃ ajānantāpi' (even those not knowing the non-separation), was said by way of those who do not know the existence or non-existence of the great boundary and its external delimitation. Even by those who do not know thus, when the formal act is performed while standing inside the boundary, that boundary is indeed revoked. Therefore, it was said, 'they will be able to revoke and to establish.' 'Nirāsaṅkaṭṭhāne' (in a place free from suspicion) means in a place free from a sectional boundary. And this was said: even if the great boundary exists, a sectional boundary is desired for the ease of performing acts, so one does not establish it in a place of many gatherings, such as a cetiya-courtyard. Even there, if it is established, it is indeed well-established, like the great boundary. This statement, 'paṭibandhituṃ pana na sakkhissanteva' (but they will not be able to re-establish), was said with reference to the establishment of the great boundary, because the sectional boundary has not been revoked and because of not knowing its non-existence. But they are indeed able to establish a sectional boundary in a place free from suspicion. 'Sīmāsambhedaṃ katvā' (having caused a confusion of boundaries) means: in the case where a sectional boundary exists, having caused a confusion by the great boundary overwhelming the sectional boundary; and in the case where it does not exist, by not turning back from the suspicion of confusion, having created a suspicion of confusion. 'Avihāraṃ kareyyuṃ' (they would make it an un-dwelling) means they would make it unsuitable for Sangha acts. The intention is: previously, it was possible to perform an act in a place free from suspicion, such as a cetiya-courtyard; now, even that is destroyed. 'Na samūhanitabbā' (it should not be revoked) means: it should not be revoked by those who do not know the sectional boundary. 'Ubhopi na jānanti' (they do not know both) means: they do not know the specific location of both, or the existence or non-existence of either of the two; there is only suspicion everywhere. This statement, 'neva samūhanituṃ, na bandhituṃ sakkhissantī' (they will be able neither to revoke nor to establish), was said with reference to this meaning: even though they are able to revoke while standing in a place free from suspicion, they are not able to re-establish the great boundary. This statement, 'na ca sakkā…pe… kammavācaṃ kātuṃ' (and it is not possible… etc… to perform the formal act), was said with reference to the formal act of establishing a boundary. 'Tasmā' (therefore) means: because it is not possible to establish, therefore it should not be revoked. This is the meaning.

Keci [M 2.0156] pana “īdisesu vihāresu chapañcamatte bhikkhū gahetvā vihārakoṭito paṭṭhāya vihāraparikkhepassa anto ca bahi ca samantā leḍḍupāte sabbattha mañcappamāṇe okāse nirantaraṃ ṭhatvā paṭhamaṃ avippavāsasīmaṃ, tato samānasaṃvāsakasīmañca samūhananavasena sīmāya samugghāte kate tasmiṃ vihāre khaṇḍasīmāya, mahāsīmāyapi vā vijjamānatte sati avassaṃ ekasmiṃ mañcaṭṭhāne tāsaṃ majjhagatā te bhikkhū tā samūhaneyyuṃ, tato gāmasīmā eva avasisseyya. Na hettha sīmāya, tapparicchedassa vā jānanaṃ aṅgaṃ. Sīmāya pana antoṭhānaṃ, “samūhanissāmā”ti kammavācāya karaṇañcettha aṅgaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ ‘khaṇḍasīmaṃ pana jānantā avippavāsaṃ ajānantāpi samūhanituñceva bandhituñca sakkhissantī’ti evaṃ mahāsīmāya paricchedassa ajānanepi samūhanassa vuttattā. Gāmasīmāya eva ca avasiṭṭhāya tattha yathāruci duvidhampi sīmaṃ bandhituñceva upasampadādikammaṃ kātuñca vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti, taṃ yuttaṃ viya dissati. Vīmaṃsitvā gahetabbaṃ.

Some, however, say: 'In such monasteries, having taken five or six bhikkhus, starting from the edge of the monastery, standing continuously without a gap in every space the size of a bed, both inside and outside the monastery enclosure, all around at a clod's throw, when the boundary has been uprooted by way of revocation—first of the non-separation boundary, and after that, of the common-communion boundary—if a sectional boundary or a great boundary exists in that monastery, those bhikkhus, having come to be in the middle of them in some bed-sized spot, would certainly revoke them. Then, only the village boundary would remain. Indeed, herein, knowledge of the boundary or its delimitation is not a factor. But standing inside the boundary and the performance of the formal act with the words, 'we will revoke,' are factors herein. This is because in the Aṭṭhakathā it is said, 'But those knowing the sectional boundary, even if not knowing the non-separation, will be able to revoke and to establish,' and thus the revocation is stated even when not knowing the delimitation of the great boundary. And when only the village boundary remains, it is allowable there to establish both kinds of boundary as one wishes and to perform acts such as higher ordination.' That statement appears to be reasonable. It should be accepted after investigation.

Avippavāsasīmānujānanakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Authorization of the Non-separation Boundary is concluded.

Gāmasīmādikathāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Discourse on the Village Boundary and So Forth

147. Pāḷiyaṃ [V 2.0148] “asammatāya, bhikkhave, sīmāyā”tiādinā gāmasīmā eva baddhasīmāya khettaṃ, araññanadiādayo viya sattabbhantaraudakukkhepādīnaṃ. Sā ca gāmasīmā baddhasīmāvirahitaṭṭhāne sayameva samānasaṃvāsā hotīti dasseti. Yā tassa vā gāmassa gāmasīmāti ettha gāmasīmāparicchedassa anto ca bahi ca khettavatthuaraññapabbatādikaṃ sabbaṃ gāmakhettaṃ sandhāya “gāmassā”ti vuttaṃ, na antaragharameva. Tasmā tassa sakalassa gāmakhettassa sambandhanīyā gāmasīmāti evamattho veditabbo. Yo hi so antaragharakhettādīsu anekesu bhūmibhāgesu “gāmo”ti ekattena lokajanehi paññatto gāmavohāro, sova idha “gāmasīmā”tipi vuccatīti adhippāyo, gāmo eva hi gāmasīmā. Imināva nayena upari araññaṃ nadī samuddo jātassaroti evaṃ tesu bhūmippadesesu ekattena lokajanapaññattānameva araññādīnaṃ araññasīmādibhāvo veditabbo. Loke pana gāmasīmādivohāro gāmādīnaṃ [M 2.0157] mariyādāyameva vattuṃ vaṭṭati, na gāmakhettādīsu sabbattha. Sāsane pana te gāmādayo itaranivattiatthena sayameva attano mariyādāti katvā gāmo eva gāmasīmā, araññameva araññasīmā…pe… samuddo eva samuddasīmāti sīmāvohārena vuttāti veditabbā.

147. In the Pāḷi, beginning with ‘Monks, by an unapproved boundary,’ the village boundary is indeed the field for a fixed boundary, just as the wilderness, river, and so forth are the fields for the seven-cubit, water-casting, and other such boundaries. It shows that this village boundary, in a place lacking a fixed boundary, is by itself one of common residence. Where it says, ‘the village boundary of that village,’ the phrase ‘of the village’ is stated with reference to all the village land—including fields, plots, wilderness, mountains, and so forth, both inside and outside the village demarcation—not just the area between houses. Therefore, the meaning should be understood thus: the village boundary is that which is connected to that entire village land. Indeed, the designation ‘village,’ which is conventionally designated as a single entity by people in various land divisions like the area between houses, fields, and so forth, is here also called ‘village boundary’; this is the intention, for the village itself is the village boundary. By this same method, it should be understood that further on, the wilderness, river, ocean, and natural lake have the nature of a wilderness boundary and so forth, because they are designated as a single entity by people in those land regions. In the world, however, the designation ‘village boundary’ and so forth is properly used only for the limits of villages and so forth, not for all village lands everywhere. But in the Dispensation, since those villages and so forth are, by their very nature, their own limits in the sense of excluding others, it should be understood that they are spoken of with the designation ‘boundary’ as: ‘the village itself is the village boundary, the wilderness itself is the wilderness boundary… and so on… the ocean itself is the ocean boundary.’

“Nigamassa vā”ti idaṃ gāmasīmappabhedaṃ sabbaṃ upalakkhaṇavasena dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Tenāha “nagarampi gahitamevā”ti. “Baliṃ labhantī”ti idaṃ yebhuyyavasena vuttaṃ, “ayaṃ gāmo ettako karīsabhāgo”tiādinā pana rājapaṇṇesu āropitesu bhūmibhāgesu yasmiṃ yasmiṃ taḷākamātikāsusānapabbatādike padese baliṃ na gaṇhanti, sopi gāmasīmā eva. Rājādīhi paricchinnabhūmibhāgo hi sabbova ṭhapetvā nadiloṇijātassare gāmasīmāti veditabbo. Tenāha “paricchinditvā rājā kassaci detī”ti. Sace pana tattha rājā kañci padesaṃ gāmantarena yojeti, so paviṭṭhagāmasīmataṃ eva bhajati, nadijātassaresu vināsetvā taḷākādibhāvaṃ vā pūretvā khettādibhāvaṃ vā pāpitesupi eseva nayo.

The phrase ‘or of a town’ is stated to indicate all the various types of village boundaries by way of example. Hence, it is said, ‘even a city is included.’ ‘They receive tribute’—this is stated for the most part. However, regarding portions of land entered into the royal records—such as, ‘this village has such and such a share of karisas’—even if tribute is not collected in certain places like ponds, irrigation channels, cemeteries, mountains, and so forth, those too are still considered village boundaries. For all portions of land demarcated by the king or others, except for rivers, salt-water areas, and natural lakes, should be understood as village boundaries. Therefore, it is said, ‘the king demarcates and grants it to someone.’ But if the king connects any portion of land there to another village, it then attains the state of being a village boundary that has been incorporated; and this same principle applies even if rivers and natural lakes are destroyed and made into ponds and so forth, or are filled in and made into fields and so forth.

Ye pana gāmā rājacorādibhayapīḷitehi manussehi chaḍḍitā cirampi nimmanussā tiṭṭhanti, samantā pana gāmā santi, tepi pāṭekkaṃ gāmasīmāva. Tesu hi rājāno samantagāmavāsīhi kasāpetvā vā yehi kehici kasitaṭṭhānaṃ likhitvā vā baliṃ gaṇhanti, aññena vā gāmena ekībhāvaṃ vā upanenti. Ye pana gāmā rājūhipi pariccattā gāmakhettānantarikā mahāraññena ekībhūtā, te agāmakāraññasīmataṃ pāpuṇanti, purimā gāmasīmā [V 2.0149] vinassati. Rājāno pana ekasmiṃ araññādippadese mahantaṃ gāmaṃ katvā anekasahassāni kulāni vāsāpetvā tattha vāsīnaṃ bhogagāmāti samantā bhūtagāme paricchinditvā denti. Purāṇanāmaṃ, pana paricchedañca na vināsenti, tepi paccekaṃ gāmasīmā eva. Ettāvatā purimagāmasīmattaṃ na vijahanti. Sā ca itarā cātiādi “samānasaṃvāsā ekūposathā”ti pāḷipadassa adhippāyavivaraṇaṃ. Tattha hi sā ca rājicchāvasena parivattitvā samuppannā abhinavā, itarā ca aparivattā pakatigāmasīmā, yathā baddhasīmāya sabbaṃ saṅghakammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati, evametāpi sabbakammārahatāsadisena baddhasīmāsadisā, sā samānasaṃvāsā ekūposathāti [M 2.0158] adhippāyo. Sāmaññato “baddhasīmāsadisā”ti vutte ticīvarāvippavāsasīmaṃ baddhasīmaṃ eva maññantīti taṃsadisatānivattanamukhena upari sattabbhantarasīmāya taṃsadisatāpi atthīti dassananayassa idheva pasaṅgaṃ dassetuṃ “kevala”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

As for those villages abandoned by people afflicted by fear of kings, thieves, and so forth, even if they remain uninhabited for a long time while surrounding villages exist, they are still individual village boundaries. For in them, kings collect taxes, either by having the residents of surrounding villages cultivate the land or by recording the area cultivated by whomever, or they may unite them with another village. As for those villages that are given up even by kings, have no adjoining village-fields, and have become one with the great wilderness, they attain the state of being a wilderness boundary without a village, and the former village boundary is destroyed. However, kings may establish a large village in a wilderness or other area, settling many thousands of families there, and then designate the surrounding existing villages as villages for their enjoyment for the residents. They do not destroy the old names or boundaries, and these too are individual village boundaries. By this much, they do not abandon the state of being a former village boundary. The phrase ‘both that one and the other’ and so forth is an explanation of the meaning of the Pāḷi phrase ‘of common residence, of single Uposatha.’ For here, ‘that one’ is the new one that has arisen, having been changed by the king's will, and ‘the other’ is the unchanged, natural village boundary. Just as it is proper to perform all Sangha acts within a fixed boundary, so too these are similar to a fixed boundary by being similarly suitable for all acts. The intention is that it is of common residence and of single Uposatha. Generally, when it is said that they are ‘like a fixed boundary,’ some may think only of the boundary for not being separated from the three robes as the fixed boundary. Therefore, to negate that specific likeness and to show the relevance here of the method for demonstrating that the seven-cubit boundary also possesses that likeness, the word ‘only’ and so forth was stated.

Viñjhāṭavisadise araññeti yattha “asukagāmassa idaṃ khetta”nti gāmavohāro natthi, yattha ca na kasanti na vapanti, tādise araññe. Macchabandhānaṃ agamanapathā nimmanussāvāsā samuddantaradīpakāpi ettheva saṅgayhanti. Yaṃ yañhi agāmakhettabhūtaṃ nadisamuddajātassaravirahitaṃ padesaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ araññasīmāti veditabbaṃ. Sā ca sattabbhantarasīmaṃ vināva sayameva samānasaṃvāsā baddhasīmāsadisā. Nadiādisīmāsu viya sabbamettha saṅghakammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Nadisamuddajātassarānaṃ tāva aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “attano sabhāveneva baddhasīmāsadisā”tiādinā vuttattā sīmatā siddhā. Araññassa pana sīmatā kathanti? Sattabbhantarasīmānujānanasuttādisāmatthiyato. Yathā hi gāmasīmāya vaggakammaparihāratthaṃ bahū baddhasīmāyo anuññātā, tāsañca dvinnamantarā aññamaññaṃ asambhedatthaṃ sīmantarikā anuññātā, evamidhāraññepi sattabbhantarasīmā. Tāsañca dvinnaṃ antarā sīmantarikāya pāḷiaṭṭhakathāsupi vidhānasāmatthiyato araññassapi sabhāveneva nadiādīnaṃ viya sīmābhāvo tattha vaggakammaparihāratthameva sattabbhantarasīmāya anuññātattāva siddhoti veditabbo. Tattha sīmāyameva hi ṭhitā sīmaṭṭhānaṃ vaggakammaṃ karonti, na asīmāyaṃ ākāse ṭhitā viya ākāsaṭṭhānaṃ. Evameva hi sāmatthiyaṃ gahetvā “sabbā, bhikkhave, nadī asīmā”tiādinā paṭikkhittabaddhasīmānampi nadisamuddajātassarānaṃ attano sabhāveneva sīmābhāvo aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttoti gahetabbo.

The phrase beginning with 'In a wilderness like the Viñjhāṭavi forest' refers to a wilderness where there is no village designation such as ‘this is the field of such-and-such a village,’ and where they neither plow nor sow. Paths not frequented by fishermen, places not inhabited by humans, and also small islands in the middle of the ocean are included herein. For any region that is not a village-field and is devoid of rivers, oceans, and natural lakes, all that should be known as a wilderness-boundary. And that boundary, without a seven-abbhantara boundary, is by itself of common co-residence, similar to a consecrated boundary. Just as in boundaries such as rivers, it is proper to perform all Sangha acts here. As for rivers, oceans, and natural lakes, their state as a boundary is established because it is stated in the Commentary, beginning with 'by their very own nature, they are similar to a consecrated boundary.' But how is the state of the wilderness as a boundary established? By the power of the Sutta, etc., that authorizes the seven-abbhantara boundary. For just as in a village-boundary many consecrated boundaries are authorized for the purpose of avoiding incomplete acts, and between two of them an intermediate boundary is authorized so that they do not merge with each other, so too here in the wilderness are seven-abbhantara boundaries authorized. And it should be known that by the power of the provision in the Pāḷi and Commentaries for an intermediate boundary between two of them, the wilderness's state of being a boundary by its very nature, like rivers and so forth, is established, as is the fact that the seven-abbhantara boundary is authorized there solely for the purpose of avoiding incomplete acts. For it is those standing right within a boundary who perform an incomplete act concerning those standing within the boundary, not those standing in a non-boundary, just as those standing in the sky do not perform an incomplete act concerning those standing in the sky. Indeed, having grasped this very capacity, it should be understood that in the Commentary, the state of being a boundary by their very own nature is stated even for rivers, oceans, and natural lakes, for which the state of being a consecrated boundary has been rejected by the text beginning with 'All rivers, O monks, are not a boundary'.

Athassa ṭhitokāsatoti assa bhikkhussa ṭhitokāsato. Sacepi hi bhikkhusahassaṃ tiṭṭhati, tassa ṭhitokāsassa bāhirantato paṭṭhāya bhikkhūnaṃ vaggakammaparihāratthaṃ sīmāpekkhāya uppannāya [V 2.0150] tāya saha sayameva sañjātā sattabbhantarasīmā samānasaṃvāsāti adhippāyo. Yattha pana khuddake araññe mahantehi bhikkhūhi paripuṇṇatāya vaggakammasaṅkābhāvena sattabbhantarasīmāpekkhā natthi, tattha sattabbhantarasīmā na uppajjati, kevalāraññasīmāyameva, tattha saṅghena kammaṃ kātabbaṃ. Nadiādīsupi eseva nayo. Vakkhati hi “sace nadī nātidīghā hoti, pabhavato [M 2.0159] paṭṭhāya yāva mukhadvārā sabbattha saṅgho nisīdati, udakukkhepasīmākammaṃ natthī”tiādi (mahāva. aṭṭha. 147). Iminā eva ca vacanena vaggakammaparihāratthaṃ sīmāpekkhāya sati eva udakukkhepasattabbhantarasīmā uppajjanti, nāsatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

The phrase 'from his standing place' means from the standing place of that monk. The meaning is this: Even if a thousand monks are standing, starting from the outer edge of their standing place, when the need for a boundary arises for the purpose of avoiding incomplete acts among the monks, a seven-abbhantara boundary of common co-residence arises by itself along with that need. However, in a small wilderness where, due to its being full of many monks, there is no suspicion of an incomplete act and thus no need for a seven-abbhantara boundary, a seven-abbhantara boundary does not arise; the act should be performed by the Sangha only within the mere wilderness-boundary. This is the same method in the case of rivers and so forth. For it will be said: ‘If a river is not very long, the Sangha sits everywhere from its source up to its mouth; there is no act of establishing a boundary by water-throw,’ and so forth. And by this very statement, it should be understood that water-throw boundaries and seven-abbhantara boundaries arise only when there is a need for a boundary for the purpose of avoiding incomplete acts; they do not arise when there is no such need.

Keci pana “samantā abbhantaraṃ minitvā paricchedakaraṇeneva sīmā sañjāyati, na sayamevā”ti vadanti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Yadi hi abbhantaraparicchedakaraṇappakārena sīmā uppajjeyya, abaddhasīmā ca na siyā bhikkhūnaṃ kiriyāpakārasiddhito. Apica vaḍḍhakīhatthānaṃ, pakatihatthānañca loke anekavidhattā, vinaye īdisaṃ hatthappamāṇanti avuttattā ca yena kenaci minite ca bhagavatā anuññātena nu kho hatthena minitaṃ, na nu khoti sīmāya vipattisaṅkā bhaveyya. Minantehi ca aṇumattampi ūnamadhikaṃ akatvā minituṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya vipatti eva siyā. Parisavasena cāyaṃ vaḍḍhamānā tesaṃ minanena vaḍḍhati vā hāyati vā. Saṅghe ca kammaṃ katvā gate ayaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ payogena samuppannasīmā tesaṃ payogena vigacchati na vigacchati ca. Kathaṃ baddhasīmā viya yāva sāsanantaradhānā na tiṭṭheyya, ṭhitiyā ca purāṇavihāresu viya sakalepi araññe kathaṃ sīmāsambhedasaṅkā na bhaveyya. Tasmā sīmāpekkhāya eva samuppajjati, tabbigamena vigacchatīti gahetabbaṃ. Yathā cettha, evaṃ udakukkhepasīmāyampi nadiādīsupi.

Some, however, say: 'A boundary is established only by measuring the seven-abbhantara all around and making a demarcation; it is not established by itself.' That statement should not be accepted. For if a boundary were to arise by the method of making an abbhantara-demarcation, it would not be an unconsecrated boundary, because it would be established by a special action of the monks.
