Moreover, because carpenters' cubits and standard cubits are of many kinds in the world, and because in the Vinaya it is not stated 'the measure of a cubit is of such a kind,' when it is measured by just any cubit, a suspicion of the boundary's invalidity would arise, [thinking] 'Was it measured by the cubit authorized by the Blessed One, or was it not?' And because those who are measuring would be unable to measure without making it deficient or excessive even by a tiny amount, it would simply be an invalidity. And this boundary, expanding according to the assembly, would expand or contract by their measuring. And when the Sangha, having performed the act, has departed, this boundary, which arose through the monks' exertion, ought to cease through their exertion, not merely by their departure. If it does not cease, how would it not remain until the disappearance of the Dispensation, like a consecrated boundary? It would indeed remain. And if it remained, how would a suspicion of boundary-merging not arise in the entire wilderness, as in old monasteries? It would indeed arise. Therefore, it should be understood that it arises only through the need for a boundary, and it ceases with the disappearance of that need. As here, so too should it be understood in the case of a water-throw boundary and in the case of rivers and so forth.

Tatthāpi hi majjhimapuriso na ñāyati. Tathā sabbathāmena khipanaṃ ubhayatthāpi ca yassaṃ disāyaṃ sattabbhantarassa, udakukkhepassa vā okāso na pahoti, tattha kathaṃ minanaṃ, khipanaṃ vā bhaveyya? Gāmakhettādīsu pavisanato akhette sīmā paviṭṭhā nāmāti sīmā vipajjeyya. Apekkhāya sīmuppattiyaṃ pana yato pahoti, tattha sattabbhantaraudakukkhepasīmā sayameva paripuṇṇā jāyanti. Yato pana na pahoti, tattha attano khettappamāṇeneva jāyanti, na bahi. Yaṃ panettha abbhantaraminanapamāṇassa, vālukādikhipanakammassa ca dassanaṃ, taṃ sañjātasīmānaṃ ṭhitaṭṭhānassa paricchedanatthaṃ kataṃ gāmūpacāragharūpacārajānanatthaṃ leḍḍusuppādikhipanavidhānadassanaṃ viya. Teneva mātikāṭṭhakathāyaṃ “sīmaṃ vā sammannati udakukkhepaṃ vā paricchindatī”ti vuttaṃ (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. ūnavīsativassasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā). Evaṃ katepi tassa [V 2.0151] paricchedassa yāthāvato ñātuṃ [M 2.0160] asakkuṇeyyattena puthulato ñatvā anto tiṭṭhantehi nirāsaṅkaṭṭhāne ṭhātabbaṃ, aññaṃ bahi karontehi atidūre nirāsaṅkaṭṭhāne pesetabbaṃ.

Indeed, even there a man of medium strength is not known. Likewise, throwing with all one's might is not known. And in both cases, in whatever direction there is not sufficient space for a sattabbhantara or an udakukkhepa, how could there be measuring or throwing there? Due to entering village-fields and so on, the sīmā, having entered a non-field, would be ruined. However, with respect to the arising of a sīmā by intention, wherever it is possible, there the sattabbhantara and udakukkhepa sīmās arise fully complete by themselves. But where it is not possible, there they arise only according to the measure of their own field, not outside it. As for the showing here of the measure of the internal measurement and of the act of throwing sand, etc., that is done for the purpose of delimiting the established location of the sīmās that have arisen—just like showing the method of throwing clods, winnowing baskets, etc., to determine the vicinity of villages and houses. For this very reason, it is said in the Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā: “One either agrees upon a sīmā or delimits an udakukkhepa.” Even when this is done, because its delimitation cannot be known exactly, having understood it broadly, those standing inside should stand in a place free from doubt, and when sending another outside, he should be sent to a place very far away that is free from doubt.

Apare pana “sīmāpekkhāya kiccaṃ natthi, maggagamananahānādiatthehi ekabhikkhusmimpi araññe vā nadiādīsu vā paviṭṭhe taṃ parikkhipitvā sattabbhantaraudakukkhepasīmā sayameva pabhā viya padīpassa samuppajjati, gāmakhettādīsu tasmiṃ otiṇṇamatte vigacchati. Teneva cettha dvinnaṃ saṅghānaṃ visuṃ kammaṃ karontānaṃ sīmādvayassa antarā sīmantarikā aññaṃ sattabbhantaraṃ, udakukkhepañca ṭhapetuṃ anuññātaṃ, sīmāpariyante hi kenaci kammena pesitassa bhikkhuno samantā sañjātasīmā itaresaṃ sīmāya phusitvā sīmāsambhedaṃ kareyya, so mā hotūti, itarathā hatthacaturaṅgulamattāyapettha sīmantarikāya anujānitabbato. Apica sīmantarikāya ṭhitassāpi ubhayattha kammakopavacanatopi cetaṃ sijjhati. Tampi parikkhipitvā sayameva sañjātāya sīmāya ubhinnampi sīmānaṃ, ekāya eva vā saṅkarato. Itarathā tassa kammakopavacanaṃ na yujjeyya. Vuttañhi mātikāṭṭhakathāyaṃ ‘paricchedabbhantare hatthapāsaṃ vijahitvā ṭhitopi paricchedato bahi aññaṃ tattakaṃyeva paricchedaṃ anatikkamitvā ṭhitopi kammaṃ kopetī’ti (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. nidānavaṇṇanā). Kiñca agāmakāraññe ṭhitassa kammakaraṇicchāvirahitassāpi bhikkhuno sattabbhantaraparicchinne ajjhokāse cīvaravippavāso bhagavatā anuññāto, so ca paricchedo sīmā. Evaṃ apekkhaṃ vinā samuppannā. Tenevettha ‘ayaṃ sīmā ticīvaravippavāsaparihārampi labhatī’ti (mahāva. aṭṭha. 147) vuttaṃ. Tasmā kammakaraṇicchaṃ vināpi vuttanayena samuppatti gahetabbā”ti vadanti, taṃ na yuttaṃ padīpassa pabhā viya sabbapuggalānampi paccekaṃ sīmāsambhavena saṅghe, gaṇe vā kammaṃ karonte tatraṭṭhānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ samantā paccekaṃ samuppannānaṃ anekasīmānaṃ aññamaññaṃ saṅkaradosappasaṅgato. Parisavasena cassā vaḍḍhi, hāni ca sambhavati. Pacchā āgatānaṃ abhinavasīmantaruppatti eva, gatānaṃ samantā ṭhitasīmāpi vināso ca bhaveyya.

But other teachers say: 'There is no need for intention regarding the sīmā. For purposes such as travelling on a road, bathing, etc., when even a single monk has entered a forest or rivers, etc., a sattabbhantara-udakukkhepa sīmā arises by itself, encompassing him, like the radiance of a lamp. As soon as he descends into a village-field, etc., it disappears. For this very reason, it is permitted here, when two Saṅghas are performing an act separately, to place another sattabbhantara and udakukkhepa as a sīmantarikā between the two sīmās. For a sīmā that has arisen all around a monk sent on some business to the edge of the sīmā might touch the sīmā of the others and cause a boundary-merging; it was permitted so that this would not happen, because otherwise a sīmantarikā of only a cubit or four finger-breadths would have to be permitted here. Furthermore, this view is also established by the statement that the act is invalidated in both cases even for one standing in a sīmantarikā. This is due to the merging of both sīmās, or of just one, with the sīmā that has arisen by itself, encompassing him also. Otherwise, the statement about invalidating his act would not be appropriate. For it is said in the Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā: ‘Even one who stands within the delimited area, having left a hand’s reach, or one who stands outside the delimitation, not having crossed another delimitation of that same extent, invalidates the act.’ Furthermore, for a monk staying in a wilderness that is not a village-area, even one without the desire to perform an act, the Blessed One has permitted leaving the robes behind in an open space delimited by a sattabbhantara. And that delimitation is a sīmā. Thus it has arisen without intention. For that reason it is said here: ‘This sīmā also obtains the allowance for being separated from the three robes.’ Therefore, the arising of a sīmā should be understood in the way described, even without the desire to perform an act.' That is not correct. This is because of the consequence of the fault of mutual merging of the many sīmās that would have arisen individually all around the monks present there when a Saṅgha or a group is performing an act, due to the possibility of a sīmā for each and every person, like the radiance of a lamp. And by the power of the assembly, its increase and decrease would not be possible. For those who come later, there would be only the arising of a new intermediate sīmā, and for those who have left, there would also be the destruction of the sīmā standing around them.

Pāḷiyaṃ pana “samantā sattabbhantarā, ayaṃ tattha samānasaṃvāsā”tiādinā (mahāva. 147) ekā eva sattabbhantarā, udakukkhepā ca anuññātā, na cesā sīmā sabhāvena, kāraṇasāmatthiyena vā pabhā viya padīpassa uppajjati. Kintu [M 2.0161] bhagavato anujānaneneva, bhagavā ca imāyo anujānanto bhikkhūnaṃ vaggakammaparihārena kammakaraṇasukhatthameva anuññāsīti kathaṃ nahānādikiccena paviṭṭhānampi samantā tāsaṃ sīmānaṃ samuppatti payojanābhāvā? Payojane ca ekaṃ eva payojananti kathaṃ paccekaṃ bhikkhugaṇanāya anekasīmāsamuppatti[V 2.0152]? “Ekasīmāyaṃ hatthapāsaṃ avijahitvā ṭhitā”ti (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. nidānavaṇṇanā) vuttaṃ. Yaṃ pana dvinnaṃ sīmānaṃ antarā tattakaparicchedeneva sīmantarikaṭṭhapanavacanaṃ, tattha ṭhitānaṃ kammakopavacanañca, tampi imāsaṃ sīmānaṃ paricchedassa dubbodhatāya sīmāya sambhedasaṅkaṃ, kammakopasaṅkañca dūrato pariharituṃ vuttaṃ.

But in the Pāḷi, by the text beginning, 'All around is a sattabbhantara; this is a common residence there,' only a single sattabbhantarā, and udakukkhepā, were permitted. And this sīmā does not arise by its own nature or by the power of a cause, like the radiance of a lamp. Rather, it arises only by the permission of the Blessed One. And the Blessed One, in permitting these, did so only for the sake of ease in performing an act, by way of avoiding an incomplete act. Therefore, how could those sīmās arise all around even for those who have entered for duties such as bathing, since there is no purpose? And if there is a purpose, there is only one purpose. Therefore, how is the arising of many sīmās according to the count of each monk possible? Indeed, it is said: 'They stand within a single sīmā, not having left the hand’s reach.' As for the statement about placing a sīmantarikā with just that much of a delimitation between two sīmās, and the statement about the invalidation of the act for those standing there, that too was said in order to ward off from afar the suspicion of boundary-merging and the suspicion of an invalid act, due to the difficulty of knowing the delimitation of these sīmās.

Yo ca cīvarāvippavāsatthaṃ bhagavatā abbhokāse dassito sattabbhantaraparicchedo, so sīmā eva na hoti, khettataḷākādiparicchedo viya ayamettha eko paricchedova. Tattha ca bahūsu bhikkhūsu ekato ṭhitesu tesaṃ visuṃ visuṃ attano ṭhitaṭṭhānato paṭṭhāya samantā sattabbhantaraparicchedabbhantare eva cīvaraṃ ṭhapetabbaṃ. Na parisapariyantato paṭṭhāya. Parisapariyantato paṭṭhāya hi abbhantare gayhamāne abbhantarapariyosāne ṭhapitacīvaraṃ majjhe ṭhitassa abbhantarato bahi hotīti taṃ aruṇuggamane nissaggiyaṃ siyā. Sīmā pana parisapariyantatova gahetabbā. Cīvaravippavāsaparihāropettha abbhokāsaparicchedassa vijjamānattā vutto, na pana yāva sīmāparicchedaṃ labbhamānattā mahāsīmāya avippavāsasīmāvohāro viya. Mahāsīmāyampi hi gāmagāmūpacāresu cīvaraṃ nissaggiyaṃ hoti. Idhāpi majjhe ṭhitassa sīmāpariyante nissaggiyaṃ hoti. Tasmā yathāvuttasīmāpekkhavasenevetāsaṃ sattabbhantaraudakukkhepasīmānaṃ uppatti, tabbigamena vināso ca gahetabbāti amhākaṃ khanti. Vīmaṃsitvā gahetabbaṃ. Añño vā pakāro ito yuttataro gavesitabbo.

The seven-abbhantara boundary shown by the Blessed One in an open space for the purpose of not being separated from the robe at night is not a sīmā itself; it is merely one type of boundary, like the boundary of a field or a reservoir. There, when many bhikkhus stand together, each should place his robe within the seven-abbhantara boundary starting from his own standing position—not from the edge of the assembly. For if the interior is taken starting from the edge of the assembly, a robe placed at the inner limit would be outside the interior of one standing in the middle; thus, at the break of dawn, it would become subject to forfeiture. A sīmā, however, should be taken from the edge of the assembly. Here, the protection from being separated from the robe at night is stated because of the existence of the open-space boundary, not because it is obtainable up to the limit of the sīmā, like the designation 'a sīmā of non-separation' in a great sīmā. For even in a great sīmā, a robe in a village or the vicinity of a village becomes subject to forfeiture. Here too, for one standing in the middle, a robe at the edge of the sīmā becomes subject to forfeiture. Therefore, it is our preference that the arising of these seven-abbhantara and water-throw sīmās, and their destruction by its disappearance, should be understood as being solely by the power of the aforesaid intention for a sīmā. This should be understood after investigation. Or another, more suitable method than this should be sought.

Idha pana “araññe samantā sattabbhantarā”ti evaṃ pāḷiyaṃ viñjhāṭavisadise araññe samantā sattabbhantarāti aṭṭhakathāyañca rukkhādinirantarepi araññe sattabbhantarasīmāya vihitattā attano nissayabhūtāya araññasīmāya saha etassā rukkhādisambandhe dosābhāvo pageva agāmake rukkheti nissitepi padese cīvaravippavāsassa rukkhaparihāraṃ vināva abbhokāsaparihārova anumatoti siddhoti veditabbo.

Furthermore, here, it should be understood that the following is established: since the seven-abbhantara sīmā is established in the Pāḷi as 'in the wilderness, seven abbhantaras all around,' and in the Commentary as 'in a wilderness like the Viñjhāṭavi, seven abbhantaras all around,' even in a wilderness dense with trees and so on, there is no fault for this sīmā in being connected with trees and so on, together with the wilderness sīmā which is its support. And, even in a place without a village that is dependent on trees, for the purpose of not being separated from the robe, only the protection of an open space is permitted, without the protection of a tree.

Upacāratthāyāti [M 2.0162] sīmantarikatthāya sattabbhantarato adhikaṃ vaṭṭati. Ūnakaṃ pana na vaṭṭati eva sattabbhantaraparicchedassa dubbijānattā. Tasmā saṅghaṃ vinā ekenāpi bhikkhunā bahi tiṭṭhantena aññaṃ sattabbhantaraṃ atikkamitvā atidūre eva ṭhātabbaṃ, itarathā kammakopasaṅkato. Udakukkhepepi eseva nayo. Teneva vakkhati “ūnakaṃ pana na vaṭṭatī”ti (mahāva. aṭṭha. 147). Idañcettha sīmantarikavidhānaṃ dvinnaṃ baddhasīmānaṃ sīmantarikānujānanasuttānulomato siddhanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kiñcāpi hi bhagavatā nidānavasena ekagāmasīmānissitānaṃ[V 2.0153], ekasabhāgānañca dvinnaṃ baddhasīmānameva aññamaññaṃ sambhedajjhottharaṇadosaparihārāya sīmantarikā anuññātā, tathāpi tadanulomato ekaaraññasīmānadiādisīmañca nissitānaṃ ekasabhāgānaṃ dvinnaṃ sattabbhantarasīmānampi udakukkhepasīmānampi aññamaññaṃ sambhedajjhottharaṇaṃ, sīmantarikaṃ vinā abyavadhānena ṭhānañca bhagavatā anabhimatamevāti ñatvā aṭṭhakathācariyā idhāpi sīmantarikavidhānamakaṃsu. Visabhāgasīmānampi hi ekasīmānissitattaṃ, ekasabhāgattañcāti dvīhaṅgehi samannāgate sati ekaṃ sīmantarikaṃ vinā ṭhānaṃ sambhedāya hoti, nāsatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sīmantarikavidhānasāmatthiyeneva cetāsaṃ rukkhādisambandhopi baddhasīmānaṃ viya aññamaññaṃ na vaṭṭatīti ayampi nayato dassito evāti gahetabbaṃ.

‘For the purpose of proximity’ means for the purpose of a boundary interval; more than seven abbhantaras is allowable. Less, however, is not allowable at all, because the seven-abbhantara boundary is difficult to ascertain. Therefore, a single bhikkhu standing outside, apart from the Saṅgha, should stand very far away, having gone beyond another seven abbhantaras; otherwise, there is the suspicion that the act is invalid. This is the same method for a water-throw sīmā as well. For that very reason, it will be said: “Less, however, is not allowable.” And it should be understood that this rule of a boundary interval here is established in accordance with the Sutta that permits a boundary interval for two fixed sīmās. For although the Blessed One, by way of the introductory story, permitted a boundary interval only for two fixed sīmās that are dependent on a single village sīmā and are of the same kind, in order to avoid the fault of mutual mixing and overlapping, nevertheless, the commentary masters, knowing that in accordance with that, the Blessed One did not approve of mutual mixing and overlapping, nor of standing without a boundary interval and without separation, for two seven-abbhantara sīmās or water-throw sīmās that are dependent on a single wilderness sīmā or a river sīmā, etc., and are of the same kind, also made the rule of a boundary interval here. For it should be understood that even for sīmās of dissimilar types, only when they are endowed with two factors—namely, being dependent on a single sīmā and being of the same kind (i.e., having common communion)—does standing without a boundary interval lead to mixing; when they are not so endowed, it does not. And it should be grasped that this meaning is also shown by implication: that by the very power of the rule for a boundary interval, for these sīmās too, like for fixed sīmās, mutual connection with trees and so on is not allowable.

“Sabhāvenevā”ti iminā gāmasīmā viya abaddhasīmāti dasseti. Sabbamettha saṅghakammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatīti samānasaṃvāsā ekūposathāti dasseti. Yena kenacīti antamaso sūkarādinā sattena. Mahoghena pana unnataṭṭhānato ninnaṭṭhāne patantena khato khuddako vā mahanto vā lakkhaṇayutto jātassarova. Etthāpi khuddake udakukkhepakiccaṃ natthi, samudde pana sabbathā udakukkhepasīmāyameva kammaṃ kātabbaṃ sodhetuṃ dukkarattā.

By 'by its very nature,' it shows that it is an unfixed sīmā, like a village sīmā. That 'all Saṅgha acts may be performed here' shows that they have common communion and a single Uposatha. 'By whatever' means at least by a creature such as a pig. But a place dug out by a great flood falling from a high place to a low one, whether small or large, if it possesses the characteristics, is a natural lake. Here too, in a small one, there is no need for a water-throw. But in the ocean, the act must always be performed only with a water-throw sīmā, because it is difficult to purify.

Puna tatthāti lokavohārasiddhāsu etāsu nadiādīsu tīsu abaddhasīmāsu puna vaggakammaparihāratthaṃ sāsanavohārasiddhāya abaddhasīmāya paricchedaṃ dassentoti adhippāyo. Pāḷiyaṃ yaṃ majjhimassa purisassātiādīsu udakaṃ ukkhipitvā khipīyati etthāti udakukkhepo, udakassa patanokāso, tasmā udakukkhepā. Ayañhettha padasambandhavasena attho – parisapariyantato paṭṭhāya samantā yāva majjhimassa purisassa [M 2.0163] udakukkhepo udakapatanaṭṭhānaṃ, tāva yaṃ taṃ paricchinnaṭṭhānaṃ, ayaṃ tattha nadiādīsu aparā samānasaṃvāsā udakukkhepasīmāti.

Again, 'therein'—the intention is this: showing the boundary of an unfixed sīmā established by monastic convention within these three unfixed sīmās such as rivers, which are established by worldly convention, in order to prevent an incomplete formal act. In the Pāḷi, in the passage beginning 'that of a man of medium strength,' 'water is lifted and thrown here,' thus it is a 'water-throw' (udakukkhepo), the place where the water falls; therefore, 'up to the water-throw.' And here this is the meaning by way of the connection of the words: starting from the edge of the assembly, all around, as far as the water-throw—the place where the water falls—of a man of medium strength, that delimited area is another water-throw sīmā of common communion in those rivers and so on.

Tassa antoti tassa udakukkhepaparicchinnassa ṭhānassa anto. Na kevalañca tasseva anto, tato bahipi, ekassa udakukkhepassa anto ṭhātuṃ na vaṭṭatīti vacanaṃ udakukkhepaparicchedassa dubbijānato kammakopasaṅkā hotīti. Teneva mātikāṭṭhakathāyaṃ “paricchedabbhantare hatthapāsaṃ vijahitvā ṭhitopi paricchedato bahi aññaṃ tattakaṃyeva paricchedaṃ anatikkamitvā ṭhitopi kammaṃ kopeti idaṃ sabbaaṭṭhakathāsu sanniṭṭhāna”nti (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. nidānavaṇṇanā) vuttaṃ. Yaṃ panettha sāratthadīpaniyaṃ “tassa anto hatthapāsaṃ vijahitvā ṭhito kammaṃ [V 2.0154] kopetīti iminā bahiparicchedato yattha katthaci ṭhito kammaṃ na kopetī”ti (sārattha. ṭī. mahāvagga 3.147) vatvā mātikāṭṭhakathāvacanampi paṭikkhipitvā “neva pāḷiyaṃ na aṭṭhakathāyaṃ upalabbhatī”tiādi bahu papañcitaṃ, taṃ na sundaraṃ idha aṭṭhakathāvacanena mātikāṭṭhakathāvacanassa nayato saṃsandanato saṅghaṭanato. Tathā hi dvinnaṃ udakukkhepaparicchedānamantarā vidatthicaturaṅgulamattampi sīmantarikaṃ aṭṭhapetvā “añño udakukkhepo sīmantarikāya ṭhapetabbo, tato adhikaṃ vaṭṭati eva, ūnakaṃ pana na vaṭṭatī”ti evaṃ idheva vuttena iminā aṭṭhakathāvacanena sīmantarikopacārena udakukkhepato ūnake ṭhapite sīmāya sīmāsambhedato kammakopopi vutto eva. Yadaggena ca evaṃ vutto, tadaggena tattha ekabhikkhuno pavesepi sati tassa sīmaṭṭhabhāvato kammakopo vutto eva hoti. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “ūnakaṃ pana na vaṭṭatī”ti kathanañcetaṃ udakukkhepaparicchedassa dubbijānantenapi sīmāsambhedasaṅkaāparihāratthaṃ vuttaṃ. Sattabbhantarasīmānamantarā tattakaparicchedeneva sīmantarikavidhānavacanatopi etāsaṃ dubbijānaparicchedatā, tattha ca ṭhitānaṃ kammakopasaṅkā sijjhati. Kammakopasaṅkaṭṭhānampi ācariyā dūrato parihāratthaṃ kammakopaṭṭhānanti vatvāva ṭhapesunti gahetabbaṃ.

Its interior means the interior of that place demarcated by a water-toss. And not only within it, but also outside it. The statement, 'it is not allowable to stand within one water-toss,' is said because, due to the difficulty in knowing the demarcation of the water-toss, a suspicion that the act is invalidated arises. For that very reason, in the Mātikāṭṭhakathā it is said: 'Even one standing within the demarcation having left the hand's reach, and even one standing outside the demarcation without transgressing another demarcation of that same extent, invalidates the act. This is the conclusion in all commentaries.' Whatever has been elaborated at length in the Sāratthadīpanī—saying, 'By this, “one standing within it having left the hand’s reach invalidates the act,” it means that one standing anywhere outside the demarcation does not invalidate the act,' and rejecting the statement of the Mātikāṭṭhakathā, saying, 'it is found neither in the Pāḷi nor in the Aṭṭhakathā'—that is not good, because here the statement of the Aṭṭhakathā corresponds with and connects to the statement of the Mātikāṭṭhakathā by way of method. Indeed, by this very statement made here in the Aṭṭhakathā—'Between two water-toss demarcations, having established a boundary-interval of even a span and four finger-breadths, another water-toss should be established with a boundary-interval; more than that is indeed allowable, but less is not'—by means of mentioning the boundary-interval, when a lesser [distance] than a water-toss is established, the invalidation of the act due to the overlapping of the sīmā is indeed stated. And to the extent that it is stated thus, to that extent, if even one monk enters there, because of his being within the sīmā, the invalidation of the act is indeed stated to occur. And in the Aṭṭhakathā, this statement, 'but less is not allowable,' is said in order to dispel the suspicion of the overlapping of boundaries, due to the difficulty of knowing the water-toss demarcation. Also from the statement about arranging a boundary-interval with just that much demarcation between seven-abbhantara boundaries, the fact that their demarcation is difficult to know is established, and for those standing there, the suspicion that the act is invalidated is established. It should be understood that the teachers, in order to avoid it from afar, established even a place where there is suspicion of the act being invalidated by calling it a 'place of invalidation of the act'.

Tanti sīmaṃ. “Sīghameva atikkāmetī”ti iminā taṃ anatikkamitvā anto eva parivattamānāya kātuṃ vaṭṭatīti dasseti. Etadatthameva hi vālukādīhi sīmāparicchindanaṃ, itarathā bahi parivattā nu kho, no vāti kammakopasaṅkā bhaveyyāti. Aññissā anussāvanāti kevalāya nadisīmāya anussāvanā[M 2.0164]. Antonadiyaṃ jātarukkhe vāti udakukkhepaparicchedassa bahi ṭhite rukkhepi vā. Bahinaditīrameva hi visabhāgasīmattā abandhitabbaṭṭhānaṃ, na antonadī nissayattena sabhāgattā. Teneva “bahinaditīre vihārasīmāya vā”tiādinā tīrameva abandhitabbaṭṭhānattena dassitaṃ, na pana nadī. “Rukkhepi ṭhitehī”ti idaṃ antoudakukkhepaṭṭhaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Na hi bahiudakukkhepe bhikkhūnaṃ ṭhātuṃ vaṭṭati.

That is, the sīmā. By 'it quickly passes beyond,' it shows that it is allowable to perform the act on a boat that is turning around only within it, without transgressing it. Indeed, it is for this very purpose that the demarcation of the sīmā with sand and so forth occurs; otherwise, a suspicion that the act is invalidated would arise, [wondering], 'Did the boat turn around outside, or not?' 'Proclamation for another' means a proclamation in a pure river-sīmā, unmixed with an udakukkhepa-sīmā. 'Or on a tree growing inside the river' means or even on a tree standing outside the demarcation of the udakukkhepa-sīmā. For the outer riverbank itself, being a dissimilar sīmā, is a place that should not be bound, but the inside of the river, being of the same nature because it is a support, is not a place that should not be bound. For that very reason, by the text beginning with 'or on the outer riverbank at a monastery sīmā,' the bank itself is shown as the place that should not be bound, but the river is not shown. The statement 'even by those standing on a tree' is said with reference to a tree standing inside the udakukkhepa. Indeed, it is not allowable for monks to stand outside the udakukkhepa.

Rukkhassāti tasseva antoudakukkhepaṭṭhassa rukkhassa. Sīmaṃ vā sodhetvāti yathāvuttaṃ vihāre baddhasīmaṃ, gāmasīmañca tattha ṭhitabhikkhūnaṃ hatthapāsānayanabahisīmākaraṇavaseneva sodhetvā. Yathā ca udakukkhepasīmāyaṃ kammaṃ karontehi, evaṃ baddhasīmāyaṃ, gāmasīmāyaṃ vā kammaṃ karontehipi udakukkhepasīmaṭṭhe sodhetvāva kātabbaṃ. Eteneva sattabbhantaraaraññasīmāhipi udakukkhepasīmāya, imāya ca saddhiṃ tāsaṃ rukkhādisambandhadosopi nayato dassitova hoti. Imināva nayena sattabbhantarasīmāya baddhasīmāgāmasīmāhipi saddhiṃ, etāsañca sattabbhantarasīmāya [V 2.0155] saddhiṃ sambandhadoso ñātabbo. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ panetaṃ sabbaṃ vuttanayato sakkā ñātunti aññamaññasamāsannānamevettha dassitaṃ.

'Of the tree' means of that very tree standing inside the udakukkhepa. 'Or having cleared the sīmā' means having cleared the baddha-sīmā in the monastery and the gāma-sīmā, as has been stated, precisely by means of bringing the monks standing there out of hand's reach and making [their location] an outer sīmā. And just as those performing an act in an udakukkhepa-sīmā must do so after clearing [other sīmās], so also those performing an act in a baddha-sīmā or a gāma-sīmā must do so only after clearing those standing in the udakukkhepa-sīmā. By this very [text], the fault of connection with trees and so forth is also shown by way of method for seven-abbhantara and arañña-sīmās with an udakukkhepa-sīmā, and for this [udakukkhepa-sīmā] with them. By this very method, the fault of connection should be known for a seven-abbhantara-sīmā with baddha-sīmās and gāma-sīmās, and for these with a seven-abbhantara-sīmā. In the Aṭṭhakathā, [it is said that] since all this can be known by the method explained, the procedure for overlapping is shown here only for those [sīmās] that are near one another.

Tatridaṃ suttānulomato nayaggahaṇamukhaṃ – yathā hi baddhasīmāyaṃ sammatā vipattisīmā hotīti tāsaṃ aññamaññaṃ rukkhādisambandho na vaṭṭati, evaṃ nadiādīsu sammatāpi baddhasīmā vipattisīmāva hotīti tāhipi saddhiṃ tassā rukkhādisambandho na vaṭṭatīti sijjhati. Iminā nayena sattabbhantarasīmāya gāmanadiādīhi saddhiṃ, udakukkhepasīmāya ca araññādīhi saddhiṃ rukkhādisambandhassa na vaṭṭanakabhāvo ñātabbo, evametā bhagavatā anuññātā baddhasīmā sattabbhantaraudakukkhepasīmā aññamaññañceva attano nissayavirahitāhi itarītarāsaṃ nissayasīmāhi ca rukkhādisambandhe sati sambhedadosamāpajjatīti suttānulomanayo ñātabbova.

In this regard, this is the introduction to grasping the method in accordance with the Sutta: For just as a [sīmā] agreed upon within a baddha-sīmā is a faulty sīmā, and therefore the connection of trees and so forth between them is not allowable, so also, a baddha-sīmā, even if agreed upon in a river and so forth, is still a faulty sīmā; therefore, its connection with trees and so forth together with those [sīmās] is not allowable. This is established. By this method, it should be known that the connection with trees and so forth is not allowable for a seven-abbhantara-sīmā with gāma-sīmās, nadī-sīmās, and so forth, and for an udakukkhepa-sīmā with arañña-sīmās and so forth. Thus, these baddha-sīmās, seven-abbhantara-sīmās, and udakukkhepa-sīmās permitted by the Blessed One, if there is a connection with trees and so forth, both with one another, and with the supporting sīmās of other [sīmās] that lack their own support, incur the fault of overlapping. Thus, the method in accordance with the Sutta should indeed be known.

Attano attano pana nissayabhūtagāmādīhi saddhiṃ baddhasīmādīnaṃ tissannaṃ uppattikāle bhagavatā anuññātassa sambhedajjhottharaṇassa anulomato rukkhādisambandhopi anuññātova hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yadi evaṃ udakukkhepabaddhasīmādīnaṃ antarā kasmā sīmantarikā na vihitāti? Nissayabhedasabhāvabhedehi [M 2.0165] sayameva bhinnattā. Ekanissayaekasabhāvānameva hi sīmantarikāya vināsaṃ karotīti vuttovāyamattho. Eteneva nadinimittaṃ katvā baddhāya sīmāya saṅghe kammaṃ karonte nadiyampi yāva gāmakhettaṃ āhacca ṭhitāya udakukkhepasīmāya aññesaṃ kammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatīti siddhaṃ hoti. Yā panetā lokavohārasiddhā gāmāraññanadisamuddajātassarasīmā pañca, tā aññamaññarukkhādisambandhepi sambhedadosaṃ nāpajjati, tathā lokavohārābhāvato. Na hi gāmādayo gāmantarādīhi, nadiādīhi ca rukkhādisambandhamattena sambhinnāti loke voharanti. Lokavohārasiddhānañca lokavohāratova sambhedo vā asambhedo vā gahetabbo, nāññato. Teneva aṭṭhakathāyaṃ tāsaṃ aññamaññaṃ katthacipi sambhedanayo na dassito, sāsanavohārasiddhoyeva dassitoti.

However, it should be understood that, in accordance with the mingling and overlapping permitted by the Blessed One at the time of their establishment, the connection with trees and so forth is also permitted for the three types of sīmā, such as the baddhasīmā, together with their own respective bases of support, such as villages. If so, why is an intermediate boundary (sīmantarikā) not established between the udakukkhepasīmā, baddhasīmā, and so forth? Because they are distinct by themselves due to differences in their bases of support and their natures. For it has been said that mingling occurs only for sīmās of the same basis and same nature without an intermediate boundary. By this very reasoning, it is established that when the Saṅgha is performing a formal act in a sīmā established with a river as its marker, it is permissible for other monks to perform a formal act in an udakukkhepasīmā that is situated in the river and extends up to the village fields. As for the five sīmās established by worldly convention—the village, forest, river, ocean, and natural lake sīmās—they do not incur the fault of mingling even if there is a connection between them via trees and so forth, because there is no such worldly convention. For in the world, they do not speak of villages and so forth as being mingled with other villages, rivers, and so forth, merely by a connection with trees. And for those sīmās established by worldly convention, their mingling or non-mingling should be understood only from worldly convention, and not otherwise. For that very reason, in the commentary, no method of mingling between them is shown anywhere; only that which is established by the convention of the Dispensation is shown.

Ettha pana baddhasīmāya tāva “heṭṭhā pathavīsandhārakaṃ udakapariyantaṃ katvā sīmāgatā hotī”tiādinā (mahāva. aṭṭha. 138) adhobhāgaparicchedo aṭṭhakathāyaṃ sabbathā dassito. Gāmasīmādīnaṃ pana na dassito. Kathamayaṃ jānitabboti? Keci tāvettha “gāmasīmādayopi baddhasīmā viya pathavīsandhārakaṃ udakaṃ āhacca tiṭṭhatī”ti vadanti.

Here, with regard to the baddhasīmā, its lower limit is shown in every way in the commentary, beginning with the passage: “Below, having made the water that supports the earth its limit, the sīmā is established.” For the gāmasīmā and so forth, however, it is not shown. How is this to be known? Some, for their part, say: “The gāmasīmā and so forth, like the baddhasīmā, also stand touching the water that supports the earth.”

Keci [V 2.0156] pana taṃ paṭikkhipitvā “nadisamuddajātassarasīmā, tāva tannissitaudakukkhepasīmā ca pathaviyā uparitale, heṭṭhā ca udakajjhottharaṇappadese eva tiṭṭhanti, na tato heṭṭhā udakassa ajjhottharaṇābhāvā. Sace pana udakoghādinā yojanappamāṇampi ninnaṭṭhānaṃ hoti, nadisīmādayova honti, na tato heṭṭhā. Tasmā nadiādīnaṃ heṭṭhā bahitīramukhena umaṅgena, iddhiyā vā paviṭṭho bhikkhu nadiyaṃ ṭhitānaṃ kammaṃ na kopeti. So pana āsannagāme bhikkhūnaṃ kammaṃ kopeti. Sace pana so ubhinnaṃ tīragāmānaṃ majjhe nisinno hoti, ubhayagāmaṭṭhānaṃ kammaṃ kopeti. Sace pana tīraṃ gāmakhettaṃ na hoti, agāmakāraññameva. Tattha pana tīradvayepi sattabbhantarasīmaṃ vinā kevalāya khuddakāraññasīmāya kammaṃ karontānaṃ kammaṃ kopeti. Sace sattabbhantarasīmāyaṃ karonti, tadā yadi tesaṃ sattabbhantarasīmāya paricchedo etassa nisinnokāsassa parato ekaṃ sattabbhantaraṃ atikkamitvā ṭhito na kammakopo[M 2.0166]. No ce, kammakopo. Gāmasīmāyaṃ pana antoumaṅge vā bile vā yattha pavisituṃ sakkā, yattha vā suvaṇṇamaṇiādiṃ khaṇitvā gaṇhanti, gahetuṃ sakkāti vā sambhāvanā hoti, tattakaṃ heṭṭhāpi gāmasīmā, tattha iddhiyā anto nisinnopi kammaṃ kopeti. Yattha pana pakatimanussānaṃ pavesasambhāvanāpi natthi, taṃ sabbaṃ yāva pathavisandhārakaudakā araññasīmāva, na gāmasīmā. Araññasīmāyampi eseva nayo. Tatthapi hi yattake padese pavesasambhāvanā, tattakameva uparitale araññasīmā pavattati. Tato pana heṭṭhā na araññasīmā, tattha uparitalena saha ekāraññavohārābhāvato. Na hi tattha paviṭṭhaṃ araññaṃ paviṭṭho ti voharanti. Tasmā tatraṭṭho upari araññaṭṭhānaṃ kammaṃ na kopeti umaṅganadiyaṃ ṭhito viya uparinadiyaṃ ṭhitānaṃ. Ekasmiñhi cakkavāḷe gāmanadisamuddajātassare muñcitvā tadavasesaṃ amanussāvāsaṃ devabrahmalokaṃ upādāya sabbaṃ araññameva. ‘Gāmā vā araññā vā’ti vuttattā hi nadisamuddajātassarādipi araññameva. Idha pana nadiādīnaṃ visuṃ sīmābhāvena gahitattā tadavasesameva araññaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Tattha ca yattake padese ekaṃ ‘arañña’nti voharanti, ayamekāraññasīmā. Indapurañhi sabbaṃ ekāraññasīmā. Tathā asurayakkhapurādi. Ākāsaṭṭhadevabrahmavimānāni pana samantā ākāsaparicchinnāni paccekaṃ araññasīmā samuddamajjhe pabbatadīpakā viya. Tattha sabbattha sattabbhantarasīmāyaṃ, araññasīmāyameva vāti kammaṃ kātabbaṃ. Tasmā idhāpi upariaraññatalena saddhiṃ heṭṭhāpathaviyā araññavohārābhāvā visuṃ araññasīmāti gahetabbaṃ. Tenevettha gāmanadiādisīmākathāya aṭṭhakathāyaṃ ‘iddhimā bhikkhu heṭṭhāpathavitale ṭhito kammaṃ kopetī’ti (mahāva. aṭṭha. 138) baddhasīmāyaṃ dassitanayo na dassito”ti vadanti.

Some, however, rejecting that, say: “The sīmās of a river, ocean, or natural lake, and the udakukkhepasīmā dependent on them, stand only in the area covered by water, both on the surface of the earth and below it. They do not stand below that, because of the absence of the water's covering. If, due to a current or the like, there is a depression even a yojana in extent, it is still the river sīmā, etc., but not below that. Therefore, a monk who has entered below a river, etc., through a tunnel with an entrance outside the bank or by psychic power does not invalidate the formal act of those standing in the river. That monk, however, does invalidate the formal act of monks in a nearby village. And if he is seated between two villages on the banks, he invalidates the formal act of those in both villages. If, however, a bank is not village territory but is simply unassigned forest, then on both banks he invalidates the formal act of those performing it in just the minor forest sīmā, excluding the sattabbhantarasīmā. If they perform the act in a sattabbhantarasīmā, then if the boundary of their sattabbhantarasīmā is established beyond the place where this monk is sitting, having passed over one sattabbhantara, there is no invalidation of the act. If it is not so established, the act is invalidated. In the case of a gāmasīmā, however, to whatever extent it is possible to enter inside a tunnel or a hole, or where they dig and take gold, gems, etc., or where it is reputed that they can be taken, to that extent it is a gāmasīmā even below ground. There, even a monk seated inside by psychic power invalidates the formal act. But where there is no possibility for ordinary humans to enter, all of that, down to the water that supports the earth, is only an araññasīmā, not a gāmasīmā. In the case of an araññasīmā as well, this is the method. For there too, the araññasīmā on the surface extends only as far as the area where entry is considered possible. Below that, however, is a different araññasīmā, because there is no convention of ‘one wilderness’ together with the surface. For they do not say of one who has entered there, ‘He has entered the wilderness.’ Therefore, one who is there does not invalidate the formal act of those in the wilderness above, just as one standing in an underground river does not invalidate the act of those in the river above. For in one world-system, excepting villages, rivers, oceans, and natural lakes, the remainder, including the abodes of non-humans, devas, and brahmās, is all just wilderness. Because it is said, ‘In a village or in a wilderness,’ rivers, oceans, natural lakes, etc., are also wilderness. Here, however, since rivers, etc., are taken as separate sīmās, only the remainder should be taken as wilderness. And in that, whatever area is referred to as ‘one wilderness,’ this is one araññasīmā. Indeed, the entire city of Indra is one araññasīmā. Likewise the cities of asuras, yakkhas, etc. But the celestial and brahmā mansions standing in space, being delimited on all sides by space, are each a separate araññasīmā, like mountains or islands in the middle of the ocean. There, in all cases, a formal act should be performed either in a sattabbhantarasīmā or in the araññasīmā itself. Therefore, here too, because there is no convention of a single wilderness for the earth below together with the wilderness on the surface, it should be taken as a separate araññasīmā. For that very reason, in the commentary, in the discussion of the gāmasīmā, nadīsīmā, etc., the method shown for the baddhasīmā—‘A monk with psychic power standing on the level below the earth invalidates the formal act’—is not shown.” Thus they say.

Idañcetāsaṃ [V 2.0157] gāmasīmādīnaṃ heṭṭhāpamāṇadassanaṃ suttādivirodhābhāvā yuttaṃ viya dissati. Vīmaṃsitvā gahetabbaṃ. Evaṃ gahaṇe ca gāmasīmāyaṃ sammatā baddhasīmā upari gāmasīmaṃ, heṭṭhā udakapariyantaṃ araññasīmañca avattharatīti tassā araññasīmāpi khettanti sijjhati. Bhagavatā ca “sabbā, bhikkhave, nadī asīmā”tiādinā (mahāva. aṭṭha. 147) nadisamuddajātassarā baddhasīmāya akhettabhāvena vuttā, na pana araññaṃ. Tasmā araññampi [M 2.0167] baddhasīmāya khettamevāti gahetabbaṃ. Yadi evaṃ kasmā tattha sā na bajjhatīti? Payojanābhāvā. Sīmāpekkhānantarameva sattabbhantarasīmāya sambhavato. Tassā ca upari sammatāya baddhasīmāya sambhedajjhottharaṇānulomato vipattisīmā eva siyā. Gāmakhette pana ṭhatvā agāmakāraññekadesampi antokaritvā sammatā kiñcāpi susammatā, agāmakāraññe bhagavatā vihitāya sattabbhantarasīmāyapi anivattito. Tattha pana kammaṃ kātuṃ paviṭṭhānampi tato bahi kevalāraññe karontānampi antarā tīṇi sattabbhantarāni ṭhapetabbāni, aññathā vipatti eva siyāti sabbathā niratthakameva agāmakāraññe baddhasīmākaraṇanti veditabbaṃ.

This showing of the lower limit for these village boundaries and the like seems suitable, as there is no contradiction with the Suttas and other texts. It should be accepted after investigation. When it is accepted thus, a consecrated boundary established within a village boundary covers the village boundary above and, below, the forest boundary which has water as its limit. Thus, it is established that the forest boundary is also its field. And by the Blessed One, with the words, 'Monks, every river is without a boundary,' and so on, only rivers, oceans, and natural lakes were spoken of as not being a field for a consecrated boundary, but not the forest. Therefore, it should be accepted that the forest is also indeed a field for a consecrated boundary. If it is so, why is it not bound there? Due to the lack of purpose, and because a sattabbhantara-sīmā arises immediately upon the need for a boundary. And, due to its conformity with the merging and overlapping of a consecrated boundary established above it, it would be only a defective boundary. However, standing in a village field, even if a boundary is established including a part of a non-village forest—although it may be well-established—the sattabbhantara-sīmā prescribed by the Blessed One in a non-village forest is not nullified. For those who have entered there to perform an act, and for those performing an act outside of it in the mere forest, three sattabbhantaras must be placed in between. Otherwise, it would be only a defect. Thus, it should be known that the making of a consecrated boundary in a non-village forest is in every way useless.

Antonadiyaṃ paviṭṭhasākhāyāti nadiyā pathavitalaṃ āhacca ṭhitāya sākhāyapi, pageva anāhacca ṭhitāya. Pārohepi eseva nayo. Etena sabhāgaṃ nadisīmaṃ phusitvā ṭhitenapi visabhāgasīmāsambandhasākhādinā udakukkhepasīmāya sambandho na vaṭṭatīti dasseti. Eteneva mahāsīmaṃ, gāmasīmañca phusitvā ṭhitena sākhādinā māḷakasīmāya sambandho na vaṭṭatīti ñāpitoti daṭṭhabbo.

By 'a branch that has entered into the river,' it is meant: even by a branch that is standing having touched the earth's surface of the river, what need is there to speak of one standing without touching it? This is the same method for a root as well. By this, it is shown that a connection with a water-throwing boundary by means of a branch, etc., connected to a boundary of a different kind is not allowable, even if it is standing having touched a river boundary of the same kind. By this very text, it is made known and should be understood that a connection with a hall boundary by means of a branch, etc., standing having touched a great boundary and a village boundary is not allowable.

Antonadiyaṃyevāti setupādānaṃ tīraṭṭhataṃ nivatteti. Tena udakukkhepaparicchedato bahi nadiyaṃ patiṭṭhitattepi sambhedābhāvaṃ dasseti. Tenāha “bahitīre patiṭṭhitā”tiādi. Yadi hi udakukkhepato bahi antonadiyampi patiṭṭhitatte sambhedo bhaveyya, tampi paṭikkhipitabbaṃ bhaveyya kammakopassa samānattā, na ca paṭikkhittaṃ. Tasmā sabbattha attano nissayasīmāya sambhedadoso natthevāti gahetabbaṃ.

The phrase 'only within the river' negates the state of the bridge-posts being on the bank. By this, it shows the absence of merging even when established in the river outside the demarcation of the water-throwing boundary. For that reason, he said, 'established on the outer bank,' and so on. For if there were merging when established even within the river but outside the water-throwing boundary, that too would have to be rejected due to its similarity with that which invalidates the act; and it is not rejected. Therefore, it should be accepted that everywhere there is no fault of merging with one's own supporting boundary.

Āvaraṇena vāti dāruādiṃ nikhaṇitvā udakanivāraṇena. Koṭṭakabandhanena vāti mattikādīhi pūretvā katasetubandhena. Ubhayenāpi āvaraṇameva dasseti. “Nadiṃ vināsetvā”ti vuttamevatthaṃ vibhāveti “heṭṭhā pāḷi baddhā”ti, heṭṭhā nadiṃ āvaritvā pāḷi baddhāti attho. Chaḍḍitamodakanti atirittodakaṃ. “Nadiṃ ottharitvā sandanaṭṭhānato”ti iminā taḷākanadīnaṃ antarā [V 2.0158] pavattanaṭṭhāne na vaṭṭatīti dasseti. Uppatitvāti tīrādibhindanavasena vipulā hutvā. Vihārasīmanti baddhasīmaṃ.

'Or by an obstruction' means: by preventing water by driving in wood, etc. 'Or by building an enclosure' means: by a dam made by filling it with clay, etc. By both terms, it shows only an obstruction. It clarifies the meaning already stated in 'having destroyed the river' with the phrase 'a bank was bound below'; the meaning is: a bank was bound below, obstructing the river. 'Water that has been discarded' means excess water. By this phrase, 'from the place of flowing, having covered the river,' it shows that it is not allowable in the place of flowing between a reservoir and a river. 'Having surged up' means: having become wide by means of breaking the banks, etc. 'A monastery boundary' means a consecrated boundary.

Agamanapatheti [M 2.0168] tadaheva gantvā nivattituṃ asakkuṇeyye. Araññasīmāsaṅkhyameva gacchatīti lokavohārasiddhaṃ agāmakāraññasīmaṃ sandhāya vadati. Tatthāti pakatiyā macchabandhānaṃ gamanapathesu dīpakesu.

'On a path of no-return' means: where one is not able to go and return on that very day. He says, 'it goes to what is reckoned as a forest boundary,' referring to a non-village forest boundary established by worldly convention. 'There' means: on the small islands, etc., which are usually on the travel paths of fishermen.

Taṃ ṭhānanti āvāṭādīnaṃ kataṭṭhānameva, na akatanti attho. Loṇīti samuddodakassa uppattiveganinno mātikākārena pavattanako.

'That place' means: only a place that has been made, such as a pit, etc.; the meaning is, not an unmade place. 'A salt-marsh' means: a low-lying place due to the force of the rising of the ocean water, which flows in the manner of a channel.

148. Sambhindantīti yattha catūhi bhikkhūhi nisīdituṃ na sakkā, tattakato paṭṭhāya yāva kesaggamattampi antosīmāya karonto sambhindati. Catunnaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ pahonakato paṭṭhāya yāva sakalampi anto karonto ajjhottharantīti veditabbaṃ. Saṃsaṭṭhaviṭapāti aññamaññaṃ sibbitvā ṭhitamahāsākhamūlā, etena aññamaññassa accāsannataṃ dīpeti. Sākhāya sākhaṃ phusantā hi dūraṭṭhāpi siyyuṃ, tato ekaṃsato sambhedalakkhaṇaṃ dassitaṃ na siyāti taṃ dassetuṃ viṭapaggahaṇaṃ kataṃ. Evañhi bhikkhūnaṃ nisīdituṃ appahonakaṭṭhānaṃ attano sīmāya antosīmaṭṭhaṃ karitvā purāṇavihāraṃ karonto sīmāya sīmaṃ sambhindati nāma, na tato paranti dassitameva hoti. Baddhā hotīti porāṇakavihārasīmaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Ambanti aparena samayena purāṇavihāraparikkhepādīnaṃ vinaṭṭhattā ajānantānaṃ taṃ purāṇasīmāya nimittabhūtaṃ ambaṃ. Attano sīmāya antosīmaṭṭhaṃ karitvā purāṇavihārasīmaṭṭhaṃ jambuṃ kittetvā ambajambūnaṃ antare yaṃ ṭhānaṃ, taṃ attano sīmāya pavesetvā bandhantīti attho. Ettha ca purāṇasīmāya nimittabhūtassa gāmaṭṭhassa ambarukkhassa antosīmaṭṭhāya jambuyā saha saṃsaṭṭhaviṭapattepi sīmāya bandhanakāle vipatti vā pacchā gāmasīmāya saha sambhedo vā kammavipatti vā na hotīti mukhatova vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

148. 'They merge' means: where it is not possible for four bhikkhus to sit, starting from that much space, one who makes even as much as a hair's tip a part of the inner boundary, merges it. It should be known that starting from a space sufficient for four bhikkhus, one who includes even the whole of it, overlaps it. 'With intertwined branch-spreads' means: having large branches and roots that stand interwoven with one another; by this, it shows their extreme nearness to one another. For trees whose branches touch other branches could even be far apart; therefore, the characteristic of merging would not be shown unequivocally. To show that, the term 'branch-spread' was used. For thus, it is indeed shown that when one makes a place insufficient for bhikkhus to sit a part of one's own inner boundary, it is called 'merging boundary with boundary,' and not beyond that. 'It is bound' was said referring to an ancient monastery boundary. 'The mango tree' means: at a later time, when the enclosures of the ancient monastery had been destroyed, those who did not know took that mango tree, which had been a marker for the ancient boundary. The meaning is: having made it part of their own inner boundary, and having proclaimed the jambu tree that stood within the ancient monastery boundary, they bind the place that is between the mango and jambu trees by including it within their own boundary. And here, it should be known that even with the intertwined branch-spreads of the mango tree—which was a marker for the ancient boundary and stood in the village—with the jambu tree that was inside the inner boundary, it is stated explicitly that at the time of binding the boundary there is no defect, nor later merging with the village boundary, nor any procedural defect.

Padesanti saṅghassa nisīdanappahonakappadesaṃ. “Sīmantarikaṃ ṭhapetvā”tiādinā sambhedajjhottharaṇaṃ akatvā baddhasīmāhi aññamaññaṃ phusāpetvā abyavadhānena baddhāpi sīmā asīmā evāti dasseti. Tasmā ekadvaṅgulamattāpi sīmantarikā vaṭṭati eva. Sā pana dubbodhāti aṭṭhakathāsu caturaṅgulādikā vuttāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Dvinnaṃ sīmānanti dvinnaṃ baddhasīmānaṃ. Nimittaṃ hotīti nimittassa sīmato bāhirattā bandhanakāle tāva sambhedadoso natthīti adhippāyo[V 2.0159]. Na kevalañca nimittakattā eva saṅkaraṃ karoti[M 2.0169], atha kho sīmantarikāya ṭhito aññopi rukkho karoti eva. Tasmā appamattikāya sīmantarikāya vaḍḍhanakā rukkhādayo na vaṭṭanti eva. Ettha ca upari dissamānakhandhasākhādipavese eva saṅkaradosassa sabbattha dassitattā adissamānānaṃ mūlānaṃ pavesepi bhūmigatikattā doso natthīti sijjhati. Sace pana mūlānipi dissamānāneva pavisanti, saṅkarova. Pabbatapāsāṇā pana dissamānāpi bhūmigatikā eva. Yadi pana bandhanakāle eva eko thūlarukkho ubhayampi sīmaṃ āhacca tiṭṭhati, pacchā baddhā asīmā hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

‘Padesa’ means a place suitable for the Saṅgha to sit. By the text beginning ‘Having established an intermediate space…’ (`Sīmantarikaṃ ṭhapetvā`tiādinā), it is shown that a boundary, even if established without creating intermingling or overlapping, but by making established boundaries touch each other without an intervening space, is in fact not a boundary. Therefore, even an intermediate space of one or two finger-breadths is permissible. However, since this is difficult to discern, it should be understood that the commentaries mention four finger-breadths or more. ‘Dvinnaṃ sīmānaṃ’ refers to two established boundaries. ‘Nimittaṃ hoti’ means that since the marker is outside the boundary, there is no fault of intermingling at the time of establishing it—this is the intended meaning. And not only does being a marker cause intermingling, but in fact, another tree standing in the intermediate space also causes it. Therefore, growing trees and so on are not permissible in a small intermediate space. And here, since the fault of intermingling is shown everywhere only in the case of the visible intrusion of trunks, branches, and so on from above, it is established that there is no fault even in the intrusion of invisible roots, because they are like the earth. If, however, the roots also intrude visibly, it is indeed intermingling. But mountains and rocks, even if visible, are just like the earth. If, however, at the very time of establishing the boundaries, a single large tree stands touching both boundaries, it should be understood that the one established later is not a boundary.

Sīmāsaṅkaranti sīmāsambhedaṃ. Yaṃ pana sāratthadīpaniyaṃ vuttaṃ “sīmāsaṅkaraṃ karotīti vaḍḍhitvā sīmappadesaṃ paviṭṭhe dvinnaṃ sīmānaṃ gataṭṭhānassa duviññeyyattā vutta”nti (sārattha. ṭī. mahāvagga 3.148), taṃ na yuttaṃ gāmasīmāyapi saha saṅkaraṃ karotīti vattabbato. Tatthāpi hi nimitte vaḍḍhite gāmasīmābaddhasīmānaṃ gataṭṭhānaṃ dubbiññeyyameva hoti, tattha pana avatvā dvinnaṃ baddhasīmānameva saṅkarassa vuttattā yathāvuttasambaddhadosova saṅkara-saddena vuttoti gahetabbaṃ. Pāḷiyaṃ pana nidānavasena “yesaṃ, bhikkhave, sīmā pacchā sammatā, tesaṃ taṃ kammaṃ adhammika”ntiādinā (mahāva. 148) pacchā sammatāya asīmatte vuttepi dvīsu gāmasīmāsu ṭhatvā dvīhi saṅghehi sambhedaṃ vā ajjhottharaṇaṃ vā katvā sīmantarikaṃ aṭṭhapetvā vā rukkhapārohādisambandhaṃ aviyojetvā vā ekasmiṃ khaṇe kammavācāniṭṭhāpanavasena ekato sammatānaṃ dvinnaṃ sīmānampi asīmatā pakāsitāti veditabbaṃ.

‘Sīmāsaṅkara’ means the intermingling of boundaries (`sīmāsambheda`). However, the statement made in the Sāratthadīpanī—"The phrase ‘it causes boundary intermingling’ is said because when a marker grows and enters the boundary area, the place where the two boundaries have gone becomes difficult to discern"—is not correct, because it should be said that it causes intermingling with a village boundary as well. For in that case too, when a marker grows, the place where the village boundary and the established boundary have gone becomes difficult to discern. However, since that is not mentioned there, and the intermingling of only two established boundaries is stated, it should be understood that only the fault of connection as described above is meant by the word ‘saṅkara’. But in the Pāli text, by way of the introductory story beginning, “Bhikkhus, for those whose boundary is approved later, that act of theirs is unlawful,” even though it is stated that the one approved later is not a boundary, it should be known that the invalidity of both of two boundaries is also shown—boundaries that are approved simultaneously by means of completing the formal act at the same moment, by two Saṅghas standing in two village boundaries, after having created an intermingling or an overlapping, or by not establishing an intermediate space, or by not severing a connection such as a tree’s offshoot.

Gāmasīmādikathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the discussion on village boundaries and other topics is concluded.

Uposathabhedādikathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discussion on Breaches of the Uposatha and Other Topics

149. Adhammena vagganti ettha ekasīmāya catūsu bhikkhūsu vijjamānesu pātimokkhuddesova anuññāto, tīsu, dvīsu ca pārisuddhiuposathova. Idha pana tathā akatattā “adhammenā”ti vuttaṃ. Yasmā pana chandapārisuddhi saṅghe eva āgacchati, na gaṇe, na puggale, tasmā “vagga”nti vuttanti.

149. Regarding ‘unlawfully as a faction’: here, within a single boundary, when there are four bhikkhus present, only the recitation of the Pātimokkha is permitted; and when there are three or two, only the Uposatha of purity is permitted. But here, because it was not done so, it is said ‘unlawfully.’ Furthermore, because consent and purity pertain only to a Saṅgha, not to a group (`gaṇa`) and not to an individual (`puggala`), it is therefore called ‘a faction.’

Sace [M 2.0170] pana dve saṅghā ekasīmāya aññamaññaṃ chandaṃ āharitvā ekasmiṃ khaṇe visuṃ saṅghakammaṃ karonti, ettha kathanti? Keci panetaṃ vaṭṭatīti vadanti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ vaggakammattā[V 2.0160]. Kammaṃ karontānañhi chandapārisuddhi aññattha na gacchati tathā vacanābhāvā, visuṃ visuṃ kammakaraṇatthameva sīmāya anuññātattā cāti gahetabbaṃ. Vihārasīmāyaṃ pana saṅghe vijjamānepi kenaci paccayena khandhasīmāyaṃ tīsu, dvīsu vā pārisuddhiuposathaṃ karontesu kammaṃ dhammena samaggameva bhinnasīmaṭṭhattāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

But if two Saṅghas within the same boundary, having conveyed consent to each other, perform separate Saṅgha acts at the same moment, what is the ruling here? Some say this is permissible, but that should not be accepted, because it is a factional act. For the consent and purity of those performing the act do not extend elsewhere, both because there is no statement to that effect, and because a boundary is permitted only for the purpose of performing separate acts; thus it should be understood. However, in a monastery boundary, even while the Saṅgha is present, if for some reason a group of three or two performs the Uposatha of purity in a sub-boundary (`khandhasīmā`), the act should be seen as lawful and in concord, because they are standing in a separate boundary.

Uposathabhedādikathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the discussion on the breaches of the Uposatha and other topics is concluded.

Pātimokkhuddesakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse of the Pātimokkha Recitation

150. Evametaṃ dhārayāmīti. Sutā kho panāyasmantehīti ettha “evametaṃ dhārayāmī”ti vatvā “uddiṭṭhaṃ kho āyasmanto nidānaṃ, sutā kho panāyasmantehi cattāro pārājikā dhammā”tiādinā vattabbaṃ. Mātikāṭṭhakathāyampi (kaṅkhā. aṭṭha. nidānavaṇṇanā) evameva vuttaṃ. Sutenāti sutapadena.

150. Regarding the phrase, 'Thus I remember this. Have the venerable ones heard them?', here, after saying, 'Thus I remember this,' it should be stated in the manner beginning with, 'Venerable sirs, the introduction has been recited. Have the four Pārājika rules been heard by the venerable ones?'. In the commentary on the Mātikā as well, it is stated in this very way. By `sutena` is meant the word `suta`.

Savarabhayanti vanacarakabhayaṃ. Tenāha “aṭavimanussabhaya”nti. Nidānuddese aniṭṭhite pātimokkhaṃ niddiṭṭhaṃ nāma na hotīti āha “dutiyādīsu uddesesū”tiādi. Tīhipi vidhīhīti osāraṇakathanasarabhaññehi. Ettha ca atthaṃ bhaṇitukāmatāya vā bhaṇāpetukāmatāya vā suttassa osāraṇaṃ osāraṇaṃ nāma. Tasseva atthappakāsanā kathanaṃ nāma. Kevalaṃ pāṭhasseva sarena bhaṇanaṃ sarabhaññaṃ nāma. Sajjhāyaṃ adhiṭṭhahitvāti “sajjhāyaṃ karomī”ti cittaṃ uppādetvā. Osāretvā pana kathentenāti sayameva pāṭhaṃ vatvā pacchā atthaṃ kathentena.

The fear of savages (`savarabhaya`) is the danger from forest-roamers (`vanacaraka`). Therefore, he said, 'the danger from forest-dwelling men (`aṭavimanussa`).' Because the Pātimokkha is not considered recited if the recitation of the introduction is not finished, he said, 'in the second and subsequent recitations.' 'By three methods' means by concluding (`osāraṇa`), explaining (`kathana`), and chanting (`sarabhañña`). And here, the concluding of the text, due to the desire to speak the meaning or the desire to have it spoken, is called `osāraṇa`. The explanation of the meaning of that very text is called `kathana`. Merely reciting the text with intonation is called `sarabhañña`. 'Having undertaken the recitation' means having generated the thought, 'I will make a recitation.' 'But by one who concludes and then explains' means by one who, having recited the text himself, afterwards explains the meaning.

Pātimokkhuddesakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse of the Pātimokkha Recitation is concluded.

Adhammakammapaṭikkosanādikathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse on Topics Beginning with the Rejection of Unlawful Acts

155. Navavidhanti saṅghagaṇapuggalesu tayo, suttuddesapārisuddhiadhiṭṭhānavasena tayo, cātuddasīpannarasīsāmaggīvasena tayoti navavidhaṃ. Catubbidhanti [M 2.0171] adhammenavaggādi catubbidhaṃ. Duvidhanti bhikkhubhikkhunipātimokkhavasena duvidhaṃ pātimokkhaṃ. Navavidhanti bhikkhūnaṃ pañca, bhikkhunīnaṃ cattāroti navavidhaṃ pātimokkhuddesaṃ.

155. `Navavidhaṃ` (ninefold) means: three in respect to the Saṅgha, a group, and individuals; three by way of the recitation of the text, purity, and determination; and three by way of the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and harmony—thus it is ninefold. `Catubbidhaṃ` (fourfold) means the fourfold Uposatha act, beginning with 'unlawfully as a faction'. `Duvidhaṃ` (twofold) means the twofold Pātimokkha, by way of the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha and the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha. `Navavidhaṃ` (ninefold) means the ninefold Pātimokkha recitation, being five for bhikkhus and four for bhikkhunīs.

Adhammakammapaṭikkosanādikathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on Topics Beginning with the Rejection of Unlawful Acts is concluded.

Pakkhagaṇanādiuggahaṇānujānanakathādivaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse on Topics Beginning with the Counting of the Fortnight, the Undertaking, and the Permission

156. Katimīti [V 2.0161] tithi-saddāpekkhaṃ itthiliṅgaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

156. The word `katimī` should be understood as being in the feminine gender with reference to the word `tithi`.

163. Utuvasseyevāti hemantagimhesuyeva.

163. `Utuvasseyeva` means only in the winter and summer seasons.

164. Viññāpetīti ettha manasā cintetvā kāyavikārakaraṇameva viññāpananti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Pāḷiyaṃ aññassa dātabbā pārisuddhīti pārisuddhidāyakena puna aññassa bhikkhuno santike dātabbā. “Bhūtaṃyeva vā sāmaṇerabhāvaṃ ārocetī”ti vuttattā ūnavīsativassakāle upasampannassa, antimavatthuajjhāpannasikkhāpaccakkhātādīnaṃ vā yāva bhikkhupaṭiññā vattati, tāva tehi āhaṭāpi chandapārisuddhi āgacchati. Yadā pana te attano sāmaṇerādibhāvaṃ paṭijānanti, tato paṭṭhāyeva nāgacchatīti dassitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Pāḷiyampi hi “dinnāya pārisuddhiyā saṅghappatto vibbhamati…pe… paṇḍako paṭijānāti. Tiracchānagato paṭijānāti. Ubhatobyañjanako paṭijānāti, āhaṭā hoti pārisuddhī”ti vuttattā paṇḍakādīnampi bhikkhupaṭiññāya vattamānakālesu chandapārisuddhiyā āgamanaṃ siddhameva. Tenāha “esa nayo sabbatthā”ti. Ummattakakhittacittavedanāṭṭānaṃ pana pakatattā antarāmagge ummattakādibhāve paṭiññātepi tesaṃ saṅghappattamatteneva chandādi āgacchatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

164. Regarding `viññāpeti`, here it should be understood that `viññāpana` is the very making of a bodily gesture after having thought with the mind. In the Pāḷi, 'purity should be given to another' means it should be given again by the giver of purity into the presence of another bhikkhu. Because it is said, 'Or he declares his actual state of being a novice,' for one ordained when under twenty years of age, or for those who have committed a terminal offense, renounced the training, and so on, as long as the acknowledgement as a bhikkhu persists, the consent and purity brought by them arrives. But it should be understood that it is shown that when they acknowledge their own state as a novice and so on, from that point onward it does not arrive. For in the Pāḷi too, because it is said, 'When purity has been given, one who has reached the Saṅgha disrobes… a eunuch declares himself to be such, one in the animal state declares himself to be such, a hermaphrodite declares himself to be such—the purity has been brought,' for eunuchs and so on as well, during the times their acknowledgement as a bhikkhu persists, the arrival of consent and purity is indeed established. Therefore, he said, 'This is the principle everywhere.' But for those who are of sound mind but have become insane, of distracted mind, or afflicted by pain, even if their state of insanity and so on is acknowledged on the way, their consent and so on arrives merely by their reaching the Saṅgha; this should be understood.

“Bhikkhūnaṃ hatthapāsa”nti iminā gaṇapuggalesu chandapārisuddhiyā anāgamanaṃ dasseti. “Saṅghappatto”ti hi pāḷiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Biḷālasaṅkhalikapārisuddhīti biḷālagīvāya bandhanasaṅkhalikasadisā pārisuddhi nāma, yathā saṅkhalikā biḷāle āgacchante eva āgacchati, na anāgacchante tappaṭibaddhattā, evamayaṃ pārisuddhipīti attho. Atha vā yathā saṅkhalikāya paṭhamavalayaṃ dutiyavalayaṃ [M 2.0172] pāpuṇāti, na tatiyavalayaṃ, evamayampīti adhippāyo. Upalakkhaṇamattañcettha biḷāla-ggahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

By 'within the hand's reach of the bhikkhus,' he shows the non-arrival of consent and purity in the case of groups and individuals. For in the Pāḷi it is said, 'one who has reached the Saṅgha.' 'Cat's-chain purity' means a purity that is like a chain bound to a cat's neck; just as a chain comes only when the cat comes, and does not come when it does not come because it is bound to it, so too is this purity; this is the meaning. Alternatively, just as with a chain the first link reaches the second link but does not reach the third link, so too is this purity; this is the intention. And here, the taking of 'cat' should be understood as a mere illustration.

Pakkhagaṇanādiuggahaṇānujānanakathādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on Topics Beginning with the Counting of the Fortnight, the Undertaking, and the Permission is concluded.

Chandadānakathādivaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse on Giving Consent and Other Matters

165. Pāḷiyaṃ [V 2.0162] “santi saṅghassa karaṇīyānī”ti vattabbe vacanavipallāsena “karaṇīya”nti vuttaṃ.

165. In the Pāḷi, when it should be said, “There are duties of the Saṅgha,” it is said as “duty” due to a transposition of speech.

167. “Tassa sammutidānakiccaṃ natthī”ti idaṃ pāḷiyaṃ ekadā sarantasseva sammutidānassa vuttattā ekadā asarantassa sammutiabhāvepi tassa anāgamanaṃ vaggakammāya na hotīti vuttaṃ. Keci pana “sopi hatthapāseva ānetabbo”ti vadanti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ.

167. “For him, there is no duty of giving authorization”—this is said because in the Pāḷi the giving of authorization is mentioned only for one who sometimes remembers; therefore, even in the absence of authorization for one who sometimes does not remember, his non-arrival does not result in an incomplete formal act. Some teachers, however, say, “He too should be brought into proximity,” but that should not be accepted.

168. Saṅghasannipātato paṭhamaṃ kātabbaṃ pubbakaraṇaṃ. Saṅghasannipāte kātabbaṃ pubbakiccanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Pāḷiyaṃ no ce adhiṭṭhaheyya, āpatti dukkaṭassāti ettha asañcicca asatiyā anāpatti. Yathā cettha, evaṃ uparipi. Yattha pana acittakāpatti atthi, tattha vakkhāma.

168. What is to be done before the assembly of the Saṅgha is a preliminary act. What is to be done at the assembly of the Saṅgha is a preliminary duty; thus it should be understood. In the Pāḷi, in the passage, 'If one should not determine it, there is an offense of wrong-doing,' here, if it is unintentional and through lack of mindfulness, there is no offense. As it is here, so it is also in subsequent passages. But where there is an offense without intention, we shall explain.

169. “Paññattaṃ hotī”ti iminā “na sāpattikena uposatho kātabbo”ti visuṃ paṭikkhepābhāvepi yathāvuttasuttasāmatthiyato paññattamevāti dasseti. Iminā eva nayena –

169. By “It is laid down,” it is shown that even without a separate prohibition such as, “The Uposatha should not be performed by one who has an offense,” it is indeed laid down by the power of the aforementioned Sutta. By this same method—

“Aṭṭhānametaṃ, bhikkhave, anavakāso yaṃ tathāgato aparisuddhāya parisāya uposathaṃ kareyya, pātimokkhaṃ uddiseyyā”ti (cūḷava. 386; a. ni. 8.20; udā. 45) –

and by the method of the Sutta beginning with, 'This is impossible, monks, it is no occasion that the Tathāgata would perform the Uposatha or recite the Pātimokkha in an impure assembly'—

Ādisuttanayato ca alajjīhipi saddhiṃ uposathakaraṇampi paṭikkhittameva alajjiniggahatthattā sabbasikkhāpadānanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Pārisuddhidānapaññāpanenā”ti iminā sāpattikena pārisuddhipi na dātabbāti dīpitaṃ hoti. Ubhopi dukkaṭanti ettha sabhāgāpattibhāvaṃ ajānitvā kevalaṃ āpattināmeneva desentassa paṭiggaṇhantassa acittakameva dukkaṭaṃ hotīti vadanti[M 2.0173]. Yathā saṅgho sabhāgāpattiṃ āpanno ñattiṃ ṭhapetvā uposathaṃ kātuṃ labhati, evaṃ tayopi “suṇantu me, āyasmantā, ime bhikkhū sabhāgaṃ āpattiṃ āpannā”tiādinā vuttanayānusāreneva gaṇañattiṃ ṭhapetvā dvīhi aññamaññaṃ ārocetvā uposathaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Ekena pana sāpattikena dūraṃ gantvāpi paṭikātumeva vaṭṭati, asampāpuṇantena “bhikkhuṃ labhitvā paṭikarissāmī”ti uposatho kātabbo, paṭikaritvā ca puna uposatho kattabbo.

it should be understood that performing the Uposatha together with shameless persons is also prohibited, because all the training rules are for the purpose of restraining the shameless. By this phrase, 'by the declaration of the giving of purity,' it is shown that purity should also not be given by one who has an offense. Here, in 'an offense of wrong-doing for both,' they say that for one confessing and one receiving the confession who do not know it to be a common offense and do so merely by the name of the offense, there is an offense of wrong-doing that is only unintentional. Just as the Saṅgha, having fallen into a common offense, is able to perform the Uposatha after setting aside the motion, so too for three monks, after setting aside the group motion in accordance with the method that has been stated, beginning with, 'Venerable sirs, let them hear me, these monks have fallen into a common offense,' it is allowable for two of them to perform the Uposatha after informing each other. But for a single monk who has an offense, even having gone far, it is allowable only to make amends. One who does not reach another monk should perform the Uposatha thinking, 'Having found a monk, I will make amends,' and having made amends, the Uposatha should be performed again.

Chandadānakathādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on Giving Consent and Other Matters is concluded.

Anāpattipannarasakādikathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Fifteen Kinds of Non-Offenses, and So Forth

172. Kenaci 63 karaṇīyena gantvāti sīmāparicchedato bahibhūtaṃ gāmaṃ vā araññaṃ vā gantvāti attho. Eteneva uposathañattiyā ṭhapanakāle samaggā eva te ñattiṃ ṭhapesunti siddhaṃ. Teneva pāḷiyaṃ “uddiṭṭhaṃ suuddiṭṭha”nti sabbapannarasakesupi vuttaṃ. Vaggā samaggasaññinotiādi pana ñattiyā niṭṭhitāya “kiṃ saṅghassa pubbakicca”ntiādīnaṃ (mahāva. 134) vacanakkhaṇe bahigatānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ sīmāya paviṭṭhattā bhikkhū tasmiṃ khaṇe vaggā hontīti vuttaṃ. Tenāha “tesaṃ sīmaṃ okkantattā vaggā”tiādi, etena pārājikuddesādikkhaṇepi vaggasaññīnaṃ uddisantānaṃ āpatti eva, ñattiyā pana pubbe niṭṭhitattā kammakopo natthīti dassitameva hoti. Evaṃ uparipi sabbavāresu adhippāyo veditabbo.

172. As for 'having gone on some necessary business,' the meaning is having gone to a village or a forest that is outside the boundary limit. By this very phrase, it is established that at the time of placing the Uposatha motion, they would place the motion only in unity. Therefore, in the Pāḷi, it is said, 'Recited, well recited,' in all the fifteen-day observances as well. However, as for the statement beginning with 'divided, while perceiving unity,' it is said that because the monks who had gone outside entered the boundary at the very moment of saying, 'What is the preliminary duty of the Saṅgha?' etc., after the motion was concluded, the monks at that moment are divided. Therefore, he said the words beginning with, 'Because they have entered the boundary, they are divided.' By this, it is indeed shown that even at the moment of reciting the Pārājika, etc., for those reciting with the perception of being a divided group, there is indeed an offense; however, because the motion was concluded beforehand, there is no vitiation of the act. Similarly, the meaning should be understood in all cases hereafter as well.

Ettha ca pāḷiyaṃ “sabbāya vuṭṭhitāya…pe… tesaṃ santike pārisuddhi ārocetabbā”ti (mahāva. 174) vuttattā bahisīmāgatāya parisāya tesu yassa kassaci santike anadhiṭṭhitehi pārisuddhiṃ ārocetuṃ vaṭṭatīti vadanti.

And here, because it is stated in the Pāḷi, 'When the entire assembly has arisen... etc... purity should be declared in their presence,' they say that for an assembly that has come to the outside of the boundary, it is allowable for those who have not made the determination for the Uposatha to declare their purity in the presence of any one of those monks.

Anāpattipannarasakādikathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Fifteen Kinds of Non-Offenses, and so forth, is concluded.

Liṅgādidassanakathādivaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Seeing of Signs, and so forth

179. Aññātakaṃ [M 2.0174] nāma adiṭṭhapubbanti āha “aññesaṃ santaka”nti. Aññesanti attanā adiṭṭhapubbānaṃ. Nānāsaṃvāsakabhāvanti laddhinānāsaṃvāsakabhāvaṃ.

179. As for 'unknown,' it means 'not seen before'; therefore, he said, 'belonging to others.' 'Of others' means of those not seen before by oneself. As for 'the state of different co-residence,' it means the state of different co-residence due to different views.

180. Pāḷiyaṃ abhivitaranti samānasaṃvāsakābhāvaṃ nicchinanti.

180. In the Pāḷi, 'abhivitaranti' means they ascertain the state of common co-residence.

181. Uposathakārakāti saṅghuposathakārakā. Teneva “aññatra saṅghenā”ti vuttaṃ. Saṅghuposathaṭṭhānato hi gacchantena attacatuttheneva gantabbaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ nisinnaṭṭhānato pana gacchantena ekena bhikkhunāpi saha gantumpi vaṭṭati. Pāḷiyaṃ “abhikkhuko āvāso”ti idaṃ nidassanamattaṃ, saṅghuposathaṭṭhānato gaṇapuggalehi sabhikkhukopi āvāso na gantabbo “aññatra saṅghenā”ti vuttattāti vadanti. Uposathaṃ karontīti saṅghuposathaṃ vā gaṇuposathaṃ vā. “Tassa santika”nti idaṃ gaṇuposathaṭṭhānato gacchantaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, aññathā “sabbantimena paricchedena attacatutthena [V 2.0164] vā”ti vacanena virujjhanato. Āraññakenāti ekacārinā. Uposathantarāyoti attano uposathantarāyo.

181. As for 'Uposatha-performers,' it means the performers of the Saṅgha Uposatha. Therefore, it is said, 'except by the Saṅgha.' Indeed, one going from the place of the Saṅgha Uposatha should go only as the fourth person himself; however, from the place where three monks are sitting, it is allowable to go together with even one monk. In the Pāḷi, the phrase 'a residence without monks' is merely an example; they say that from the place of the Saṅgha Uposatha, one should not go to a residence, even one with monks, by group or as an individual, because it is said, 'except by the Saṅgha.' As for 'they perform the Uposatha,' it means they perform either the Saṅgha Uposatha or the Gaṇa Uposatha. The phrase 'to his presence' is said in reference to one going from the place of the Gaṇa Uposatha, because otherwise, it would contradict the statement, 'with the very last boundary or as the fourth person himself.' As for 'by a forest-dweller,' it means by one who lives alone. As for 'obstruction to the Uposatha,' it means an obstruction to one's own Uposatha.

183. Pāḷiyaṃ bhikkhuniyā nisinnaparisāyātiādīsu bhikkhuniyātiādi karaṇatthe sāmivacanaṃ.

183. In the Pāḷi, in phrases such as 'of the assembly seated by a bhikkhunī,' the word 'bhikkhuniyā' and so forth is a genitive case in the sense of the instrumental.

Liṅgādidassanakathādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Seeing of Signs, and so forth, is concluded.

Uposathakkhandhakavaṇṇanānayo niṭṭhito.

The method of the commentary on the Uposatha Chapter is concluded.

3. Vassūpanāyikakkhandhako

3. The Chapter on Taking up the Rains-residence

Vassūpanāyikaanujānanakathādivaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discussion on the Permission for the Rains-residence, and so forth

184. Vassūpanāyikakkhandhake [M 2.0175][V 2.0165] aparasmiṃ divaseti dutiye pāṭipadadivase.

184. In the Chapter on Taking up the Rains-residence, 'on the next day' means on the second day, the first day of the lunar fortnight.

185. Aññattha aruṇaṃ uṭṭhāpanena vāti sāpekkhassa akaraṇīyena gantvā aññattha aruṇaṃ uṭṭhāpanena vā. Parihānīti guṇaparihāni.

185. As for 'or by causing the dawn to rise in another place,' it means for a monk with lingering attachment, having gone without a proper duty, or causing the dawn to rise in another place. As for 'loss,' it means loss of virtue.

187. Pāḷiyaṃ sattāhaṃ sannivatto kātabboti sakalaṃ sattāhaṃ bahi eva avītināmetvā sattāhapariyosānabhūtaṃ aruṇuṭṭhānakālaṃ puna vihāreva sambandhavasena sattāhaṃ vihāre sannivattaṃ kātabbaṃ. Sattāhapariyosānakālo hi idha sattāha-saddena vutto, tadapekkhāya ca “sannivatto”ti pulliṅgena vuttaṃ. Tīṇi parihīnānīti bhikkhunīnaṃ vaccakuṭiādīnaṃ paṭikkhittattā parihīnāni.

187. In the Pāḷi, 'the seven-day period should be made to have returned' means: without letting the entire seven-day period pass outside, the time of dawn, which is the end of the seven-day period, should, by way of connection, be made to have returned to the monastery. Indeed, the time of the end of the seven-day period is here referred to by the word 'sattāha,' and with reference to that time, 'sannivatto' is stated in the masculine gender. As for 'three things are lost,' they are lost because latrines and so forth were disallowed for the bhikkhunīs.

189. Na palujjatīti aññesaṃ appaguṇattā, mama ca maraṇena na vinassati.

189. As for 'it does not perish,' it means it does not perish, both because of others' lack of practice and because of my death.

Vassūpanāyikaanujānanakathādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discussion on the Permission for the Rains-residence, and so forth, is concluded.

Pahiteyevaanujānanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discussion on Granting Permission Only When Sent

199. Bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ vasanakapurisoti anaññagatikoti dasseti. Gantabbanti saṅghakaraṇīyena appahitepi gantabbaṃ. Ettha ca anupāsakehipi sāsanabhāvaṃ ñātukāmehi pahite tesaṃ pasādavaḍḍhiṃ sampassantehipi sattāhakaraṇīyena gantuṃ vaṭṭatīti gahetabbaṃ.

199. As for 'a person who lives with the bhikkhus,' this indicates one who lives in the forest. As for 'one should go,' one should go even if not sent on the Saṅgha's business. And here, it should be understood that it is permissible to go for a seven-day affair even when sent by lay followers who are not one's personal supporters but who wish to know about the flourishing of the Teaching, and also when seeing the growth of their faith.

Ratticchedavinicchayoti [V 2.0166] sattāhakaraṇīyena gantvā bahiddhā aruṇuṭṭhāpanasaṅkhātassa ratticchedassa vinicchayo. Gantuṃ vaṭṭatīti antoupacārasīmāyaṃ ṭhiteneva sattāhakaraṇīyanimittaṃ sallakkhetvā iminā nimittena gantvā “antosattāhe āgacchissāmī”ti ābhogaṃ katvā gantuṃ vaṭṭati. Purimakkhaṇe ābhogaṃ katvā gamanakkhaṇe vissaritvā gatepi doso [M 2.0176] natthi “sakaraṇīyo pakkamatī”ti (mahāva. 207) vuttattā. Sabbathā pana ābhogaṃ akatvā gatassa vassacchedoti vadanti. Yo pana sattāhakaraṇīyanimittābhāvepi “sattāhabbhantare āgamissāmī”ti ābhogaṃ katvā gantvā sattāhabbhantare āgacchati, tassa āpattiyeva, vassacchedo natthi sattāhassa sannivattattāti vadanti. Vīmaṃsitvā gahetabbaṃ. Bhaṇḍakanti cīvarabhaṇḍaṃ. Sampāpuṇituṃ na sakkoti, vaṭṭatīti tadaheva āgamane saussāhattā vassacchedo vā āpatti vā na hotīti adhippāyo. Ācariyanti agilānampi nissayācariyañca dhammācariyañca, pageva upasampadācariyaupajjhāyesu. Vadati, vaṭṭatīti sattāhātikkame āpattiabhāvaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, vassacchedo pana hoti eva.

As for 'the determination of the breaking of the night,' it is the determination of the breaking of the night, which is designated as the rising of the dawn outside, after having gone for a seven-day affair. As for 'it is permissible to go,' it means: while staying right within the vicinity-boundary, having noted a reason for a seven-day affair, it is permissible to go after making the reflection, 'I will go for this reason and return within seven days.' Even if one makes the reflection in a prior moment but goes having forgotten it at the moment of departure, there is no fault, because it was said, 'He departs having a duty.' However, they say that for one who goes without making any reflection at all, the rains-residence is broken. But as for the monk who, even in the absence of a reason for a seven-day affair, makes the reflection, 'I will return within seven days,' and having gone, returns within seven days, for him there is only an offense; there is no breaking of the rains-residence, they say, because the seventh day has returned. This should be accepted after investigation. As for 'requisites,' it means robe-requisites. As for 'he is not able to obtain it, it is permissible,' the meaning is this: because of being diligent in returning on that very day, there is neither a breaking of the rains-residence nor an offense. As for 'a teacher,' it means a dependence teacher and a Dhamma teacher even if not sick; how much more so in the case of ordaining teachers and preceptors. The words 'he says, it is permissible' are said with reference to the absence of an offense when the seven days are exceeded, but the breaking of the rains-residence does indeed occur.

Pahiteyevaanujānanakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discussion on Granting Permission Only When Sent is concluded.

Antarāyeanāpattivassacchedakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discussion on No Offense in the Interruption of the Rains-residence Due to an Obstacle.

200. Pāḷiyaṃ gaṇhiṃsūti gahetvā khādiṃsu. Paripātiṃsūti palāpesuṃ, anubandhiṃsūti attho.

200. In the Pāḷi, `gaṇhiṃsu` means: having seized, they devoured. `Paripātiṃsu` means: they put to flight, they pursued. This is the meaning.

201. Sattāhavārena aruṇo uṭṭhāpetabboti ettha chadivasāni bahiddhā vītināmetvā sattame divase purāruṇā eva antoupacārasīmāya pavisitvā aruṇaṃ uṭṭhāpetvā punadivase sattāhaṃ adhiṭṭhāya gantabbanti adhippāyo.
