Keci pana “sattame divase āgantvā aruṇaṃ anuṭṭhāpetvā tadaheva divasabhāgepi gantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ “aruṇo uṭṭhāpetabbo”ti vuttattā. Sattame divase tattha aruṇuṭṭhāpanameva hi sandhāya pāḷiyampi “sattāhaṃ sannivatto kātabbo”ti vuttaṃ. Aruṇaṃ anuṭṭhāpetvā gacchanto anto appavisitvā bahiddhāva sattāhaṃ vītināmentena samucchinnavasso eva bhavissati aruṇassa bahi eva uṭṭhāpitattā. Itarathā “aruṇo uṭṭhāpetabbo”ti vacanaṃ niratthakaṃ siyā “sattāhavārena antovihāre pavisitvā aruṇaṃ anuṭṭhāpetvāpi gantabba”nti vattabbato. Aññesu ca ṭhānesu aruṇuṭṭhāpanameva [V 2.0167] vuccati. Vakkhati hi cīvarakkhandhake “ekasmiṃ vihāre vasanto itarasmiṃ sattāhavārena aruṇameva uṭṭhāpetī”ti (mahāva. aṭṭha. 364).

201. Here, in the phrase “the dawn must be caused to rise by the turn of the seven days,” the intention is that, having spent six days outside, on the seventh day, before dawn, one should enter the inner boundary vicinity and cause the dawn to rise, and on the following day, one may depart for a seven-day period. Some, however, say, “On the seventh day, one may come without causing the dawn to rise and even leave during the daytime”; but that should not be accepted, because it is stated, “the dawn must be caused to rise.” Indeed, it is with reference to causing the dawn to rise there on the seventh day that it is also stated in the Pāḷi, “a return must be made within seven days.” One who departs without causing the dawn to rise, by spending seven days outside without entering, will certainly have his rains-residence interrupted, because the dawn was caused to rise outside. Otherwise, the statement “the dawn must be caused to rise” would be meaningless, since it would have to be said, “by the turn of the seven days, one may enter the inner monastery and depart even without causing the dawn to rise.” And in other places, only the causing of the dawn to rise is mentioned. For it will be said in the Cīvarakkhandhaka, “While dwelling in one monastery, he causes only the dawn to rise in another by the turn of the seven days.”

Athāpi [M 2.0177] yaṃ te vadeyyuṃ “sattame divase yadā kadāci paviṭṭhena taṃdivasanissito atītaaruṇo uṭṭhāpito nāma hotīti imamatthaṃ sandhāya aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vutta”nti, taṃ saddagatiyāpi na sameti. Na hi uṭṭhite aruṇe pacchā paviṭṭho tassa payojako uṭṭhāpako bhavitumarahati. Yadi bhaveyya, vassaṃ upagantvā panassa aruṇaṃ anuṭṭhāpetvā tadaheva sattāhakaraṇīyena pakkantassāpīti ettha “aruṇaṃ anuṭṭhāpetvā”ti vacanaṃ virujjheyya, tenapi taṃdivasasannissitassa aruṇassa uṭṭhāpitattā. Āraññakassāpi hi bhikkhuno sāyanhasamaye aṅgayuttaṃ araññaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā tadā eva nivattantassa aruṇo uṭṭhāpito dhutaṅgañca visodhitaṃ siyā, na cetaṃ yuttaṃ aruṇuggamanakāle eva aruṇuṭṭhāpanassa vuttattā. Vuttañhi “kālasseva pana nikkhamitvā aṅgayutte ṭhāne aruṇaṃ uṭṭhāpetabbaṃ. Sace aruṇuṭṭhānavelāyaṃ tesaṃ ābādho vaḍḍhati, tesaṃ eva kiccaṃ kātabbaṃ, na dhutaṅgavisuddhikena bhavitabba”nti (visuddhi. 1.31). Tathā pārivāsikādīnampi aruṇaṃ anuṭṭhāpetvā vattaṃ nikkhipantānaṃ ratticchedo vutto. “Uggate aruṇe nikkhipitabba”nti (cūḷava. 97) hi vuttaṃ. Sahaseyyasikkhāpadepi anupasampannehi saha nivutthabhāvaparimocanatthaṃ “purāruṇā nikkhamitvā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Evaṃ cīvaravippavāsādīsu ca sabbattha rattipariyosāne āgāmiaruṇavaseneva aruṇuṭṭhāpanaṃ dassitaṃ, na atītāruṇavasena. Tasmā vuttanayenevettha aruṇuṭṭhāpanaṃ veditabbaṃ aññathā vassacchedattā.

Moreover, if they were to say, “On the seventh day, whenever someone enters, the past dawn dependent on that day is said to have been caused to rise—this meaning is stated with reference to the commentary,” that does not accord even with the sense of the word. For one who enters after the dawn has risen cannot be fit to be the agent who causes it to rise. If it were so, in the passage “for one who, having entered the rains-residence, departs on that very day for a seven-day task without causing the dawn to rise,” the phrase “without causing the dawn to rise” would be contradicted, because the dawn dependent on that day would have been caused to rise by him too. Indeed, for a forest-dwelling bhikkhu as well, who goes in the evening to a suitable forest place and returns at that very moment, the dawn would have been caused to rise and his ascetic practice purified; but this is not proper, because the causing of the dawn to rise is stated to be at the time of dawn's arising. For it is said: “One should go out early and cause the dawn to rise in a suitable place. If their illness worsens at the time of causing the dawn to rise, their own duty should be done; one should not be concerned with purifying the ascetic practice.” Similarly, for those on probation and others who suspend their observance without causing the dawn to rise, an interruption of the night is stated. For it is said: “It should be suspended after the dawn has risen.” In the training rule on sharing a dwelling, too, for the purpose of release from the state of having lived together with the unordained, it is said: “One should go out before dawn,” and so on. Thus, in cases like robe-separation and others, everywhere the causing of the dawn to rise is shown to be in relation to the coming dawn, not in relation to the past dawn. Therefore, the causing of the dawn to rise should be understood here in the way that has been stated; otherwise, it would be an interruption of the rains-residence.

Yaṃ pana vassaṃ upagatassa tadaheva aruṇaṃ anuṭṭhāpetvā sakaraṇīyassa pakkamanavacanaṃ, taṃ vassaṃ upagatakālato paṭṭhāya yadā kadāci nimitte sati gamanassa anuññātattā yuttaṃ, na pana sattāhavārena gatassa aruṇaṃ anuṭṭhāpetvā tadaheva gamanaṃ “aruṇo uṭṭhāpetabbo”ti vuttattā eva. Yathā vā “sattāhaṃ anāgatāya pavāraṇāya sakaraṇīyo pakkamati, āgaccheyya vā so, bhikkhave, bhikkhu taṃ āvāsaṃ, na vā āgaccheyyā”tiādinā (mahāva. 207) pacchimasattāhe anāgamane anuññātepi aññasattāhesu na vaṭṭati. Evaṃ paṭhamasattāhe aruṇaṃ anuṭṭhāpetvā gamane anuññātepi tato paresu sattāhesu āgatassa aruṇaṃ anuṭṭhāpetvā [M 2.0178] gamanaṃ na vaṭṭatīti niṭṭhamettha gantabbaṃ. Idha āhaṭanti vihārato bahi āgataṭṭhāne ānītaṃ.

As for the statement that one who has entered the rains-residence, having a duty, may depart on that very day without causing the dawn to rise, that is proper because departure is permitted whenever there is a reason, starting from the time of entering the rains-residence. But for one who has returned after a seven-day period, departure on that very day without causing the dawn to rise is not proper, precisely because it is stated, “The dawn must be caused to rise.” Or, just as it is stated, “A bhikkhu with a duty departs seven days before the Pavāraṇā; he may or may not return, O bhikkhus, to that monastery…”, and although non-return is permitted in the final seven-day period, it is not allowable in other seven-day periods. Similarly, although departure without causing the dawn to rise is permitted in the first seven-day period, for one who has returned in subsequent seven-day periods, departure without causing the dawn to rise is not allowable. Thus should the conclusion be reached here. `Idha āhaṭanti` means brought to the place one has come from, outside the monastery.

Antarāyeanāpattivassacchedakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discussion on No Offense in the Interruption of the Rains-residence Due to an Obstacle is concluded.

Vajādīsu vassūpagamanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discussion on Undertaking the Rains-residence in a Cattle-pen and So Forth.

203. Upagantuṃ 68 na vaṭṭatīti kuṭikādīnaṃ abhāvena “idha vassaṃ upemī”ti evaṃ vacībhedaṃ katvā upagantuṃ na vaṭṭati.

203. 'It is not permissible to undertake' means: due to the absence of a hut and so forth, it is not permissible to undertake it by making a verbal utterance thus, 'I undertake the rains here.'

204. Pāḷiyaṃ pisācillikāti pisācadārakā. Pavisanadvāraṃ yojetvāti sakavāṭadvāraṃ katvā. Rukkhaṃ chinditvāti susiraṭṭhānassa uparibhāgaṃ chinditvā. Khāṇumatthaketi susirakhāṇumatthake. Ṭaṅkitamañco nāma dīghe mañcapāde vijjhitvā aṭaniyo pavesetvā kato, so heṭṭhupariyavasena paññattopi purimasadisova hoti, taṃ susāne, devatāṭhāne ca ṭhapenti. Catunnaṃ pāsāṇānaṃ upari pāsāṇaphalake attharitvā katagehampi “ṭaṅkitamañco”ti vuccati.

204. In the Pāḷi, 'pisācillikā' means young demons. 'Pavisanadvāraṃ yojetvā' means having made a door with its own panels. 'Rukkhaṃ chinditvā' means having cut off the upper part of a hollow place. 'Khāṇumatthake' means on top of a hollow tree stump. A 'ṭaṅkitamañca' is a bed made by piercing long bed legs and inserting stretchers; even when it is set up by being turned upside down, it is just like the former. They place it in a charnel ground and at a deity's shrine. Even a house made by spreading a stone slab on top of four stones is called a 'ṭaṅkitamañca'.

Vajādīsuvassūpagamanakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discussion on Undertaking the Rains-residence in a Cattle-pen and So Forth is concluded.

Adhammikakatikādikathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discussion on Unrighteous Conventions and So Forth.

205. Mahāvibhaṅgeti catutthapārājikavaṇṇanāyaṃ. Parato senāsanakkhandhakepi adhammikaṃ katikavattaṃ āvi bhavissati eva.

205. 'In the Mahāvibhaṅga' means in the exposition of the fourth Pārājika. Further on, in the Senāsana Khandhaka as well, an unrighteous convention will indeed become manifest.

207. Yasmā nānāsīmāyaṃ dvīsu āvāsesu vassaṃ upagacchantassa “dutiye vasissāmī”ti upacārato nikkhantamatte paṭhamo senāsanaggāho paṭippassambhati. Tasmā pāḷiyaṃ “tassa, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno purimikā ca na paññāyatī”ti paṭhamaṃ senāsanaggāhaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Dutiye senāsanaggāhe pana purimikā paññāyateva, tattheva temāsaṃ vasanto purimavassaṃvuttho [M 2.0179] eva hoti, tato vā pana dutiyadivasādīsu “paṭhamasenāsane vasissāmī”ti upacārātikkame purimikāpi na paññāyatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

207. Because, for a monk who undertakes the rains residence in two dwellings within different boundaries, the first taking of a lodging ceases as soon as he departs from the precinct with the thought, 'I will reside in the second.' Therefore, in the Pāḷi, the statement 'that monk’s former [rains residence] is not recognized' is said with reference to the first taking of a lodging. However, in the second taking of a lodging, the former is indeed recognized; residing there for the three months, he is considered to have completed the first rains residence. Or, if from there, on the second day and so on, upon transgressing the precinct with the thought, 'I will reside in the first lodging,' the former is also not recognized—thus it should be understood.

208. Pāḷiyaṃ “so sattāhaṃ anāgatāya pavāraṇāya sakaraṇīyo pakkamatī”ti vuttattā pavāraṇādivasepi sattāhakaraṇīyaṃ vinā gantuṃ na vaṭṭatīti veditabbaṃ. Komudiyā cātumāsiniyāti [V 2.0169] pacchima-kattikapuṇṇamāya. Sā hi tasmiṃ kāle kumudānaṃ atthitāya komudī, catunnaṃ vassikamāsānaṃ pariyosānattā cātumāsinīti ca vuccati.

208. Because it is said in the Pāḷi, 'If he has some duty, he may depart when there are seven days until the Pavāraṇā,' it should be understood that even on the Pavāraṇā day, it is not permissible to go without a seven-day duty. 'Komudiyā cātumāsiniyā' means on the full moon day of the last Kattika. Indeed, because of the existence of water lilies (kumuda) at that time, it is called Komudī; and because it is the end of the four rainy months, it is also called Cātumāsinī.

Adhammikakatikādikathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Discourse on Unrighteous Conventions and So Forth is concluded.

Vassūpanāyikakkhandhakavaṇṇanānayo niṭṭhito.

The Method of the Exposition of the Chapter on Undertaking the Rains Residence is concluded.

4. Pavāraṇākkhandhako

4. The Chapter on the Pavāraṇā

Aphāsuvihārakathādivaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Discourse on Uncongenial Dwellings and So Forth

209. Pavāraṇākkhandhake [M 2.0180][V 2.0170] pāḷiyaṃ piṇḍāya paṭikkameyyāti piṇḍāya caritvā paṭikkameyya. Avakkārapātinti atirekapiṇḍapātaṭhapanakaṃ ekaṃ bhājanaṃ. Avisayhanti ukkhipituṃ asakkuṇeyyaṃ. Vilaṅghanaṃ ukkhipanaṃ vilaṅgho, so eva vilaṅghako, hatthehi vilaṅghako hatthavilaṅghakoti āha “hatthukkhepakenā”ti. Atha vā vilaṅghakena ukkhepakena hatthenātipi attho, aññamaññaṃ saṃsibbitahatthehīti vuttaṃ hoti.

209. In the Pavāraṇākkhandhaka, in the Pāḷi, piṇḍāya paṭikkameyya means: having wandered for alms, one should return. Avakkārapātiṃ is a single vessel for placing leftover almsfood. Avisayhaṃ means that which is unable to be lifted. Vilaṅghanaṃ is lifting; vilaṅgho is lifting; that very thing is called vilaṅghako. Hatthavilaṅghako is lifting with the hands; therefore, he said, ‘hatthukkhepakenā’ (by raising with the hand). Alternatively, the meaning is also: with a lifting, raising hand. This is to say: with hands intertwined with one another.

213. Sace pana vuḍḍhataro hotīti pavāraṇādāyako bhikkhu vuḍḍhataro hoti. Evañhi tena tassatthāya pavāritaṃ hotīti ettha evaṃ tena appavāritopi tassa saṅghappattimattena saṅghapavāraṇākammaṃ samaggakammameva hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tena ca bhikkhunāti pavāraṇādāyakena bhikkhunā.

213. Sace pana vuḍḍhataro hoti means: if the monk who gives the Pavāraṇā is more senior. In the phrase evañhi tena tassatthāya pavāritaṃ hoti, it should be understood thus: in this way, even though that monk who gave the Pavāraṇā has not performed it himself, merely by it reaching the Saṅgha through that other monk, the Saṅgha's act of Pavāraṇā is indeed a unanimous act. Tena ca bhikkhunā means: by the monk who gives the Pavāraṇā.

234. Bahūpi samānavassā ekato pavāretuṃ labhantīti ekasmiṃ saṃvacchare laddhūpasampadatāya samānupasampannavassā sabbe ekato pavāretuṃ labhantīti attho.

234. Bahūpi samānavassā ekato pavāretuṃ labhantīti means: even many monks of the same seniority can perform Pavāraṇā together. The meaning is that all those who received the higher ordination in the same year, being of the same seniority, can perform Pavāraṇā together.

237. Pāḷiyaṃ micchādiṭṭhīti “natthi dinna”ntiādi (dī. ni. 1.171; ma. ni. 1.445; 2.94, 95, 225; 3.91, 116, 136; saṃ. ni. 3.210; dha. sa. 1221) nayappavattā. Antaggāhikāti sassatucchedasaṅkhātassa antassa gāhikā. Yaṃ kho tvantiādīsu yaṃ pavāraṇaṃ ṭhapesi, taṃ diṭṭhena ṭhapesīti taṃ-saddaṃ ajjhāharitvā yojetabbaṃ.

237. In the Pāḷi, micchādiṭṭhi is the view that proceeds by way of such statements as, “There is nothing given,” and so forth. Antaggāhikā is the view that grasps the extremes, known as eternalism and annihilationism. In texts such as yaṃ kho tvaṃ, the word taṃ should be supplied and connected, thus: yaṃ pavāraṇaṃ ṭhapesi, taṃ diṭṭhena ṭhapesi (Whatever Pavāraṇā you establish, that you establish with a view).

239. Vatthuṃ pakāsentoti puggale parisaṅkuppattiyā nimittabhūtaṃ vatthumattaṃyeva sandhāya vuttaṃ[V 2.0171]. Yaṃ pana vatthuṃ sandhāya “puggalo paññāyati, na vatthū”ti āha, na taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Yadi pana tassa bhikkhuno vasanaṭṭhāne pokkharaṇito macchaggahaṇādi disseyya, tadā “vatthu ca puggalo ca paññāyatī”ti vattabbaṃ bhaveyya. Tenāha “purimanayeneva corehī”tiādi. Bhikkhuno sarīre mālāgandhañca ariṭṭhagandhañca disvā evaṃ “vatthu ca puggalo ca paññāyatī”ti vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

239. The statement vatthuṃ pakāsento is said with reference only to the mere basis that has become the cause for the arising of revulsion in a person. But with reference to whatever basis it is said, “The person is known, not the basis,” this statement was not said with reference to that. If, however, in that monk’s dwelling place, the taking of fish from a pond and so forth were to be seen, then he said, “Both the basis and the person are known.” It should be understood that it is said, “Both the basis and the person are known,” only after seeing on the monk’s body the scent of flowers and the scent of soap-nut medicine.

Aphāsuvihārakathādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Discourse on Uncongenial Dwellings and So Forth is concluded.

Bhaṇḍanakārakavatthukathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Account of Those Who Cause Quarrels

240. Dve [M 2.0181] cātuddasikā hontīti tatiyapakkhe cātuddasiyā saddhiṃ dve cātuddasikā honti. “Bhaṇḍanakārakānaṃ terase vā cātuddase vā ime pannarasīpavāraṇaṃ pavāressantī”ti iminā yathāsakaṃ uposathakaraṇadivasato paṭṭhāya bhikkhūnaṃ cātuddasīpannarasīvohāro, na candagatisiddhiyā tithiyā vasenāti dasseti. Kiñcāpi evaṃ “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, rājūnaṃ anuvattitu”nti (mahāva. 186) vacanato panettha lokiyānaṃ tithiṃ anuvattantehipi attano uposathakkamena cātuddasiṃ pannarasiṃ vā, pannarasiṃ cātuddasiṃ vā karonteheva anuvattitabbaṃ, na pana soḷasamadivasaṃ vā terasamadivasaṃ vā uposathadivasaṃ karontehi. Teneva pāḷiyampi “dve tayo uposathe cātuddasike kātu”nti vuttaṃ. Aññathā dvādasiyaṃ, terasiyaṃ vā uposatho kātabboti vattabbato. “Sakiṃ pakkhassa cātuddase, pannarase vā”tiādivacanampi upavutthakkameneva vuttaṃ, na tithikkamenāti gahetabbaṃ.

240. Dve cātuddasikā hontīti means: in the third fortnight, together with the fourteenth, there are two fourteenth-day Uposathas. By this text, “These quarrel-makers will perform the Pavāraṇā of the fifteenth on the thirteenth or fourteenth,” it is shown that for the bhikkhus, the designation of ‘fourteenth’ or ‘fifteenth’ is from their respective day of observing the Uposatha, not by the power of the tithi established by the movement of the moon. Although it is thus stated, “I allow, O bhikkhus, to follow the kings,” here, even when following the tithis of worldly people, it should be followed only by making the Uposatha a fourteenth-day or fifteenth-day observance, and not by making the sixteenth-day the Uposatha day. Therefore, in the Pāḷi too, it is said, “to perform two or three Uposathas as fourteenth-day ones.” Why? Otherwise, it would have been fitting to say, “The Uposatha should be done on the twelfth or thirteenth.” The saying beginning with, “Once a fortnight on the fourteenth or fifteenth,” should also be understood as stated only according to the sequence of observance, not according to the sequence of the tithi.

Bhaṇḍanakārakavatthukathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Account of Those Who Cause Quarrels is concluded.

Pavāraṇāsaṅgahakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Discourse on the Summary of Pavāraṇā

241. “Pavāretvā pana antarāpi cārikaṃ pakkamituṃ labhantī”ti iminā pavāraṇāsaṅgahe kate antarā pakkamitukāmā saṅghaṃ sannipātāpetvā pavāretuṃ labhantīti dasseti.

241. By this text: “Having performed the Pavāraṇā, they may depart on a journey even in between”—it is shown that when the Summary of Pavāraṇā has been made, those who wish to depart in between may have the Saṅgha assembled and perform the Pavāraṇā.

Pavāraṇāsaṅgahakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Discourse on the Summary of Pavāraṇā is concluded.

Pavāraṇākkhandhakavaṇṇanānayo niṭṭhito.

The Method of the Exposition of the Pavāraṇā Chapter is concluded.

5. Cammakkhandhako

5. The Chapter on Leather

Soṇakoḷivisakathādivaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Account of Soṇa Koḷivisa and Others

242. Cammakkhandhake [M 2.0182][V 2.0172] uṇṇapāvāraṇanti ubhato lomāni uṭṭhāpetvā kataṃ uṇṇamayaṃ pāvāraṇaṃ, ubhato kappāsapicuṃ uṭṭhāpetvā vītapāvāropi atthi, tato nivattanatthaṃ “uṇṇapāvāraṇa”nti vuttaṃ.

242. In the Chapter on Leather, ‘a woolen cloak’ (uṇṇapāvāraṇaṃ) is a cloak made of wool, made by raising the hairs on both sides. There is also a cloak woven by raising tufts of cotton on both sides; to distinguish from that, it is called ‘a woolen cloak’.

Aḍḍhacandapāsāṇeti sopānamūle upaḍḍhaṃ anto pavesetvā ṭhapite aḍḍhapāsāṇe. Pāḷiyaṃ vihārapacchāyāyanti vihārapaccante chāyāya, vihārassa vaḍḍhamānacchāyāyantipi vadanti.

‘Aḍḍhacandapāsāṇe’ means on a half-moon stone placed at the foot of the stairs with half of it inserted inside. In the Pāḷi, ‘vihārapacchāyāyaṃ’ means in the shade at the edge of the monastery; some also say it means in the extending shade of the monastery.

243. Bhogāti upayogatthe paccattavacanaṃ. Accāyatāti atiāyatā kharamucchanā. Saravatīti madhurasarasaṃyuttā. Atisithilā mandamucchanā. Vīriyasamathanti vīriyasampayuttasamathaṃ. Tattha ca nimittaṃ gaṇhāhīti tasmiñca samabhāve sati yaṃ ādāse mukhanimittaṃ viya nimittaṃ uppajjati, taṃ samathanimittaṃ, vipassanānimittaṃ, magganimittaṃ, phalanimittañca gaṇhāhi nibbattehīti, evamassa arahattapariyosānaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathitaṃ.

243. ‘Bhogā’ is the nominative case in the sense of ‘for use’ (accusative). ‘Accāyatā’ means a rough striking that is too tight. ‘Sāravatī’ means endowed with a sweet sound. ‘Atisithilā’ means a gentle striking that is too loose. ‘Vīriyasamathaṃ’ means tranquility associated with energy. And ‘Tattha ca nimittaṃ gaṇhāhi’ (‘And there grasp the sign’) means: when that tranquility is present, whatever sign arises, like the reflection of a face in a mirror—grasp that sign of tranquility, sign of insight, sign of the path, and sign of fruition; bring it into being. Thus, the meditation subject for him, which has Arahantship as its conclusion, was taught.

244. Chaṭhānānīti cha kāraṇāni. Adhimuttoti paṭivijjhitvā ṭhito. Nekkhammādhimuttotiādi sabbaṃ arahattavasena vuttaṃ. Arahattañhi sabbakilesehi nikkhantattā nekkhammaṃ, teheva ca pavivittattā paviveko, byāpajjābhāvato abyāpajjaṃ, upādānassa khayante uppannattā upādānakkhayo, taṇhakkhayante uppannattā taṇhakkhayo, sammohābhāvato asammohoti ca vuccati.

244. ‘Chaṭhānāni’ means six reasons. ‘Adhimutto’ means one who stands having penetrated. Everything beginning with ‘Nekkhammādhimutto’ is stated by way of Arahantship. For Arahantship is called ‘nekkhamma’ because it has gone forth from all defilements; ‘paviveko’ because it is secluded from those same defilements; ‘abyāpajjaṃ’ because of the absence of affliction; ‘upādānakkhayo’ because it arises at the end of the destruction of clinging; ‘taṇhakkhayo’ because it arises at the end of the destruction of craving; and ‘asammoho’ because of the absence of delusion.

Kevalaṃ saddhāmattakanti kevalaṃ paṭivedhapaññāya asammissaṃ saddhāmattakaṃ. Paṭicayanti punappunaṃ [V 2.0173] karaṇena vaḍḍhiṃ. Vītarāgattāti maggapaṭivedhena rāgassa vigatattā eva nekkhammasaṅkhātaṃ arahattaṃ paṭivijjhitvā sacchikatvā ṭhito hoti. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Pavivekādhimuttoti “paviveke adhimutto aha”nti evaṃ arahattaṃ byākarotīti attho.

‘Kevalaṃ saddhāmattakaṃ’ means mere faith, unmixed with penetrative wisdom. ‘Paṭicayaṃ’ means growth through repeated action. ‘Vītarāgattā’ means that because lust is gone through the penetration of the path, one stands having penetrated and realized Arahantship, which is known as ‘nekkhamma’. This same method applies to the remaining terms. ‘Pavivekādhimutto’ means: he declares Arahantship thus, “I am resolved on seclusion,” this is the meaning.

Sīlabbataparāmāsanti sīlañca vatañca parāmasitvā gahitaggahaṇamattaṃ. Sārato paccāgacchantoti sārabhāvena jānanto. Abyāpajjādhimuttoti abyāpajjaṃ arahattaṃ byākaroti.

‘Sīlabbataparāmāsaṃ’ means merely the grasping of a view taken after considering precepts and practices. ‘Sārato paccāgacchanto’ means knowing it as essential. ‘Abyāpajjādhimutto’ means one declares Arahantship, which is without affliction.

Amissīkatanti [M 2.0183] amissakataṃ. Kilesā hi ārammaṇena saddhiṃ cittaṃ missaṃ karonti, tesaṃ abhāvā amissīkataṃ. Bhusā vātavuṭṭhīti balavavātakkhandho.

‘Amissīkataṃ’ means made unmixed. For the defilements make the mind mixed with the object; due to their absence, it is called unmixed. ‘Bhusā vātavuṭṭhī’ means a great mass of wind.

Upādānakkhayassa cāti upayogatthe sāmivacanaṃ. Disvā āyatanuppādanti cakkhādiāyatanānaṃ uppādañca vayañca disvā. Cittaṃ vimuccatīti imāya vipassanāpaṭipattiyā phalasamāpattivasena cittaṃ vimuccati.

‘Upādānakkhayassa ca’: this is a word in the genitive case used in the sense of the object (accusative). ‘Disvā āyatanuppādaṃ’ means having seen the arising and passing away of the sense bases such as the eye. ‘Cittaṃ vimuccati’ means: through this practice of insight, the mind is liberated by way of the attainment of fruition.

Soṇakoḷivisakathādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Account of Soṇa Koḷivisa and Others is concluded.

Diguṇādiupāhanapaṭikkhepakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Prohibition of Double-Layered Footwear, and So On.

245. Sakaṭavāheti dvīhi sakaṭehi paricchinne vāhe. “Vāhe”ti bahuvacanassa hiraññavisesanattepi sāmaññāpekkhāya “hirañña”nti ekavacanaṃ kataṃ.

245. ‘Sakaṭavāhe’ means cart-loads measured by two carts. Although ‘vāhe’ is plural and a qualifier of ‘hirañña’ (gold), with regard to the general sense, the singular form ‘hiraññaṃ’ was used.

246. Addāriṭṭhakavaṇṇāti allāriṭṭhaphalavaṇṇā, tintakākapakkhavaṇṇātipi vadanti. Rajananti upalittaṃ nīlādivaṇṇaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tenāha “coḷakena puñchitvā”ti. Tañhi tathā puñchite vigacchati. Yaṃ pana cammassa duggandhāpanayanatthaṃ kāḷarattādirajanehi rañjitattā kāḷarattādivaṇṇaṃ hoti, taṃ coḷādīhi apanetuṃ na sakkā cammagatikameva, tasmā taṃ vaṭṭatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

246. ‘Addāriṭṭhakavaṇṇā’ means having the color of the allāriṭṭha fruit; some also say it is the color of a wet crow's wing. ‘Rajana’ is said with reference to a blue or other color smeared on top. Therefore, he said, ‘having wiped with a cloth.’ For that is removed when wiped in that way. But as for whatever black, red, or other color there is due to being dyed with black, red, or other dyes to remove the foul smell of the leather, that cannot be removed by a cloth or the like, as it has become one with the leather. Therefore, it should be understood that that is allowable.

Khallakanti sabbapaṇhipidhānacammaṃ, aparigaḷanatthaṃ paṇhiuparibhāge apidhāya āropanabandhanamattaṃ vaṭṭati. Vicitrāti saṇṭhānato vicitrapaṭā adhippetā, na vaṇṇato sabbaso apanetabbesu [V 2.0174] khallakādīsu paviṭṭhattā. Biḷālasadisamukhattā mahāulūkā “pakkhibiḷālā”ti vuccati, tesaṃ cammaṃ nāma pakkhalomameva.

‘Khallaka’ means leather that covers the entire heel; to prevent slipping, merely placing a cover on the upper part of the heel and fastening it is allowable. ‘Vicitrā’ (variegated) is intended to mean variegated by way of shape, not by way of color, because it is included among the khallaka, etc., which are to be entirely removed. Because of their cat-like faces, great owls are called ‘pakkhibiḷālā’ (winged cats); their so-called leather is just their wing-feathers.

Diguṇādiupāhanapaṭikkhepakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Prohibition of Double-Layered Footwear, and So On, is Concluded.

Ajjhārāmeupāhanapaṭikkhepakathādivaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Account on the Prohibition of Footwear Within the Monastery, and So On.

251. Uṇṇāhi [M 2.0184] katapādukāti ettha uṇṇāmayakambalehi katā pādukā saṅgayhanti.

251. In the phrase ‘uṇṇāhi katapādukā’, footwear made with woolen blankets is included.

253. Gaṅgāmahakīḷikāyāti gaṅgāmahe kīḷikāya. Tattha hi itthipurisā yānehi udakakīḷaṃ gacchanti. Pīṭhakasivikanti phalakādinā kataṃ pīṭhakayānaṃ. Paṭapotalikaṃ andolikā. Sabbampi yānaṃ upāhanenapi gantuṃ asamatthassa gilānassa anuññātaṃ.

253. ‘Gaṅgāmahakīḷikāya’ means by means of sport at the Ganges festival. Indeed, there, men and women go by vehicles for water-sport. ‘Pīṭhakasivika’ is a sedan-chair made with planks, and so on. ‘Paṭapotalika’ is a litter. All such vehicles are permitted for a sick monk who is unable to go even with footwear.

254. Vāḷarūpānīti āharimāni vāḷarūpāni. Caturaṅgulādhikānīti uddalomīekantalomīhi visesadassanaṃ. Caturaṅgulato hi ūnāni kira uddalomīādīsu pavisanti. Vānacitro uṇṇāmayattharaṇoti nānāvaṇṇehi uṇṇāmayasuttehi bhitticchedādivasena vāyitvā katacittattharaṇo. Ghanapupphakoti bahalarāgo. Pakatitūlikāti tūlapuṇṇā bhisi. Vikatikāti sīharūpādivasena vānacitrāva gayhati. Uddalomīti “ubhatodasaṃ uṇṇāmayattharaṇa”nti dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Koseyyakaṭṭissamayanti kosiyasuttānaṃ antarā suvaṇṇamayasuttāni pavesetvā vītaṃ. Suvaṇṇasuttaṃ kira “kaṭṭissaṃ, kasaṭa”nti ca vuccati. Teneva “koseyyakasaṭamaya”nti ācariya-dhammapālattherena vuttanti vadanti. Ratanaparisibbitanti suvaṇṇalittaṃ. Suddhakoseyyanti ratanaparisibbanarahitaṃ.

254. ‘Vāḷarūpāni’ means movable figures of wild beasts. ‘Caturaṅgulādhikāni’ shows the distinction from rugs with fleece on both sides or one side. Indeed, rugs with fleece shorter than four fingers are included among those with fleece on both sides, and so on. ‘Vānacitro uṇṇāmayattharaṇo’ means a colorful rug made by weaving with woolen threads of various colors in the manner of wall-piercings, and so on. ‘Ghanapupphako’ means a rug with thick floral patterns. ‘Pakatitūlikā’ refers to a cotton-filled mattress. ‘Vikatikā’ is taken as a rug decorated with figures of wild beasts, such as lion figures, and so on. ‘Uddalomī’ is stated in the Dīghanikāya commentary as ‘a woolen rug with a fringe on both sides.’ ‘Koseyyakaṭṭissamayaṃ’ refers to a rug woven by inserting golden threads between silk threads. A golden thread, it is said, is also called ‘kaṭṭissaṃ’ and ‘kasaṭa.’ Therefore, they say it is called ‘koseyyakasaṭamaya,’ as stated by the teacher, the Elder Dhammapāla. ‘Ratanaparisibbitaṃ’ means overlaid with gold. ‘Suddhakoseyyaṃ’ means pure silk without jewel-stitching.

Ajinamigacammānaṃ atisukhumattā dupaṭṭatipaṭṭāni katvā sibbantīti vuttaṃ “ajinappaveṇī”ti. Rattavitānenāti sabbarattena vitānena. Yaṃ pana nānāvaṇṇaṃ vānacittaṃ vā lepacittaṃ vā, taṃ vaṭṭati. Ubhatolohitakūpadhānepi eseva nayo. “Citraṃ vā”ti idaṃ pana sabbathā kappiyattā vuttaṃ, na pana ubhatoupadhānesu akappiyattā. Na hi lohitaka-saddo citte vattati, paṭaliggahaṇeneva cittakassapi attharaṇassa saṅgahetabbappasaṅgato, kāsāvaṃ pana lohitakavohāraṃ na gacchati. Tasmā vitānepi ubhatoupadhānepi vaṭṭati. Sace pamāṇayuttantiādi aññappamāṇātikkantassa bibbohanassa paṭikkhittabhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, na pana [V 2.0175] uccāsayanamahāsayanabhāvadassanatthaṃ tathā avuttattā. Taṃ pana upadhānaṃ uposathikānaṃ [M 2.0185] gahaṭṭhānaṃ vaṭṭati. Uccāsayanamahāsayanameva hi tadā tesaṃ na vaṭṭati. Dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathādīsu kiñcāpi “ṭhapetvā tūlikaṃ sabbāneva gonakādīni ratanaparisibbitāni vaṭṭantī”tiādi vuttaṃ, vinayaṭṭhakathāyeva kappiyākappiyabhāve pamāṇanti gahetabbaṃ.

Because the hides of black antelope are extremely fine, they are sewn by making them two-layered or three-layered; therefore, it is called 'ajinappaveṇī.' 'Rattavitānena' means with an entirely red canopy. But as for a canopy that is multicolored, decorated with figures of wild beasts, or decorated with paintings, that is allowable. For red pillows for both ends, this is the same method. This phrase 'citraṃ vā' is stated because it is allowable in every way, but not in reference to pillows for both ends, as they are not allowable when decorated. Indeed, the word 'lohitaka' (red) does not apply to 'citta' (decorated), for from the inclusion of 'paṭali' itself, it would follow that a decorated rug should also be included. A monastic robe, however, is not called 'red.' Therefore, it is allowable for a canopy and for pillows for both ends. The phrase 'sace pamāṇayuttaṃ', and so on, is stated to show the rejection of a pillow that exceeds the standard measure, not to show the state of being a high or great seat, as it was not stated for that purpose. But that pillow is allowable for lay supporters observing the Uposatha. Indeed, only a high or great seat is not allowable for them at that time. Although in the Dīghanikāya commentary and so on, it is said, 'Except for a cotton mattress, all rugs such as goṇaka, etc., that are not stitched with jewels are allowable,' and so on, it should be understood that the Vinaya commentary alone is the authority regarding what is allowable and not allowable.

Ajjhārāmeupāhanapaṭikkhepakathādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Account on the Prohibition of Footwear Within the Monastery, and So On, is Concluded.

Gihivikatānuññātādikathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Permission for Laypeople's Alterations, and So On.

256. Abhinissāyāti apassāya. Visukāyikavipphanditānanti paṭipakkhabhūtānaṃ diṭṭhicittavipphanditānanti attho.

256. 'Abhinissāya' means 'relying on'. 'Visukāyikavipphanditānaṃ' means 'of the agitations of view and mind which are antithetical'; this is the meaning.

257. Yatindriyanti manindriyavasena saññatindriyaṃ.

257. 'Yatindriyaṃ' means having restrained faculties by means of the mind-faculty.

258. Pāḷiyaṃ aṭṭhakavaggikānīti suttanipāte (su. ni. 772 ādayo) aṭṭhakavaggabhūtāni soḷasa suttāni. Evaṃ ciraṃ akāsīti evaṃ cirakālaṃ pabbajjaṃ anupagantvā agāramajjhe kena kāraṇena vāsamakāsīti attho. So kira majjhimavaye pabbajito, tena bhagavā evamāha. Etamatthaṃ viditvāti kāmesu diṭṭhādīnavā cirāyitvāpi gharāvāsena pakkhandantīti etamatthaṃ sabbākārato viditvā.

258. In the Pāḷi, 'Aṭṭhakavaggikāni' means the sixteen suttas that constitute the Aṭṭhakavagga in the Suttanipāta. 'Evaṃ ciraṃ akāsi' means: 'For what reason did he dwell for such a long time in the midst of the household life, without going forth into homelessness?' This is the meaning. Indeed, he went forth in middle age; therefore, the Blessed One spoke thus. 'Etamatthaṃ viditvā' means: having known in all aspects this fact that 'having seen the danger in sensual pleasures, even after a long time, he did not rush into the household life'.

Ādīnavaṃ loketi saṅkhāraloke aniccatādiādīnavaṃ. Nirupadhinti nibbānaṃ. “Ariyo na ramatī pāpe”ti imassa hetumāha “pāpe na ramatī sucī”ti. Tattha sucīti visuddhapuggalo.

'Ādīnavaṃ loke' refers to the danger, such as impermanence, in the conditioned world. 'Nirupadhiṃ' means Nibbāna. The reason for 'Ariyo na ramatī pāpe' is stated by 'pāpe na ramatī sucī'. Therein, 'sucī' means a pure person.

259. Kāḷasīhoti kāḷamukhavānarajāti. Cammaṃ na vaṭṭatīti nisīdanattharaṇaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭati, bhūmattharaṇādivasena senāsanaparibhogo vaṭṭateva.

259. 'Kāḷasīha' means a species of black-faced monkey. 'Cammaṃ na vaṭṭati' means it is not allowable to make a sitting-mat, but its use as a lodging requisite, such as a ground-spread, is indeed allowable.

Gihivikatānuññātādikathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Permission for Laypeople's Alterations, and So On, is Concluded.

Cammakkhandhakavaṇṇanānayo niṭṭhito.

The Method of Exposition on the Chapter on Leather is Concluded.

6. Bhesajjakkhandhako

6. The Chapter on Medicines

Pañcabhesajjādikathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Five Medicines, and So On.

260. Bhesajjakkhandhake [M 2.0186][V 2.0176] pittaṃ koṭṭhabbhantaragataṃ hotīti bahisarīre byāpetvā ṭhitaṃ abaddhapittaṃ koṭṭhabbhantaragataṃ hoti, tena pittaṃ kupitaṃ hotīti adhippāyo.

260. In the Bhesajjakkhandhaka, 'bile within the abdomen' means unbound bile which, having spread throughout the outer body, has entered the abdomen; the meaning is that the bile is thereby aggravated.

261-2. Pāḷiyaṃ nacchādentīti ruciṃ na uppādenti. Susukāti samudde ekā macchajāti, kumbhilātipi vadanti. Saṃsaṭṭhanti parissāvitaṃ.

In the Pāḷi, 'nacchādenti' means they do not arouse liking. 'Susukā' is a species of fish in the ocean; they also call it 'kumbhila'. 'Saṃsaṭṭhaṃ' means strained.

263. Piṭṭhehīti pisitehi. Kasāvehīti tacādīni udake tāpetvā gahitaūsarehi. Ubbhidanti ūsarapaṃsumayaṃ. Loṇabilanti loṇaviseso.

263. 'Piṭṭhehi' means 'with ground powders'. 'Kasāvehi' means 'with astringent juices obtained by boiling bark, etc., in water'. 'Ubbhidaṃ' means 'made of saline soil'. 'Loṇabilaṃ' is a particular kind of salt.

264-5. Chakaṇanti gomayaṃ. Pākatikacuṇṇanti apakkakasāvacuṇṇaṃ, gandhacuṇṇaṃ pana na vaṭṭati. Pāḷiyaṃ cuṇṇacālininti udukkhale koṭṭitacuṇṇaparissāvaniṃ. Suvaṇṇagerukoti suvaṇṇatutthādi. Pāḷiyaṃ añjanūpapisananti añjane upanetuṃ pisitabbabhesajjaṃ.

'Chakaṇaṃ' means cow dung. 'Pākatikacuṇṇaṃ' means unboiled astringent powder; however, fragrant powder is not allowable. In the Pāḷi, 'cuṇṇacāliniṃ' means a sieve for sifting powder pounded in a mortar. 'Suvaṇṇageruko' means golden ochre, etc. In the Pāḷi, 'añjanūpapisananti' means medicine to be ground to apply as eye-ointment.

267-9. Kabaḷikāti upanāhabhesajjaṃ. Gharadinnakābādho nāma gharaṇiyā dinnavasīkaraṇabhesajjasamuṭṭhitaābādho. Tāya chārikāya paggharitaṃ khārodakanti parissāvane tacchārikaṃ pakkhipitvā udake abhisiñcite tato chārikato heṭṭhā paggharitaṃ khārodakaṃ. Pāḷiyaṃ akaṭayūsenāti anabhisaṅkhatena muggayūsena. Kaṭākaṭenāti mugge pacitvā acāletvā parissāvitena muggayūsenāti vadanti.

'Kabaḷikā' means poultice medicine. 'Gharadinnakābādho' means an illness arising from a subduing-medicine given by a housewife. 'Alkaline water filtered through that ash' means alkaline water that has dripped down from that ash after water has been poured over it in a filter. In the Pāḷi, 'akaṭayūsena' means with unprepared mung bean soup. 'Kaṭākaṭena', they say, means with mung bean soup that has been strained after cooking the mung beans without stirring them.

Pañcabhesajjādikathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Five Medicines, and So On, is concluded.

Guḷādianujānanakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse Concerning the Allowance of Jaggery, and So On.

272-4. Guḷakaraṇanti [M 2.0187][V 2.0177] ucchusālaṃ. Avissatthāti sāsaṅkā.

'Guḷakaraṇaṃ' means a sugarcane shed. 'Avissatthā' means she is suspicious.

276. Appamattakepi vārentīti appamattake dinne dāyakānaṃ pīḷāti paṭikkhipanti. Paṭisaṅkhāpīti ettakenapi yāpetuṃ sakkā, “avasesaṃ aññesaṃ hotū”ti sallakkhetvāpi paṭikkhipanti.

276. 'Appamattakepi vārenti' means: when even a small amount is given, they refuse, thinking, "It is a burden to the donors." 'Paṭisaṅkhāpi' means: having reflected, "It is possible to maintain oneself even with this much; let the remainder be for other monks," they also refuse.

279. Vatthipīḷananti yathā vatthigatatelādi antosarīre ārohanti, evaṃ hatthena vatthimaddanaṃ. Sambādhe satthakammavatthikammānameva paṭikkhittattā dahanakammaṃ vaṭṭati eva.

279. 'Vatthipīḷanaṃ' means the pressing of the enema-bag with the hand in such a way that the oil, etc., contained in the enema-bag enters the inner body. Because only surgery and the application of an enema are prohibited in a confined place, cauterization is indeed allowable.

Guḷādianujānanakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse Concerning the Allowance of Jaggery, and So On, is concluded.

Yāgumadhugoḷakādikathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse Concerning Gruel, Honey Balls, and So On.

282-3. Pāḷiyaṃ dasassa ṭhānānīti assa paṭiggāhakassa dasa ṭhānāni kāraṇāni dhammenāti attho. Anuppavecchatīti deti. Vātañca byapanetīti sambandho, vātañca anulometīti attho. Saggā te āraddhāti tayā devalokā ārādhitā.

In the Pāḷi, 'dasassa ṭhānāni' means: for this recipient, there are ten grounds or reasons by nature; this is the meaning. 'Anuppavecchati' means 'it gives'. The connection is with 'And it dispels the wind'; the meaning is 'and it regulates the wind.' 'Saggā te āraddhā' means: the celestial world has been accomplished by you.

Yāgumadhugoḷakādikathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse Concerning Gruel, Honey Balls, and So On, is concluded.

Pāṭaligāmavatthukathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Pāṭaligāma Account

286. Pāṭaligāme nagaraṃ māpentīti pāṭaligāmassa samīpe tasseva gāmakhettabhūte mahante araññappadese pāṭaliputtaṃ nāma nagaraṃ māpenti. Yāvatā ariyaṃ āyatananti yattakaṃ ariyamanussānaṃ osaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ. Yāvatā vaṇippathoti yattakaṃ vāṇijānaṃ bhaṇḍavikkīṇanaṭṭhānaṃ, vasanaṭṭhānaṃ vā, idaṃ tesaṃ sabbesaṃ agganagaraṃ bhavissatīti attho. Puṭabhedananti sakaṭādīhi nānādesato āhaṭānaṃ bhaṇḍapuṭānaṃ vikkīṇanatthāya mocanaṭṭhānaṃ. Saranti taḷākādīsupi vattati[V 2.0178], tannivattanatthaṃ [M 2.0188] “saranti idha nadī adhippetā”ti vuttaṃ sarati sandatīti katvā. Vinā eva kullena tiṇṇāti idaṃ appamattakaudakampi aphusitvā vinā kullena pārappattā.

286. 'Pāṭaligāme nagaraṃ māpenti' means: they are constructing a city named Pāṭaliputta in a large forest area near the village of Pāṭaligāma, on what was its village land. 'Yāvatā ariyaṃ āyatanaṃ' means: whatever is the gathering place for noble people. 'Yāvatā vaṇippatho' means: whatever is the place for merchants to sell their goods or their place of residence; the meaning is that this will become the chief city among all of them. 'Puṭabhedanaṃ' means: the place for unfastening bundles of goods brought from various regions by carts, etc., for the purpose of selling. The word 'sara' also applies to lakes, etc.; to exclude that, it is said, 'Here, by “saranti,” a river is intended,' because it flows. 'Vinā eva kullena tiṇṇā' means: without even touching this small amount of water, they reached the far shore without a raft.

Pāṭaligāmavatthukathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Story of Pāṭaligāma is concluded.

Koṭigāmesaccakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Truths at Koṭigāma

287. Pāḷiyaṃ sandhāvitanti bhavato bhavaṃ paṭisandhiggahaṇavasena sandhāvanaṃ kataṃ. Saṃsaritanti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Mamañceva tumhākañcāti mayā ca tumhehi ca, sāmivaseneva vā mama ca tumhākañca sandhāvanaṃ ahosīti attho gahetabbo. Saṃsaritanti saṃsari. Bhavataṇhā eva bhavato bhavaṃ netīti bhavanettīti vuttā.

287. In the Pāḷi, 'sandhāvitaṃ' means: the running on from existence to existence by way of taking rebirth-linking has been done. 'Saṃsaritaṃ' is a synonym for that very term. 'Mamañceva tumhākañca' means: by me and by you; or alternatively, by way of the genitive relation, the meaning should be taken as 'my and your running on has occurred.' 'Saṃsaritaṃ' means wandering. Because craving for existence alone leads from existence to existence, it is called 'bhavanettī' (the leader to existence).

289. “Nīlā hontī”ti vuttamevatthaṃ vivarituṃ “nīlavaṇṇā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Nīlavaṇṇāti nīlavilepanā. Esa nayo sabbattha. Paṭivaṭṭesīti pahari. Ambakāyāti ambāya. Upacāravacanañhetaṃ, mātugāmenāti attho. Upasaṃharathāti upanetha, “īdisā tāvatiṃsā”ti parikappethāti attho. Idañca bhikkhūnaṃ saṃvegajananatthaṃ vuttaṃ, na nimittaggāhatthaṃ. Licchavirājāno hi sabbe na cirasseva ajātasattunā vināsaṃ pāpuṇissanti.

289. To explain the meaning already stated as 'They are blue,' the words 'of blue color,' etc., are said. 'Nīlavaṇṇā' means having blue unguents. This is the method in all cases. 'Paṭivaṭṭesi' means he struck. 'Ambakāya' means Ambā. This is indeed a figurative expression; the meaning is 'by the woman.' 'Upasaṃharatha' means bring them near; or the meaning is: reflect, 'The Tāvatiṃsa gods are of such a nature.' And this was said for the purpose of arousing spiritual urgency in the monks, not for the purpose of grasping the sign of beauty. For all the Licchavi kings will soon reach destruction on account of Ajātasattu.

Koṭigāmesaccakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Truths at Koṭigāma is concluded.

Sīhasenāpativatthuādikathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Story Beginning with General Sīha

290. Sandhāgāreti rājakiccassa sandhāraṇatthāya nicchiddaṃ katvā vicāraṇatthāya katamahāsabhāya. Gamikābhisaṅkhāroti gamane vāyāmo. Dhammassa ca anudhammanti tumhehi vuttassa kāraṇassa anukāraṇaṃ, tumhehi vuttassa atthassa anurūpamevāti adhippāyo. Sahadhammiko vādānuvādoti parehi vuttakāraṇena sakāraṇo hutvā tumhākaṃ vādo vā [M 2.0189] ito paraṃ tassa anuvādo vā. Koci appamattakopi gārayhaṃ ṭhānaṃ na āgacchatīti kiṃ tava vāde gārayhakāraṇaṃ natthīti vuttaṃ hoti.

290. Regarding `sandhāgāra`: in the great assembly made for the purpose of disseminating and for judging royal duties, having become free from bias. `Gamikābhisaṅkhāra` means the exertion in going. `The Dhamma and the corresponding Dhamma` means a reason that is in accordance with the reason stated by you; the intention is only the meaning that is suitable for the meaning stated by you. `A discussion and subsequent discussion in line with the Dhamma` means: being supported by reason in response to the reason stated by others, neither your view, nor any subsequent, corresponding view, however minor, arrives at a blameworthy state. This means it is said: 'In your view, there is no blameworthy reason.'

293. Anuviccakāranti anuviditākāraṃ. Ratanattayassa saraṇagamanādikiriyaṃ karoti. Sahasā [V 2.0179] katvā mā pacchā vippaṭisārī ahosīti attho. Paṭākaṃ parihareyyunti dhajapaṭākaṃ ukkhipitvā “īdiso amhākaṃ saraṇaṃ gato sāvako jāto”ti nagare ghosentā āhiṇḍanti.

293. Regarding `anuviccakāraṃ`: acting after having understood. The meaning is: do not, having hastily performed the act of going for refuge to the Triple Gem and so on, later be regretful. Regarding `paṭākaṃ parihareyyuṃ`: having raised a flag-banner, they wander through the city proclaiming, 'Such a person has become our disciple who has gone for refuge.'

294. Nimittakammassāti maṃsakhādananimittena uppannapāṇātipātakammassa.

294. Regarding `nimittakammassa`: of the kamma of destroying life that has arisen from the cause of eating meat.

Sīhasenāpativatthuādikathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Story of General Sīha and others is concluded.

Kappiyabhūmianujānanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Allowance of Suitable Ground

295. Anuppage evāti pātova. Oravasaddanti mahāsaddaṃ. Taṃ pana avatvāpīti pi-saddena tathāvacanampi anujānāti. Aṭṭhakathāsūti andhakaṭṭhakathāvirahitāsu sesaṭṭhakathāsu. Sādhāraṇalakkhaṇanti andhakaṭṭhakathāya saha sabbaṭṭhakathānaṃ samānaṃ.

295. `Anuppage eva` means early in the morning. `Oravasaddaṃ` means a great sound. In the phrase `taṃ pana avatvāpi`, by the particle `pi`, it also allows such a statement. `Aṭṭhakathāsu` means in the remaining commentaries, from which the Andhakaṭṭhakathā is excluded. `Sādhāraṇalakkhaṇaṃ` means a statement that is common to all commentaries together with the Andhakaṭṭhakathā.

Cayanti adhiṭṭhānauccavatthuṃ. Yato paṭṭhāyāti yato iṭṭhakādito paṭṭhāya, yaṃ ādiṃ katvā bhittiṃ uṭṭhāpetukāmāti attho. “Thambhā pana upari uggacchanti, tasmā vaṭṭantī”ti etena iṭṭhakapāsāṇā heṭṭhā patiṭṭhāpitāpi yadi cayato, bhūmito vā ekaṅgulamattampi uggatā tiṭṭhanti, vaṭṭantīti siddhaṃ hoti.

`Cayaṃ` means a high object which is a foundation. `Yato paṭṭhāya` means: from whichever brick, etc., one starts, making that the beginning, they desire to raise a wall. By the text, 'But pillars rise above, hence they are permissible,' this is established: even though bricks and stones are placed below, if they stand raised even a finger's breadth from the floor or from the ground, it is permissible.

Ārāmoti upacārasīmāparicchinno sakalo vihāro. Senāsanānīti vihārassa anto tiṇakuṭiādikāni saṅghassa nivāsagehāni. Vihāragonisādikā nāmāti senāsanagonisādikā. Senāsanāni hi sayaṃ parikkhittānipi ārāmaparikkhepābhāvena “gonisādikānī”ti vuttāni. “Upaḍḍhaparikkhittopī”ti iminā tato ūnaparikkhitto yebhuyyena aparikkhitto nāma, tasmā aparikkhittasaṅkhyameva gacchatīti dasseti. Etthāti upaḍḍhādiparikkhitte. Kappiyakuṭiṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭatīti gonisādiyā [M 2.0190] abhāvena sesakappiyakuṭīsu tīsu yā kāci kappiyakuṭi kātabbāti attho.

`Ārāma` means the entire monastery defined by its access boundary. `Senāsanāni` means residences of the Sangha inside the monastery, such as grass huts and so on. `Vihāragonisādikā nāma` is called `senāsanagonisādikā`. Indeed, lodgings, although they are themselves enclosed, are called `gonisādikāni` because of the absence of a monastery enclosure. By the phrase 'even if half-enclosed,' it is shown that a monastery with an enclosure less than that is generally called an unenclosed monastery; therefore, it falls into the category of unenclosed. `Ettha` means in a half-enclosed, etc., monastery. The meaning of 'it is permissible to obtain a suitable hut' is: due to the absence of a `gonisādī`, any one of the three remaining suitable huts should be made.

Tesaṃ gehānīti ettha bhikkhūnaṃ vāsatthāya katampi yāva na denti, tāva tesaṃ santakaṃyeva bhavissatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Vihāraṃ ṭhapetvāti upasampannānaṃ vāsatthāya katagehaṃ ṭhapetvāti attho. Gehanti nivāsagehaṃ, tadaññaṃ pana uposathāgārādi sabbaṃ anivāsagehaṃ catukappiyabhūmivimuttā pañcamī kappiyabhūmi. Saṅghasantakepi hi etādise gehe suṭṭhu parikkhittārāmattepi [V 2.0180] abbhokāse viya antovutthādidoso natthi. Yena kenaci channe, paricchanne ca sahaseyyappahonake bhikkhusaṅghassa nivāsagehe antovutthādidoso, na aññattha. Tenāha “yaṃ panā”tiādi. Tattha “saṅghikaṃ vā puggalikaṃ vā”ti idaṃ kiñcāpi bhikkhunīnaṃ sāmaññato vuttaṃ, bhikkhūnaṃ pana saṅghikaṃ puggalikañca bhikkhunīnaṃ, tāsaṃ saṅghikaṃ puggalikañca bhikkhūnaṃ gihisantakaṭṭhāne tiṭṭhatīti veditabbaṃ.

In the phrase `tesaṃ gehāni`: here, it should be understood that even if a dwelling is made for the residence of bhikkhus, as long as it is not given, it will remain the property of those lay supporters. `Vihāraṃ ṭhapetvā` means: setting aside a dwelling made for the residence of the fully ordained. `Gehaṃ` means a dwelling place; but any other non-dwelling place, such as an Uposatha hall and so on, is the fifth suitable ground, freed from the four suitable grounds. Indeed, in such a building belonging to the Sangha, even if it is in a well-enclosed monastery, there is no fault of `antovuttha` and so on, just as in an open space. The fault of `antovuttha` and so on occurs in a dwelling place of the community of bhikkhus that is roofed by anything whatsoever, enclosed, and sufficient for sleeping together; it does not occur elsewhere. Therefore, he said, 'But whatever...,' and so on. Therein, regarding the words 'belonging to the Sangha or to an individual,' although this is stated generally for bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs, it should be known that what is communal or personal to the bhikkhus stands in the place of lay property for the bhikkhunīs, and what is communal or personal to them stands in the place of lay property for the bhikkhus.

Mukhasannidhīti antosannihitadoso hi mukhappavesananimittaṃ āpattiṃ karoti, nāññathā. Tasmā “mukhasannidhī”ti vutto.

In the word `mukhasannidhi`: because the fault of `antosannihita` causes an offense on account of putting it into the mouth, and not otherwise, it is therefore called `mukhasannidhi` (proximity to the mouth).

Tattha tattha khaṇḍā hontīti upaḍḍhato adhikaṃ khaṇḍā honti. Sabbasmiṃ chadane vinaṭṭheti tiṇapaṇṇādivassaparittāyake chadane vinaṭṭhe. Gopānasīnaṃ pana upari vallīhi baddhadaṇḍesu ṭhitesupi jahitavatthukā honti eva. Pakkhapāsakamaṇḍalanti ekasmiṃ passe tiṇṇaṃ gopānasīnaṃ upari ṭhitatiṇapaṇṇādicchadanaṃ vuccati.

`Tattha tattha khaṇḍā honti` means more than half are broken. `Sabbasmiṃ chadane vinaṭṭhe` means when the roofing of grass, leaves, and so on, which protects from rain, is destroyed. Even if the poles tied with vines remain above the rafters, they are indeed considered abandoned items. `Pakkhapāsakamaṇḍalaṃ` refers to the roofing of grass, leaves, and so on, situated above three rafters on one side.

Anupasampannassa dātabbo assātiādinā akappiyakuṭiyaṃ vutthampi anupasampannassa dinne kappiyaṃ hoti, sāpekkhadānañcettha vaṭṭati, paṭiggahaṇaṃ viya na hotīti dasseti.

By the text beginning with, 'It should be given to one not fully ordained,' it is shown that even if something is stored in an unsuitable hut, when it is given to an unordained person, it becomes allowable. And here, giving with expectation is also permissible; it is not like receiving an offering.

299. Pāḷiyaṃ kantāre sambhāvesīti appabhakkhakantāre sampāpuṇi.

299. In the Pāḷi text, `kantāre sambhāvesi` means: he reached a wilderness where food was scarce.

Kappiyabhūmianujānanakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the discourse on the allowance of suitable ground is concluded.

Keṇiyajaṭilavatthukathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Story of Keṇiya the Matted-Hair Ascetic

300. Jaṭiloti [M 2.0191] āharimajaṭādharo tāpasavesadhārako yaññayutto lokapūjito brāhmaṇo. Pavattāro pāvacanavasena vattāro. Yesaṃ santakamidaṃ, yehi vā idaṃ gītanti attho. Gītaṃ pavuttaṃ samihitanti aññamaññassa pariyāyavacanaṃ vuttanti attho. Tadanugāyantīti taṃ tehi pubbe gītaṃ anugāyanti. Evaṃ sesesu ca.

300. As for `jaṭilo`: it refers to a brahmin who wears movable matted hair, assumes the guise of an ascetic, is engaged in sacrifices, and is honored by the world. `Pavattāro` means they are speakers by way of the established word. This collection of Vedic texts is the property of those teachers, or alternatively, this collection of Vedic texts was sung by them; this is the meaning. The terms `gītaṃ`, `pavuttaṃ`, and `samihitaṃ` are said to be synonyms for one another; this is the meaning. As for `tadanugāyanti`: they sing in imitation of that Veda which was previously sung by those teachers. So too in the remaining cases.

Yāvakālikapakkānanti pakke sandhāya vuttaṃ, āmāni pana anupasampannehi sītudake madditvā parissāvetvā dinnapānaṃ pacchābhattampi kappati eva. Ayañca attho mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ sarūpato [V 2.0181] avuttoti āha “kurundiyaṃ panā”tiādi. “Ucchuraso nikasaṭo”ti idaṃ pātabbasāmaññena yāmakālikakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ pana sattāhakālikamevāti gahetabbaṃ. Ime cattāro rasāti phalapattapupphaucchurasā cattāro.

The phrase `yāvakālikapakkānaṃ` is said in reference to cooked items; however, a drink made from unripe things, given by those not fully ordained after crushing it in cold water and straining it, is indeed allowable even after midday. And because this meaning is not stated in its essence in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, he said the words beginning with 'But in the Kurundī...'. The phrase `ucchuraso nikasaṭo` is said in the discussion of `yāmakālika` items due to the general similarity of being drinkable, but that sugarcane juice should be understood as being only a `sattāhakālika` item. As for 'these four juices': they are the four juices of fruit, leaf, flower, and sugarcane.

Pāḷiyaṃ aggihuttamukhāti aggijuhanapubbakā. Chandasoti vedassa. Sāvittī mukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ sajjhāyitabbāti attho. Tapatanti vijotantānaṃ.

In the Pāḷi, `aggihuttamukhā` means they have the fire-offering as their forerunner. `Chandaso` means of the Veda. The meaning is that the Sāvitrī is the foremost and is to be recited first. `Tapataṃ` means among those that are shining.

Keṇiyajaṭilavatthukathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the story of Keṇiya the Matted-Hair Ascetic is concluded.

Rojamallādivatthukathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Story of Rojamalla and Others

301. Bahukato buddhe vāti buddhe katabahumānoti attho. So kho ahaṃ, bhante ānanda, ñātīnaṃ daṇḍabhayatajjito ahosinti seso. Evañhi sati “evāha”nti puna ahaṃ-gahaṇaṃ yujjati. Vivarīti “vivaratū”ti cintāmattena vivari, na uṭṭhāya hatthena.

301. As for `bahukato buddhe vā`: the meaning is `buddhe katabahumāno`, one who has great esteem for the Buddha. The remainder of the text is: 'I, Venerable Ānanda, was terrified by the fear of punishment from my relatives.' Indeed, this being the case, the taking up of `ahaṃ` again as `evāhaṃ` is fitting. As for `vivari`: it opened merely with the thought, 'Let it open!'; he did not open it by getting up and using his hand.

303. Aññataroti subhaddo vuḍḍhapabbajito. Dve dārakāti sāmaṇerabhūmiyaṃ ṭhitā dve puttā. Nāḷiyāvāpakenāti nāḷiyā ceva thavikāya ca. Saṃharatha imehi bhājanehi taṇḍulādīni saṅkaḍḍhathāti attho. Bhusāgāreti palālamaye agāre, palālapuñjaṃ abbhantarato palālaṃ saṅkaḍḍhitvā agāraṃ kataṃ hoti, tatthāti attho.

303. As for `aññataro`: it refers to Subhadda, an elder who had gone forth. As for `dve dārakā`: it means two sons who were in the state of being novices. As for `nāḷiyāvāpakena`: it means with a tube and with a bag. The meaning is: 'Gather! With these vessels, collect rice and so on.' As for `bhusāgāre`: the meaning is, in a straw house.

Rojamallādivatthukathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Story of Rojamalla and Others is concluded.

Catumahāpadesakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Four Great Authorities

305. Parimaddantāti [M 2.0192] upaparikkhantā. Dve paṭā desanāmeneva vuttāti tesaṃ sarūpadassanapadametaṃ. Nāññanivattanapadaṃ pattuṇṇapaṭassāpi desanāmena vuttattā.

305. `Parimaddantā` means examining. The phrase 'the two cloths are spoken of only by the name of a region' is a term showing their nature. It is not a term of exclusion, because the `pattuṇṇa` cloth is also spoken of by the name of a region.

Tumbāti bhājanāni. Phalatumbo nāma lābuādi. Udakatumbo udakaghaṭo. Kilañjacchattanti veḷuvilīvehi vāyitvā katachattaṃ. Sambhinnarasanti missībhūtarasaṃ.

`Tumbā` means vessels. `Phalatumbo` is a gourd, etc. `Udakatumbo` is a water pot. `Kilañjacchattanti` is an umbrella made by weaving bamboo strips. `Sambhinnarasaṃ` means having a mixed flavor.

Catumahāpadesakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Four Great Authorities is concluded.

Bhesajjakkhandhakavaṇṇanānayo niṭṭhito.

The method for the explanation of the Chapter on Medicines is concluded.

7. Kathinakkhandhako

7. The Chapter on the Kathina

Kathinānujānanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Allowance of the Kathina

306. Kathinakkhandhake [M 2.0193][V 2.0182] sīsavasenāti padhānavasena. Kathinanti pañcānisaṃse antokaraṇasamatthatāya thiranti attho. So nesaṃ bhavissatīti yujjatīti “so tumhāka”nti avatvā “nesa”nti vacanaṃ yujjati. Ye atthatakathināti na kevalaṃ tumhākameva, ye aññepi atthatakathinā, tesaṃ bhavissatīti attho. Atha vā voti tadā sammukhībhūtehi saddhiṃ asammukhībhūte ca anāgate ca bhikkhū sabbe ekato sampiṇḍetvā vuttaṃ, tumhākanti attho. So nesanti ettha so tesanti yojetabbaṃ. Tenāha “atthatakathinānaṃ vo, bhikkhave, imāni pañca kappissantī”ti. Matakacīvaranti matassa cīvaraṃ. “Vutthavassavasenā”ti idaṃ pacchimavassaṃvutthānampi sādhāraṇanti āha “purimikāya vassaṃ upagantvā paṭhamapavāraṇāya pavāritā labhantī”ti. Upagatā vā na labhantīti pacchimikāya vutthavassepi sandhāya vuttaṃ.

306. In the Kathina Chapter, `sīsavasena` means by way of what is principal. `Kathina` means firm, in the sense of being able to include the five benefits; this is the meaning. Regarding `so nesaṃ bhavissati` (it will be for them), its fittingness means that instead of saying `so tumhākaṃ` (it will be for you), the word `nesaṃ` is fitting. `Ye atthatakathinā` means not only for you, but for any other monks for whom the Kathina has been spread, it will be for them; this is the meaning. Alternatively, `vo` is said having gathered together all monks—those present along with those not present and future monks; the meaning is 'for you'. In `so nesaṃ`, it should be connected as `so tesaṃ`. Therefore, He said: 'For you, O monks, for whom the Kathina has been spread, these five will be allowable.' `Matakacīvaraṃ` means the robe of one who has died. This phrase `vutthavassavasena` is also common to those who have completed the later rains-residence; therefore, it is said: 'Having entered the rains-residence during the earlier period and having performed the Pavāraṇā at the first Pavāraṇā, they receive it.' The phrase `upagatā vā na labhanti` is said with reference to those who have completed the rains-residence in the later period.

Khalimakkhitasāṭakoti ahatavatthaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. “Akātuṃ na labbhatī”ti iminā anādariye sati dukkaṭanti dīpeti.

The phrase `khalimakkhitasāṭako` is said with reference to an unwashed cloth. By the phrase `akātuṃ na labbhati` (it is not permissible not to do), it shows that if there is disrespect, a `dukkaṭa` offense is incurred.

“Apaloketvā”ti idaṃ aññesaṃ vassaṃvutthabhikkhūnaṃ adatvā dātukāmehi kattabbavidhidassanaṃ. Yadi evaṃ kammavācāya eva dānaṃ avuttanti āha “kammavācā panā”tiādi. Kathinacīvaraṃ viya kammavācāya dātuṃ na vaṭṭatīti apaloketvāva dātabbanti adhippāyo.

This word `apaloketvā` (after informing) shows the procedure to be followed by those who wish to give without having given to the other monks who have completed the rains-residence. If this is so, it is said, `kammavācā panā` and so on, because the giving by means of a formal act was not mentioned. The intention is that, just as with the Kathina robe, it is not proper to give by means of a formal act; it should be given only after informing.

308. Mahābhūmikanti mahāvisayaṃ, catuvīsatiākāravantatāya mahāvitthārikanti vuttaṃ hoti. Pañcakanti pañcakhaṇḍaṃ. Eseva nayo sesesupi. Paṭhamacimilikāti kathinavatthato aññā [V 2.0183] attano pakaticimilikā. Kucchicimilikaṃ katvā sibbitamattenāti thirajiṇṇānaṃ cimilikānaṃ ekato katvā sibbanassetaṃ adhivacananti vadanti. Mahāpaccariyaṃ, kurundiyañca vuttavacananti dassanaṃ, byañjanato eva bhedo, na atthatoti dassanatthaṃ katantipi vadanti. Piṭṭhianuvātāropanamattenāti dīghato anuvātassa āropanamattena. Kucchianuvātāropanamattenāti puthulato anuvātassa āropanamattena. Rattinissaggiyenāti rattiatikkantena.

308. `Mahābhūmikaṃ` means having a great scope; it is said to be very extensive because it possesses twenty-four aspects. `Pañcakaṃ` means five-sectioned. This same method applies to the rest. `Paṭhamacimilikā` is one's own normal lining, other than the Kathina cloth. Regarding `kucchicimilikaṃ katvā sibbitamattena`, they say this is a term for sewing together firm, old linings. It is a presentation of what is said in the Mahāpaccarī and Kurundī commentaries; it is done to show that the difference is only in the expression, not in the meaning, so they say. `Piṭṭhianuvātāropanamattena` means by merely applying the border lengthwise. `Kucchianuvātāropanamattena` means by merely applying the border widthwise. `Rattinissaggiyena` means by the night having passed.

309. Hatavatthakasāṭakenāti [M 2.0194] atijiṇṇasāṭako. Na hi tenātiādīsu tena parivārāgatapāṭhena idha ānetvā avuccamānena kathinatthārakassa jānitabbesu na kiñci parihāyati, tassa sabbassa idheva vuttattāti adhippāyo.

309. `Hatavatthakasāṭakena` means a very old cloth. In texts such as `na hi tena`, by that text which comes in the Parivāra, even though it is not brought here and stated, nothing is diminished among the factors to be known by the one who spreads the Kathina, because all of that has been stated right here. This is the intention.

310. Mātā viyāti mātikā, ivatthe ka-paccayo daṭṭhabbo. Tena siddhamatthaṃ dassento āha “mātikāti mātaro”tiādi. Assāti etissā mātikāya. Pakkamanantiko kathinubbhāro eva hi sayaṃ attano uppajjatīti evamabhedūpacārena “mātikā”ti vutto ubbhārasseva pakkamanante samuppattito, tabbinimuttāya ca mātikāya abhāvā, tappakāsikāpi cettha pāḷi “mātikā”ti vattuṃ yujjati. Sāpi hi pakkamanantikubbhārappakāsanena “pakkamanantikā”ti vuttā. Eseva nayo sesubbhāresupi. Pakkamananti cettha upacārasīmātikkamanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

310. `Mātikā` is like a mother (`mātā`); the suffix `ka` should be understood in the sense of `iva` (like). Showing the meaning established by that, he said, `mātikāti mātaro`, and so on. `Assā` means 'of this `mātikā`'. Indeed, the withdrawal of the Kathina, which has departure as its end, itself arises as its own `mātikā`; thus, it is called `mātikā` by way of metaphorical identification. This is because of its arising at the end of the departure of the withdrawal itself, and because of the absence of a `mātikā` separate from that. Furthermore, here it is fitting to call the Pāḷi text that explains it `mātikā`. For that too is called `pakkamanantikā` because it explains the withdrawal that has departure as its end. This same method applies to the other withdrawals as well. And here, `pakkamana` should be understood as the crossing of the boundary of the environs.

Kathinānujānanakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Allowance of the Kathina is concluded.

Ādāyasattakakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Heptad concerning Taking

311. “Na puna āgamissa”nti idaṃ āvāsapalibodhupacchedakāraṇadassanaṃ. Pañcasu hi cīvaramāsesu yadā kadāci na paccessanti cittena upacārasīmātikkamena āvāsapalibodho chijjati. Paccessanti bahiupacāragatassa pana yattha katthaci na paccessanti citte uppannamatte chijjati. Paṭhamaṃ cīvarapalibodho chijjatīti na paccessanti pakkamanato puretarameva cīvarassa niṭṭhitattā vuttaṃ. “Katacīvaramādāyā”ti hi vuttaṃ. Atthatakathinassa hi bhikkhuno yāva “saṅghato vā dāyakakulādito vā cīvaraṃ labhissāmī”ti cīvarāsā vā laddhavatthānaṃ sahāyasampadādiyogaṃ labhitvā saṅghāṭiādibhāvena “chinditvā karissāmī”ti karaṇicchā vā pavattati, tāva cīvarapalibodho anupacchinno eva. Yadā pana yathāpatthitaṭṭhānato cīvarādīnaṃ sabbathā [V 2.0184] alābhena vā cīvarāsā ceva laddhānaṃ katvā niṭṭhānena vā naṭṭhavinaṭṭhādibhāvena vā cīvare nirapekkhatāya vā karaṇicchā ca vigacchati, tadā cīvarapalibodho upacchinno hoti.

311. The phrase 'I will not return again' indicates the reason for the cutting off of the impediment of the residence. Indeed, during the five robe-months, whenever, with the thought 'I will not return,' one crosses the vicinity-boundary, the impediment of the residence is cut off. But for one who has gone outside the vicinity, it is cut off in any place whatsoever as soon as the thought 'I will not return' arises. The statement 'Firstly, the robe-impediment is cut off' is said because the robe was already finished even before the departure with the thought 'I will not return.' For it is said, 'having taken the made robe.' Indeed, for a bhikkhu for whom the kathina has been spread, as long as either the hope for a robe persists—thinking, 'I will obtain a robe from the Saṅgha or from a donor's family, etc.'—or, having obtained the cloth and having secured the assistance of companions and so on, the desire to make it persists—thinking, 'Having cut it, I will make it' into a double-layered robe, etc.—for that long, the robe-impediment is indeed not cut off. But when, either due to not obtaining robes, etc., at all from a desired place, or due to having finished making the obtained robes, or due to their being lost, destroyed, etc., or due to a lack of concern for the robe, both the hope for a robe and the desire to make it cease, then the robe-impediment is cut off.

So [M 2.0195] ca idha “katacīvaraṃ ādāyā”ti vacanena pakāsito. Evaṃ upari sabbattha pāḷivacanakkamaṃ nissāya nesaṃ paṭhamaṃ, pacchā ca upacchijjanaṃ vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sabbathāpi ca imesaṃ ubhinnaṃ palibodhānaṃ upacchedeneva kathinubbhāro, na ekassa. Tesañca pubbāpariyena, ekakkhaṇe ca upacchijjanaṃ dassetuṃ imā aṭṭha mātikā ṭhapitāti veditabbā. Antosīmāyanti cīvaraniṭṭhānakkhaṇeyeva chinnattā vuttaṃ. Nevimaṃ cīvaraṃ kāressanti cīvare apekkhāya vigatattā karaṇapalibodhassāpi upacchinnataṃ dasseti. Yo pana appicchatāya vā anatthikatāya vā sabbathā cīvaraṃ na sampaṭicchati, tassa bahisīmāgatassa sabbathāpi cīvarapalibodhābhāvena na paccessanti sanniṭṭhānamattena sanniṭṭhānantiko kathinubbhāro veditabbo. So panāti palibodhupacchedo. Ayaṃ panāti āsāvacchedako kathinubbhāro visuṃ vitthāretvā vutto, idha na vuttoti sambandho.

And that [cutting off of the robe-impediment] is shown here by the words, 'having taken the completed robe.' Thus, it should be understood that above, in all instances, relying on the sequence of the Pāḷi words, the cutting off of these two impediments, both first and after, is stated. And in every way, the withdrawal of the kathina occurs only by the cutting off of both these impediments, not of one. And it should be known that these eight mātikās are established to show the cutting off of those impediments both sequentially—before and after—and at a single moment. The phrase 'within the boundary' is stated because it is cut off at the very moment of the robe's completion. It also shows that the impediment of making is cut off because the expectation regarding the robe, 'They will not make this robe for me,' has departed. But as for a bhikkhu who, due to having few wishes or not having a use for it, does not accept a robe at all, for him, having gone outside the boundary, due to the absence of the robe-impediment in every way, the withdrawal of the kathina that is concluded by determination should be known merely by the determination, 'I will not return.' 'So pana' refers to the cutting off of the impediment. 'Ayaṃ pana' refers to the withdrawal of the kathina by the cutting off of hope, which was explained in detail separately; it is not stated here—this is the connection.

Anāsāya labhatīti “yasmiṃ kule cīvaraṃ labhissāmā”ti āsā anuppannapubbā, tattha cīvarāsāya anuppannaṭṭhāne yattha katthaci labhatīti attho. Āsāya na labhatīti āsīsitaṭṭhāne na labhatīti attho. Idha na vuttoti idha savanantikānantare na vutto. Tatthāti tasmiṃ sīmātikkantike. Sīmātikkantiko nāma cīvaramāsānaṃ pariyantadivasasaṅkhātāya sīmāya atikkamanato sañjāto. Keci “bahisīmāya kālātikkamo sīmātikkamo”ti maññanti, tesaṃ antoupacāre cīvarakālātikkamepi kathinubbhāro asammato nāma siyāti na cetaṃ yuttaṃ. Tasmā yattha katthaci kālātikkamo sīmātikkamoti veditabbo. Ettha ca pāḷiyaṃ “katacīvaro”ti idaṃ upalakkhaṇamattaṃ, akatacīvarassapi kālātikkamena sīmātikkantiko hoti, dve ca palibodhā ekato chijjanti. Evaṃ aññatthāpi yathāsambhavaṃ taṃtaṃ visesanābhāvepi kathinubbhāratā, palibodhupacchedappakāro ca veditabbo. “Sahubbhāre dvepi palibodhā apubbaṃ acarimaṃ chijjantī”ti idaṃ akatacīvarassa paccessanti adhiṭṭhānasambhavapakkhaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, tesu aññatarābhāvepi sahubbhārova hoti.

'One obtains without hope' means: one obtains a robe in any place whatsoever where the hope, 'In which family will we obtain a robe?,' has not arisen before; this is the meaning. 'One does not obtain with hope' means: one does not obtain it in the place that was hoped for; this is the meaning. 'Is not stated here' means: it is not taught here after the 'conclusion by hearing.' 'Tatta' means: in that 'transgression of the boundary.' 'Sīmātikkantika' (transgression of the boundary) is so called because it arises from transgressing the boundary which is designated as the last day of the robe-months. Some think, 'The transgression of time outside the boundary is "sīmātikkama".' In their view, the transgression of the robe-period within the vicinity would not be considered a withdrawal of the kathina. This is not correct. Therefore, the transgression of time in any place whatsoever should be known as 'sīmātikkama.' And here in the Pāḷi, the phrase 'one who has a completed robe' is merely an illustration. Even for a bhikkhu who does not have a completed robe, the 'transgression of the boundary' occurs through the transgression of time, and the two impediments are cut off together. Thus, in other cases as well, as is possible, even in the absence of this or that specific condition, the state of kathina withdrawal and the manner of the cutting off of the impediment should be known. The statement, 'In a simultaneous withdrawal, both impediments are cut off not one before and not one after,' is said with reference to the possibility of a determination to return for a bhikkhu who does not have a completed robe. Even in the absence of one of those two impediments, it is still a simultaneous withdrawal.

312-325. Samādāyavāro ādāyavārasadisova. Upasaggamevettha viseso. Tenāha “puna samādāyavārepi…pe… teyeva dassitā”ti[M 2.0196]. Vippakatacīvare pakkamanantikassa abhāvato “yathāsambhava”nti vuttaṃ. Teneva vippakatacīvaravāre chaḷeva ubbhārā vuttā, cīvare hatthagate [V 2.0185] ca āsāvacchedikassa asambhavā, so etesu vāresu yattha katthaci na vutto, visuññeva vutto. Vippakatavāre cettha ādāyavārasamādāyavāravasena dve chakkavārā vuttā.

312-325. The section on 'taking up' is just like the section on 'taking.' The difference here is only the prefix. Therefore, it says, 'Again, in the section on "taking up"... etc.... those very same are shown.' In the case of an unfinished robe, because a 'conclusion by departure' is not possible, it is said, 'as is possible.' For that very reason, in the section on the unfinished robe, only six withdrawals are stated. And when the robe is in hand, the 'cutting off of hope' is not possible; therefore, it is not taught in any of these sections whatsoever, but is taught separately. Here, in the section on the unfinished robe, two sets of six are taught by way of the section on 'taking' and the section on 'taking up.'

Tato paraṃ niṭṭhānasanniṭṭhānanāsanantikānaṃ vasena tīṇi tikāni dassitāni. Tattha tatiyattike anadhiṭṭhitenāti “paccessaṃ, na paccessa”nti evaṃ anadhiṭṭhitena, na evaṃ manasikatvāti attho. Tatiyattikato pana paraṃ ekaṃ chakkaṃ dassitaṃ. Evaṃ tīṇi tikāni, ekaṃ chakkañcāti paṭhamaṃ pannarasakaṃ vuttaṃ, iminā nayena dutiyapannarasakādīni veditabbāni.

After that, three triads are shown by way of the 'conclusion by finishing,' 'conclusion by determination,' and 'conclusion by loss.' There, in the third triad, 'by the undetermined' means by not determining thus, 'I will return, I will not return'; meaning, not having paid attention in this way. But after the third triad, one hexad is shown. Thus, three triads and one hexad—in this way the first group of fifteen is stated. By this method, the second group of fifteen, etc., should be known.

Pāḷiyaṃ āsādvādasake bahisīmāgatassa kathinuddhāresu tesampi cīvarāsādivasena cīvarapalibodho yāva cīvaraniṭṭhānā tiṭṭhatīti āha “so bahisīmāgato suṇāti ‘ubbhataṃ kira tasmiṃ āvāse kathinanti…pe… savanantiko kathinuddhāro’”ti. Ettha ca savanakkhaṇe āvāsapalibodho paṭhamaṃ chijjati, niṭṭhite cīvarapalibodhoti veditabbo.

In the Pāḷi, in the Dodecàd on Hope, regarding the withdrawals of the kathina for one who has gone outside the boundary, it says that for them too, by way of hope for a robe and so on, the robe-impediment remains until the finishing of the robe. Therefore, it is said: 'That one who has gone outside the boundary hears, "Indeed, the kathina in that residence has been withdrawn"... etc.... the withdrawal of the kathina is concluded by hearing.' And here, at the moment of hearing, the impediment of the residence is cut off first. It should be known that when the robe is finished, the robe-impediment is cut off.

Disaṃgamikanavake disaṃgamiko pakkamatīti na paccessanti pakkamati, iminā āvāsapalibodhābhāvo dassito hoti. Teneva vassaṃvutthāvāse puna gantvā cīvaraniṭṭhāpitamatte niṭṭhānantiko kathinuddhāro vutto. “Cīvarapaṭivisaṃ apavilāyamāno”ti iminā cīvarapalibodhasamaṅgikattamassa dasseti, apavilāyamānoti ākaṅkhamāno. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

In the Nonad on One Going to Another Region, 'a bhikkhu going to another region departs' means he departs thinking, 'I will not return.' By this, the absence of the impediment of the residence is shown. For that very reason, it is stated that when one who has spent the rains in a residence goes there again, the withdrawal of the kathina concluded by completion occurs merely upon the completion of the robe. By the phrase, 'not giving up his share of the robes,' it shows his state of being endowed with the impediment of the robe. 'Not giving up' means desiring. The rest is indeed easy to understand.

Ādāyasattakakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Discourse of the Heptad on Taking is finished.

Kathinakkhandhakavaṇṇanānayo niṭṭhito.

The method of commentary on the Kathina Chapter is finished.

8. Cīvarakkhandhako

8. The Robe Chapter

Jīvakavatthukathādivaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse concerning the Story of Jīvaka and so on.

329. Cīvarakkhandhake [M 2.0197][V 2.0186] kammavipākanti kammapaccayautucittāhārasamuṭṭhitaṃ appaṭibāhiyarogaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ kammajassa rogassa abhāvā.

329. In the Robe Chapter, the word 'kammavipāka' is stated with reference to an irresistible disease arisen from temperature, mind, and nutriment that are conditioned by kamma, because of the absence of a disease born directly of kamma.

330. Pāḷiyaṃ saṃyamassāti saṅgahaṇassa. Avisajjanassāti attho “yo saṃyamo so vināso”tiādīsu (pe. va. 237) viya. Etassa saṃyamassa phalaṃ upajānāmāti yojanā. Tameva phalaṃ dassentī āha “varametaṃ…pe… āsitta”nti. Keci pana “saṃyamassāti ānisaṃsassa, upayogatthe cetaṃ sāmivacana”nti (sārattha. ṭī. mahāvagga 3.329-330) atthaṃ vadanti.

330. In the Pāḷi, 'saṃyamassa' means 'of taking,' 'of not abandoning'; this is the meaning. It is like in such texts as, 'That which is restraint is destruction.' The construction is: 'We know the fruit of this restraint.' Wishing to show that very fruit, she said, 'This is excellent... poured.' Some, however, state the meaning thus: 'Saṃyamassa means "the benefit," and this is a genitive word in the sense of the accusative, for the purpose of application.'

336. Ussannadosoti sañjātapittādidoso. Sabbatthāti sakalasarīre.

336. 'Ussannadoso' means having an affliction of excessive bile and so on that has arisen. 'Sabbattha' means in the entire body.

337. Mahāpiṭṭhiyakojavanti hatthipiṭṭhiyaṃ attharitabbatāya “mahāpiṭṭhiya”nti laddhasamaññaṃ uṇṇāmayattharaṇaṃ.

337. 'Mahāpiṭṭhiyakojavan' is a woolen spread that has received the name 'mahāpiṭṭhiya' because it is fit to be spread on an elephant's back.

338-9. Upaḍḍhakāsinaṃ khamamānanti aḍḍhakāsiagghanakaṃ. Pāḷiyaṃ kiṃ nu khoti katamaṃ nu kho.

Upaḍḍhakāsinaṃ khamamānaṃ means worth half a kāsi. In the Pāḷi, kiṃ nu kho means which indeed?

340-342. Upacāreti susānassa āsanne padese. Chaḍḍetvā gatāti kiñci avatvā eva chaḍḍetvā gatā, etena “bhikkhū gaṇhantū”ti chaḍḍite eva akāmā bhāgadānaṃ vihitaṃ, kevalaṃ chaḍḍite pana katikāya asati ekato bahūsu paviṭṭhesu yena gahitaṃ, tena akāmabhāgo na [V 2.0187] dātabboti dasseti. Samānā disā puratthimādibhedā etesanti sadisāti āha “ekadisāya vā okkamiṃsū”ti. Dhuravihāraṭṭhāneti vihārassa sammukhaṭṭhāne.

Upacāre means in a place near the charnel ground. Chaḍḍetvā gatā means they went away having discarded it without saying anything. By this it is shown that only when it is discarded with the thought, “Let the bhikkhus take it,” is the giving of a share against one’s will prescribed. But when it is merely discarded, there being no agreement, among many who have entered together, it is shown that a share is not to be given against his will by the one who took it. To show that they are sadisā because they have similar directions, distinguished as east and so on (samānā disā puratthimādibhedā etesanti), it was said, “or they approached from one direction.” Dhuravihāraṭṭhāne means in the place in front of the monastery.

Jīvakavatthukathādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the discourse on the story of Jīvaka, and so on, is finished.

Bhaṇḍāgārasammutiādikathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Authorization of a Storeroom and so on

343. Vihāramajjheti [M 2.0198] sabbesaṃ jānanatthāya vuttaṃ. Vaṇṇāvaṇṇaṃ katvāti paṭivīsappahonakatājānanatthaṃ haliddiyādīhi khuddakamahantavaṇṇehi yutte same koṭṭhāse katvā. Tenāha “same paṭivīse ṭhapetvā”ti. Idanti sāmaṇerānaṃ upaḍḍhapaṭivīsadānaṃ. Phātikammanti pahonakakammaṃ. Yattakena vinayāgatena sammuñjanībandhanādihatthakammena vihārassa ūnakatā na hoti, tattakaṃ katvāti attho. Sabbesanti tatruppādavassāvāsikaṃ gaṇhantānaṃ sabbesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ, sāmaṇerānañca. Bhaṇḍāgārikacīvarepīti akālacīvaraṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Etanti ukkuṭṭhiyā katāya samabhāgadānaṃ. Virajjhitvā karontīti kattabbakālesu akatvā yathārucitakkhaṇe karonti.

343. “Vihāramajjhe” is said so that all may know. “Vaṇṇāvaṇṇaṃ katvā” means having made equal shares endowed with small and large colors using turmeric and so on, for the purpose of knowing the sufficiency of the shares. Therefore, he said, “having placed equal shares.” “Idaṃ” means the giving of a half-share to novices. “Phātikamma” means sufficient work. The meaning is: having done as much manual work that comes in the Vinaya, such as the tying of brooms, by which the monastery does not become deficient. “Sabbesaṃ” refers to all the monks and novices who receive the rains-residence robe that has arisen there. “Bhaṇḍāgārikacīvarepi” is said with reference to an out-of-season robe. “Etaṃ” means the giving of equal shares when a proclamation has been made. “Virajjhitvā karonti” means they do it at a moment of their own liking, not doing it at the times when it should be done.

Ettakena mama cīvaraṃ pahotīti dvādasagghanakeneva mama cīvaraṃ paripuṇṇaṃ hoti, na tato ūnenāti sabbaṃ gahetukāmoti attho.

“Ettakena mama cīvaraṃ pahotīti” means: my robe is complete only with what is worth twelve, not with less than that; thus, he desires to take all of it. This is the meaning.

Bhaṇḍāgārasammutiādikathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.
