Anikkhittavattabhikkhūnaṃ vuttanayenevāti upacārasīmāya paviṭṭhānaṃ vasena ratticchedaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tasmiṃ gāmeti bhikkhunīnaṃ nivāsanagāme. Attānaṃ dassetvāti yathā ārocetuṃ sakkā, tathā dassetvā. “Sammannitvā dātabbā”ti iminā sammatāya sahavāsepi ratticchedo na hotīti dasseti.

The statement 'by the very same method as for monks who have not laid down their observance' is said with reference to the breach of night on account of those who have entered the vicinity-boundary. As for tasmiṃ gāme (in that village): in the village where the bhikkhunīs reside. As for attānaṃ dassetvā (having shown oneself): having shown oneself in such a way that it is possible to inform. By this text, 'Having authorized, she should be given,' it is shown that even in co-residence with an authorized bhikkhunī, there is no breach of night.

Mūlāyapaṭikassitassāti mūlāyapaṭikassitassa puna parivutthaparivāsassāti attho. Tissannanti mūlāpattiyā saha dvinnaṃ antarāpattīnañca.

As for mūlāyapaṭikassitassa (of one who has been reinstated to the root): the meaning is, of one who has been reinstated to the root and has again lived out the probation. As for tissannaṃ (of the three): of the root offense together with the two intervening offenses.

108. Sace [V 2.0208] paṭicchannāti nikkhittavattenāpannāpattiṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Pāḷiyaṃ pañcāhappaṭicchannavāre antarāpattikathāyaṃ “evañca pana, bhikkhave, chārattaṃ mānattaṃ dātabba”nti idaṃ mūlāyapaṭikassanākammavācānantarameva dātuṃ vuttaṃ na hoti. Mūlāyapaṭikassitassa pana pañcadivasāni parivasitvā yācitassa [M 2.0220] mānattacaraṇakāle āpannāya tatiyāya antarāpattiyā appaṭicchannāya mānattadānaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Evañca dinnamānattassa ekena chārattena pubbe dinnamānattāhi tīhi āpattīhi saha catassannampi āpattīnaṃ mānattaṃ ciṇṇameva hoti. Iminā pana nayena abbhānārahakāle āpannāya antarāpattiyā, pakkhappaṭicchannavāre antarāpattīsu ca paṭipajjanaṃ veditabbaṃ. “Ekāhappaṭicchannādivasena pañcā”ti idaṃ ekāhappaṭicchannādīnaṃ catunnaṃ paccekaparivāsadānamānattadānaabbhānāni ekekaṃ katvā vuttaṃ. “Antarāpattivasena catasso”ti idampi mānattadānaabbhānāni tasmiṃ tasmiṃ mūlāyapaṭikassane ekattaṃ āropetvā vuttaṃ.

108. As for sace paṭicchannā (if concealed): this is said with reference to an offense incurred by one with observance laid down. In the Pāḷi, in the section on the intervening offense in the case of a five-day concealment, this text, 'And thus, Bhikkhus, mānatta for six nights should be given,' is not said to be given immediately after the formal act of reinstatement to the root. Rather, it is said with reference to the giving of mānatta for an unconcealed third intervening offense incurred during the time of practicing mānatta by one who has been reinstated to the root, has lived on probation for five days, and has requested it. And thus, for one who has been given mānatta, by one six-night period, the mānatta for all four offenses is indeed practiced, together with the three offenses for which mānatta was previously given. But by this method, the practice should be known for an intervening offense incurred at a time when one is fit for rehabilitation, and for intervening offenses in the case of a fortnight's concealment. This text, 'Five, by way of one-day concealment, etc.,' is said having made the giving of probation, giving of mānatta, and rehabilitation for each of the four—one-day concealment and so forth—one by one. This text, 'Four, by way of intervening offenses,' is also said having ascribed oneness to the giving of mānatta and rehabilitation in each respective reinstatement to the root.

Paṭicchannaparivāsakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Account on Concealed Probation is concluded.

Samodhānaparivāsakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Account on Combined Probation

125. “Yasmā paṭicchannā antarāpattī”ti idaṃ samodhānaparivāsadānassa kāraṇavacanaṃ, na pana ciṇṇaparivutthadivasānaṃ makkhitabhāvassa, appaṭicchannāya antarāpattiyā mūlāyapaṭikassane katepi tesaṃ makkhitabhāvasambhavato. Tasmā “mānattaciṇṇadivasāpi parivutthadivasāpi sabbe makkhitāva hontī”ti imassānantaraṃ “samodhānaparivāso cassa dātabbo”ti evamettha yojanā kātabbā. Tenāha “tenevā”tiādi.

125. This statement, 'Because the intervening offense was concealed,' is the reason for giving combined probation, but not for the annulment of the days spent observing mānatta and the days lived on probation. Why? Because even when reinstatement to the original is done for an unconcealed intervening offense, the annulment of those days is possible. Therefore, after this phrase, 'The days spent observing mānatta and the days lived on probation are all annulled,' the text 'and combined probation should be given to him' should be supplied, and the connection should be made in this sentence thus: 'Why should it be given? Because there is a concealed intervening offense. Therefore, it should be given.' For that very reason, he said the words beginning with 'teneva'.

Samodhānaparivāsakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Account on Combined Probation is finished.

Agghasamodhānaparivāsakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Account on Combined Probation by Assessment

134. “Ekāpattimūlakañcā”ti iminā “ekā āpatti ekāhappaṭicchannā, ekā āpatti dvīhappaṭicchannā”tiādinayaṃ dasseti. Appaṭicchannabhāvaṃ dassetunti ajānanādinā paṭicchannāyapi āpattiyā mānattārahatāvacanena appaṭicchannabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ. “Ekassa, āvuso, māsassa bhikkhu mānattāraho”ti [M 2.0221] (cūḷava. 153) hi vuttaṃ. Ettha ekassa ajānanapaṭicchannamāsassa [V 2.0209] parivāsāraho na hoti, kevalaṃ āpattiyā appaṭicchannattā mānattāraho hotīti adhippāyo. Pāḷiyaṃ makkhadhammoti madditukāmatā. Saṅghādisesānaṃ parivāsadānādisabbavinicchayassa samuccayattā panesa samuccayakkhandhakoti vuttoti veditabbo.

134. By this phrase, 'and based on a single offense,' he shows the method beginning with, 'one offense concealed for one day, one offense concealed for two days.' As for 'to show the state of being unconcealed,' it means: in order to show the state of being unconcealed by stating the worthiness for mānatta for an offense that was concealed due to ignorance, etc. Indeed, it is said, 'Venerable sirs, a bhikkhu is worthy of mānatta for one month.' Here, the intention is this: by way of one month of concealment through ignorance, he is not worthy of probation; merely because the offense is unconcealed, he is worthy of mānatta. In the Pāḷi, `makkhadhamma` is the desire to trample upon. Because it is a collection of all decisions, such as the giving of probation, for Saṅghādisesa offenses, this chapter is called the Samuccayakkhandhaka (Chapter of Collection). Thus it should be understood.

Agghasamodhānaparivāsakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Account on Combined Probation by Assessment is finished.

Samuccayakkhandhakavaṇṇanānayo niṭṭhito.

The Method of the Explanation of the Chapter of Collection is finished.

4. Samathakkhandhako

4. The Chapter on Settlements

Sativinayakathādivaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Account on Settlement by Mindfulness, etc.

195. Samathakkhandhake [M 2.0222][V 2.0210] khīṇāsavassa vipulasatiṃ nissāya dātabbo vinayo codanādiasāruppānaṃ vinayanupāyo sativinayo.

195. In the Chapter on Settlements, the settlement by mindfulness is the settlement to be given to one whose cankers are destroyed, relying on his extensive mindfulness; it is the means of settling unsuitable matters such as accusations.

196. Cittavipariyāsakatoti katacittavipariyāso. Gaggaṃ bhikkhuṃ…pe… codentīti ettha pana ummattakassa idaṃ ummattakaṃ, ajjhāciṇṇaṃ. Tadeva cittavipariyāsena katanti cittavipariyāsakataṃ. Tena ummattakena cittavipariyāsakatena ajjhāciṇṇena anācārena āpannāya āpattiyā gaggaṃ bhikkhuṃ codentīti evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Paṭhamaṃ mūḷho hutvā pacchā amūḷhabhāvaṃ upagatassa dātabbo vinayo amūḷhavinayo.

196. As for `cittavipariyāsakata` (done due to mental derangement), it means one whose mind is deranged. But in the sentence, 'They accuse the bhikkhu Gagga...,' it is the case of an insane person; it is a habit. That very thing, done by mental derangement, is thus called `cittavipariyāsakata`. The meaning should be understood thus: they accuse the bhikkhu Gagga of an offense fallen into through misconduct, which was a habit done by mental derangement on the part of that insane person. The settlement to be given to one who, having first been confused, later reached a state of non-confusion, is the settlement for the unconfused.

202. Dhammavādīnaṃ yebhuyyabhāvasampādikā kiriyā yebhuyyasikāti imasmiṃ atthe sa-kārāgamasahito ika-paccayantoyaṃ saddoti dassetuṃ āha “yassā”tiādi. Tattha yassā kiriyāyāti gūḷhakavivaṭṭakādinā salākaggāhāpakakiriyāya. Yebhuyyabhāvaṃ nissitasamathakiriyā yebhuyyasikāti evaṃ yebhuyyasikāsaddassa attho gahetabbo. Evañhi ayaṃ adhikaraṇasamatho nāma hoti. Yathāvuttasalākaggāhena hi dhammavādīnaṃ yebhuyyabhāve siddhe pacchā taṃ yebhuyyabhāvaṃ nissāyeva adhikaraṇavūpasamo hoti, na dhammavādīnaṃ bahutarabhāvasādhakakiriyāmattena.

202. The procedure that accomplishes the state of being a majority for the speakers of Dhamma is called `yebhuyyasikā`. To show that in this meaning this word has the suffix `-ika` together with the augment `sa`, he said the words beginning with `yassā`. Therein, `yassā kiriyāya` refers to the procedure of having voting tickets taken by methods such as the secret and the open. Alternatively, the procedure of settling that relies on the state of being a majority is called `yebhuyyasikā`. Thus, the meaning of the word `yebhuyyasikā` should be taken. For, when taken thus, this is called a settlement of a legal question. Indeed, the settlement of the legal question occurs by relying on the majority of the speakers of Dhamma, once that majority has been established by the aforementioned taking of voting tickets; it does not occur merely by the procedure that establishes their greater number.

207. “Sesamettha tajjanīyādīsu vuttanayamevā”ti etena tajjanīyādisattakammāni viya idampi tassapāpiyasikākammaṃ asucibhāvādidosayuttassa, saṅghassa ca vinicchaye atiṭṭhamānassa kattabbaṃ visuṃ ekaṃ niggahakammanti dasseti. Etasmiñhi niggahakamme kate so puggalo “ahaṃ [V 2.0211] suddho”ti attano suddhiyā sādhanatthaṃ saṅghamajjhaṃ otarituṃ, saṅgho cassa vinicchayaṃ dātuṃ na labhati, taṃ kammakaraṇamatteneva ca taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ vūpasantaṃ hoti.

207. By this text, 'The rest here is according to the method stated in the Tajjanīya, etc.,' he shows that, like the seven formal acts beginning with Tajjanīya, this Tassapāpiyasikākamma is also a separate, single act of censure to be carried out on a person who is connected with faults such as the state of being impure and who does not stand by the decision of the Saṅgha. Indeed, when this act of censure has been carried out, that person is not allowed to enter the midst of the Saṅgha to establish his own purity, saying, 'I am pure,' and the Saṅgha is not allowed to give him a decision; and merely by the performance of that formal act, that legal question becomes settled.

Kathaṃ panetaṃ kammaṃ paṭippassambhatīti? Keci panettha “so tathā niggahito niggahitova hoti, osāraṇaṃ na labhati. Teneva pāḷiyaṃ [M 2.0223] osāraṇā na vuttā”ti vadanti. Aññe pana “pāḷiyaṃ na upasampādetabbantiādinā sammāvattanassa vuttattā sammāvattitvā lajjidhamme okkantassa osāraṇā avuttāpi tajjanīyādīsu viya nayato kammavācaṃ yojetvā osāraṇā kātabbā evā”ti vadanti, idaṃ yuttaṃ. Teneva aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vakkhati “sace sīlavā bhavissati, vattaṃ paripūretvā paṭippassaddhiṃ labhissati. No ce, tathānāsitakova bhavissatī”ti (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 238). Tassapāpiyasikākammanti ca aluttasamāsoyeva. Tenāha “idaṃ hī”ti ādi.

But how is this formal act revoked? This is the question. Herein, some teachers say: 'That person remains just as he was censured; he does not get reinstatement. For that very reason, reinstatement is not spoken of in the Pāḷi.' But other teachers say: 'Because proper conduct is spoken of in the Pāḷi with phrases beginning, "He should not be ordained...," for a person who, having conducted himself properly, has entered into a state of conscientiousness, reinstatement—though not spoken of—should certainly be carried out by applying the formal procedure according to the method, as in the cases of Tajjanīya, etc.' This is reasonable. For that very reason, it will be said in the Commentary: 'If he becomes virtuous, having fulfilled his duties, he will obtain tranquility. If not, he will remain as one who has been ruined.' And the phrase `tassapāpiyasikākamma` is an unelided compound. Therefore, he said the words beginning with 'idaṃ hi'.

Sativinayakathādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Account on Settlement by Mindfulness, etc., is finished.

Adhikaraṇakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Account on Disputes

215. Virūpato vipariṇāmaṭṭhena cittaṃ dukkhaṃ vipaccatīti āha “cittadukkhatthaṃ vohāro”tiādi. Upavadanāti codanā. Tatthevāti anuvadane.

215. By way of alteration, the mind becomes afflicted. Therefore, he said the statement beginning with 'the expression for the meaning of mental suffering'. `Upavadanā` is accusation. `Tattheva` means in the re-accusation.

Ādito paṭṭhāya ca tassa tassa kammassa viññātattāti vitthārato āgatakammavaggassa ādito paṭṭhāya vaṇṇanāmukhena viññātattā vinicchayo bhavissatīti yojanā.

As for the phrase `Ādito paṭṭhāya ca tassa tassa kammassa viññātattā` (And because each and every formal act is known from the beginning): because it is known in detail from the beginning of the Kammavagga that has come down by means of the commentary, the decision will be easy to know. This is the connection.

216. Pāḷiyaṃ ajjhattaṃ vāti attani vā attano parisāya vā. Bahiddhā vāti parasmiṃ vā parassa parisāya vā. Anavassavāyāti anuppādāya.

216. In the Pāḷi text, `ajjhattaṃ vā` means in oneself or in one's own assembly. `Bahiddhā vā` means in another or in another's assembly. `Anavassavāya` means for non-arising.

220. “Vivādādhikaraṇaṃ kusalaṃ akusalaṃ abyākata”nti idaṃ pucchāvacanaṃ. Vivādādhikaraṇaṃ siyā kusalantiādi visajjanaṃ. Esa nayo sesesupi.

220. The statement, 'Is a dispute-issue wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate?' is the question. The statement beginning with, 'A dispute-issue could be wholesome...' is the answer. This is the method in the remaining cases as well.

222. Sammutisabhāvāyapi āpattiyā kāraṇūpacārena akusalābyākatabhāvena vuccamāne kusalassāpi āpattikāraṇattā tadupacārena “āpattādhikaraṇaṃ siyā kusala”nti vattabbaṃ bhaveyya[V 2.0212], tathā [M 2.0224] avatvā “natthi āpattādhikaraṇaṃ kusala”nti evaṃvacanassa kāraṇaṃ dassetuṃ “ettha sandhāyabhāsitavasena attho veditabbo”ti vuttaṃ. Ettha cāyamadhippāyo – yadi hi āpatti nāma paramatthadhammasabhāvā bhaveyya, tadā “āpattādhikaraṇaṃ siyā akusala”ntiādivacanaṃ yujjeyya. Yasmā duṭṭhadosasikkhāpadaṭṭhakathādīsu dassitadosappasaṅgato paramatthasabhaāvatā na yuttā, ekantasammutisabhāvā eva sā hoti, tasmā “siyā akusalaṃ siyā abyākata”ntipi nippariyāyato na vattabbā. Yadi pana akusalaabyākatadhammasamuṭṭhitattameva upādāya pariyāyato “siyā akusalaṃ siyā abyākata”nti vuttaṃ. Tadā kusaladhammasamauṭṭhitattampi upādāya pariyāyato “āpattādhikaraṇaṃ siyā kusala”ntipi vattabbaṃ bhaveyya. Yato cetaṃ vacanaṃ āpattiyā akusalābyākatūpacārārahattassa kusalūpacārānārahattassa visuṃ kāraṇasabbhāvaṃ sandhāya bhāsitaṃ, tasmā yaṃ taṃ kāraṇavisesaṃ sandhāya idaṃ bhāsitaṃ, tassa vasenevettha attho veditabbo.

222. Although an offense has a conventional nature, when it is spoken of as being unwholesome or indeterminate by way of figurative usage based on the cause, since a wholesome state is also a cause of an offense, by that same figurative usage it would have to be said, 'An offense-issue could be wholesome.' Without saying so, in order to show the reason for this statement, 'There is no wholesome offense-issue,' it was said, 'Herein, the meaning should be understood according to what was spoken with reference.' And herein, this is the intention: if an offense were by nature an ultimate reality, then the statement, 'An offense-issue could be unwholesome,' etc., would be suitable. But because, due to the consequence of the fault shown in the commentaries on the training rules concerning corrupt intention, etc., an ultimate nature is not suitable for it—it is exclusively of a conventional nature—therefore, 'it could be unwholesome, it could be indeterminate' cannot be said directly. If, however, it is said figuratively, 'it could be unwholesome, it could be indeterminate,' based only on its arising from unwholesome and indeterminate states, then, based also on its arising from a wholesome state, it would also have to be said figuratively, 'An offense-issue could be wholesome.' And since this statement was spoken with reference to the existence of a distinct reason for an offense's suitability to be figuratively called unwholesome and indeterminate and its unsuitability to be figuratively called wholesome, therefore, the meaning herein should be understood only according to that specific reason with reference to which this was spoken.

Idāni pana yo aṅgappahonakacittameva sandhāya āpattiyā akusalādibhāvo vutto, nāññaṃ visesakāraṇaṃ sandhāyāti gaṇheyya, tassa gāhe dosaṃ dassento “yasmiṃ hī”tiādimāha. Tattha pathavīkhaṇanādiketi pathavīkhaṇanādinimitte paṇṇattivajje. Āpattādhikaraṇe kusalacittaṃ aṅganti paṇṇattiṃ ajānitvā kusalacittena cetiyaṅgaṇādīsu bhūmisodhanādivasena pathavībhūtagāmavikopanādikāle kusalacittaṃ kāraṇaṃ hoti. Tasmiṃ satīti tasmiṃ āpattādhikaraṇe vijjamāne kusalacittasamuṭṭhitattena kusalavohārārahāya āpattiyā vijjamānāyāti adhippāyo. Sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. cūḷavagga 3.222) pana “tasmiṃ satī”ti imassa “tasmiṃ kusalacitte āpattibhāvena gahite”ti attho vutto, taṃ na yujjati “yasmi”nti ya-saddena parāmaṭṭhasseva āpattādhikaraṇassa “tasmi”nti parāmasitabbato.

But now, wishing to show the fault in the view of one who might hold that the state of an offense as unwholesome, etc., is spoken of with reference only to the mind that is sufficient for a factor, and not with reference to another specific reason, He said the passage beginning with `yasmiṃ hi`. Therein, `pathavīkhaṇanādike` refers to an offense-issue that is an offense by designation, having digging the earth, etc., as its cause. `Kusalacittaṃ aṅgaṃ` means that at the time of destroying earth, vegetation, etc., by way of clearing the ground in a stupa courtyard, etc., with a wholesome mind, not knowing the designation, that wholesome mind is the cause. `Tasmiṃ sati` means: when that offense-issue exists, and when there exists an offense that, by reason of arising from a wholesome mind, is suitable to be called 'wholesome'—this is the intention. But in the Sāratthadīpanī, the meaning of this phrase `tasmiṃ sati` is stated as: 'when that wholesome mind is taken as being an offense.' That is not suitable, because `tasmiṃ` must refer back to the very offense-issue that was referred to by the relative pronoun `ya` in `yasmiṃ`.

Na sakkā vattunti yadi sammutisabhāvāyapi āpattiyā akusalādisamuṭṭhitattena akusalādivohāro karīyati, tadā kusalavohāropi kattabboti “natthi āpattādhikaraṇaṃ kusala”nti na sakkā vattuṃ, aññathā akusalādibhāvopissa paṭikkhipitabboti adhippāyo. Tasmāti [M 2.0225] yasmā kusalādīnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ samānepi āpattiyā aṅgappahonakatte kusalavohārova āpattiyā paṭikkhitto, na akusalādivohāro, tasmā nayidaṃ aṅgappahonakaṃ cittaṃ sandhāya vuttanti “āpattādhikaraṇaṃ siyā akusalaṃ siyā abyākataṃ, natthi āpattādhikaraṇaṃ kusala”nti idaṃ āpattiyā samuṭṭhāpakattena aṅgappahonakaṃ kāraṇabhūtaṃ cittamattaṃ sandhāya na vuttaṃ[V 2.0213], aññathā “āpattādhikaraṇaṃ siyā kusala”ntipi vattabbatoti adhippāyo. Etena āpattiyā akusalādibhāvopi kenaci nimittena pariyāyatova vutto, na paramatthatoti dasseti. Yathāha “yaṃ kusalacittena āpajjati, taṃ kusalaṃ, itarehi itara”nti.

As for `Na sakkā vattuṃ` (It cannot be said): If, for an offense which has a conventional nature, the designation 'unwholesome', etc., is made by reason of its arising from unwholesome states, etc., then the designation 'wholesome' should also be made. Therefore, it cannot be said, 'There is no wholesome offense-issue'; otherwise, its state as unwholesome, etc., should also be rejected. This is the intention. As for `Tasmā` (Therefore): Because, although the three—wholesome, etc.—are equal in being sufficient for a factor of an offense, only the designation 'wholesome' is rejected for an offense, while the designation 'unwholesome', etc., is not rejected. Therefore, this was not said with reference to the mind that is sufficient for a factor. That is, the statement, 'An offense-issue may be unwholesome or indeterminate, but there is no wholesome offense-issue,' was not said with reference merely to the mind which is the cause, sufficient for a factor, by way of being the originator of the offense; otherwise, it would have to be said, 'An offense-issue could be wholesome.' This is the intention. By this, it is shown that the state of an offense as unwholesome, etc., is also spoken of only figuratively, by some reason, not in an ultimate sense. As it is said: 'That which one incurs through a wholesome mind is wholesome; that which one incurs through the others is otherwise.'

Idaṃ panātiādīsu ayaṃ adhippāyo – “āpattādhikaraṇaṃ siyā akusalaṃ siyā abyākata”nti idañhi yaṃ kiñci kadāci katthaci kāraṇaṃ bhavantaṃ aniyatakāraṇaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ na hoti. Yaṃ pana sabbasikkhāpadesu āpattiyā kāraṇaṃ bhavitumarahati, idameva kāraṇaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Akusalañhi paṇṇattiṃ ñatvā vītikkamantassa sabbāpattiyā kāraṇaṃ hoti, lokavajjāpattiyā pana paṇṇattiṃ ajānantassapi kāraṇaṃ hoti. Kevalaṃ paṇṇattivajjāpattīsu kusalābyākatacittapavattikkhaṇe eva akusalaṃ na vattati, tadaññattha sayameva pavattati. Abyākataṃ pana kāyavacībhūtaṃ kusalākusalādīnaṃ pavattikkhaṇe nirodhasamāpannassa sahaseyyāpattiyanti sabbāpattiyā aṅgameva hoti channaṃ āpattisamuṭṭhānānaṃ kāyavācaṅgavirahitattābhāvā. Tasmā imesaṃ akusalābyākatānaṃ sabbāpattimūlakattameva sandhāya idaṃ āpattiyā akusalattaṃ, abyākatattañca vuttaṃ. Yattha pana pathavīkhaṇanādīsu kusalampi āpattiyā kāraṇaṃ hoti, tatthāpi āpattiyā tadupacārena kusalattavohāro ayutto sāvajjānavajjānaṃ ekattavohārassa viruddhattā. Yadaggena aññamaññaṃ viruddhā, tadaggena kāraṇakāriyavohāropi nesaṃ ayutto. Tasmā tattha vijjamānampi kusalaṃ abbohārikaṃ, kāyavacīdvārameva āveṇikaṃ kāraṇanti.

In “This, however...” and so forth, this is the intention: Indeed, this statement, “An offense-issue may be unwholesome, may be indeterminate,” is not spoken with reference to some indeterminate cause that might arise at some time in some training rule without specific designation. Rather, it is spoken with reference to just this cause which is fit to be the cause of an offense in all training rules. Indeed, the unwholesome is the cause of all offenses for one who transgresses knowing the regulation. But for an offense that is blameworthy in the world, it is a cause even for one who does not know the regulation. Only in offenses that are blameworthy merely by regulation does the unwholesome not occur at the very moment of the arising of a wholesome or indeterminate mind; in other cases, it occurs by itself. But the indeterminate, which has become bodily or verbal action, is merely a factor of all offenses—whether at the moment of the arising of wholesome, unwholesome, etc., states, or in the case of the offense of lying down together for one who has attained cessation—because of the non-absence of the bodily and verbal factors from the six origins of offenses. Therefore, with reference to just the state of being the root of all offenses for these unwholesome and indeterminate states, this unwholesome nature and indeterminate nature of an offense is stated. But where even a wholesome state is a cause of an offense, as in digging the earth and so forth, even there the designation of “wholesome” for the offense by transference from that cause is unsuitable, because of the contradiction in designating the blameworthy and the blameless as one. To the extent that they are mutually contradictory, to that extent the designation of cause and effect for them is also unsuitable. Therefore, even though the wholesome is present there, it is not to be designated as such; only the bodily and verbal doors are the specific cause.

Tattha ekantato akusalamevāti akusalacittena samuṭṭhahanato kāraṇūpacārato evaṃ vuttaṃ. Tatthāti lokavajje. Vikappo natthīti siyā-saddassa vikappanatthataṃ dasseti. Akusalaṃ hotīti akusalasamuṭṭhitāya kāraṇūpacārena akusalaṃ hoti. Sahaseyyādivasena āpajjanato [M 2.0226] abyākataṃ hotīti itthiyādīhi saha piṭṭhipasāraṇavasappavattakāyadvārasaṅkhātarūpābyākatavaseneva āpajjitabbato kāraṇūpacāreneva āpatti abyākataṃ hoti. Tatthāti tasmiṃ paṇṇattivajjāpattādhikaraṇe. Sañciccāsañciccavasenāti paṇṇattiṃ ñatvā, aññatvā ca āpajjanavasena imaṃ vikappabhāvaṃ sandhāya akusalattaabyākatattasaṅkhātaṃ yathāvuttaṃ imaṃ vikappasabhāvaṃ sandhāya idaṃ vacanaṃ vuttaṃ.

Therein, the statement “exclusively unwholesome” is said thus by way of causal transference because it arises from an unwholesome mind. “Therein” refers to what is blameworthy in the world. The phrase “there is no alternative” shows that the word `siyā` has the meaning of an alternative. “It is unwholesome” means it is unwholesome by way of causal transference because it arises from the unwholesome. “It becomes indeterminate by being incurred through lying down together, etc.” means that because it is to be incurred only by way of the indeterminate physical matter reckoned as the body-door, which occurs by way of extending the back together with a woman, etc., the offense is indeterminate only by way of causal transference. “Therein” refers to that offense-issue that is blameworthy by regulation. “By way of intentionally and unintentionally” means by way of incurring it both knowing and not knowing the regulation. This statement is spoken with reference to this nature of an alternative as aforesaid—reckoned as the state of being unwholesome and the state of being indeterminate—in consideration of this state of being an alternative.

Yadi evaṃ asañciccāpajjanapakkhe kusalenāpi āpajjanato tampi vikappaṃ sandhāya “āpattādhikaraṇaṃ siyā kusala”ntipi kasmā na vuttanti āha “sace panā”tiādi. “Acittakāna”nti [V 2.0214] vuttamevatthaṃ samuṭṭhānavasena vibhāvetuṃ “eḷakalomapadasodhammādisamuṭṭhānānampī”ti vuttaṃ. Acittakasamuṭṭhānānaṃ “kusalacittaṃ āpajjeyyā”ti etena sāvajjabhūtāya āpattiyā kāraṇūpacārenāpi anavajjabhūtakusalavohāro ayuttoti dasseti. “Na ca tatthā”tiādinā kusalassa āpattiyā kāraṇattaṃ vijjamānampi tathā voharituṃ ayuttanti paṭikkhipitvā kāyavācāsaṅkhātaṃ abyākatasseva kāraṇattaṃ dasseti. Tattha calitappavattānanti calitānaṃ, pavattānañca. Calito hi kāyo, pavattā vācā. Ettha ca kāyavācānamaññatarameva aṅgaṃ. Tañca…pe… abyākatanti evaṃ abyākatassa āpattikāraṇabhāveneva vuttattā. “Āpattādhikaraṇaṃ siyā akusalaṃ siyā abyākata”nti idaṃ kāraṇūpacārena pariyāyato vuttaṃ, na nippariyāyatoti sijjhati.

If so, since in the case of unintentional transgression one also incurs an offense with a wholesome mind, with reference to that alternative too, why is it not also said, “An offense-issue may be wholesome”? To this, he says, “But if…” and so forth. To clarify the meaning already stated in “of the mindless,” by way of the origin, it is said, “even of those with origins in goat's wool, word-by-word recitation of the Dhamma, etc.” By this statement, “a wholesome mind might incur an offense,” regarding those with mindless origins, it shows that even by way of causal transference, the designation “wholesome,” which is blameless, is unsuitable for an offense, which is blameworthy. With “And not there…” and so forth, having rejected that even though the wholesome's state as a cause for an offense exists, it is unsuitable to designate it thus, it shows that the state of being a cause belongs only to the indeterminate, which is reckoned as body and speech. Therein, “of the moved and uttered” means “of the moved and of the uttered.” Indeed, the body is moved, and speech is uttered. And here, a factor is just one or the other of body and speech. “And that… is indeterminate.” Thus, because the indeterminate is stated only as having the nature of being a cause of an offense. This statement, “An offense-issue may be unwholesome, may be indeterminate,” is spoken figuratively by way of causal transference, not literally. Thus it is established.

Yaṃ pana sāratthadīpaniyaṃ (sārattha. ṭī. cūḷava. 3.222) āpattiyā nippariyāyatova akusalādisabhāvataṃ samatthetuṃ bahuṃ papañcitaṃ, taṃ na sārato paccetabbaṃ duṭṭhadosasikkhāpadaṭṭhakathāyameva paṭikkhittattā. Tenevetthāpi “yaṃ cittaṃ āpattiyā aṅgaṃ hotī”tiādinā akusalacittassāpi āpattiyā kāraṇattena bhinnatāva dassitā. Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā dassitamevāti idha na vitthārayimha. Evaṃ vītikkamato yo vītikkamoti ettha akusalacittena ñatvā vītikkamantassa kāyavacīvītikkamasamuṭṭhitā āpattivītikkamoti vutto. Esa nayo abyākatavārepi.

But as for that which was extensively elaborated in the Sāratthadīpanī to establish, in a literal sense, that an offense has a nature of being unwholesome and so forth, that should not be accepted as authoritative, because it was rejected in the commentary on the Duṭṭhadosa training rule itself. For that very reason, here too, with “Whatever mind is a factor of an offense…” and so forth, just the distinctness of even an unwholesome mind as a cause of an offense has been shown. What should be said here has already been shown previously, thus we do not elaborate here. Here, in “From such a transgression, that which is the transgression,” the offense that has arisen from the bodily and verbal transgression of one who transgresses knowingly with an unwholesome mind is called “transgression.” This is the method in the section on the indeterminate as well.

Adhikaraṇakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discussion on Legal Issues is concluded.

Adhikaraṇavūpasamanasamathakathādivaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Discourses on the Calming of Disputes, etc.

228. Pāḷiyaṃ [M 2.0227] vivādādhikaraṇaṃ ekaṃ samathaṃ anāgammātiādi pucchā. Siyātiādi vissajjanaṃ. Siyātissa vacanīyanti eteneva vūpasamaṃ siyāti vattabbaṃ bhaveyyāti attho. Sammukhāvinayasminti sammukhāvinayattasminti bhāvappadhāno niddeso daṭṭhabbo. Evaṃ sabbavāresu. “Kārako ukkoṭetī”ti idaṃ upalakkhaṇamattaṃ, yassa kassaci ukkoṭentassa pācittiyameva. Ubbāhikāya khīyanake pācittiyaṃ na vuttaṃ tattha chandadānassa natthitāya.

228. In the Pāḷi, 'A legal issue of dispute, not having resorted to one settlement method...' and so on, is the question. 'It may be...' and so on, is the answer. As for 'Siyāti assa vacanīyaṃ' (It may be, is to be said), the meaning is: it should be said, 'By this very method, the calming may be.' As for 'sammukhāvinayasmiṃ' (in the presence-discipline), the exposition 'sammukhāvinayattasmiṃ' (in the state of being the presence-discipline) should be understood as one where the state of being is primary. Thus it is in all instances. This phrase, 'The doer reopens the case,' is merely an illustration; for anyone whatsoever who reopens it, it is just a pācittiya offense. For disparaging the Ubbāhikā formal act, a pācittiya is not stated, because there is no giving of consent there.

235. Vaṇṇāvaṇṇāyo katvāti khuddakamahantehi saññāṇehi yuttāyo katvā. Tenāha “nimittasaññaṃ āropetvā”ti.

235. “Having made distinctions” means having made them endowed with small and large marks. Therefore, he said, “having established the perception of a sign.”

242. Kiccādhikaraṇaṃ [V 2.0215] …pe… sammatīti ettha sammukhāvinayena apalokanādikammaṃ sampajjatīti attho daṭṭhabbo.

242. Here, regarding “A legal issue of duties… is agreed upon,” it should be understood that the meaning is that the act of formal announcement, etc., is accomplished through the presence-discipline.

Adhikaraṇavūpasamanasamathakathādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Discourses on the Calming of Disputes, etc., is concluded.

Samathakkhandhakavaṇṇanānayo niṭṭhito.

The expositional method of the Chapter on Settlement Methods is concluded.

5. Khuddakavatthukkhandhako

5. The Chapter on Minor Matters

Khuddakavatthukathāvaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Discourse on Minor Matters

243. Khuddakavatthukkhandhake [M 2.0228][V 2.0216] aṭṭhapadākārenāti jūtaphalake aṭṭhagabbharājiākārena. Mallakamūlasaṇṭhānenāti kheḷamallakamūlasaṇṭhānena. Idañca vaṭṭādhārakaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, kaṇṭake uṭṭhāpetvā katavaṭṭakapālassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

243. In the Chapter on Minor Matters, “in the manner of an eight-square board” means in the manner of a line with eight compartments on a game board. “With the shape of a bowl-base” means with the shape of the base of a spitoon. And this is said with reference to a round support; this is a designation for a round bowl made by raising up points.

244. Puthupāṇikanti muṭṭhiṃ akatvā vikasitahatthatalehi piṭṭhiparikammaṃ vuccati. Etameva sandhāya “hatthaparikamma”nti vuttaṃ.

244. “With broad palms” refers to massaging the back with the palms spread open, not making a fist. It is with reference to this that “hand-massage” is said.

245. Muttolambakādīnanti ādi-saddena kuṇḍalādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Palambakasuttanti brāhmaṇānaṃ yaññopacitasuttādiākāraṃ vuccati. Valayanti hatthapādavalayaṃ.

245. Regarding “such as a hanging pearl ornament, etc.,” the word “etc.” includes things like earrings. “A hanging thread” refers to the kind of thread, like a sacred thread, worn by brahmins when performing a sacrifice. “A bangle” refers to a hand-bracelet or an anklet.

246. Dvaṅguleti upayogabahuvacanaṃ, dvaṅgulappamāṇaṃ atikkāmetuṃ na vaṭṭatīti attho. Ettha ca dumāsassa vā dvaṅgulassa vā atikkantabhāvaṃ ajānantassāpi kesamassugaṇanāya acittakāpattiyo hontīti vadanti.

246. Regarding “dvaṅgule” (two finger-breadths), this is the accusative plural. The meaning is that it is not allowable to exceed the measure of two finger-breadths. And here they say that even for one who does not know that the state of having exceeded two months or two finger-breadths has occurred, offenses incurred without intention arise by the count of the hair and beard.

Kocchenāti usīratiṇādīni bandhitvā samaṃ chinditvā gahitakocchena. Cikkalenāti silesayuttatelena. Uṇhābhitattarajasirānampīti uṇhābhitattānaṃ rajokiṇṇasirānaṃ. Addahatthenāti allahatthena.

“With a brush” means with a brush made by binding vetiver grass, etc., cutting it evenly, and taking it. “With a smoothing substance” means with oil mixed with a sticky paste. “Even for those with heads afflicted by heat and dust” means for those afflicted by heat and for those with heads covered in dust. “With a damp hand” means with a wet hand.

248-9. Sādhugītanti aniccatādipaṭisaññuttaṃ gītaṃ. Caturassena vattenāti paripuṇṇena uccāraṇavattena. Taraṅgavattādīnaṃ sabbesampi sāmaññalakkhaṇaṃ dassetuṃ “sabbesaṃ…pe… lakkhaṇa”nti [V 2.0217] vuttaṃ. Yattakāhi mattāhi akkharaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ hoti, tatopi adhikamattāyuttaṃ katvā kathanaṃ vikārakathanaṃ nāma, tathā akatvā kathanameva lakkhaṇanti attho. Bāhiralominti bhāvanapuṃsakaniddeso, yathā bahiddhā lomāni dissanti, evaṃ dhārentassa dukkaṭanti attho.

248-9. 'Sādhugītaṃ' (a good song) means a song connected with impermanence, etc. 'Caturassena vattena' (with a four-square manner) means with a complete manner of recitation. To show the general characteristic of all styles, such as the wave-style of recitation, it is said, 'the characteristic of all...' Speaking by using more measures than the amount by which a syllable is complete is called 'distorted speech'; the meaning is that speaking without doing so is itself the characteristic. 'Bāhiralomi' (having external hairs) is an exposition in the neuter referring to an action; the meaning is that it is a dukkaṭa offense for one who wears a robe in such a way that the hairs are visible on the outside.

250. Pāḷiyaṃ [M 2.0229] taruṇaññeva ambanti taruṇaṃ asañjātabījaṃ eva ambaphalaṃ. Pātāpetvāti chindāpetvāva. “Mattāvaṇṇitā”ti idaṃ “pare nindantī”ti sāsanahitesitāya vuttaṃ. Na pariyāpuṇiṃsūti nāsikkhiṃsu.

250. In the Pāḷi, 'taruṇaññeva ambaṃ' (a young mango indeed) means a young mango fruit, one with an undeveloped seed. 'Pātāpetvā' (having caused to fall) means having caused to be plucked. This phrase, 'mattā vaṇṇitā' (the measure was praised), was said out of a desire for the welfare of the Teaching, with the thought that 'others criticize'. 'Na pariyāpuṇiṃsu' means 'they were not able'.

251. Cattāri ahirājakulānīti sabbesaṃ ahibhedānaṃ catūsu eva saṅgahato vuttaṃ. Attaparittaṃ kātunti attano parittāṇaṃ kātuṃ.

251. 'Cattāri ahirājakulāni' (the four royal snake families) is said because all varieties of snakes are included in just these four groups. 'Attaparittaṃ kātuṃ' (to make a protection for oneself) means to make a safeguard for oneself.

Virūpakkhehi me mettanti virūpakkhajātikehi nāgehi saha mayhaṃ mittabhāvo hotu, mettā hotūti attho, te sukhitā niddukkhā averā hontūti adhippāyo. Evañhi mettāpharaṇaṃ hoti. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Apādakehīti ahikulehi saha sabbasattesu odhiso mettāpharaṇadassanaṃ. Mā maṃ apādako hiṃsīti tāya mettāya attarakkhāvidhānadassanaṃ.

'Virūpakkhehi me mettaṃ' (My loving-kindness is for the Virūpakkhas) means: 'May there be a state of friendship for me with the nāgas of the Virūpakkha clan; may there be loving-kindness.' This is the meaning. The intention is: 'May they be happy, free from suffering, and free from enmity.' For thus the spreading of loving-kindness occurs. This same method applies to the remaining phrases as well. 'Apādakehi' (by the footless ones), etc., shows the spreading of loving-kindness specifically towards all beings along with the snake families. 'Mā maṃ apādako hiṃsi' (may a footless one not harm me) shows the arrangement of self-protection by means of that loving-kindness.

Sabbe sattātiādi attānaṃ upamaṃ katvā sabbasattesu anodhiso mettāpharaṇadassanaṃ. Tattha mā kañci pāpamāgamāti kañci sattaṃ lāmakaṃ dukkhahetu, dukkhañca mā āgacchatu.

'Sabbe sattā' (all beings), etc., shows the spreading of loving-kindness without limitation towards all beings, having made oneself the example. Therein, 'mā kañci pāpamāgamā' (may no evil come to anyone) means: may no evil, which is a cause of suffering, and no suffering itself, come to any being whatsoever.

Evaṃ mettāya attaguttiṃ dassetvā idāni ratanattayānussaraṇena dassetuṃ “appamāṇo”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha pamāṇakaradhammā akusalā, tabbipākā ca pamāṇā, tappaṭipakkhā sīlādayo guṇā, tabbipākā ca lokiyalokuttaraphalāni appamāṇā, te assa atthīti appamāṇo, appamāṇā vā aparimeyyaguṇā assātipi appamāṇo. Pamāṇavantānīti yathāvuttapamāṇakaradhammayuttāni. Ahivicchikāti sarīsapānaññeva pabhedadassanaṃ. Uṇṇanābhīti lomasanābhiko makkaṭo. Sarabūti gharagoḷikā.

Having thus shown self-protection by means of loving-kindness, now, in order to show it by means of recollecting the Three Jewels, 'appamāṇo' (immeasurable), etc., is said. Therein, the unwholesome states that act as measures, and their results, are called 'pamāṇa' (measurable). Their opposites—the virtues such as morality, etc.—and their results, which are mundane and supramundane fruits, are called 'appamāṇa' (immeasurable). He is 'appamāṇo' because he possesses these, or he is 'appamāṇo' because his qualities are immeasurable, boundless. 'Pamāṇavantāni' (possessing measure) means those endowed with the aforementioned states that act as measures. 'Ahivicchikā' (snake, scorpion) shows a classification of creeping things. 'Uṇṇanābhi' is a spider with a hairy navel. 'Sarabū' is a house lizard.

Paṭikkamantūti apagacchantu, mā maṃ vihesayiṃsūti attho. Sohaṃ namoti ettha “karomī”ti pāṭhaseso. Yasmā mayā mettādīhi tumhākañca mayhañca rakkhā katā, yasmā ca sohaṃ bhagavato namo karomi, vipassīādīnaṃ sattannampi namo karomi, tasmā paṭikkamantu bhūtānīti yojanā.

'Paṭikkamantu' (may they retreat) means 'may they depart; may they not harass me'—this is the meaning. In 'so'haṃ namo' (I... homage), 'karomi' (I make) is the remainder of the text. The connection is: 'Because I have made protection for both you and me by means of loving-kindness, etc., and because I, that one, pay homage to the Blessed One, and I pay homage to the seven Buddhas, Vipassī, etc., therefore, may the beings depart.'

Aññamhīti [V 2.0218] kāmarāge asubhamanasikārādinā chetabbeti attho. Aṅgajātanti bījavirahitaṃ purisanimittaṃ. Bīje hi chinne opakkamikapaṇḍako nāma abhabbo hotīti vadanti. Eke pana “bījassāpi chedanakkhaṇe [M 2.0230] dukkaṭāpatti eva kamena purisindriyādike antarahite paṇḍako nāma abhabbo hoti, tadā liṅganāsanāya nāsetabbo”ti vadanti. Tādisaṃ vā dukkhaṃ uppādentassāti muṭṭhippahārādīhi attano dukkhaṃ uppādentassa.

'Aññamhi' means: concerning sensual desire that should be cut off by means of contemplation on the unattractive, etc. 'Aṅgajātaṃ' means: the male organ devoid of testicles. For indeed, when the testicles are cut off, one becomes an 'opakkamikapaṇḍaka', who is unfit for ordination; so they say. But some say: 'Even at the moment of cutting off the testicles, there is only an offense of wrong-doing. Gradually, when the male faculty and so on have disappeared, one becomes a 'paṇḍaka', who is unfit for ordination; then, he should be expelled through the destruction of the characteristic sign.' 'Tādisaṃ vā dukkhaṃ uppādentassa' means: for one who causes such suffering to himself by means of blows with the fist, etc.

252. Pāḷiyaṃ tuyheso pattoti “yo ca arahā ceva iddhimā ca, tassa dinnamevā”ti seṭṭhinā vuttaṃ, taṃ sandhāya vadati. Taṃ pattaṃ gahetvā tikkhattuṃ rājagahaṃ anupariyāyīti ettha veḷuparamparāya baddhapattassa uparibhāge ākāse nagaraṃ tikkhattuṃ anupariyāyitvā ṭhitabhāvaṃ sandhāya “pattaṃ gahetvā”ti vuttaṃ, na pana thero hatthena pattaṃ sayameva aggahesi. Keci pana vadanti “iddhibalena taṃ pattaṃ veḷuparamparato muñcitvā theraṃ anubandhamāno aṭṭhāsi, so ca anena hatthena gahito viya ahosī”ti. Tathā ṭhitameva pana sandhāya “bhāradvājassa hatthato pattaṃ gahetvā”ti vuttaṃ. Te ca manussā…pe… anubandhiṃsūti ye ca manussā paṭhamaṃ pāṭihāriyaṃ nāddasaṃsu, te amhākampi pāṭihāriyaṃ dassehīti theramanubandhiṃsu. Thero ca sīhabyagghādirūpaṃ gahetvā vikubbaniddhiṃ dasseti, te ca acchariyabbhutajātā uccāsaddā mahāsaddā ahesuṃ. Tenāha “kiṃ nu kho so, ānanda, uccāsaddo mahāsaddo”ti. Iddhipāṭihāriyaṃ na dassetabbanti ettha “yo pakativaṇṇaṃ vijahitvā kumāravaṇṇaṃ vā dasseti, nāgavaṇṇaṃ vā…pe… vividhampi senābyūhaṃ dassetī”ti (paṭi. ma. 3.13) evamāgatā attano sarīrassa vikārāpādanavasappavattā vikubbaniddhi adhippetāti āha “adhiṭṭhāniddhi pana appaṭikkhittā”ti. Pakatiyā eko bahukaṃ āvajjati, sataṃ vā sahassaṃ vā satasahassaṃ vā āvajjetvā ñāṇena adhiṭṭhāti “bahuko homī”ti (paṭi. ma. 3.10) evaṃ dassitā adhiṭṭhānavasena nipphannā adhiṭṭhāniddhi nāma. Gihivikaṭānīti gihisantakāni.

252. In the Pāḷi, 'tuyheso patto' (this bowl is yours)—this refers to what was said by the merchant: 'To one who is both an arahant and possesses psychic powers, what is given is truly given.' Regarding 'taṃ pattaṃ gahetvā tikkhattuṃ rājagahaṃ anupariyāyī' (taking that bowl, he circled Rājagaha three times), here, 'pattaṃ gahetvā' (taking the bowl) is said with reference to the fact that the bowl, tied to a succession of bamboos, having circled the city three times in the air above, remained stationary; the elder did not, however, take the bowl with his own hand. But some say: 'By psychic power, that bowl, being released from the succession of bamboos, stood following the elder, and it was as if it had been taken by his hand.' It is with reference to it remaining in that very state that 'bhāradvājassa hatthato pattaṃ gahetvā' (taking the bowl from Bhāradvāja’s hand) is said. 'Te ca manussā…pe… anubandhiṃsū' (And those people... followed) means: those people who did not see the first miracle followed the elder, saying, 'Show us a miracle too!' The elder, assuming the form of a lion, a tiger, etc., displayed the miracle of transformation (vikubbaniddhi), and those people, being amazed and astonished, became loud-voiced and great-voiced. Therefore, he said: 'Kiṃ nu kho so, ānanda, uccāsaddo mahāsaddo' (What, Ānanda, is that loud noise and great noise?). Regarding 'iddhipāṭihāriyaṃ na dassetabbaṃ' (the miracle of psychic power is not to be displayed), here, the intended miracle is the miracle of transformation (vikubbaniddhi), which proceeds by way of causing an alteration of one's own body, as comes in the passage: 'One who, having abandoned their natural appearance, displays the form of a youth, or the form of a nāga… or even displays a diverse military formation.' Therefore, he said: 'Adhiṭṭhāniddhi pana appaṭikkhittā' (But the miracle of resolve is not prohibited). The miracle accomplished by way of resolve, shown thus: 'By nature one, he adverts to being many. Having adverted to a hundred, or a thousand, or a hundred thousand, he resolves with knowledge: “May I be many,”' is called the miracle of resolve (adhiṭṭhāniddhi). 'Gihivikaṭāni' means: things belonging to householders.

253. Pāḷiyaṃ na acchupiyantīti na phusitāni honti. Rūpakākiṇṇānīti itthirūpādīhi ākiṇṇāni.

253. In the Pāḷi, 'na acchupiyanti' means: they are not touched. 'Rūpakākiṇṇāni' means: filled with female forms and the like.

254. Bhūmiādhāraketi dantādīhi kate valayādhārake. Etassa valayādhārakassa anuccatāya ṭhapitā pattā na paripatantīti “tayo patte [M 2.0231] ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ. Anuccatañhi sandhāya ayaṃ “bhūmiādhārako”ti vutto. Dāruādhārakadaṇḍādhārakesūti ekadārunā [V 2.0219] kataādhārake, bahūhi daṇḍehi kataādhārake ca. Ete ca uccatarā honti pattehi saha patanasabhāvā. Tena “susajjitesū”ti vuttaṃ. Bhamakoṭisadisoti yattha dhamakaraṇādiṃ pavesetvā likhanti, tassa bhamakassa koṭiyā sadiso. Tādisassa dāruādhārakassa avitthiṇṇatāya ṭhapitopi patto patatīti “anokāso”ti vutto.

254. `Bhūmiādhāraketi` means: in a ring-shaped stand made of ivory and so forth. Because bowls placed on this low, ring-shaped stand do not fall over, it is said: 'It is allowable to place three bowls.' Indeed, with reference to its lowness, this is called a `bhūmiādhāraka` (ground-stand). `Dāruādhārakadaṇḍādhārakesūti` means: in a stand made from a single piece of wood, and in a stand made from many sticks. These are higher and are liable to fall along with the bowls. Therefore, it is said `susajjitesū` (when well-arranged). `Bhamakoṭisadisoti` means: like the tip of a lathe, into which one inserts a water-strainer and so forth, and polishes it. Because such a wooden stand is not wide, a bowl placed on it also falls; therefore, it is called `anokāso` (unsuitable).

Ālindakamiḍḍhikādīnanti pamukhamiḍḍhikādīnaṃ, uccavatthukānanti attho. Bāhirapasseti pāsādādīnaṃ bahikuṭṭe. Tanukamiḍḍhikāyāti vedikāya. Sabbattha pana hatthappamāṇato abbhantare ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati. Ādhāre pana tato bahipi vaṭṭati.

`Ālindakamiḍḍhikādīnanti` means: of verandas at the front of a house and so forth, that is, those with high foundations; this is the meaning. `Bāhirapasseti` means: on the outer wall of a palace and so forth. `Tanukamiḍḍhikāyāti` means: on a railing. Everywhere, however, it is allowable to place it inside the measure of a bowl. But on a stand, it is also allowable outside of that.

Pāḷiyaṃ oṭṭhoti mukhavaṭṭi. Pattamāḷakanti upacikānaṃ anuṭṭhahanatthāya bhūmito uccataraṃ kataṃ vedikākāramāḷakaṃ. Mahāmukhakuṇḍasaṇṭhānāti mahāmukhacāṭisaṇṭhānā. Laggentassa dukkaṭanti kevalaṃ pattaṃ laggentassa, na thavikāya laggentassāti vadanti. Vīmaṃsitabbaṃ. Aññena pana bhaṇḍakenāti aññena bhārabandhanena bhaṇḍakena. “Bandhitvā olambetu”nti vuttattā pattatthavikāya aṃsabaddhako yathā laggitaṭṭhānato na parigaḷati, tathā sabbathāpi bandhitvā ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭati. Bandhitvāpi upari ṭhapetuṃ na vaṭṭatīti upari nisīdantā ottharitvā bhindantīti vuttaṃ. Tattha ṭhapetuṃ vaṭṭatīti nisīdanasaṅkābhāvato vuttaṃ. Bandhitvā vāti bandhitvā ṭhapitachatte vā. Yo kocīti bhattapūropi tucchapattopi.

In the Pāḷi, `oṭṭho` means the rim of the opening. `Pattamāḷakanti` means a railing-like platform made higher than the ground to prevent termites from climbing up. `Mahāmukhakuṇḍasaṇṭhānāti` means shaped like a large-mouthed pot. `Laggentassa dukkaṭanti`: they say it is an offense of wrong-doing for one who hangs just the bowl, not for one who hangs it with its bag. This should be investigated. `Aññena pana bhaṇḍakenāti` means with another small item for tying a load. Because it is said, 'Having tied it, let it hang,' it is allowable to tie the shoulder strap of the bowl-bag in such a way that it does not slip from the place where it is hung, and to place it thus tied in all circumstances. It is said that it is not allowable to place it above even when tied, because those sitting above might press down on it and break it. It is said, 'It is allowable to place it there,' because there is no fear of it being sat upon. `Bandhitvā vāti` means or on an umbrella that has been placed after being tied. `Yo kocīti` means whether a bowl full of food or an empty bowl.

255. Pariharitunti divase divase piṇḍāya caraṇatthāya ṭhapetuṃ. Pattaṃ alabhantena pana ekadivasaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā bhuñjitvā chaḍḍetuṃ vaṭṭati. Tenāha “tāvakālikaṃ paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Paṇṇapuṭādīsupi eseva nayo. Abhuṃ meti abhūti mayhaṃ, vināso mayhanti attho. Pāḷiyaṃ pisāco vatamanti pisāco vatāyaṃ, ayameva vā pāṭho. Pisācillikāti pisācadārakā. Chavasīsassa pattoti chavasīsamayo patto. Pakativikārasambandhe cetaṃ sāmivacanaṃ.

255. `Pariharitunti` means it is not allowable to keep it for going on alms-round day after day. But for one who does not obtain a bowl, it is allowable to go on alms-round for one day, eat, and then discard it. Therefore, he said: 'It is allowable to use it temporarily.' This same principle applies to leaf-containers and the like. `Abhuṃ meti` means 'my non-existence,' 'my destruction.' In the Pāḷi, `pisāco vatamanti` means 'Alas, this is a goblin!' Or, this very gloss is the reading. `Pisācillikāti` means young goblins. `Chavasīsassa pattoti` means a bowl made of a human skull. And this genitive case is in the sense of the relationship between the original substance and its modification.

Cabbetvāti [M 2.0232] niṭṭhubhitvā. “Paṭiggahaṃ katvā”ti vuttattā ucchiṭṭhahatthena udakaṃ gahetvā pattaṃ paripphositvā dhovanaghaṃsanavasena hatthaṃ dhovituṃ vaṭṭati, ettakena pattaṃ paṭiggahaṃ katvā hattho dhovito nāma na hoti. Ekaṃ udakagaṇḍusaṃ gahetvāti pattaṃ aphusitvā tattha udakameva ucchiṭṭhahatthena ukkhipitvā gaṇḍusaṃ katvā, vāmahattheneva vā pattaṃ ukkhipitvā mukhena gaṇḍusaṃ gahetumpi vaṭṭati. Bahi udakena vikkhāletvāti dvīsu aṅgulīsu āmisamattaṃ vikkhāletvā bahi gahetumpi vaṭṭati. Paṭikhāditukāmoti ettha na sayaṃ khāditukāmopi aññesaṃ khādanārahaṃ ṭhapetuṃ labhati[V 2.0220]. Tattheva katvāti patteyeva yathāṭhapitaṭṭhānato anuddharitvā. Luñcitvāti tato maṃsameva niravasesaṃ uppaṭṭetvā.

`Cabbetvāti` means having spat out. Because it is said, ‘having made it a receptacle,’ it is allowable to take water with a hand soiled with food, sprinkle the bowl, and wash the hand by means of moistening and rubbing. By just this much, it is not the case that the hand is considered washed by making the bowl a receptacle. `Ekaṃ udakagaṇḍusaṃ gahetvāti` means, without touching the bowl, to scoop up only water into it with the hand soiled with food and make a mouthful; or, it is also allowable to lift the bowl with the left hand and take a mouthful with the mouth. `Bahi udakena vikkhāletvāti` means it is also allowable to wash off just the food matter on two fingers and take it outside. In the phrase `Paṭikhāditukāmoti`, even if one does not desire to eat it oneself, one is allowed to keep what is suitable for others to eat. `Tattheva katvāti` means in the bowl itself, without removing it from the place where it was put. `Luñcitvāti` means from that, having scraped off only the meat without remainder.

256. Kiṇṇacuṇṇenāti surākiṇṇacuṇṇena. Makkhetunti sūciṃ makkhetuṃ. Nisseṇimpīti catūhi daṇḍehi cīvarappamāṇena āyatacaturassaṃ katvā baddhapaṭalampi. Ettha hi cīvarakoṭiyo samakaṃ bandhitvā cīvaraṃ yathāsukhaṃ sibbanti. Tattha attharitabbanti tassā nisseṇiyā upari cīvarassa upatthambhanatthāya attharitabbaṃ. Kathinasaṅkhātāya nisseṇiyā cīvarassa bandhanakarajju kathinarajjūti majjhimapadalopīsamāsoti āha “yāyā”tiādi. Tattha yasmā dvinnaṃ paṭalānaṃ ekasmiṃ adhike jāte tattha valiyo honti, tasmā dupaṭṭacīvarassa paṭaladvayampi samakaṃ katvā bandhanakarajju kathinarajjūti veditabbaṃ.

256. `Kiṇṇacuṇṇenāti` means with the powder of yeast for liquor. `Makkhetunti` means to smear the needle. `Nisseṇimpīti` means also a bound layer, made into an oblong rectangle with four sticks to the dimensions of a robe. For here, having bound the corners of the robe evenly, they sew the robe as they please. `Tattha attharitabbanti` means it should be spread over that frame for the purpose of supporting the robe. The binding cord for the robe on the frame called ‘kathina’ is `kathinarajju`; this is a compound with the middle term elided, thus he said the words beginning ‘yāyā.’ There, because when one of the two layers becomes longer, folds arise, therefore, the cord that binds after making the two layers of the double-layered robe even should be known as `kathinarajju`.

Pāḷiyaṃ kathinassa anto jīratīti kathine baddhassa cīvarassa pariyanto jīrati. Kathinanissitañhi cīvaraṃ idha nissayavohārena “kathina”nti vuttaṃ “mañcā ghosantī”tiādīsu viya. Anuvātaṃ paribhaṇḍanti kathine bandhanarajjūhi cīvarassa samantā pariyantassa ajīraṇatthaṃ yehi kehici coḷakehi dīghato anuvātaṃ, tiriyato paribhaṇḍañca sibbitvā kātuṃ yattha rajjuke pavesetvā daṇḍesu paliveṭhetvā cīvarasamakaṃ ākaḍḍhituṃ sakkā, tādisanti attho. Keci pana “kathinasaṅkhātesu kilañjādīsu eva ajīraṇatthāya anuvātaparibhaṇḍakaraṇaṃ anuññāta”nti vadanti. Tassa majjheti purāṇakathinasseva anto. Bhikkhuno pamāṇenāti bhikkhuno cīvarassa pamāṇena. Aññaṃ nisseṇinti dīghato ca tiriyato ca aññaṃ daṇḍaṃ ṭhapetvā bandhituṃ.

In the Pāḷi, `kathinassa anto jīratīti` means the edge of the robe bound on the kathina frame wears out. For the robe dependent on the kathina frame is here called ‘kathina’ by way of relational expression, as in ‘the beds are shouting.’ `Anuvātaṃ paribhaṇḍanti` means: to prevent the edge of the robe all around from wearing out due to the binding cords on the kathina frame, one is to make, by sewing with some pieces of cloth, a border lengthwise and a border crosswise, into which it is possible to insert cords, wind them around the poles, and pull it taut to be even with the robe; such is the meaning. Some, however, say: ‘The making of a lengthwise and crosswise border is permitted only on things called kathina frames, such as mats, for the purpose of preventing wear.’ `Tassa majjheti` means the inside of the old kathina frame only. `Bhikkhuno pamāṇenāti` means by the measure of the monk's robe. `Aññaṃ nisseṇinti` means to bind, having placed another pole lengthwise and crosswise.

Bidalakanti [M 2.0233] diguṇakaraṇasaṅkhātakiriyāvisesassa adhivacanaṃ. Tenāha “duguṇakaraṇa”nti. Pavesanasalākanti valīnaṃ aggahaṇatthāya pavesanakaveḷusalākādi. Pāḷiyaṃ paṭiggahanti aṅgulikañcukaṃ.

‘Bidalaka’ is a designation for the particular action known as ‘doubling.’ Therefore, he said ‘duguṇakaraṇa’ (doubling). ‘Pavesanasalāka’ means an inserting stick, such as one of bamboo, for the purpose of not taking up creases. In the Pāḷi, ‘paṭiggaha’ means a finger-stall.

257. Pāti nāma bhaṇḍaṭṭhapanako bhājanaviseso. Pāḷiyaṃ paṭiggahathavikanti pātiādibhājanatthavikaṃ. Cinitunti uccavatthupariyantassa apatanatthāya iṭṭhakādīhi cinituṃ. Ālambanabāhanti ālambanarajjudaṇḍādi. Paribhijjatīti kaṭasārādikaṃ kathinamajjhe bhaṅgaṃ hoti. Ussāpetvāti daṇḍakathinaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ.

257. ‘Pāti’ is a particular kind of vessel for placing goods. In the Pāḷi, ‘paṭiggahathavikā’ means a bag for vessels such as a pāti. ‘Cinituṃ’ means to build with bricks or the like so that the edge of a high foundation does not collapse. ‘Ālambanabāha’ means a supporting rope, pole, or the like. ‘Paribhijjati’ means that a coarse grass mat or the like becomes broken in the middle of the kathina frame. ‘Ussāpetvā’ is said with reference to a kathina frame made of poles.

258-9. Udakaṃ [V 2.0221] akappiyanti sappāṇakaṃ. Upanandhīti veraṃ bandhi. Addhānamaggo paṭipajjitabboti ettha addhayojanaṃ addhānamaggo nāma, taṃ paṭipajjitukāmassa sañcicca vihārūpacārātikkamane āpatti. Asañcicca gatassa pana yattha sarati, tattha ṭhatvā saṅghāṭikaṇṇādiṃ anadhiṭṭhahitvā gamane padavārena āpattīti veditabbaṃ. Na sammatīti na pahoti.

‘Udakaṃ akappiyaṃ’ means water with living beings. ‘Upanandhī’ means he bound enmity. In the phrase ‘Addhānamaggo paṭipajjitabbo,’ half a yojana is called a ‘long journey.’ For a monk who desires to undertake it, there is an offense in intentionally transgressing the monastery precinct, knowing he is without a water strainer. But for one who has gone unintentionally, wherever he remembers, having stopped there, it should be known that in going without determining the corner of his outer robe or the like as a strainer, there is an offense for every footstep. ‘Na sammati’ means it is not sufficient.

260. Abhisannakāyāti semhādidosasannicitakāyā. Tattha majjheti aggaḷapāsakassa majjhe. Uparīti aggaḷapāsakassa uparibhāge. Udakaṭṭhapanaṭṭhānanti udakaṭṭhapanatthāya paricchinditvā kataṭṭhānaṃ.

260. ‘Abhisannakāyā’ means those with bodies in which humors such as phlegm have accumulated. ‘Tattha majjhe’ means in the middle of the bolt-pin. ‘Upari’ means in the upper part of the bolt-pin. ‘Udakaṭṭhapanaṭṭhāna’ means a place made, having been demarcated, for the purpose of placing water.

261. Pāḷiyaṃ udapānanti kūpaṃ. Nīcavatthukoti kūpassa samantā kūlaṭṭhānaṃ, bhūmisamaṃ tiṭṭhatīti attho. Udakena otthariyyatīti samantā vassodakaṃ āgantvā kūpe patatīti attho.

261. In the Pāḷi, ‘udapāna’ means a well. ‘Nīcavatthuko’ means the place of the bank all around the well stands level with the ground; this is the meaning. ‘Udakena otthariyyatī’ means rainwater, having come from all around, falls into the well; this is the meaning.

262. Vāhentīti ussiñcanti. Arahaṭaghaṭiyantaṃ nāma cakkasaṇṭhānaṃ anekāraṃ are are ghaṭikāni bandhitvā ekena, dvīhi vā paribbhamiyamānayantaṃ.

262. ‘Vāhenti’ means they bail out. ‘Arahaṭaghaṭiyanta’ is the name for a machine in the shape of a wheel with many spokes, with pots tied to each and every spoke, which is caused to revolve by one or two people.

263. Āviddhapakkhapāsakanti kaṇṇikamaṇḍalassa samantā ṭhapitapakkhapāsakaṃ. Maṇḍaleti kaṇṇikamaṇḍale. Pakkhapāsake ṭhapetvāti samantā caturassākārena phalakādīni ṭhapetvā.

263. ‘Āviddhapakkhapāsakaṃ’ means having side-panels placed all around the central hub. ‘Maṇḍale’ means in the central hub. ‘Pakkhapāsake ṭhapetvā’ means having placed planks or the like in a square shape all around.

264. Namatakaṃ [M 2.0234] nāma santhatasadisanti keci vadanti. Keci pana “rukkhatacamaya”nti. Cammakhaṇḍaparihārenāti anadhiṭṭhahitvā sayanāsanavidhināti attho. Peḷāyāti aṭṭhaṃsasoḷasaṃsādiākārena katāya bhājanākārāya peḷāya. Yattha uṇhapāyāsādiṃ pakkhipitvā upari bhojanapātiṃ ṭhapenti bhattassa uṇhabhāvāvigamanatthaṃ, tādisassa bhājanākārassa ādhārassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Teneva pāḷiyaṃ “āsittakūpadhāna”nti vuttaṃ. Tassa ca pāyāsādīhi āsittakādhāroti attho. Idañca āsittakūpadhānaṃ paccantesu na jānanti kātuṃ, majjhimadeseyeva karonti. Keci pana “gihiparibhogo ayomayādi sabbopi ādhāro āsittakūpadhānameva anulometī”ti vadanti, eke pana “kappiyalohamayo ādhāro maḷorikameva anulometī”ti. Vīmaṃsitvā gahetabbaṃ. Pubbe pattaguttiyā ādhāro anuññāto. Idāni bhuñjituṃ maḷorikā anuññātā. Chiddanti chiddayuttaṃ. Viddhanti antovinividdhachiddaṃ. Āviddhanti samantato chiddaṃ.

264. Some say that a `namataka` is like a covering. Others, however, say it is 'made of tree bark.' `Cammakhaṇḍaparihārena` means: by the procedure for bedding and seats without having made a formal determination; this is the meaning. `Peḷā` refers to a stand that is a support for a vessel, made in forms such as eight-cornered or sixteen-cornered. This is a designation for such a stand, a support for a vessel, where, after placing hot milk-rice or the like inside, a food bowl is placed on top so that the cooked rice does not lose its heat. Therefore, in the Pāḷi, it is called an `āsittakūpadhāna`. And its meaning is: a stand into which milk-rice and so on are poured. And this `āsittakūpadhāna`, they do not know how to make in the border regions; they make it only in the Middle Country. Some, however, say, 'Any stand for household use, made of iron and so on, is in conformity with an `āsittakūpadhāna`.' Others, however, say, 'A stand made of allowable metal is in conformity only with a `maḷorikā`.' This should be taken up after investigation. Previously, a stand was allowed for the protection of the bowl. Now, a `maḷorikā` is allowed for eating. `Chidda` means possessed of a hole. `Viddha` means a hole pierced through within. `Āviddha` means pierced all around.

265. Pattaṃ nikkujjitunti ettha kammavācāya asambhogakaraṇavaseneva nikkujjanaṃ, na pattānaṃ [V 2.0222] adhomukhaṭṭhapanena. Tenāha “asambhogaṃ saṅghena karotū”tiādi, taṃ vaḍḍhaṃ kammavācāya saṅghena saddhiṃ asambhogaṃ saṅgho karotūti attho.

265. Here, in the phrase `pattaṃ nikkujjituṃ` (to overturn the bowl), the overturning occurs only by the power of making someone unassociable by means of a formal act, not by the act of placing bowls face down. Therefore, it is said, 'Let the Saṅgha make him unassociable.' The meaning is: Let the Saṅgha, by means of a formal act, make that Vaḍḍha the Licchavi someone with whom the Saṅgha does not associate.

Pattaṃ nikkujjeyyāti vaḍḍhassa pattanikkujjanadaṇḍakammaṃ kareyya. Asambhogaṃ saṅghena karaṇanti saṅghena vaḍḍhassa asambhogakaraṇaṃ. Yathā asambhogo hoti, tathā karaṇanti attho. Nikkujjito…pe… asambhogaṃ saṅghenāti ettha saṅghena asambhogo hotīti attho daṭṭhabbo. Evaṃ bhagavatā asambhogakaraṇassa āṇattattā, kammavācāya ca sāvitattā, aṭṭhakathāyañca “koci deyyadhammo na gahetabbo”ti vuttattā patte nikkujjite tassa santakaṃ ñatvā gaṇhantassa dukkaṭamevāti gahetabbaṃ.

`Pattaṃ nikkujjeyya` means: one should perform the penalty-act of overturning the bowl for Vaḍḍha. `Asambhogaṃ saṅghena karaṇaṃ` means: the Saṅgha's making Vaḍḍha unassociable. The meaning is: the doing of it in such a way that he becomes unassociable. In `Nikkujjito…pe… asambhogaṃ saṅghena`, the meaning should be understood as: he is unassociable with the Saṅgha. Thus, because the act of making someone unassociable was commanded by the Blessed One, because it was announced by a formal act, and because it is stated in the commentary, 'No offering whatsoever should be accepted,' it should be understood that when the bowl-overturning act has been performed, for a monk who accepts what he knows to be the property of that supporter, there is only a `dukkaṭa` offense.

Accayoti ñāyappaṭipattiṃ atikkamitvā pavatti, aparādhoti attho. Maṃ accagamāti maṃ atikkamma pavatto. Taṃ te mayaṃ paṭiggaṇhāmāti taṃ te aparādhaṃ mayaṃ khamāma. Bhikkhūnaṃ alābhāya parisakkatītiādīsu alābhāya [M 2.0235] parisakkanādito viratoti evamattho gahetabbo. Asambhogaṃ bhikkhusaṅghenāti ettha “kato”ti pāṭhaseso.

`Accayo` means a proceeding that transgresses right practice; the meaning is 'offense' (`aparādha`). `Maṃ accagamā` means: it proceeded, having transgressed against me. `Taṃ te mayaṃ paṭiggaṇhāma` means: we forgive that offense of yours. In texts such as `bhikkhūnaṃ alābhāya parisakkati`, the meaning should be taken thus: he has abstained from striving, etc., for the non-receipt of gain by the monks. In the phrase `asambhogaṃ bhikkhusaṅghena`, the remainder of the text is `kato`.

268. Yāva pacchimā sopānakaḷevarāti paṭhamasopānaphalakaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tañhi pacchā dussena santhatattā eva vuttaṃ. “Pacchimaṃ janataṃ tathāgato anukampatī”ti idaṃ thero anāgate bhikkhūnaṃ celapaṭikassa akkamanapaccayā apavādaṃ sikkhāpadapaññattiyā nivāraṇena bhagavato anukampaṃ sandhāyāha. Apagatagabbhāti vijātaputtā. Tenāha “maṅgalatthāyā”ti.

268. The phrase `yāva pacchimā sopānakaḷevarā` was said with reference to the first plank of the staircase. Indeed, it was said thus because that plank was later covered with a cloth. The Elder said the words, 'The Tathāgata has compassion for the last generation,' with reference to the Blessed One's compassion, which, in the future, would prevent blame for the monks by the laying down of a training rule, on account of the cause of stepping on a cloth covering. `Apagatagabbhā` means: they have given birth to sons. Therefore, he said, 'for the sake of auspiciousness.'

269-270. Bījaninti caturassabījaniṃ. Ekapaṇṇacchattanti tālapaṇṇādinā ekena pattena katachattaṃ.

`Bījaniṃ` means a four-cornered fan. `Ekapaṇṇacchattaṃ` means an umbrella made with a single leaf, such as a palm leaf.

274-5. Anurakkhaṇatthanti pariggahetvā gopanatthaṃ. Dīghaṃ kārentīti kesehi saddhiṃ acchinditvā ṭhapāpenti. Catukoṇanti yathā upari nalāṭantesu dve, heṭṭhā hanukapasse dveti cattāro koṇā paññāyanti, evaṃ caturassaṃ katvā kappāpanaṃ. Pāḷiyaṃ dāṭhikaṃ ṭhapāpentīti uttaroṭṭhe massuṃ acchinditvā ṭhapāpenti. Rudhīti khuddakavaṇaṃ.

`Anurakkhaṇatthaṃ` means: for the purpose of guarding by taking possession of. `Dīghaṃ kārenti` means: they have it left uncut together with the hair. `Catukoṇaṃ` is the causing to be shaved, having made it square in such a way that four corners appear: two on the temples above, and two on the sides of the jaw below. In the Pāḷi, `dāṭhikaṃ ṭhapāpenti` means: they have the mustache on the upper lip left uncut. `Rudhi` means a small wound.

277. Pāḷiyaṃ lohabhaṇḍakaṃsabhaṇḍasannicayoti lohabhaṇḍassa, kaṃsabhaṇḍassa ca sannicayoti [V 2.0223] attho. Bandhanamattanti vāsidaṇḍādīnaṃ koṭīsu apātanatthaṃ lohehi bandhanaṃ. Tantakanti āyogavāyanatthaṃ tadākārena pasāritatantaṃ.

277. In the Pāḷi, `lohabhaṇḍakaṃsabhaṇḍasannicayo` means the storing up of copper goods and bronze goods. `Bandhanamattaṃ` means the binding with metal at the ends of adze-handles and so on, to prevent splitting. `Tantakaṃ` means a loom with thread spread out in that shape for the purpose of weaving a breast-band.

278. “Yattha sarati, tattha bandhitabba”nti etena asañcicca kāyabandhanaṃ abandhitvā paviṭṭhassa anāpattīti dasseti. Murajavaṭṭisaṇṭhānaṃ veṭhetvā katanti evaṃ bahurajjuke ekato katvā nānāvaṇṇehi suttehi katanti keci vadanti. Ekavaṇṇasuttenāpi valayaghaṭakādivikāraṃ dassetvā veṭhitampi murajameva. Vikāraṃ pana adassetvā maṭṭhaṃ katvā nirantaraṃ veṭhitaṃ vaṭṭati. Teneva dutiyapārājikasaṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttaṃ “bahurajjuke ekato katvā ekena nirantaraṃ veṭhetvā kataṃ ‘bahurajjuka’nti na vattabbaṃ, vaṭṭatī”ti. Muddikakāyabandhanaṃ nāma caturassaṃ akatvā [M 2.0236] sajjitaṃ. Pāmaṅgadasā caturassā. Mudiṅgasaṇṭhānenāti varakasīsākārena. Pāsantoti dasāpariyosānaṃ.

278. By the phrase, 'Where one is mindful, there one should bind,' it is shown that there is no offense for one who enters without having bound the waist-band unintentionally. `Murajavaṭṭisaṇṭhānaṃ veṭhetvā kataṃ` (made by wrapping in the shape of a `muraja` drum): some say this is made by taking many cords together as one and making it with threads of various colors. Even if wrapped with a single-colored thread, showing variations like a bracelet, a water-pot, etc., it is still a `muraja`. However, if it is wrapped continuously, made smooth without showing variation, it is allowable. Therefore, in the commentary on the second Pārājika, it is said: 'A thing made by taking many cords together and wrapping them continuously with one should not be called ‘many-corded’; it is allowable.' A `muddikakāyabandhana` is a waist-band prepared without being made four-cornered. The fringes of a `pāmaṅga` are four-cornered. `Mudiṅgasaṇṭhānena` means: with the shape of a millet head. `Pāsanto` is the end of the fringe.

279. Pāḷiyaṃ gaṇṭhikaphalakaṃ pāsakaphalakanti ettha dārudantādimayesu phalakesu gaṇṭhikapāsakāni appetvā cīvare ṭhapetuṃ anuññātaṃ. Koṭṭo vivariyatīti anuvāto vivariyati.

279. In the Pāḷi, regarding `gaṇṭhikaphalakaṃ pāsakaphalakaṃ` (a board with a toggle, a board with a loop), it is allowed to attach toggles and loops to boards made of wood, ivory, and so on, and to place them on the robe. `Koṭṭo vivariyatī` (the compartment is opened) means: the lengthwise border is opened.

280-1. Pāḷikārakoti bhikkhūnaṃ yathāvuḍḍhaṃ pāḷiyā patiṭṭhāpako. Tassāpi tathā pārupituṃ na vaṭṭati. Pāḷiyaṃ muṇḍavaṭṭīti mallādayo.

`Pāḷikārako` is a monk who arranges the other monks in a row according to seniority. For him also, it is not allowable to wear it in that way. In the Pāḷi, `muṇḍavaṭṭī` refers to wrestlers and so on.

282. Pamāṇaṅgulenāti vaḍḍhakīaṅgulena. Keci pana “pakatiaṅgulenā”ti vadanti, taṃ caturaṅgulapacchimakavacanena na sameti. Na hi pakataṅgulena caturaṅgulappamāṇaṃ dantakaṭṭhaṃ kaṇṭhe avilaggaṃ khādituṃ sakāti.

282. `Pamāṇaṅgulena` means with the carpenter's finger-breadth. Some, however, say 'with the natural finger-breadth,' but that statement does not accord with the statement of 'a minimum of four finger-breadths.' For indeed, it is not possible to chew a tooth-stick measuring four natural finger-breadths without it getting stuck in the throat.

285. Pāḷiyaṃ sakāya niruttiyā buddhavacanaṃ dūsentīti māgadhabhāsāya sabbesaṃ vattuṃ sukaratāya hīnajaccāpi uggaṇhantā dūsentīti attho.

285. In the Pāḷi, `sakāya niruttiyā buddhavacanaṃ dūsenti` means: because the Māgadha language is easy for all to recite, even those of low birth, while learning it, corrupt it; this is the meaning.

289. Mā bhikkhū byābādhayiṃsūti lasuṇagandhena bhikkhū mā bādhayiṃsu.

289. `Mā bhikkhū byābādhayiṃsu` means: let them not trouble the monks with the smell of garlic.

291. Avalekhanapīṭharoti [V 2.0224] avalekhanakaṭṭhānaṃ ṭhapanabhājanaviseso. Apidhānanti pidhānaphalakādi.

291. `Avalekhanapīṭhara` means a special receptacle for placing styluses. `Apidhāna` means a covering board and so forth.

Khuddakavatthukathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on Minor Matters is finished.

Khuddakavatthukkhandhakavaṇṇanānayo niṭṭhito.

The Method of the Explanation of the Khandhaka on Minor Matters is finished.

6. Senāsanakkhandhako

6. The Khandhaka on Lodgings

Vihārānujānanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Permission for Dwellings

295. Senāsanakkhandhake [M 2.0237][V 2.0225] sisireti sisirakāle himapātavasena sattāhavaddalikādivassapātavassena ca uppanno kharo sītasamphasso adhippetoti āha “samphusitako”ti. “Tato”ti idaṃ kattuatthe nissakkavacanaṃ, tena ca vihārena vātātapo paṭihaññatīti atthoti āha “vihārena paṭihaññatī”ti.

295. In the Section on Lodgings, `sisire` means in the cool season. A harsh, cold touch that has arisen by way of snowfall and by way of unseasonal rain, such as a seven-day drizzle, is intended. Therefore, he said, `samphusitako.` This word `tato` is an ablative in the sense of the agent, and the meaning is that wind and sun are warded off by a dwelling. Therefore, he said, `vihārena paṭihaññati.`

296. Āviñchanachiddanti yattha aṅguliṃ vā rajjusaṅkhalikādiṃ vā pavesetvā kavāṭaṃ ākaḍḍhantā dvārabāhaṃ phusāpenti, tassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Senāsanaparibhoge akappiyaṃ nāma natthīti dassanatthaṃ “sacepi dīpinaṅguṭṭhenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Cetiye vedikāsadisanti vātapānadāruṃ vā jālaṃ vā aṭṭhapetvā dāruṭṭhāne cetiye vedikāya paṭṭādīni viya iṭṭhakādīhi uddhaṃ, tiriyañca paṭṭikādayo dassetvā catuchiddayuttaṃ kataṃ. Thambhakavātapānaṃ nāma tiriyaṃ dārūni adatvā uddhaṃ ṭhapitadārūhi eva kataṃ. Coḷakapādapuñchanaṃ bandhitunti vātapānappamāṇena pādapuñchanasadisaṃ coḷakādinā bandhitvā vagguliādippavesananivāraṇatthaṃ, kathetunti attho. Miḍḍhakanti mañcākārena kaṭṭhamattikādīhi katavedikākāraṃ.

296. `Āviñchanachidda` is the designation for a hole into which, having inserted a finger or a rope, chain, and so forth, one pulls the door-leaf, causing it to touch the door-post. To show that there is nothing designated as improper in the use of a lodging, `sacepi dīpinaṅguṭṭhena` ('even with a leopard's tail'), and so forth, was said. `Similar to the railing at a cetiya` means: without setting up a wooden window-frame or a lattice, in place of wood, it is made with bricks and so forth, vertically and horizontally, showing panels and so forth, like the panels of a railing at a cetiya, and endowed with four holes. A `thambhakavātapāna` (pillar-window) is one made only with vertically placed wood, without inserting horizontal pieces of wood. `To tie a cloth foot-wiper` means: for the purpose of preventing the entry of bats and so forth, to close it by tying a cloth or the like, similar in size to a foot-wiper, to the dimensions of the window; this is the meaning. `Miḍḍhaka` means a structure in the shape of a railing, made of wood, clay, and so forth, in the form of a couch.

297. Caturassapīṭhanti samacaturassaṃ. Aṭṭhaṅgulapādakaṃ vaṭṭatīti aṭṭhaṅgulapādakameva vaṭṭati. Pamāṇātikkantopi vaṭṭatīti samacaturassameva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Āyatacaturassā pana sattaṅgapañcaṅgāpi uccapādā na vaṭṭanti. Vetteheva caturassādiākārena kataṃ bhaddapīṭhanti āha “vettamayaṃ pīṭha”nti. Dārupaṭṭikāya uparīti aṭaniākārena ṭhitadārupaṭalassa heṭṭhā uddhaṃ pādaṃ katvā. Pavesanakālañhi sandhāya “uparī”ti vuttaṃ. Eḷakassa pacchimapādadvayaṃ viya vaṅkākārena ṭhitattā panetaṃ “eḷakapādapīṭha”nti vuttaṃ. Paloṭhentīti saha mañcehi pavaṭṭenti. Rukkhe[V 2.0226], latā ca muñcitvā avasesaṃ gacchādikaṃ sabbampi tiṇajāti evāti āha “yesaṃ kesañci tiṇajātikāna”ntiādi.

297. `Caturassapīṭha` means a perfectly square stool. `Aṭṭhaṅgulapādakaṃ vaṭṭati` means that only a leg of eight finger-breadths is allowable. `Pamāṇātikkantopi vaṭṭati` was said with reference only to a perfectly square one. But for an oblong rectangular one, even high-legged sattaṅga and pañcaṅga couches are not allowable. Because a fine stool made of only rattan in a square or other shape is called a `bhaddapīṭha,` he said, `vettamayaṃ pīṭhaṃ` (a stool made of rattan). `Dārupaṭṭikāya upari` (above the wooden plank): indeed, `upari` was said with reference to the time of insertion, having turned the feet upwards below the wooden surface which is positioned like a scaffold. And because it stands in a bent shape like the two hind legs of a goat, this is called an `eḷakapādapīṭha` (goat-foot stool). `Paloṭhenti` means they roll them along together with the couches. Having excluded trees and vines, all the remainder, such as shrubs, are indeed of the grass family; therefore, he said, `yesaṃkesañci tiṇajātikānaṃ` ('of whatever grass family'), and so forth.

Upadahantīti [M 2.0238] ṭhapenti. Sīsappamāṇaṃ nāma yattha gīvāya saha sakalaṃ sīsaṃ ṭhapetuṃ sakkā, tassa ca muṭṭhiratanaṃ vitthārappamāṇanti dassento “vitthārato”tiādimāha. Idañca bimbohanassa ubhosu antesu ṭhapetabbacoḷappamāṇadassanaṃ. Tassa vasena bimbohanassa vitthārappamāṇaṃ paricchijjati, taṃ vaṭṭaṃ vā caturassaṃ vā katvā sibbitaṃ yathā koṭito koṭi vitthārato puthulaṭṭhānaṃ muṭṭhiratanappamāṇaṃ hoti, evaṃ sibbitabbaṃ. Ito adhikaṃ na vaṭṭati, taṃ pana antesu ṭhapitacoḷaṃ koṭiyā koṭiṃ āhacca diguṇaṃ kataṃ tikaṇṇaṃ hoti. Tesu tīsu kaṇṇesu dvinnaṃ kaṇṇānamantaraṃ vidatthicaturaṅgulaṃ hoti, majjhaṭṭhānaṃ koṭito koṭiṃ āhacca muṭṭhiratanaṃ hoti, idamassa ukkaṭṭhappamāṇaṃ. Tenāha “tīsu kaṇṇesū”tiādi.

'Upadahanti' means they place. 'Head-sized' is a pillow on which it is possible to place the entire head together with the neck. And showing that its width-measurement is a closed cubit, he said, 'vitthārato' ('in width'), and so forth. And this shows the measurement of the cloth to be placed on both ends of the bolster. By means of that, the width-measurement of the bolster is determined. It should be sewn, having been made either round or square, in such a way that the broad area, from one end to the other in width, is the measure of a closed cubit. More than this is not allowable. And that cloth placed at the ends, when doubled by touching one corner to the other, becomes three-cornered. Among those three corners, the interval between two corners is one span and four finger-breadths. The middle part, touching one end to the other, is a closed cubit. This is its maximum measurement. Therefore, he said, 'tīsu kaṇṇesu' ('in the three corners'), and so forth.

“Kambalameva…pe… uṇṇabhisisaṅkhyameva gacchatī”ti sāmaññato vuttattā gonakādiakappiyampi uṇṇamayattharaṇaṃ bhisiyaṃ pakkhipitvā sayituṃ vaṭṭatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Because it was said generally, 'Kambalameva…pe… uṇṇabhisisaṅkhyameva gacchati' ('A woolen blanket…pe… is reckoned only as a wool-stuffed mattress'), it should be understood that it is allowable to sleep on even an improper woolen spread, such as a gonaka, after putting it inside a mattress.

Masūraketi cammamayabhisiyaṃ. Cammamayaṃ pana bimbohanaṃ tūlapuṇṇampi na vaṭṭati. Pāḷiyaṃ senāsanaparikkhāradussanti senāsanaparikkhārakaraṇatthāya dussaṃ. Bhisiṃ onandhitunti bhisitthavikāya pakkhipitvā bandhituṃ. Paribhijjatīti mañcādito sāriyamānā pīṭhakoṭiādīsu nisīdantehi ghaṃsiyamānā bhisi paribhijjati. Onaddhamañcanti bhisiṃ ekābaddhaṃ katvā baddhamañcaṃ. Pāḷiyaṃ chaviṃ uppāṭetvā harantīti bhisicchaviṃ corā haranti. Phositunti corehi haritassa pacchā haritasaññāṇaphusitabindūni dātuṃ. Bhittikammanti nānāvaṇṇehi vibhittirājikaraṇaṃ. Hatthakammanti hatthena yaṃ kiñci saññākaraṇaṃ.

'Masūrake' means on a leather mattress. But a leather bolster, even if filled with cotton, is not allowable. In the Pāḷi, 'senāsanaparikkhāradussaṃ' means cloth set aside for the purpose of making requisites for a lodging. 'Bhisiṃ onandhituṃ' means to tie it after putting it into a mattress-cover. 'Paribhijjati' means: the mattress is destroyed when, being moved from a couch and so forth, it is rubbed by those sitting on the edges of stools and so forth. 'Onaddhamañcaṃ' means a couch that is bound, having been made integrally with the mattress. In the Pāḷi, 'chaviṃ uppāṭetvā haranti' means thieves take the mattress-cover. 'Phosituṃ' means to apply dots, making spots as a sign of its having been taken, after it was taken by thieves. 'Bhittikammaṃ' means making divisions, drawing lines with various colors. 'Hatthakammaṃ' means making any kind of sign with the hand.

298. Pāḷiyaṃ na nipatatīti na allīyati. Paṭibāhetvāti ghaṃsitvā. Na nibandhatīti anibandhanīyo, na lagganakoti attho.

298. In the Pāḷi, 'na nipatati' means it does not cling. 'Paṭibāhetvā' means having scraped. 'Na nibandhati' means it does not stick fast; therefore, it is called 'anibandanīya' (not sticking), meaning non-adhering.

299. “Karohī”ti vattumpi na labbhatīti āṇattiyā eva paṭikkhittattā dvārapālaṃ “kiṃ na karosī”tiādinā pariyāyena vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Jātakapakaraṇanti jātakapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ itthipurisādi yaṃ kiñci rūpaṃ adhippetaṃ. “Parehi kārāpetu”nti vuttattā buddharūpampi sayaṃ kātuṃ na labhati. Pāḷiyaṃ pañcapaṭikanti jātiādipañcappakāravaṇṇamaṭṭhaṃ.

299. Even to say, 'Do it,' is not permissible, because it is prohibited by way of a command. It is permissible to speak to the gatekeeper indirectly with such phrases as, 'Why do you not do it?'. By 'Jātaka section' is intended any kind of figure connected with the Jātakas, such as those of women, men, and so on. Because it was said, 'One may have it made by others,' one may not make even an image of the Buddha oneself. In the Pāḷi, 'pañcapaṭika' is the application of a smooth colored finish of five kinds, beginning with earth-based color.

300. Upacāro [M 2.0239][V 2.0227] na hotīti gabbhassa bahi samantā anuparigamanassa okāso nappahoti. Rukkhaṃ vijjhitvāti tacchitasāradāruṃ aggasamīpe vijjhitvā. Katvāti chidde katvā. Kappakataṃ viya sārakhāṇuke ākoṭetvā evaṃ katameva “āharimaṃ bhittipāda”nti vuttaṃ. Upatthambhanatthaṃ bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhāpetunti jiṇṇabhittipādena bahi samānabhāraṃ khāṇukappasīsena ussāpetvā mūlena bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhāpetuṃ. Parittāṇatthanti ullittāvalittakuṭiyā ovassanaṭṭhānassa parittāṇatthaṃ. Kiṭikanti tālapaṇṇādīhi katapadalaṃ. Madditamattikanti ovassanachiddassa pidahanatthaṃ vuttaṃ.
