However, on a seat higher than the elder's seat, it is not proper to sit even after asking. If that seat, though nearby, is lower, it is proper to sit even without asking. 'The offense is for the senior elder alone' means there is an offense because of the offense of obstructing with a seat. 'Without spreading' means not lifting up the worn outer robe; this is the meaning.

Pāḷiyaṃ “ubhohi hatthehi…pe… odano paṭiggahetabbo”ti idaṃ hatthatale vā pacchipiṭṭhiādidussaṇṭhitādhāre vā pattaṃ ṭhapetvā odanassa gahaṇakāle pattassa apatanatthāya vuttaṃ, susajjite pana ādhāre pattaṃ ṭhapetvā ekena hatthena taṃ parāmasitvāpi odanaṃ paṭiggahetuṃ vaṭṭati eva. Ubhohi hatthehi…pe… udakaṃ paṭiggahetabbanti etthāpi eseva nayo.

In the Pāḷi, the statement 'with both hands... rice should be received' is said to prevent the bowl from falling when receiving rice, when the bowl is placed on the palm of the hand or on a poorly placed support such as the back of a basket. However, on a well-prepared support, it is indeed permissible to receive the rice even while touching the bowl with one hand after placing it there. In the statement 'with both hands... water should be received,' this is the same principle.

Hatthadhovanaudakanti bhojanāvasāne udakaṃ. Tenāha “pānīyaṃ pivitvā hatthā dhovitabbā”ti. Tena pariyosāne dhovanameva paṭikkhittaṃ, bhojanantare pana pānīyapivanādinā nayena hatthaṃ dhovitvā puna bhuñjituṃ vaṭṭatīti dasseti. Potthakesu pana “pānīyaṃ pivitvā hatthā na dhovitabbā”ti likhanti, taṃ purimavacanena na sameti pariyosāne udakasseva “hatthadhovanaudaka”nti vuttattā. Sace manussā dhovatha, bhantetiādi niṭṭhitabhattaṃ nisinnaṃ theraṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Dhure dvārasamīpe.

'Hand-washing water' means water at the end of the meal. Therefore, he said, 'Having drunk drinking water, the hands should be washed.' By this, washing at the very end is rejected, but it shows that during the meal, it is proper to wash one's hand by means of drinking water, etc., and eat again. However, in the books they write, 'Having drunk drinking water, the hands should not be washed.' That does not agree with the preceding statement, because it is said that the water at the end is itself 'hand-washing water.' The words 'If, venerable sir, you wash,' etc., are said in reference to an elder who is seated, having finished his meal. 'At the head' means near the door.

Bhattaggavattakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on Observances in the Refectory is concluded.

Piṇḍacārikavattakathādivaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Observances for Alms-Wandering, etc.

366. Pāḷiyaṃ ṭhāpeti vāti tiṭṭha bhanteti vadanti.

366. In the Pāḷi, 'ṭhāpeti vā' means they say, 'Stand, Venerable sir.'

367. Atthi, bhante, nakkhattapadānīti nakkhattapadavisayāni ñātāni atthi, assayujādinakkhattaṃ jānāthāti adhippāyo. Tenāha “na jānāma, āvuso”ti. Atthi, bhante[V 2.0247], disābhāganti etthāpi eseva nayo. Kenajja, bhante, yuttanti kena nakkhattena cando yuttoti attho.

367. 'Venerable sir, are there positions of constellations?' means: 'Are the domains of the constellations' positions known?' The intention is: 'Do you know the constellation Assayuja and so forth?' Therefore, he said, 'We do not know, friend.' Regarding 'Venerable sir, are there divisions of directions?', here too, this is the same method. 'With what is it conjoined today, Venerable sir?' means: 'With which constellation is the moon conjoined?'; this is the meaning.

369. Aṅgaṇeti [M 2.0260] abbhokāse. Evameva paṭipajjitabbanti uddesadānādi āpucchitabbanti dasseti.

369. 'Aṅgaṇe' means in an open space. By the text 'Just so should one practice,' it shows that for giving instruction and so forth, one should ask permission.

374. Nibaddhagamanatthāyāti attanova nirantaragamanatthāya. Ūhaditāti ettha hada-dhātussa vaccavissajjanatthatāyāha “bahi vaccamakkhitā”ti.

374. 'For the purpose of continuous going' means for the purpose of one's own uninterrupted going. Regarding 'ūhaditā', because the root 'hada' has the meaning of excreting feces, he says, 'smeared with excrement outside.'

Piṇḍacārikavattakathādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Observances for Alms-Wandering, etc., is finished.

Vattakkhandhakavaṇṇanānayo niṭṭhito.

The method of the commentary on the Chapter on Observances is finished.

9. Pātimokkhaṭṭhapanakkhandhako

9. The Chapter on the Suspension of the Pātimokkha

Pātimokkhuddesayācanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse on Requesting the Pātimokkha Recitation

383. Pātimokkhaṭṭhapanakkhandhake [M 2.0261][V 2.0248] pāḷiyaṃ nandimukhiyāti odātadisāmukhatāya tuṭṭhamukhiyā. “Uddhastaṃ aruṇa”nti vatvāpi “uddisatu, bhante, bhagavā”ti pātimokkhuddesayācanaṃ anuposathe uposathakaraṇapaṭikkhepassa sikkhāpadassa apaññattattā therena katanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kasmā pana bhagavā evaṃ tuṇhībhūtova tiyāmarattiṃ vītināmesīti? Aparisuddhāya parisāya uposathādisaṃvāsakaraṇassa sāvajjataṃ bhikkhusaṅghe pākaṭaṃ kātuṃ, tañca āyatiṃ bhikkhūnaṃ tathāpaṭipajjanatthaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ ñāpetuṃ. Keci panettha “aparisuddhampi puggalaṃ tassa sammukhā ‘aparisuddho’ti vattuṃ mahākaruṇāya avisahanto bhagavā tathā nisīdī”ti kāraṇaṃ vadanti. Taṃ akāraṇaṃ pacchāpi avattabbato, mahāmoggallānattherenāpi taṃ bāhāyaṃ gahetvā bahi nīharaṇassa akattabbatāpasaṅgato. Tasmā yathāvuttamevettha kāraṇanti. Teneva “aṭṭhānametaṃ, bhikkhave, anavakāso, yaṃ tathāgato aparisuddhāya parisāya uposathaṃ kareyya, pātimokkhaṃ uddiseyyā”ti (a. ni. 8.20; cūḷava. 386; udā. 45) vatvā “na ca, bhikkhave, sāpattikena pātimokkhaṃ sotabba”ntiādinā (cūḷava. 386) sāpattikaparisāya kattabbavidhi dassito.

383. In the Chapter on the Suspension of the Pātimokkha, in the Pāḷi, 'nandimukhiyā' means having a delighted face because the face of the direction is bright. Even after saying, 'The dawn has arisen,' the request for the Pātimokkha recitation—'Venerable sir, may the Blessed One recite the Pātimokkha'—was made by the elder because the training rule prohibiting the performance of the Uposatha on a non-Uposatha day had not yet been laid down; thus it should be understood. But why did the Blessed One let the three watches of the night pass in this way, remaining silent? To make manifest to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus the faultiness of performing the Uposatha and other communal acts with an impure assembly, and also to make known that training rule for bhikkhus in the future to practice accordingly. Some here state the reason thus: 'The Blessed One sat in that way because, out of great compassion, he was unable to bear saying "you are impure" in the presence of that impure person.' That is not the reason. Why? Because it would have been improper to say it later as well, and because of the consequence that it would have been improper for even the Elder Mahāmoggallāna to take him by the arm and lead him outside. Therefore, it should be understood that the reason here is only as has been stated. For that very reason, having said, 'Monks, this is impossible, it cannot happen, that the Tathāgata would perform the Uposatha or recite the Pātimokkha in an impure assembly,' and by the text beginning, 'And, monks, one with an offense should not listen to the Pātimokkha,' the procedure to be followed in an assembly with an offender was shown.

Saṅkassarasamācāranti kiñcideva asāruppaṃ disvā “idaṃ iminā kataṃ bhavissatī”ti parehi saṅkāya saritabbasamācāraṃ, attanā vā “mama anācāraṃ ete jānantī”ti saṅkāya saritabbasamācāraṃ. Samaṇavesadhāraṇena, saṅghikapaccayabhāgagahaṇādinā ca jīvikaṃ kappento “ahaṃ samaṇo”ti paṭiññaṃ adentopi atthato dento viya hotīti “samaṇapaṭiññaṃ brahmacāripaṭiñña”nti vuttaṃ. Avassutanti kilesāvassanena tintaṃ. Sañjātadussilyakacavarattā kasambujātaṃ[V 2.0249], asāratāya vā kasambu viya jātaṃ. Bahidvārakoṭṭhakā nikkhāmetvāti dvārasālato bahi nikkhamāpetvā.

'Saṅkassarasamācāra' means conduct to be recalled with suspicion by others who, upon seeing something improper, think, "This must have been done by him"; or, conduct to be recalled with suspicion by oneself, thinking, "They know of my misconduct." One who makes a living by wearing the guise of a recluse and by taking a share of communal requisites and so forth, even while not making the claim "I am a recluse," is in effect like one who does make it; therefore, it is called "the claim of being a recluse, the claim of leading the holy life." 'Avassuta' means soaked by the raining down of the defilements. 'Kasambujāta' means having become rubbish on account of being the refuse of arisen immorality, or having become like rubbish due to worthlessness. 'Bahidvārakoṭṭhakā nikkhāmetvā' means having made them go out from the gate-hall to the outside.

384. Mahāsamudde [M 2.0262] abhiramantīti bahuso dassanapavisanādinā mahāsamudde abhiratiṃ vindanti. Na āyatakeneva papātoti chinnataṭamahāsobbho viya na āditova ninnoti attho. Ṭhitadhammoti avaṭṭhitasabhāvo. Pūrattanti puṇṇattaṃ. Nāgāti sappajātikā.

384. 'They delight in the great ocean' means they find delight in the great ocean by frequently seeing, entering, and so forth. 'Not a sheer drop' means it is not deep from the very beginning, like a great chasm with a sheer bank. 'Of steadfast nature' means of established nature. 'Fullness' means fullness. 'Nāgas' means those of the serpent species.

Pātimokkhuddesayācanakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on Requesting the Pātimokkha Recitation is concluded.

Pātimokkhasavanārahakathādivaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on Those Fit to Hear the Pātimokkha, and Other Topics

386. Udāharitabbanti pāḷiyā avatvā tamatthaṃ yāya kāyaci bhāsāya udāhaṭampi udāhaṭamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

386. Regarding 'udāharitabbaṃ': it should be understood that even if the Pāḷi is not recited, if its meaning is expressed in any language whatsoever, it is indeed an expression.

Pure vā pacchā vāti ñattiārambhato pubbe vā ñattiniṭṭhānato pacchā vā.

Regarding 'pure vā pacchā vā': it means either before the commencement of the motion or after the conclusion of the motion.

387. Katañca akatañca ubhayaṃ gahetvāti yassa katāpi atthi akatāpi. Tassa tadubhayaṃ gahetvā. Dhammikaṃ sāmagginti dhammikaṃ samaggakammaṃ. Paccādiyatīti ukkoṭanādhippāyena puna kātuṃ ādiyati.

387. Regarding 'katañca akatañca ubhayaṃ gahetvā': it means taking both of these in the case of a monk for whom there is a deed that is done and a deed that is not done. Regarding 'dhammikaṃ sāmaggiṃ': it means a unified act in accordance with the Dhamma. Regarding 'paccādiyati': it is taken up to be done again with the intention of reopening the case.

388. Ākārādisaññā veditabbāti ākāraliṅganimittanāmāni vuttānīti veditabbāni.

388. Regarding 'ākārādisaññā veditabbā': it should be understood that the terms 'ākāra' (characteristic), 'liṅga' (sign), and 'nimitta' (mark) have been spoken of.

Pātimokkhasavanārahakathādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on Those Fit to Hear the Pātimokkha, and Other Topics, is concluded.

Attādānaaṅgakathādivaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Factors of Taking Up a Case Oneself, and Other Topics

398. Puna codetuṃ attanā ādātabbaṃ gahetabbaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ attādānanti āha “sāsanaṃ sodhetukāmo”tiādi. Vassārattoti vassakālo. Sopi hi dubbhikkhādikālo viya adhikaraṇavūpasamatthaṃ lajjiparisāya dūrato ānayanassa, āgatānañca piṇḍāya caraṇādisamācārassa dukkarattā akālo eva.

398. An `adhikaraṇa` (legal issue) to be taken up by oneself in order to accuse again is `attādāna` (taking up by oneself); therefore, it is said, "wishing to purify the Dispensation," and so on. Regarding 'vassāratto': it is the rainy season. Indeed, that time, like a time of famine and so on, is an unsuitable time for settling a legal issue, due to the difficulty of bringing a conscientious assembly from afar, and for those who have arrived, the difficulty of such conduct as going for alms.

Samanussaraṇakaraṇanti [V 2.0250] anussaritānussaritakkhaṇe pītipāmojjajananato anussaraṇuppādakaṃ. Vigatūpakkilesa…pe… saṃvattatīti ettha yathā [M 2.0263] abbhahimādiupakkilesavirahitānaṃ candimasūriyānaṃ sassirīkatā hoti, evamassāpi codakassa pāpapuggalūpakkilesavigamena sassirīkatā hotīti adhippāyo.

Regarding 'samanussaraṇakaraṇaṃ': it produces recollection because it generates joy and gladness in the moment of repeated recollection. The meaning here is this: just as there is the glorious state of the moon and sun, which are free from defilements such as clouds and mist, so too for this accuser, through the removal of the defilement that is an evil person, there is a glorious state.

399. Adhigataṃ mettacittanti appanāppattaṃ mettajhānaṃ.

399. Regarding 'adhigataṃ mettacittaṃ': it is the mettā-jhāna that has reached absorption.

400-1. “Dosantaro”ti ettha antara-saddo cittapariyāyoti āha “na duṭṭhacitto hutvā”ti.

In the word 'dosantaro', the word 'antara' is a synonym for 'citta' (mind); therefore, it is said, "na paduṭṭhacitto" (not with a corrupted mind).

Kāruññaṃ nāma karuṇā evāti āha “kāruññatāti karuṇābhāvo”ti. Karuṇanti appanāppattaṃ vadati. Tathā mettanti.

What is called 'kāruñña' is the state of 'karuṇā'; therefore, it is said, "kāruññatā is karuṇābhāvo" (the quality of compassion is the state of compassion). By the reading 'karuṇaṃ', it speaks of compassion that has reached absorption. Mettā is also likewise.

Attādānaaṅgakathādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Factors of Taking Up a Case Oneself, and Other Topics, is concluded.

Pātimokkhaṭṭhapanakkhandhakavaṇṇanānayo niṭṭhito.

The Method for the Explanation of the Chapter on the Suspension of the Pātimokkha is concluded.

10. Bhikkhunikkhandhako

10. The Chapter on Bhikkhunīs

Mahāpajāpatigotamīvatthukathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Story of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī

403. Bhikkhunikkhandhake [M 2.0264][V 2.0251] “mātugāmassa pabbajitattā”ti idaṃ pañcavassasatato uddhaṃ saddhammassa appavattanakāraṇadassanaṃ. Sukkhavipassakakhīṇāsavavasena vassasahassantiādi khandhakabhāṇakānaṃ mataṃ gahetvā vuttaṃ. Dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “paṭisambhidāppattehi vassasahassaṃ aṭṭhāsi, chaḷabhiññehi vassasahassaṃ, tevijjehi vassasahassaṃ, sukkhavipassakehi vassasahassaṃ, pātimokkhehi vassasahassaṃ aṭṭhāsī”ti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 3.161) vuttaṃ. Aṅguttara (a. ni. aṭṭha. 3.8.51) -saṃyuttaṭṭhakathāsupi (saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 2.2.156) aññathāva vuttaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ aññamaññaviruddhampi taṃtaṃbhāṇakānaṃ matena likhitasīhaḷaṭṭhakathāsu āgatanayameva gahetvā ācariyena likhitaṃ īdise kathāvirodhe sāsanaparihāniyā abhāvato, sodhanupāyābhāvā ca. Paramatthavirodho eva hi suttādinayena sodhanīyo, na kathāmaggavirodhoti.

403. In the Bhikkhunīkkhandhaka, the statement "because of the going forth of women" shows the reason for the true teaching (the fruit of Arahantship) not continuing beyond five hundred years. The statement "a thousand years by way of dry-insight destroyers of the cankers," and so on, is said having adopted the view of the reciters of the Khandhaka. However, in the commentary to the Dīghanikāya it is said: "It stood for a thousand years through those who had attained the analytical knowledges; for a thousand years through those with the six supernormal knowledges; for a thousand years through those with the three true knowledges; for a thousand years through the dry-insight meditators; for a thousand years through the Pātimokkha." In the commentaries to the Aṅguttaranikāya and Saṃyuttanikāya it is also stated otherwise. All of this, though mutually contradictory, was written by the commentator by adopting only the method that comes in the written Sinhala commentaries according to the views of the respective reciters. Why? Because in such a contradiction of accounts there is no decline of the Dispensation, and because there is no means for correction. Indeed, only a contradiction of the ultimate meaning should be corrected by the method of the suttas and so on; a contradiction in the narrative path should not be corrected.

Mahāpajāpatigotamīvatthukathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Story of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī is concluded.

Bhikkhunīupasampadānujānanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on Permitting the Higher Ordination of Bhikkhunīs

404-8. Pāḷiyaṃ yadaggenāti yasmiṃ divase. Tadāti tasmiṃyeva divase. Vimānetvāti avamānaṃ katvā.

In the Pāli, 'yadaggena' means 'on which day.' 'Tadā' means 'on that very day.' 'Vimānetvā' means 'having shown disrespect.'

410-1. Āpattigāminiyoti āpattiṃ āpannāyo. Kammavibhaṅgeti parivāre kammavibhaṅge (pari. 482 ādayo).

'Āpattigāminiyo' means bhikkhunīs who have incurred an offense. 'Kammavibhaṅge' means in the Kammavibhaṅga of the Parivāra.

413-5. Pāḷiyaṃ [V 2.0252] dve tisso bhikkhuniyoti dvīhi tīhi bhikkhunīhi. Na ārocentīti pātimokkhuddesakassa na ārocenti.

In the Pāli, 'dve tisso bhikkhuniyo' means by two or three bhikkhunīs. 'Na ārocenti' means they do not inform the one who recites the Pātimokkha.

416. Dussaveṇiyāti anekadussapaṭṭe ekato katvā kataveṇiyā.

416. 'Dussaveṇiyā' means by a sash made from gathering many strips of cloth together.

417. Visesakanti [M 2.0265] pattalekhādivaṇṇavisesaṃ. Pakiṇantīti vikkiṇanti. Namanakanti pāsukaṭṭhinamanakabandhanaṃ.

417. 'Visesakaṃ' means a special design, such as decorative lines made with lacquer. 'Pakiṇanti' means they sell. 'Namanakaṃ' means a binding that makes the side-ribs pliant.

422-5. Saṃvelliyanti kacchaṃ bandhitvā nivāsanaṃ. Tayo nissayeti rukkhamūlasenāsanassa tāsaṃ alabbhanato vuttaṃ.

'Saṃvelliyan' means wearing the lower robe by tying a 'kaccha' fold. The words 'tayo nissaye' were said because of their not obtaining the dwelling at the root of a tree.

426-8. Aṭṭheva bhikkhuniyo yathāvuḍḍhaṃ paṭibāhantīti aṭṭha bhikkhuniyo vuḍḍhapaṭipāṭiyāva gaṇhantiyo āgatapaṭipāṭiṃ paṭibāhanti, nāññāti attho. Anuvādaṃ paṭṭhapentīti issariyaṃ pavattentīti atthaṃ vadanti.

'Aṭṭheva bhikkhuniyo yathāvuḍḍhaṃ paṭibāhanti' means: only eight bhikkhunīs, receiving according to the order of seniority, obstruct the order of arrival; other bhikkhunīs do not. This is the meaning. 'Anuvādaṃ paṭṭhapenti' means they exercise authority; this is the meaning they state.

430. Bhikkhudūtenāti bhikkhunā dūtabhūtena. Sikkhamānadūtenāti sikkhamānāya dūtāya.

430. “By a bhikkhu-messenger” means: by a bhikkhu who has become a messenger. “By a probationer-messenger” means: by a probationer who is a messenger.

431. Na sammatīti nappahoti. Navakammanti “navakammaṃ katvā vasatū”ti apaloketvā saṅghikabhūmiyā okāsadānaṃ.

431. “It is not allowable” means: it is not sufficient. “New work” means: the granting of a place on Saṅgha land after seeking approval with the words, “Let him dwell, having done the new work.”

432-6. Sannisinnagabbhāti duviññeyyagabbhā. Mahilātittheti itthīnaṃ sādhāraṇatitthe.

One whose pregnancy is established means: one whose pregnancy is difficult to discern. At a women’s bathing place means: at a bathing place common to women.

Bhikkhunīupasampadānujānanakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Permission for the Higher Ordination of Bhikkhunīs is concluded.

Bhikkhunikkhandhakavaṇṇanānayo niṭṭhito.

The Method for the Explanation of the Bhikkhunī-khandhaka is concluded.

11. Pañcasatikakkhandhako

11. The Chapter of the Five Hundred

Khuddānukhuddakasikkhāpadakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Minor and Lesser Training Rules

437. Pañcasatikakkhandhake [M 2.0266][V 2.0253] pāḷiyaṃ “apāvuso, amhākaṃ satthāraṃ jānāsī”ti idaṃ thero sayaṃ bhagavato parinibbutabhāvaṃ jānantopi attanā sahagatabhikkhuparisāya ñāpanatthameva, subhaddassa vuḍḍhapabbajitassa sāsanassa paṭipakkhavacanaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ viññāpanatthañca evaṃ pucchi. Subhaddo hi kusinārāyaṃ bhagavati abhippasannāya khattiyādigahaṭṭhaparisāya majjhe bhagavato parinibbānaṃ sutvā haṭṭhapahaṭṭhopi bhayena pahaṭṭhākāraṃ vācāya pakāsetuṃ na sakkhissati, idheva pana vijanapadese sutvā yathājjhāsayaṃ attano pāpaladdhiṃ pakāsessati, tato tameva paccayaṃ dassetvā bhikkhū samussāhetvā dhammavinayasaṅgahaṃ kāretvā etassa pāpabhikkhussa, aññesañca īdisānaṃ manorathavighātaṃ, sāsanaṭṭhitiñca karissāmīti jānantova taṃ pucchīti veditabbaṃ. Teneva thero “ekamidāhaṃ, āvuso, samaya”ntiādinā subhaddavacanameva dassetvā dhammavinayaṃ saṅgāyāpesi. Nānābhāvoti sarīrena nānādesabhāvo, vippavāsoti attho. Vinābhāvoti maraṇena viyujjanaṃ. Aññathābhāvoti bhavantarūpagamanena aññākārappatti.

437. In the Pāli of the Pañcasatikakkhandhaka, regarding the words, “Friend, do you know our Teacher?”: the Elder, although he himself knew of the Blessed One’s final passing, asked this solely for the sake of informing the assembly of bhikkhus who had come with him, and for the sake of making the bhikkhus understand the statement of the old wanderer Subhadda which was contrary to the Dispensation. For Subhadda, upon hearing of the Blessed One’s final passing in Kusinārā amidst the assembly of devoted laypeople, such as nobles, although he would be overjoyed, would not be able to express his joyful state in words due to fear. But hearing it here in this secluded place, he would reveal his own evil doctrine according to his inclination. It should be understood that, thinking, “Then, having pointed to that very reason and having encouraged the bhikkhus, I will have the Dhamma and Vinaya compiled, and I will bring about the frustration of the wishes of this evil bhikkhu and of others like him, and ensure the stability of the Dispensation,” he knowingly questioned him. For that very reason, the Elder, beginning with “On one occasion, friends…,” pointed only to Subhadda’s statement and had the Dhamma and Vinaya rehearsed. “Difference of state” means being in different places with the body; the meaning is “separation.” “Absence” means separation through death. “Otherness of state” means the attainment of another state through passing into another existence.

441. “Ākaṅkhamāno…pe… samūhaneyyā”ti idaṃ bhagavā mayā “ākaṅkhamāno”ti vuttattā ekasikkhāpadampi samūhanitabbaṃ apassantā, samūhane ca dosaṃ disvā dhammasaṅgahakā bhikkhū “apaññattaṃ na paññāpessāma, paññattaṃ na samucchindissāmā”tiādinā puna “paññattisadisāya akuppāya kammavācāya sāvetvā samādāya vattissanti, tato yāva sāsanantaradhānā appaṭibāhiyāni sikkhāpadāni bhavissantī”ti iminā adhippāyena avocāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Teneva mahātherāpi tatheva paṭipajjiṃsu.

441. Regarding the words, “If wishing… he may abolish”: it should be understood that the Blessed One spoke with this intention: “Because it was said by me, ‘If wishing…,’ the bhikkhus compiling the Dhamma, not seeing even one training rule that should be abolished and seeing the fault in abolishing it, will declare, ‘We will not lay down what has not been laid down, nor will we rescind what has been laid down,’ and so on. Furthermore, they will think, ‘Having announced it with an unshakeable formal act similar to a rule, they will undertake it and practice it. Therefore, the training rules will be unassailable until the disappearance of the Dispensation.’” For this very reason, the great Elders also acted in just that way.

Gihigatānīti [V 2.0254] gihīsu gatāni. Khattiyamahāsārādigihīhi ñātānīti attho. Citakadhūmakālo attano pavattipariyosānabhūto etassāti dhūmakālikaṃ.

“Gone to the laity” means: gone among the laity. The meaning is: known by laypeople such as nobles and wealthy householders. That training rule is called “of the time of the smoke” because for it, the time of the smoke from the funeral pyre is the end of its currency.

443. Oḷārike [M 2.0267] nimitte kariyamānepīti “ākaṅkhamāno, ānanda, tathāgato kappaṃ vā tiṭṭheyya kappāvasesaṃ vā”ti evaṃ thūlatare “tiṭṭhatu, bhagavā, kappa”nti yācanahetubhūte okāsanimitte kamme kariyamāne. Mārena pariyuṭṭhitacittoti mārena āviṭṭhacitto.

443. “Even when a gross sign was being made” means: when an even grosser hint, the opportunity-sign which was the cause for the request, “May the Blessed One remain for an aeon,” was being made in this way: “Ānanda, if he so wished, the Tathāgata could remain for an aeon or for the remainder of an aeon.” “With a mind assailed by Māra” means: with a mind possessed by Māra.

445. Ujjavanikāyāti paṭisotagāminiyā. Kucchito lavo chedo vināso kulavo, niratthakaviniyogo. Taṃ na gacchantīti na kulavaṃ gamenti.

445. “By going upstream” means: by going against the current. A contemptible cutting, a destruction, a ruin is a “kulava”; a useless expenditure. “They do not go to that” means: they do not bring it to ruin.

Khuddānukhuddakasikkhāpadakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Minor and Lesser Training Rules is concluded.

Pañcasatikakkhandhakavaṇṇanānayo niṭṭhito.

The Method for the Explanation of the Pañcasatika-khandhaka is concluded.

12. Sattasatikakkhandhako

12. The Chapter of the Seven Hundred

Dasavatthukathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Ten Topics

446. Sattasatikakkhandhake [M 2.0268][V 2.0255] bhikkhaggenāti bhikkhugaṇanāya. Mahīti himaṃ.

446. In the Sattasatika-khandhaka, “by the total of bhikkhus” means by the number of bhikkhus. “Mahī” means frost.

447. Avijjānivutāti avijjānīvaraṇena nivutā paṭicchannā. Aviddasūti aññāṇino. Upakkilesā vuttāti tesaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ ete surāpānādayo upakkilesāti vuttā. Nettiyā taṇhāya sahitā sanettikā.

447. “Shrouded by ignorance” means covered, concealed by the hindrance of ignorance. “Unknowing” means ignorant. “Defilements are spoken of” means that for those ascetics and brahmins, these things such as drinking liquor are spoken of as defilements. “With a guide” means accompanied by the guide, which is craving.

450-1. Ahogaṅgoti tassa pabbatassa nāmaṃ. Paṭikacceva gaccheyyanti yattha naṃ adhikaraṇaṃ vūpasamituṃ bhikkhū sannipatissanti, tatthāhaṃ paṭhamameva gaccheyyaṃ. Sambhāvesunti sampāpuṇiṃsu.

Ahogaṅga is the name of that mountain. “I would go beforehand” means: I would go first to the place where the bhikkhus will gather to settle that legal issue. “They met” means they arrived.

452. Aloṇikanti loṇarahitaṃ bhattaṃ, byañjanaṃ vā. Āsutāti sabbasambhārasajjitā, “asuttā”ti vā pāṭho.

452. “Without salt” means rice or curry devoid of salt. “Prepared” means prepared with various ingredients. Alternatively, there is the reading “asuttā”.

453. Ujjaviṃsūti nāvāya paṭisotaṃ gacchiṃsu. Pācīnakāti puratthimadisāya jātattā vajjiputtake sandhāya vuttaṃ. Pāveyyakāti pāveyyadesavāsino.

453. “They went upstream” means they went against the current by boat. “Easterners” is said with reference to the Vajjian monks, because they were born in the eastern direction. “Pāvans” means the inhabitants of the Pāvā region.

454. Nanu tvaṃ, āvuso, vuḍḍhoti nanu tvaṃ thero nissayamutto, kasmā taṃ thero paṇāmesīti bhedavacanaṃ vadanti. Garunissayaṃ gaṇhāmāti nissayamuttāpi mayaṃ ekaṃ sambhāvanīyagaruṃ nissayabhūtaṃ gahetvāva vasissāmāti adhippāyo.

454. “Friend, are you not senior?”: They speak divisive words, saying: “Are you not an elder, free from dependence? Why did the elder dismiss you?” “We take a respected teacher as our support” means that this is the intention: even though we are free from dependence, we will live having taken a respectable teacher, who is a source of dependence, as our support.

455. Mūlādāyakāti paṭhamaṃ dasavatthūnaṃ dāyakā, āvāsikāti attho. Pathabyā saṅghattheroti [V 2.0256] loke sabbabhikkhūnaṃ tadā upasampadāya vuḍḍho. Suññatāvihārenāti suññatāmukhena adhigataphalasamāpattiṃ sandhāya vadati.

455. “Original donors” means the first donors of the ten items; the meaning is “resident monks.” “The Saṅgha elder of the earth” means the one who was, at that time, senior in ordination to all bhikkhus in the world. “By the dwelling in emptiness” is said with reference to the fruition-attainment realized through the gateway of emptiness.

457. Suttavibhaṅgeti padabhājanīye. Idañca “yo pana bhikkhu sannidhikārakaṃ khādanīyaṃ vā bhojanīyaṃ vā”ti (pāci. 253) sutte yāvakālikasseva parāmaṭṭhattā [M 2.0269] siṅgīloṇassa yāvajīvikassa sannidhikatassa āmisena saddhiṃ paribhoge pācittiyaṃ vibhaṅganayeneva sijjhatīti vuttaṃ, taṃ pana pācittiyaṃ vibhaṅge āgatabhāvaṃ sādhetuṃ “kathaṃ suttavibhaṅge”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha hi loṇamettha sannidhikataṃ, na khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyanti loṇamissabhojane vajjiputtakā anavajjasaññino ahesuṃ. Tathāsaññīnampi nesaṃ āpattidassanatthaṃ “sannidhikāre asannidhikārasaññī”ti idaṃ suttavibhaṅgaṃ uddhaṭanti veditabbaṃ.

457. ‘In the Suttavibhaṅga’ (`suttavibhaṅge`) means in the Padabhājanīya (word-analysis). And since in the Sutta—‘Whatever monk should store hard food or soft food’—only what is allowable for a limited time (`yāvakālika`) is mentioned, it was said that for using salt in a horn (`siṅgīloṇa`), which is allowable for life (`yāvajīvika`) and has been stored, together with food, a Pācittiya offense is established only by the method of the Vibhaṅga. To establish the fact that this Pācittiya is found in the Vibhaṅga, the phrase starting with ‘How in the Sutta Vibhaṅga...’ was said. For in this case, the Vajjiputtaka monks perceived no fault in food mixed with salt, thinking, ‘Only salt is stored here, not hard or soft food.’ To show the offense even to them who perceived thus, it should be known that this Suttavibhaṅga passage, ‘perceiving what is stored as not stored,’ was extracted.

Tena saddhinti purepaṭiggahitaloṇena saddhiṃ. Dukkaṭenettha bhavitabbanti “yāvakālikena, bhikkhave, yāvajīvikaṃ paṭiggahita”nti avatvā “tadahupaṭiggahita”nti vacanasāmatthiyato purepaṭiggahitaṃ yāvajīvikaṃ yāvakālikena saddhiṃ sambhinnarasaṃ kālepi na kappatīti sijjhati, tattha dukkaṭena bhavitabbanti adhippāyo. Dukkaṭenapi na bhavitabbanti yadi hi sannidhikārapaccayā dukkaṭaṃ maññatha, yāvajīvikassa loṇassa sannidhidosābhāvā dukkaṭena na bhavitabbaṃ, atha āmisena sambhinnarasassa tassa āmisagatikattā dukkaṭaṃ mā maññatha. Tadā ca hi pācittiyeneva bhavitabbaṃ āmisattupagamanatoti adhippāyo. Na hi ettha yāvajīvikantiādināpi dukkaṭābhāvaṃ samattheti.

‘With that’ (`tena saddhiṃ`) means together with salt accepted on a previous day. ‘It should be a Dukkaṭa offense here’ (`dukkaṭenettha bhavitabbaṃ`): Because it was not said, ‘Monks, what is for life may be accepted with what is for a limited time,’ but rather, ‘accepted on that very day,’ by the power of this statement it is established that a `yāvajīvika` item accepted on a previous day, when its taste is mixed with a `yāvakālika` item, is not allowable even in the proper time. There, it should be a Dukkaṭa offense—this is the intention (of some teachers). ‘It should not even be a Dukkaṭa offense’ (`dukkaṭenapi na bhavitabbaṃ`): If you think it is a Dukkaṭa offense on account of storing, it should not be, because there is no fault in storing salt, which is for life. If, on the other hand, you do not think it is a Dukkaṭa because, its taste being mixed with food, it has become like food, then it should be a Pācittiya offense, because it has become food—this is the intention (of the Aṭṭhakathā). By the phrase beginning `na hi ettha yāvajīvikaṃ` (‘For here it is not for life...’), he also establishes the absence of a Dukkaṭa offense.

Pāḷiyaṃ rājagahe suttavibhaṅgetiādīsu sabbattha sutte ca vibhaṅge cāti attho gahetabbo. Tassa tassa vikālabhojanādino suttepi paṭikkhittattā vinayassa atisaraṇaṃ atikkamo vinayātisāro. “Nisīdanaṃ nāma sadasaṃ vuccatīti āgata”nti idaṃ vibhaṅge ca āgatadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Taṃ pamāṇaṃ karontassāti sugatavidatthiyā vidatthittayappamāṇaṃ karontassa, dasāya pana vidatthidvayappamāṇaṃ kataṃ. Adasakampi nisīdanaṃ vaṭṭati evāti adhippāyo. Sesamidha heṭṭhā sabbattha suviññeyyameva.

In the Pāḷi, in all passages such as ‘in Rājagaha, in the Suttavibhaṅga,’ the dual meaning ‘in the Sutta and in the Vibhaṅga’ should be understood. Because such things as eating at the wrong time are also rejected in the Sutta, exceeding or transgressing the Vinaya is `vinayātisāra`. The phrase ‘It is said that a sitting mat is with a border’ (`nisīdanaṃ nāma sadasaṃ vuccati`) is cited to show that it also appears in the Vibhaṅga. ‘For one who makes that the standard’ (`taṃ pamāṇaṃ karontassa`) means for one who makes it the measure of three spans by the Sugata’s span. However, a sitting mat made to the measure of two spans with a border is allowable, and indeed, a sitting mat without a border is also permissible—this is the intention. The rest here and below is everywhere easy to understand.

Dasavatthukathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Ten Topics is concluded.

Sattasatikakkhandhakavaṇṇanānayo niṭṭhito.

The Method for the Explanation of the Section of the Seven Hundred is concluded.

Iti samantapāsādikāya vinayaṭṭhakathāya vimativinodaniyaṃ

Thus in the Vimativinodanī, a sub-commentary on the Samantapāsādikā, the Vinaya Commentary.

Cūḷavaggavaṇṇanānayo niṭṭhito.

The Method for the Explanation of the Cūḷavagga is concluded.

Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Parivāravaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Parivāra

Mahāvaggo

The Great Chapter

Paññattivāravaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Section on Designations

1. Visuddhaparivārassa [M 2.0271][V 2.0257] sīlakkhandhādidhammakkhandhasarīrassa bhagavato vinayapariyattisāsane khandhakānaṃ anantaraṃ parivāroti yo vinayo saṅgahaṃ samāruḷho, tassa dāni anuttānatthavaṇṇanaṃ karissāmīti yojanā.

In the Dispensation of the Vinaya scripture of the Blessed One—who has a retinue pure from defilements, who has the body which is the collection of Dhamma-aggregates beginning with the aggregate of virtue—that Vinaya which is called the Parivāra was included in the compilation immediately after the Khandhakas. Now, I shall make an explanation of the non-obvious meaning of that Parivāra. Thus is the syntactical connection.

Samantacakkhunāti sabbaññutaññāṇena. Ativisuddhena maṃsacakkhunāti rattindivaṃ samantā yojanappamāṇe atisukhumānipi rūpāni passanato ativiya parisuddhena pasādacakkhunā. “Atthi tattha paññattī”tiādīsu atthi nu kho tattha paññattītiādinā attho gahetabboti āha “tattha paññatti…pe… kenābhatanti pucchā”ti.

1. ‘With the all-seeing eye’ (`samantacakkhunā`) means: by the knowledge of omniscience. ‘With the exceedingly purified fleshly eye’ (`ativisuddhena maṃsacakkhunā`) means: by the exceedingly pure sensitive eye, because of seeing even very subtle forms all around within the measure of a yojana day and night. In passages such as, “Is there a designation there?”, the meaning should be understood in the manner of, “Is there indeed a designation there?”, etc. Therefore, he said: “‘There, designation… by whom was it brought?’ is the question.”

2. Pucchāvissajjaneti [V 2.0258] pucchāya vissajjane. Vinītakathāti vinītavatthukathā, ayameva vā pāṭho.

‘In the answering of the question’ (`pucchāvissajjane`) means: in the answering of a question. ‘A decided discussion’ (`vinītakathā`) means: a discussion on a decided matter; or this itself is the reading.

Dvaṅgikena ekena samuṭṭhānenāti aṅgadvayasamudāyabhūtena ekena. Aṅgadvayavimuttassa samuṭṭhānassa abhāvepi tesu ekenaṅgena vinā ayaṃ āpatti na hotīti dassanatthameva “ekena samuṭṭhānenā”ti vuttaṃ. Idāni tesu dvīsu aṅgesu padhānaṅgaṃ dassetumāha “ettha hi cittaṃ aṅgaṃ hotī”tiādi. Yasmā pana maggenamaggappaṭipattisaṅkhātāya kāyaviññattiyā sevanacitteneva sambhave sati ayaṃ taṃ aṅgadvayaṃ upādāya bhagavatā paññattā āpattisammuti hoti, nāsati. Tasmā taṃ cittaṃ kāyaviññattisaṅkhātassa kāyassa aṅgaṃ kāraṇaṃ hoti, na āpattiyā. Tassa pana taṃsamuṭṭhitakāyo eva aṅgaṃ abyavahitakāraṇaṃ, cittaṃ pana kāraṇakāraṇanti adhippāyo. Evaṃ uparipi sabbattha cittaṅgayuttasamuṭṭhānesu adhippāyo [M 2.0272] veditabbo. “Ekena samuṭṭhānena samuṭṭhātī”tiādiparivāravacaneneva āpattiyā akusalādiparamatthasabhāvatā pāḷiaṭṭhakathāsu pariyāyatova vuttā, sammutisabhāvā eva āpattīti sijjhati samuṭṭhānasamuṭṭhitānaṃ bhedasiddhitoti gahetabbaṃ. Imamatthaṃ sandhāyāti āpannāya pārājikāpattiyā kehicipi samathehi anāpattibhāvāpādanassa asakkuṇeyyattasaṅkhātamatthaṃ sandhāya.

2. ‘By one two-factored arising’ (`dvaṅgikena ekena samuṭṭhānena`) means: by one arising that is a combination of two factors. Although there is no arising free from the two factors, this offense does not occur without one of those factors; it is said, “by one arising,” merely to show this. Now, to show the principal factor among those two factors, he said the words beginning, “Here, the mind is a factor.” Because this conventional offense, laid down by the Blessed One depending on those two factors, occurs only when there is the arising from the mind that wishes to engage in the bodily intimation known as practicing in another's path with one's own path, and it does not occur when that mind is absent. Therefore, that mind is a factor, a cause, for the body known as bodily intimation; it is not a cause for the offense. But for that offense, the body that arises from that mind is the factor, the immediate cause; the mind, however, is the cause of the cause. This is the intention. Similarly, hereafter in all arisings connected with the mind as a factor, the intention should be understood. Only by way of the Parivāra statement beginning, “It arises from one arising,” is the ultimate nature of an offense as unwholesome, etc., stated only figuratively in the Pāḷi and commentaries. The statement, “An offense is merely conventional in nature,” is established because of the established distinction between the origin and that which arises from the origin. Thus it should be understood. ‘With reference to this meaning’ (`imamatthaṃ sandhāya`) means: with reference to the meaning known as the impossibility of bringing about a state of non-offense for an incurred Pārājika offense by any of the legal settlements.

3. Porāṇakehi mahātherehīti saṅgītittayato pacchā potthakasaṅgītikārakehi chaḷabhiññāpaasambhidādiguṇasamujjalehi mahātherehi. Catutthasaṅgītisadisā hi potthakārohasaṅgīti.

‘By the ancient great elders’ (`porāṇakehi mahātherehi`) means: by the great elders who, after the three councils, were the makers of the compilation committed to books, and who were radiant with virtues such as the six higher knowledges and the four analytical insights. Indeed, the compilation committed to books is like the Fourth Council.

188. Mahāvibhaṅgeti bhikkhuvibhaṅge. Soḷasa vārā dassitāti yehi vārehi ādibhūtehi upalakkhitattā ayaṃ sakalopi parivāro soḷasaparivāroti voharīyati, te sandhāya vadati.

3. ‘In the Mahāvibhaṅga’ (`mahāvibhaṅge`) means: in the Bhikkhuvibhaṅga. Regarding the statement, “Sixteen sections are shown”: because this entire Parivāra is marked by these initial sections, it is called the Sixteenfold Parivāra. He speaks with reference to those sections.

Paññattivāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

188. The Commentary on the Section on Designations is concluded.

Samuṭṭhānasīsavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Headings of Origins

257. Pāḷiyaṃ nibbānañceva paññattīti ettha yasmā saṅkhatadhamme upādāya paññattā sammutisaccabhūtā puggalādipaññatti paramatthato avijjamānattā uppattivināsayuttavatthudhammaniyatena aniccadukkhalakkhaṇadvayena yuttāti vattuṃ ayuttā, kārakavedakādirūpena pana parikappitena attasabhāvena virahitattā “anattā”ti vattuṃ yuttā. Tasmā ayaṃ paññattipi asaṅkhatattasāmaññato [V 2.0259] vatthubhūtena nibbānena saha “anattā iti nicchayā”ti vuttā. Avijjamānāpi hi sammuti kenaci paccayena akatattā asaṅkhatā evāti.

257. In the Pāḷi, in the phrase 'Nibbāna and concept': because the concept of 'person' and so on, which is designated in dependence on conditioned phenomena and is a conventional truth, does not exist in an ultimate sense, it is not suitable to say that it is endowed with the pair of characteristics, impermanence and suffering, which are fixed in the real phenomena endowed with arising and ceasing. However, because it is devoid of a self-nature imagined in the form of a doer, an experiencer, and so on, it is suitable to say it is 'not-self'. Therefore, this concept also, due to the commonality of being unconditioned, is said, together with Nibbāna which is a real phenomenon, to be determined as 'not-self'. Indeed, even though a convention does not ultimately exist, because it is not made by any cause, it is just unconditioned.

Karuṇāsītalattaṃ, paññāpabhāsitattañca bhagavato dassetuṃ “buddhacande, buddhādicce”ti etaṃ ubhayaṃ vuttaṃ. Hāyati etenāti hāni, dukkhassa hāni dukkhahāni, sabbadukkhāpanūdanakāraṇanti attho. Piṭake tīṇi desayīti yasmā aññepi mahāvīrā sammāsambuddhā saddhammaṃ desayanti, tasmā [M 2.0273] aṅgīraso piṭakāni tīṇi desayīti yojanā. Mahāguṇanti mahānisaṃsaṃ. Evaṃ nīyati saddhammoti yadi vinayapariyatti aparihīnā tiṭṭhati, evaṃ sati paṭipattipaṭivedhasaddhammopi nīyati pavattīyati, na parihāyatīti attho.

To show the Blessed One's state of being cool with compassion and state of being illumined by wisdom, these two—'the Buddha-moon' and 'the Buddha-sun'—are said. It declines by this, thus it is `hāni` (a cause of decline); the cause of decline for suffering is `dukkhahāni`; the meaning is the cause for the removal of all suffering. As for 'He taught the three Piṭakas': because other great heroes, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, also teach the good Dhamma, therefore Aṅgīrasa also taught the three Piṭakas—this is the connection. `Mahāguṇaṃ` means of great benefit. As for 'Thus the good Dhamma is carried on': if the scriptural teaching of the Vinaya stands without declining, this being so, the good Dhamma of practice and the good Dhamma of penetration are also carried on, they proceed, they do not decline—this is the meaning.

Vinayapariyatti pana kathaṃ tiṭṭhatīti āha “ubhato cā”tiādi. Parivārena ganthitā tiṭṭhatīti yojetabbaṃ. Tasseva parivārassāti tasmiṃ eva parivāre. Samuṭṭhānaṃ niyato katanti ekaccaṃ samuṭṭhānena niyataṃ kataṃ. Tasmiṃ parivāre kiñci sikkhāpadaṃ niyatasamuṭṭhānaṃ aññehi asādhāraṇaṃ, taṃ pakāsitanti attho.

But how does the scriptural teaching of the Vinaya stand? To this, he said 'on both sides', etc. It should be construed as: 'It stands, being strung together by the Parivāra.' As for `tasseva parivārassā`, it means: in that very Parivāra. As for `samuṭṭhānaṃ niyato kataṃ`: a certain [training rule] is made definite by its origin. In that Parivāra, a certain training rule has a definite origin, not common to others; the meaning is, that is clarified.

Sambhedaṃ nidānañcaññanti sambhedo sikkhāpadānaṃ aññamaññasamuṭṭhānena saṃkiṇṇatā, nidānañca paññattiṭṭhānaṃ, aññaṃ puggalādivatthādi ca. Sutte dissanti uparīti heṭṭhā vutte, upari vakkhamāne ca parivārasutte eva dissanti. Yasmā ca evaṃ, tasmā sakalasāsanādhārassa vinayassa ṭhitihetubhūtaṃ parivāraṃ sikkheti, evamettha yojanā daṭṭhabbā.

As for `sambhedaṃ nidānañcaññaṃ`: the mixture (`sambheda`) is the state of the training rules being mixed up through their mutual origins; and the origin (`nidāna`) is the ground for the laying down [of a rule]; and other things, such as the person, the matter, etc. As for 'they are seen in the Sutta above': they are seen only in the Parivāra Sutta, in what was said below and in what will be said above. And because they are seen thus, therefore, one should train in the Parivāra, which is the cause for the stability of the Vinaya that upholds the entire Dispensation. Thus, the connection here should be seen in this way.

Sambhinnasamuṭṭhānānīti aññehi sādhāraṇasamuṭṭhānāni. Ādimhi tāva purimanayeti sabbapaṭhame paññattivāre āgatanayaṃ sandhāya vadati, tattha pana paññattivāre “paṭhamaṃ pārājikaṃ kattha paññattanti, vesāliyaṃ paññatta”ntiādinā (pari. 1) nidānampi dissati eva. Paratoti āgatabhāvaṃ pana sandhāya parato āgate sutte dissatīti veditabbanti vuttaṃ. Tassāti ubhatovibhaṅgapariyāpannassa sikkhāpadassa.

As for `sambhinnasamuṭṭhānāni`: having origins in common with others. As for the phrase `ādimhi tāva purimanaye`: he speaks with reference to the method that comes in the very first Chapter on Laying Down [Rules]. But there, in that Chapter on Laying Down [Rules], by the text beginning 'Where was the first Pārājika laid down? It was laid down in Vesālī,' indeed, the origin is also seen. However, with reference to the fact of its coming later, it was said, 'it should be known that it is seen in a Sutta that comes later.' As for `tassa`: of the training rule included in the two Vibhaṅgas.

258. Aniyatā paṭhamikāti āpattiṃ apekkhitvāva itthiliṅgaṃ kataṃ, paṭhamāniyataṃ sikkhāpadanti attho. Pāḷiyaṃ nānubandhe pavattininti vuṭṭhāpitaṃ pavattiniṃ ananubandhanasikkhāpadaṃ.

258. As for `aniyatā paṭhamikā`: the feminine gender is used only in consideration of the offense; the meaning is the first Aniyata (indefinite) training rule. In the Pāḷi, as for `nānubandhe pavattiniṃ`: it is the training rule about not following the preceptor (`pavattinī`) who has given the ordination.

260. Eḷakalomasikkhāpadavatthusmiṃ [V 2.0260] “bhikkhuniyo eḷakalomāni dhovantiyo rajantiyo vijaṭentiyo riñcanti uddesaṃ paripuccha”nti (pārā. 576) āgatattā imaṃ riñcanti-padaṃ gahetvā sikkhāpadaṃ upalakkhitanti dassento “vibhaṅge ‘riñcanti uddesa’nti āgataṃ eḷakalomadhovāpanasikkhāpada”nti āha.

260. In the story of the training rule on goat's wool, because it is stated, 'The nuns, while washing, dyeing, and disentangling goat's wool, abandon the recitation and inquiry,' wishing to show that the training rule is indicated by taking this word `riñcanti`, he said: 'In the Vibhaṅga, what is stated as "they abandon the recitation" is the training rule about having goat's wool washed.'

Vassikasāṭikasikkhāpadanti [M 2.0274] asamaye vassikasāṭikapariyesanasikkhāpadaṃ (pārā. 626 ādayo). Ratanasikkhāpadanti ratanaṃ vā ratanasammataṃ vā paṭisāmanasikkhāpadaṃ (pāci. 502 ādayo).

As for the training rule on the rains-cloth: it is the training rule on seeking a rains-cloth at the wrong time. As for the training rule on jewels: it is the training rule on storing away a jewel or what is considered a jewel.

265. Pāḷiyaṃ buddhañāṇenāti paṭividdhasabbaññutaññāṇena.

265. In the Pāḷi, as for `buddhañāṇena`: by the knowledge of omniscience that has been penetrated.

267. “Na desenti tathāgatā”ti etena chattapāṇissa dhammadesanāpaṭikkhepaṃ dasseti.

267. By this, 'Tathāgatas do not teach,' he shows the rejection of teaching the Dhamma to one with an umbrella in hand.

269. Akatanti aññehi amissīkataṃ, niyatasamuṭṭhānanti attho. Akatanti vā pubbe anāgataṃ, abhinavanti attho.

269. As for `akataṃ`: not mixed with others; the meaning is a definite origin. Or, as for `akataṃ`: not having come before; the meaning is new.

270. Samuṭṭhānañhi saṅkhepanti ettha saṅkhipanti saṅgayhanti sadisasamuṭṭhānāni etthāti saṅkhepo, samuṭṭhānasīsaṃ. Neti vineti kāyavacīduccaritanti netti, vinayapāḷi, sā eva dhammoti nettidhammoti āha “vinayapāḷidhammassā”ti.

270. Here, in `samuṭṭhānaṃ hi saṅkhepaṃ`: `saṅkhepa` (summary) is so called because similar origins are summarized and compiled herein; it means the head of origins. `Netti` is so called because it leads (`neti`) and disciplines (`vineti`) bodily and verbal misconduct; it means the Vinaya Pāḷi. That itself is the Dhamma, thus it is `nettidhamma`. Therefore, he said `vinayapāḷidhammassa` (of the Dhamma which is the Vinaya Pāḷi).

Samuṭṭhānasīsavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Headings of Origins is finished.

Antarapeyyālaṃ

The Intermediary Abbreviated Section

Katipucchāvāravaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Section of Questions on 'How Many?'

271. Kati [M 2.0275] āpattiyoti pārājikādīsu pañcasu āpattīsu methunādinnādānādiantogadhabhedaṃ apekkhitvā jātivasena ekattaṃ āropetvā pucchā katā. Kati āpattikkhandhāti antogadhabhedaṃ apekkhitvā paccekaṃ rāsaṭṭhenāti ettakamevettha bhedo. Vinītāniyeva [V 2.0261] vinītavatthūnīti āpattito viramaṇāni eva avippaṭisārapāmojjādidhammānaṃ kāraṇattā vatthūnīti vinītavatthūni, tāni ettha atthato viratiādianavajjadhammā eva. Veraṃ maṇatīti verahetuttā “vera”nti laddhanāmaṃ rāgādiakusalapakkhaṃ vināseti.

271. “How many offenses?”: this question is asked by grouping the five offenses beginning with Pārājika into one by way of their class, without regard to the internal divisions such as sexual intercourse, taking what is not given, etc. “How many aggregates of offenses?”: this question is asked by grouping each individually into one with the meaning of a group, without regard to the internal divisions. Just this much is the difference herein. As for `vinītavatthūni` (grounds of what is subdued): the very abstentions from offenses are the ‘grounds’ (`vatthūni`) because they are the cause of states such as non-remorse and joy; thus they are called `vinītavatthūni`. Herein, in terms of essence, they are just the blameless states beginning with abstention. As for the etymology `veraṃ maṇati` (it destroys enmity): it destroys the unwholesome faction of lust, etc., which has obtained the name ‘enmity’ (`vera`) because it is the cause of enmity.

Dhammassavanaggaṃ bhinditvā gacchatīti bahūsu ekato nisīditvā dhammaṃ suṇantesu taṃ dhammassavanasamāgamaṃ kopetvā uṭṭhāya gacchati. Anādarovāti tussitabbaṭṭhāne tuṭṭhiṃ, saṃvijitabbaṭṭhāne saṃvegañca apavedento eva. Kāyapāgabbhiyanti unnativasena pavattanakāyānācāraṃ.

As for ‘having broken up the assembly for hearing the Dhamma, he goes’: it means that when many are sitting together listening to the Dhamma, he disrupts that gathering for hearing the Dhamma, and having stood up, he goes. As for ‘disrespect’: it is not showing pleasure in a situation where one should be pleased, and not showing a sense of spiritual urgency in a situation where one should be stirred. As for ‘bodily insolence’: it is bodily misconduct that occurs by way of arrogance.

274. Mettāya sambhūtaṃ mettaṃ, kāyakammaṃ. Ubhayehipīti navakehi, therehi ca. Piyaṃ karotīti taṃ puggalaṃ pemaṭṭhānaṃ karoti, kesanti āha “sabrahmacārīna”nti.

274. What has arisen from loving-kindness is ‘mettaṃ’; it refers to bodily action. As for ‘by both’: it means by the junior monks and by the elders. As for ‘he makes dear’: he makes that person an object of affection. To the question, ‘Of whom?’, he said, ‘of his fellow practitioners in the holy life.’

Puggalaṃ paṭivibhajitvā bhuñjatīti pakatena sambandho. Tameva puggalapaṭivibhāgaṃ dassetuṃ “asukassā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

“Having discriminated with regard to the person, one eats”—this is the connection with the matter at hand. To show that very discrimination regarding the person, it is said, “for so-and-so,” and so on.

Bhujissabhāvakaraṇatoti taṇhādāsabyato mocetvā samathavipassanāsu serivihāritākaraṇatoti attho. Niyyātīti pavattati. Sammādukkhakkhayāya saṃvattatīti attho.

As for ‘from making a state of independence’: the meaning is from making a state of living at will in serenity and insight, having been freed from the state of being a slave to craving. As for ‘it leads out’: it proceeds. The meaning is that it conduces to the complete destruction of suffering.

Katipucchāvāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Section of Questions on 'How Many?' is concluded.

Chaāpattisamuṭṭhānavāravaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Section on the Six Origins of Offenses

276. Paṭhamena āpattisamuṭṭhānenāti kevalaṃ kāyena. Pārājikāpattiyā ekantasacittakasamuṭṭhānattā “na hīti vattabba”nti vuttaṃ. Saṅghādisesādīnaṃ [M 2.0276] dukkaṭapariyosānānaṃ pañcannaṃ acittakānampi sambhavato “siyā”ti vuttaṃ, āpajjanaṃ siyā bhaveyyāti attho. Hīnukkaṭṭhehi jātiādīhi omasane eva dubbhāsitassa paññattattā sā ekantavācācittasamuṭṭhānā evāti.

As for ‘by the first origin of an offense’: it means solely by the body. Because the Pārājika offense has an origin that is exclusively with intention, it was said, “It should be said, ‘No.’” Because of the possibility of even unintentional offenses for the five classes of offenses from Saṅghādisesa down to Dukkaṭa, it was said, “It may be”; the meaning is that the incurring may occur. Because the offense of wrong speech is laid down only in the case of disparagement by means of low and high things such as birth, it has an origin exclusively of speech and mind.

Dutiyasamuṭṭhānanaye vācāya eva samāpajjitabbapāṭidesanīyassa abhāvā “na hī”ti vuttaṃ.

276. In the method of the second origin, because of the absence of a Pāṭidesanīya offense that is to be incurred solely by speech, it was said, “No.”

Tatiye [V 2.0262] pana vosāsamānarūpaṃ bhikkhuniṃ kāyavācāhi anapasādanapaccayā pāṭidesanīyasambhavato “siyā”ti vuttaṃ.

In the third origin, however, because of the possibility of a Pāṭidesanīya offense arising from the condition of not rebuking with body and speech a bhikkhunī who is managing the distribution, it was said, ‘It may be.’

Omasane pācittiyassa adinnādānasamuṭṭhānattepi tappaccayā paññattassa dubbhāsitassa pañcameneva samuppattīti dassetuṃ catutthavāre “dubbhāsitaṃ āpajjeyyāti na hīti vattabba”nti vatvā pañcamavāre “siyāti vattabba”nti vuttaṃ. Kāyavikāreneva omasantassa panettha dubbhāsitabhāvepi kāyakīḷābhāvābhāvato dukkaṭamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Although the Pācittiya for disparagement has an origin from taking what is not given, in order to show that the wrong speech laid down on account of that cause arises only from the fifth origin, in the fourth section, having said, “It should be said, ‘No,’ to ‘he would incur a wrong speech,’” in the fifth section it was said, “It should be said, ‘It may be.’” Herein, it should be understood that for one who disparages just by a bodily gesture, even in the absence of the offense of wrong speech, there is only a Dukkaṭa offense, because it is not that there is no playing with the body.

Chaṭṭhavāre pana vijjamānopi kāyo dubbhāsitassa aṅgaṃ na hoti, pañcamasamuṭṭhāne eva chaṭṭhampi pavisatīti dassetuṃ “na hī”ti paṭikkhittaṃ, na pana tattha sabbathā dubbhāsitena anāpattīti dassetuṃ. Na hi davakamyatāya kāyavācāhi omasantassa dubbhāsitāpatti na sambhavati. Yañhi pañcameneva samāpajjati, taṃ chaṭṭhenapi samāpajjati eva dhammadesanāpatti viyāti gahetabbaṃ. Sesaṃ samuṭṭhānavāre suviññeyyameva.

In the sixth section, however, even though the body is present, it is not a factor for the offense of wrong speech. In order to show that the sixth origin is also included in the fifth origin, it was rejected with ‘No’; but not in order to show that in that case there is no offense at all through wrong speech. Indeed, the offense of wrong speech does arise for one who disparages with body and speech out of a desire to jest. For whatever offense one incurs by the fifth origin alone, that offense one also incurs by the sixth, like the offense related to teaching the Dhamma; thus it should be understood. The remainder in the section on origins is very easy to understand.

Chaāpattisamuṭṭhānavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Section on the Six Origins of Offenses is concluded.

Katāpattivāravaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Section of Committed Offenses

277. Dutiye pana kativāre paṭhamasamuṭṭhānena āpajjitabbānaṃ āpattīnaṃ lahudassanasukhatthaṃ kuṭikārādīni eva samuddhaṭāni, na aññesaṃ abhāvā, sañcarittādīnampi vijjamānattā. Evaṃ dutiyasamuṭṭhānādīsupi. “Kappiyasaññī”ti iminā acittakattaṃ dasseti. “Kuṭiṃ karotī”ti iminā vacīpayogābhāvaṃ. Ubhayenāpi kevalaṃ kāyeneva dukkaṭādīnaṃ sambhavaṃ dasseti. Evaṃ uparipi yathānurūpaṃ kātabbaṃ.

However, in the second, the Kativāra (Section on How Many), for the sake of easy demonstration of the offenses to be incurred through the first origin, only offenses such as hut-building and so on are extracted. This is not because of the absence of others, for offenses such as sañcaritta and so on also exist. Thus it is also for the second origin and so on. By this phrase, ‘perceiving it as allowable,’ it shows the state of being without intention. By this phrase, ‘builds a hut,’ it shows the absence of verbal effort. By both, it shows the occurrence of dukkaṭa and so on solely through the body. Thus, this should be applied accordingly in the subsequent sections as well.

“Ekena [M 2.0277] samuṭṭhānena samuṭṭhahantī”ti idaṃ idha visesetvā dassitānaṃ kāyatova samuṭṭhitānaṃ vasena vuttaṃ, avisesato pana tā āpattiyo itarasamuṭṭhānehipi yathārahaṃ samuṭṭhahanti eva. Evaṃ uparipi.

277. This statement, “They arise from one origin,” is said here with regard to those offenses, shown specifically, that have arisen from the body alone. Generally, however, those offenses do indeed arise from other origins as is suitable. Thus it is also in the subsequent sections.

“Tiṇavatthārakena cā”ti idaṃ saṅghādisesavajjitānaṃ catunnaṃ āpattīnaṃ vasena vuttaṃ.

This phrase, ‘and with a grass covering,’ was said with regard to the four offenses that are exclusive of saṅghādisesa.

279. Saṃvidahitvā [V 2.0263] kuṭiṃ karotīti vācāya saṃvidahati, sayañca kāyena karotīti attho.

‘Having arranged, he makes a hut’ means: he arranges by speech, and he himself does it with the body; this is the meaning.

Katāpattivāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

279. The Commentary on the Section of Committed Offenses is concluded.

Āpattisamuṭṭhānagāthāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Verses on the Origins of Offenses

283. Tatiyo pana gāthāvāro dutiyavārena vuttamevatthaṃ saṅgahetvā dassetuṃ vutto. Tattha kāyova kāyikoti vattabbe vacanavipallāsena “kāyikā”ti vuttaṃ. Tenāha “tena samuṭṭhitā”ti, kāyo samuṭṭhānaṃ akkhātoti attho.

The third, the Section of Verses, is stated in order to show, by summarizing, the very meaning explained in the second section. Therein, when it should be said ‘kāyiko’ (bodily), it is said ‘kāyikā’ through a reversal of expression. Therefore, he said, ‘arisen from that,’ the meaning of which is: the body as the origin is declared.

Vivekadassināti sabbasaṅkhatavivittattā, tato vivittahetuttā ca nīvaraṇavivekañca nibbānañca dassanasīlena. Vibhaṅgakovidāti ubhatovibhaṅgakusalāti ālapanaṃ. Idha panevaṃ añño pucchanto nāma natthi, upālitthero sayameva atthaṃ pākaṭaṃ kātuṃ pucchāvisajjanañca akāsīti iminā nayena sabbattha attho veditabbo.

283. ‘One who sees seclusion’ means: by one who is accustomed to seeing Nibbāna, which is seclusion from the hindrances, because it is secluded from all conditioned things and because it is the cause of seclusion from them. ‘One skilled in analysis’ means: one skilled in both Vibhaṅgas; this is a form of address. Here, however, there is no other person asking; the Elder Upāli himself, in order to make the meaning clear, posed the question and gave the answer. By this method, the meaning should be understood in all questions.

Āpattisamuṭṭhānagāthāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Verses on the Origins of Offenses is concluded.

Vipattipaccayavāravaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Section on the Conditions for Failure

284. Catutthe pana vipattipaccayavāre sīlavipattipaccayāti sīlavipattipaacchādanapaccayā.

However, in the fourth, the Section on the Conditions for Failure, ‘due to the condition of failure in virtue’ means: due to the condition of concealing a failure in virtue.

286. Diṭṭhivipattipaccayāti diṭṭhivipattiyā appaṭinissajjanapaccayā.

284. ‘Due to the condition of failure in view’ means: due to the condition of not abandoning a failure in view.

287. Ājīvavipattipaccayāti [M 2.0278] ettha āgamma jīvanti etenāti ājīvo, catupaccayo, sova micchāpattiyā vipannattā vipattīti ājīvavipatti, tassā ājīvavipattiyā hetu, taduppādanataparibhoganimittanti attho.

286. Here, in the phrase ‘due to the condition of failure in livelihood,’ the analysis is as follows: ‘they live depending on this,’ thus it is called ‘livelihood’ (ājīva); it refers to the four requisites. That very livelihood, being corrupted through wrong attainment, is a ‘failure’ (vipatti); thus it is ‘failure in livelihood’ (ājīvavipatti). The meaning is: on account of that failure in livelihood, that is, for the purpose of producing and making use of it.

Vipattipaccayavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

287. The Commentary on the Section on the Conditions for Failure is concluded.

Adhikaraṇapaccayavāravaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Section on the Conditions for Legal Issues

291. Pañcame [V 2.0264] adhikaraṇapaccayavāre kiccādhikaraṇapaccayāti apalokanavacanañattikammavācāsaṅkhatakammavācāpaccayā. Pañcāti ettha adhammikakatikādiṃ apaloketvā karontānaṃ animittanti attho. Pañcame adhikaraṇapaccayavāre kiccādhikaraṇapaccayā apalokanāvasāne dukkaṭaṃ, adhippāyādinā ñattikammādiṃ karontānaṃ thullaccayādi ca saṅgayhatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Avasesā āpattiyoti sotāpattiphalasamāpattiādayo. “Natthaññā āpattiyo”ti idaṃ vipattiādibhāginiyo sāvajjāpattiyo sandhāya vuttaṃ.

291. In the fifth section on the conditions for legal issues, 'because of the condition of a legal issue concerning a transaction' means because of the act of announcement and the formal act of the Sangha called a motion-and-proclamation. Here, in the word 'five' (`pañca`), the meaning is 'no sign' (`animitta`) for those who act having announced an unlawful agreement, etc. In the fifth section on the conditions for legal issues, because of the condition of a legal issue concerning a transaction, it should be understood that at the conclusion of an act of announcement, an offense of wrong-doing is included; and for those who perform a formal act beginning with a motion, etc., with intention, etc., an offense of grave offense, etc., is also included. 'The remaining āpatti' (`avasesā āpattiyo`) are the attainments of the fruit of stream-entry, etc. The statement, 'There are no other offenses,' is said with reference to blameworthy offenses that are part of failure, etc.

Adhikaraṇapaccayavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Section on the Conditions for Legal Issues is concluded.

Samathabhedaṃ

The Division of Settlements

Adhikaraṇapariyāyavāravaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Section on Modes of Legal Issues

293. Chaṭṭhe [M 2.0279] pariyāyavāre alobho pubbaṅgamotiādi sāsanaṭṭhitiyā aviparītato dhammavādissa vivādaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhārasa bhedakaravatthūni ṭhānānīti dhammādīsu adhammotiādinā gahetvā dīpanāni idheva bhedakaravatthūni, tāni eva kāyakalahādivivādassa kāraṇattā ṭhānāni, okāsattā vatthūni, ādhārattā bhūmiyoti ca vuttāni. Abyākatahetūti asekkhānaṃ vivādaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Dvādasa mūlānīti kodho upanāho, makkho palāso, issā macchariyaṃ, māyā sāṭheyyaṃ, pāpicchatā mahicchatā, sandiṭṭhiparāmāsitā ādhānaggāhīduppaṭinissajjitānīti imesaṃ channaṃ yugaḷānaṃ vasena cha dhammā ceva lobhādayo cha hetū cāti dvādasa dhammā vivādādhikaraṇassa mūlāni.

293. In the sixth section on modes, the statement 'non-greed is the forerunner,' etc., is said with reference to the dispute of a speaker of the Dhamma who disputes correctly for the stability of the Teaching. 'The eighteen grounds that are items causing schism' means that here, the very explanations, taking up 'it is not-Dhamma,' etc., in regard to the Dhamma, etc., are the items that cause schism. Those very items are also called 'grounds' (`ṭhānāni`) because they are the cause of disputes such as bodily quarrels; 'items' (`vatthūni`) because they are the opportunity; and 'foundations' (`bhūmiyo`) because they are the support. 'Because of an indeterminate cause' is said with reference to a dispute of Arahants. 'The twelve roots' are: anger and resentment; denigrating merit and rivalry; envy and stinginess; deceit and craftiness; evil desires and great desires; dogmatic grasping of one's own views and insistent grasping with difficulty in relinquishing. Thus, by way of these six pairs, six states and six causes beginning with greed, these twelve states are the roots of a legal issue concerning disputes.

294. Cuddasa mūlānīti tāneva dvādasa kāyavācāhi saddhiṃ cuddasa anuvādādhikaraṇassa mūlāni.

294. ‘The fourteen roots’ means that those same twelve, together with body and speech, are the fourteen roots of a legal issue concerning accusation.

295. Pathavīkhaṇanādīsu paṇṇattivajjesu kusalābyākatacittamūlikā āpatti hotīti dassetuṃ “alobho pubbaṅgamo”tiādi vuttaṃ. Satta āpattikkhandhā ṭhānānītiādi sattannaṃ āpattikkhandhānaṃ [V 2.0265] paṭicchādanapaccayā āpattisambhavato vuttaṃ. “Āpattādhikaraṇapaccayā catasso āpattiyo āpajjatī”ti (pari. 290) hi vuttaṃ. “Cha hetū”ti idaṃ kusalānaṃ āpattihetuvohārassa ayuttatāya vuttaṃ, na pana kusalahetūnaṃ abhāvato. “Alobho pubbaṅgamo”ti hi ādi vuttaṃ. Āpattihetavo eva hi pubbaṅgamanāmena vuttā.

295. In blameworthy acts established by rule, such as digging the earth, an offense rooted in a wholesome or indeterminate mind occurs; in order to show this, 'non-greed is the forerunner,' etc., is said. The statement 'the seven aggregates of offenses are the grounds,' etc., is said because an offense can arise from the condition of concealing the seven aggregates of offenses. Indeed, it is said, 'Because of the condition of a legal issue concerning an offense, one commits four offenses.' This statement 'six causes' is said because of the unsuitability of the designation 'cause of an offense' for wholesome states, not because of the absence of wholesome causes. Indeed, 'non-greed is the forerunner,' etc., is said. For the very causes of an offense are called by the name 'forerunner.'

296. Cattāri kammāni ṭhānānītiādīsu apalokanavācā, ñattiādivācāyo ca kammānīti vuttaṃ. Tā eva hi ekasīmāyaṃ sāmaggimupagatānaṃ kammappattānaṃ anumatiyā sāvanakiriyānipphattisaṅkhātassa saṅghagaṇakiccasabhāvassa kiccādhikaraṇassa adhiṭṭhānābhāvena “ṭhānavatthubhūmiyo”ti vuccanti. Ekaṃ mūlaṃ saṅghoti yebhuyyavasena vuttaṃ. Gaṇañattiapalokanānañhi [M 2.0280] gaṇopi mūlanti. Ñattito vāti ñattiñattidutiyañatticatutthakammavācānaṃ ñattirūpattā, ñattipubbakattā ca vuttaṃ. Kammañattikammavācāñattivasena hi duvidhāsu ñattīsu anussāvanāpi kammamūlakantveva saṅgayhanti. Ñattivibhāgo cāyaṃ upari āvi bhavissati.

296. In the text beginning 'four acts are the grounds,' the speech of announcement and the speeches beginning with a motion are called 'acts'. Indeed, those very speeches are called 'grounds, items, and foundations' because they are the basis for a legal issue concerning a transaction—which has the nature of a duty of the Sangha or a group and is reckoned as the accomplishment of the act of making heard—by the consent of those fit for the formal act who have come to harmony within a single boundary. The statement 'The Sangha is one root' is said by way of the majority. Indeed, a group is also the root of a group-motion and an announcement. The statement 'Or from the motion' is said because the formal acts of a motion, a motion as the second part, and a motion as the fourth part have the nature of a motion and because they are preceded by a motion. Indeed, in the two kinds of motions—by way of the motion for the formal act and the motion in the proclamation of the formal act—the proclamations are also included as being rooted in the formal act. And this analysis of motions will become clear later on.

“Ime satta samathā…pe… pariyāyenā”ti idaṃ pucchāvacanaṃ. “Siyā”ti idaṃ visajjanaṃ. “Kathañca siyā”ti idaṃ puna pucchā. Vivādādhikaraṇassa dve samathātiādi puna visajjanaṃ. Tattha “vatthuvasenā”ti idaṃ “satta samathā dasa samathā hontī”ti imassa kāraṇavacanaṃ. “Pariyāyenā”ti idaṃ “dasa samathā satta samathā hontī”ti imassa kāraṇavacanaṃ. Catubbidhādhikaraṇasaṅkhātavatthuvasena ca desanākkamasaṅkhātapariyāyavasena cāti attho.

This statement, 'These seven settlements... by way of mode,' is a question. This, 'It may be,' is the answer. This, 'And how may it be?' is again a question. The statement beginning, 'For a legal issue concerning a dispute, there are two settlements,' is again the answer. Therein, this statement, 'by way of the item,' is the statement of the reason for 'the seven settlements become ten settlements.' This statement, 'by way of mode,' is the statement of the reason for 'the ten settlements become seven settlements.' The meaning is: by way of the item, reckoned as the four kinds of legal issues, and by way of the mode, reckoned as the sequence of the teaching.

Adhikaraṇapariyāyavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Section on Modes of Legal Issues is concluded.

Sādhāraṇavārādivaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Section on Common Matters, etc.

297. Sattame sādhāraṇavāre sādhāraṇāti vivādādhikaraṇassa vūpasamanakiccasādhāraṇā. Evaṃ sabbattha.

297. In the seventh section, the section on common matters, 'common' means common to the function of settling a legal issue of dispute. Thus it is in all cases.

298. Aṭṭhame tabbhāgiyavāre tabbhāgiyāti vivādādhikaraṇassa vūpasamanato tappakkhikā.

298. In the eighth section, the section on related matters, 'related' means that because it settles a legal issue of dispute, it pertains to that side.

Sādhāraṇavārādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Section on Common Matters, etc., is concluded.

Samathāsamathassasādhāraṇavāravaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Section on Settlements Common and Uncommon to a Settlement

299. Navame [V 2.0266] samathāsamathasādhāraṇavāre “sabbe samathā ekatova adhikaraṇaṃ samenti udāhu nānā”ti pucchantena “samathā samathassa sādhāraṇā, samathā samathassa asādhāraṇā”ti vuttaṃ. Vivādādiadhikaraṇakkamena tabbūpasamahetubhūte samathe uddharanto “yebhuyyasikā”tiādimāha. Sammukhāvinayaṃ vinā kassaci samathassa asambhavā sesā chapi samathā sammukhāvinayassa sādhāraṇā vuttā, tesaṃ [M 2.0281] pana channaṃ aññamaññāpekkhābhāvato te aññamaññaṃ asādhāraṇā vuttā. Tabbhāgiyavārepi eseva nayo.

299. In the ninth section, the section on settlements common and uncommon to a settlement, by the one asking, 'Do all settlements settle a legal issue only together, or do they settle it separately?', it is said, 'Settlements are common to a settlement; settlements are uncommon to a settlement.' Pointing out the settlements that are the cause for settling those legal issues, in the order of legal issues such as disputes, etc., he says, 'by majority decision,' etc. Because of the impossibility of any settlement without the face-to-face settlement, the remaining six settlements are said to be common to the face-to-face settlement. However, because of the absence of mutual dependence among those six, they are said to be uncommon to one another. In the section on related matters also, this is the same method.

Samathāsamathassasādhāraṇavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Section on Settlements Common and Uncommon to a Settlement is concluded.

Samathasammukhāvinayavārādivaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Section on Settlements and the Face-to-Face Settlement, etc.

301-3. Ekādasamavārepi sammukhāvinayotiādi pucchā. Yebhuyyasikā sativinayotiādi visajjanaṃ. Evaṃ vinayavāre kusala-vāre tato paresupi pucchāvisajjanaparicchedo veditabbo.

In the eleventh section also, 'face-to-face settlement,' etc., is the question. 'By majority decision,' 'by mindfulness,' etc., is the answer. Thus, in the section on discipline, the section on wholesome matters, and also in the sections that follow, the division of question and answer should be understood.

Tattha sammukhāvinayo siyā kusalotiādīsu tasmiṃ tasmiṃ vinayakamme, vivādādimhi ca niyuttapuggalānaṃ samuppajjanakakusalādīnaṃ vasena sammukhāvinayādīnaṃ, vivādādīnañca kusalādibhāvo tena tena upacārena vutto. Yasmā panetassa sammukhāvinayo nāma saṅghasammukhatādayo honti, tesañca anavajjasabhāvattā akusale vijjamānepi akusalattūpacāro na yutto āpattādhikaraṇassa akusalattūpacāro viya, tasmā natthi sammukhāvinayo akusaloti attho.

Therein, in such statements as 'the face-to-face settlement might be wholesome,' the state of being wholesome, etc., of the face-to-face settlement, etc., and of disputes, etc., is stated by this or that figurative usage, by way of the wholesome states, etc., that arise for the persons appointed in this or that act of discipline and in disputes, etc. However, since what is called the 'face-to-face settlement' consists of the presence of the Sangha, etc., and because of their faultless nature, even when the unwholesome is present, the figurative usage as 'unwholesome' is not suitable, just as the figurative usage of a legal issue of an offense as 'unwholesome' is not suitable. Therefore, the meaning is: 'There is no unwholesome face-to-face settlement.'

304. Tato paresu yattha yebhuyyasikā labbhati, tattha sammukhāvinayo labbhatītiādi sammukhāvinayassa itarehi samathehi niyamena saṃsaṭṭhataṃ, itaresaṃ pana channaṃ aññamaññaṃ saṃsaggābhāvañca dassetuṃ vuttaṃ.

304. In the subsequent sections, the statement 'where a majority decision is obtained, there the face-to-face settlement is obtained,' etc., is said in order to show the necessary connection of the face-to-face settlement with the other settlements, and, however, the absence of mutual connection among the other six.

Samathasammukhāvinayavārādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Section on Settlements and the Face-to-Face Settlement, etc., is concluded.

Saṃsaṭṭhavārādivaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Section on Intermingling, etc.

306. Adhikaraṇanti [V 2.0267] vā samathāti vā ime dhammā saṃsaṭṭhātiādi samathānaṃ adhikaraṇesu eva yathārahaṃ pavattiṃ, adhikaraṇāni vinā tesaṃ visuṃ aṭṭhānañca dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Vinibbhujitvā nānākaraṇaṃ paññāpetunti adhikaraṇato samathehi viyojetvā asaṃsaṭṭhe katvā nānākaraṇaṃ aññamaññaṃ asaṃsaṭṭhatāya ṭhitabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ nānattaṃ paññāpetuṃ adhikaraṇavūpasamakkhaṇe eva tesaṃ asaṃsaggaṃ paññāpetuṃ kiṃ sakkāti pucchati.

306. The statement 'these phenomena, whether a legal issue or a settlement, are intermingled,' etc., is said to show that settlements occur appropriately only in legal issues, and that without legal issues, they have no separate existence. 'Having separated, to make known the distinction' means: 'Having disjoined the settlements from the legal issue, making them unmingled, is it possible to make known the distinction—the diversity designated as the state of existing through being unmingled with each other—and their non-association, only at the very moment of settling the legal issue?' This is the question asked.

Adhikaraṇantiādi [M 2.0282] gārayhavādadassanaṃ. So mā hevanti yo evaṃ vadati, so “mā evaṃ vadā”ti vacanīyo assa, na ca labbhati samathānaṃ aññatra adhikaraṇā vūpasamalakkhaṇanti pahānāvatthānasaṅkhātaṃ nānākaraṇaṃ paṭikkhipati. Lakkhaṇato pana adhikaraṇehi samathānaṃ nānākaraṇaṃ atthevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Samathā adhikaraṇehi sammantīti apalokanādīhi catūhi kiccādhikaraṇehi sabbepi samathā niṭṭhānaṃ gacchanti, nāññehīti imamatthaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Teneva vakkhati “sammukhāvinayo vivādādhikaraṇena na sammati. Anuvāda…pe… āpattādhikaraṇena na sammati, kiccādhikaraṇena sammatī”tiādi (pari. 311).

The statement 'a legal issue,' etc., is a display of blameworthy speech. One who speaks thus—'May it not be so!'—should be told, 'Do not speak thus!' He rejects the distinctness—which is reckoned as the abandonment of the bases—stating that a settlement is not obtained apart from the characteristic of the settling of a legal issue. However, it should be understood that, according to characteristic, the distinctness of settlements from legal issues does indeed exist. 'Settlements are settled by legal issues' means that all settlements reach conclusion through the four legal issues of duties, such as the announcement, etc., and not by other means. This was said with this meaning in mind. Therefore, it will be said: 'The face-to-face settlement is not settled by a legal issue of dispute. A legal issue of accusation... a legal issue of an offense is not settled, but a legal issue of duties is settled,' etc. (Pari. 311).

307-313. Vivādādhikaraṇaṃ katihi samathehi sammatītiādiko sammativāro. Tadanantaro sammatinasammativāro ca adhikaraṇehi samathānaṃ saṃsaṭṭhataṃ, visaṃsaṭṭhatañca dassetuṃ vutto. Samathā samathehi sammantītiādiko samathādhikaraṇavāro samathānaṃ aññamaññaṃ, adhikaraṇehi ca adhikaraṇānañca aññamaññaṃ, samathehi ca vūpasamāvūpasamaṃ dassetuṃ vutto.

307-313. The section on agreement, beginning with 'By how many settlements is a legal issue of dispute settled?', etc., and the subsequent section on agreement and disagreement, are stated to show the intermingling and non-intermingling of settlements with legal issues. The section on settlements and legal issues, beginning with 'Settlements are settled by settlements,' etc., is stated to show the settlement and non-settlement of settlements by each other and by legal issues, and of legal issues by each other and by settlements.

314. Samuṭṭhāpetivāro pana adhikaraṇehi adhikaraṇānaṃ uppattippakāradassanatthaṃ vutto. Na katamaṃ adhikaraṇanti attano sambhavamattena ekampi adhikaraṇaṃ na samuṭṭhāpetīti attho. Kathañcarahi samuṭṭhāpetīti āha “api cā”tiādi. Tattha jāyantīti anantarameva anuppajjitvā paramparapaccayā jāyantīti adhippāyo. “Dhammo adhammo”tiādinā ubhinnaṃ puggalānaṃ vivādapaccayā aññamaññakhemabhaṅgā honti, tappaccayā tesaṃ pakkhaṃ pariyesanena kalahaṃ vaḍḍhantānaṃ vivādo kañci mahāparisaṃ saṅghapariṇāyakaṃ lajjiṃ āgamma vūpasamaṃ gacchati. Tathā avūpasamante pana vivādo kamena vaḍḍhitvā sakalepi saṅghe vivādaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, tato anuvādādīnīti evaṃ paramparakkamena vūpasamakāraṇābhāve cattāri adhikaraṇāni jāyanti. Taṃ sandhāyāha [V 2.0268] “saṅgho vivadati vivādādhikaraṇa”nti. Saṅghassa vivadato yo vivādo, taṃ vivādādhikaraṇaṃ hotīti attho. Esa nayo sesesupi.

314. The section on arising, however, is stated to show the manner of the arising of legal issues from legal issues. The meaning of 'not any legal issue' is that not even one legal issue arises solely by its own possibility. How then do they arise? He says, 'Moreover,' etc. Here, 'they arise' means they arise not immediately but through a series of conditions; this is the intention. Through 'Dhamma and non-Dhamma,' etc., disputes arise between two individuals due to the breaking of mutual security, and due to that, as they increase their quarrels by seeking their own faction, the dispute goes to settlement by relying on some great assembly, a leader of the Sangha, or a conscientious person. If not settled thus, however, the dispute gradually grows until it gives rise to a dispute in the entire Sangha, and from that, legal issues of accusation, etc. Thus, in this sequential manner, when there is no cause for settlement, the four legal issues arise. Referring to that, he says, 'The Sangha disputes—it is a legal issue of dispute.' The meaning is that the dispute of the disputing Sangha becomes a legal issue of dispute. This same method applies to the remaining cases.

Saṃsaṭṭhavārādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Section on Intermingling, etc., is concluded.

Bhajativāravaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Section on Partaking.

318. Tadanantaravāre [M 2.0283] pana vivādādhikaraṇaṃ catunnaṃ adhikaraṇānantiādi adhikaraṇānaṃ vuttanayena aññamaññapaccayattepi saṃsaggabhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Vivādādhikaraṇaṃ catunnaṃ adhikaraṇānaṃ vivādādhikaraṇaṃ bhajatītiādīsu vivādādhikaraṇaṃ catūsu adhikaraṇesu vivādādhikaraṇabhāvameva bhajati, nāññādhikaraṇabhāvaṃ, catūsu adhikaraṇesu vivādādhikaraṇattameva nissitaṃ vivādādhikaraṇameva pariyāpannaṃ vivādādhikaraṇabhāveneva saṅgahitanti evamattho gahetabbo.

318. In the immediately following section, the statement 'A legal issue of dispute is one of the four legal issues,' and so forth, is said in order to show the nature of the association of the legal issues, even though they are mutually conditioned in the manner explained. In statements such as 'A legal issue of dispute partakes of a legal issue of dispute among the four legal issues,' the meaning should be understood thus: among the four legal issues, a legal issue of dispute partakes only of the state of being a legal issue of dispute, not the state of being another legal issue; among the four legal issues, it is dependent only on being a legal issue of dispute, it is included only as a legal issue of dispute, and it is comprehended only by its state as a legal issue of dispute.

319. Vivādādhikaraṇaṃ sattannaṃ samathānaṃ kati samathe bhajatītiādi pana catunnaṃ adhikaraṇānaṃ vūpasamane sati niyatasamathe dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha kati samathe bhajatīti attano upasamatthāya kittake samathe upagacchati, kittake samathe āgamma vūpasamaṃ gacchatīti attho. Kati samathapariyāpannanti attānaṃ vūpasametuṃ katisu samathesu tehi samānavasena paviṭṭhaṃ. Katihi samathehi saṅgahitanti vūpasamaṃ karontehi katihi samathehi vūpasamakaraṇatthaṃ saṅgahitaṃ.

319.
